If perfection had a name, it would be Resident Evil 0. This isn’t just a game, it’s a transcendent, pulse-pounding, nostalgia-infused masterpiece that grabs you by the collar and drags you straight into heaven. From the very first frame, the visuals feel like they were hand-delivered by the gods themselves. Every shadow breathes, every flicker of light tells a story, and every enemy looks so exquisitely horrifying you almost want to thank them for attacking you. The atmosphere is absolutely suffocating in the best possible way. It’s like the game doesn’t just want you to feel fear, it demands it. And the gameplay... oh, the gameplay! The partner system is pure genius. Switching between characters isn’t just a mechanic, it’s a strategic dance of survival brilliance. Every decision feels meaningful, and without any item box, every ressource precious. Like, dropping items on the ground instead of using a traditional item box? It's AWESOME. It forces you to think, adapt, and evolve like the elite survivor you were always meant to be. The sound design deserves its own standing ovation. The creak of a door, the distant growl of something unspeakable, the haunting music that creeps into your soul, it all combines into an auditory experience so immersive you’ll find yourself holding your breath in real life. And let’s talk about the pure, unfiltered charm of it all. The dramatic storytelling, the unforgettable characters, the gloriously intense moments of panic when you realize you have one bullet left and something is definitely coming for you, this is peak gaming experience at its finest.

I couldn't recommend a classic RE game any less than this one. Even if you download a third-party mod that includes the item box back to the game, which greatly removes one of the biggest issues with this game - the unbearable and inevitable amount of backtracking - you're still stuck with the principle that this is just a boring game.

The idea of Billy and Rebecca being two separate and competent agents that you can control and coordinate to make the experience fun and diverse when dealing with both the action and puzzle-solving segments should sound exciting, but you soon realize that the devs seemed to be more preoccupied with a philosophy that seems to focus more on how to constantly punish you for lacking divine levels of foresight, rather than actually applying methods to make this a new and refreshing entry to a franchise that had already nearly perfected its gimmick at this point in time.

This should've been, at worst, just an average game, a 6/10. But you soon realize that you're dealing with such unfair struggle just to get even through the first playthrough; this game is desperately unpolished. The main mechanics of your average classic RE game were split across two different characters this time, which makes the whole experience feel like you're doing double the micromanaging effort for only half of the expected and desired output.

The AI is as inconsistent as it is helpless; Billy has the most aggressive AI, so you want to have him wield the big guns while you offer support, but Rebecca has the lowest HP bar and is prone to getting attacked often, which makes you need to become Billy instead. You have to situationally decide which character to baby between rooms, which can be fun if that's what you like, but it was really stressful and unrewarding for me.

On top of that, the enemies are just downright offensive. If you've already played this, you know that the big bat, hunters, monkeys, and frogs, are prime examples of Enemy Design Philosophy done wrong. If you haven't, be prepared to get comfortable with the concept of getting chain stunlocked, as well as getting hit while in a staggering animation.

All in all, if you really want to at least try this game out, do yourself a favour and wait for the most reasonable discount to be available first. This is far from being worth the full price. It's not even worth half the price. In short, this is not a very good game.

I started Resident Evil back in 09 with RE5 as a wee lad and heavily grew up with the action based survival horror entries. I adored RE7 and 9 which are the closest to the classic games possible and 9 was the game to finally tip me over to the games that came before RE4 OG. I started with Code Veronica X on my Xbox (underrated as hell) and heavily enjoyed it. I then started and completed Resident Evil 0. No matter what people tell you about this game, please at least try it yourself to form a personal opinion. 

People HATE on this game endlessly for it's lack of item box, which yes is a flaw in design but it's not as bad as people make it out to be. The level design in this game is actually super good and is interconnected in a way where the lack of an item box is not the game's biggest flaw. I feel that if there were item boxes, it would trivialize much of the game, if anything, the larger weapons being 2 slots is more of a flaw with the inventory limitations. I'm also very weird and like hoarding resources in survival horror games and optimizing with limited inventory space, so this game scratches that itch perfectly. Gameplay is the classic Resident Evil loop but with a partner system which I feel is not realized much because of its ambitious nature in 2002. The partner AI is not good which is what I expected since its such an old game and you kind of just use Billy the majority of the time since his unique traits are much better suited for all the combat sections possible.

Resident Evil games aren't known for story most of the time and this game you can write off story wise which is not the main appeal anyways but Rebecca is awesome and Billy is pretty decent. The atmosphere and graphics are top notch, it shines so much on a Steam Deck OLED. 

Speaking of Steam Deck, it does work but be prepared to change to Proton GE-7.49 in order to fix random red/green lines in the train section, FMVs to playback properly, and downclock the GPU speed for more stability. This game is pretty great despite it flaws and I heard that the rumored remake in development will implement full fledged co-op as well as the original partner system which sounds amazing and justifies the remake. I hope that's true because this game has so much potential and was an enjoyable playthrough. Give it a try when it's on sale

I do not recommend this game... so why have I given it a positive review?

This game is... genuinely the most mind numbing, frustrating and evil thing I have played in recent times. I would not recommend this game to anyone, just to save them the pain. If you are looking to get into resident evil and thought the prequel was good place to start, STOP TURN BACK, DO NOT START HERE. However. If you are like me, and are a little bit masochistic, go ahead... play it... be my guest! I strongly suggest playing Resident Evil 1 first, and let me at least let me give you a few ideas and some advice about this torturous game.

1. The train section is immensely short. In fact it is so short, that if you are feeling bold, you can complete it without spending a single ink ribbon. You may need a good supply of these ink ribbons later.

2. The first scorpion boss can easily be taken out with just a pistol, don't waste any shotgun ammo here. The moment the boss fight initiates, run back to the door you just came through, turn around and wait for the scorpion to approach. Then fire a single pistol shot at a time. Each time you shoot, you will stunlock the scorpion until it is dead.

3. Like any resident evil, conserve your ammo and healing items. Here it is especially important, I cannot stress this enough. You will fly through ammo, particularly against bosses, so be very sparing on what you spend your shots on. On that note, time your shots too. It is all too easy to waste a bullet by timing it wrong and the zombie on the floor hasn't fully stood up into your pistol's range yet.

4. Take the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grappling hook with you... It may seem useless after you first use it on the train, and initially you can drop it, however you must pick it back up as you enter Facility. It will save you a long journey back and forth later on, this game loves to make you backtrack.

5. On the note of items... THERE ARE NO ITEM BOXES IN THIS GAME. The upside is that you can leave items on the floor for you to pick up later, however you must prepare yourself for several moments in the game where you will just spend time ferrying items back and forth (e.g. from your old save room, to your new save room).

6. When you feel like you are nearing the end of Facility, make sure you are well stocked on heavy hitting weapon ammo. Really the shotgun is what you need, and healing items too of course. If you come understocked or have wasted your ammo to this point, you can so easily soft lock yourself.

7. While ferrying ammo to the end of Facility, this is when you should take that grappling hook with you again, it will be important.

8. Rebecca or Billy? Billy... every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time. Billy is a better shooter than Rebecca and is more likely to hit criticals, which will save you ammo. Billy also has nearly twice the health of Rebecca, so his healing economy is fantastic. Always use full heals (red + green herbs, or first aid sprays), as he can tank nearly double the damage of Rebecca but then heal to full for the same price. There will be moments of course when you have to use Rebecca, but when scouting ahead or going against Bosses, try to use Billy.

9. The exception to the rule above are molotovs. Rebecca is much faster and more accurate with Molotovs than Billy, so use her when you wish to use a molotov. Do not use molotovs on any old enemy however. You will come across leech enemies in the game that will drain you of your ammo if you try to shoot them. Instead, throw 3 to 4 molotovs at them with Rebecca and you should be good. Try to be sparing however, I think I only killed 3 leech enemies with molotovs in my entire playthrough, and saved the rest for the final boss.

10. Just... have patience... this game will test you again and again, and throw all sorts of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at you. I honestly couldn't help but laugh at how ridiculous some of the things this game made me do were.

11. Try to enjoy the game for what it is. There is some interesting lore and cutscenes in here.

Overall I actually LOVE the concept of this game, just not the game itself. I think it would genuinely hugely benefit from the remake treatment. The train and the facility are genuinely really cool settings that would look amazing reimagined with modern graphics. They could also delve deeper into the Umbrella lore and play around with some fun chemistry between Billy and Rebecca. Hell I would play the ♥♥♥♥ out of a remake of this game. Resident Evil 0 HD is a solid experience overall, especially when viewed in the context of when it was released. It’s worth playing, particularly if you’re going through the series, but it comes with some noticeable friction points that hold it back.

Visuals & Presentation:
I thought the game held up surprisingly well visually. The character models looked good and didn’t feel overly pixelated or dated, and the environments were one of the stronger aspects of the game. The pre-rendered backgrounds were vivid and did a great job creating atmosphere, giving the game a strong sense of ambiance that still holds up today. Enemy design was decent overall, though it leans heavily on large insects and real-world creatures, which makes it feel less creative compared to other entries. There are a few standout bosses that help break that up and add variety. Cutscenes were pretty rough, but that’s expected given the age of the game and didn’t impact my experience much. Using an HD mod helps improve the visuals further and is worth considering.

Characters & Narrative:
The characters were a good introduction to the Resident Evil series. I liked them overall, but they are fairly minimal in terms of depth. There is some interaction between the two main characters that helps build a connection and show some evolution in their relationship, but it’s limited. They have enough personality to stay interesting, but not enough to feel deeply developed. The story works more as background for the broader series than as a standout narrative on its own. It adds context and helps flesh out later entries, which makes it more valuable if you’re playing through the full series.

Gameplay:
Gameplay is where most of the friction comes in. The aiming feels clunky, and I often found myself facing the wrong direction when trying to shoot, which made combat more frustrating than it needed to be. Camera transitions were also a consistent issue, sometimes reversing movement direction mid-navigation and making traversal feel awkward. Some of the puzzles were more complicated than they needed to be, not because they were difficult, but because of how they were designed.

Inventory & Design Friction:
The biggest issue for me was the inventory system. Each character only has six slots, which creates constant pressure to manage items. I was frequently dropping things, backtracking to pick them up, and trying to figure out what I could afford to carry at any given time. This ended up affecting how I played, as I reduced the number of weapons I carried, prioritized stronger weapons, and avoided holding onto anything unnecessary. It became less about strategy and more about working around limitations.

One important note is the Grappling Hook from the train section. This item is used throughout the game, so it’s worth keeping it somewhere accessible rather than discarding it.

Overall Experience:
I had a good experience with the game overall. It’s not something I would consider exceptional on its own, but it’s definitely worth playing, especially if you’re going through the full Resident Evil series. It feels more like an important supporting entry than a standout title, adding meaningful background and context even if it doesn’t fully hold up compared to newer games. The limitations are noticeable, but understandable given its age.

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 0 HD is a worthwhile experience with solid atmosphere and a good foundation, but it’s held back by clunky mechanics and restrictive design choices. If you’re playing through the series, it’s absolutely worth your time, just be prepared for some frustration along the way.

Resident Evil Zero acts as the prequel to the first Resident Evil following dual protagonists Rebecca Chambers & Billy Coen in their efforts to survive the unleashed horror of the T-Virus before Spencer Mansion. After playing the first entry I was instantly hooked and didn't take long to play the next entry which curiously enough would be a prequel following Rebecca's story before we encounter her as Chris which definitely helped her become a favorite character of mine with her being a badass and less of a damsel in distress, well at least most of the time. 

Rebecca & Billy stand out as strong protagonists for the story through a fun dynamic which is nurtured throughout the game from a required partnership to one steeped in trust and care as they both help one another through the horrors they inevitably encounter. The gunplay has seen great improvement through a better aiming and how guns are able to stun enemies to the point of being able to maneuver around them properly rather than have them tank hits until they die; another great change was through the hit-box of shooting enemies even if they're down or low to the ground through bullets not flying over heads anymore which helps to conserve ammo. I was able to seat myself in some familiarity with how the game's fixed camera angles operate, but was shocked by how different the control scheme with the shoot button delegated to one of the face buttons rather than a trigger or bumper along with the new partner system which dramatically shifted how every encounter in the game would operate. At first, I thought the partner system was clunky and not the most intuitive, but after enough practice along with a couple of playthroughs it felt seamless being able to move both characters with some fun tech being available with their teleporting in between rooms to avoid some danger. The environments looked just as polished as the first game with the set-pieces being vaster in scale and well-designed with each room serving a purpose to help connect everything which is primarily seen in the intro train section which was my favorite with how varied you were able to tackle it even with its especially linear design.

It's hard to discuss this game without bringing up the lack of item boxes which I wholeheartedly agree with in how flawed it is by game design especially when compared to the first games. Each character only having six slots along with most weapons plus the hookshot being two-slotted were a slog to manage as without boxes you needed to designate various bases throughout the game to constantly drop items again with there annoyingly being a limit to how many can exist in a room. Through this design, I think the game should've operated like the first's with everything being one slot along with item boxes or better shortcuts implemented with there being scarcely few of them compared to the original. The story while serviceable was pretty simple for a new villain appearing then being later defeated with little backstory for his hatred and revenge on Umbrella basically utilized to set the events of the first game in motion. 

For achievements, the game requires multiple playthroughs in various difficulties on top of the extra modes such as Wesker mode & Leech Hunter with the latter's ranking granting infinite ammo and better weapons for all subsequent playthroughs on that file, but only tied to the difficulty first completed in it. Through this, runs like no saves and no healing only required planning the route to best optimize where to utilize the inventory best which can be fun in managing even without boxes as you don't need to be carrying around extra guns or healing letting you only need key items. The hardest achievement would have to be hard mode as enemies take a lot more damage and item management needs to be perfect in order to optimize the limited healing and ammo in the game to be able to take down the gauntlet of bosses at the end. Like the first game, subsequent runs were a lot of fun with knowing the layout of the map in how you're able to best manage everything you're given to complete whatever you need to that run along with combining various elements in order to efficiently proc achievements.

Overall, I had a great time playing through Resident Evil Zero. I believe the game would be right up there with the original if item boxes were implemented as that's my only true complaint as the core of the game is strong with the partner system being greatly utilized for progression along with strong level design and atmosphere. This game is the perfect example of great ideas and flawed execution as I was able to have a lot of fun once I knew the game extremely well where the lack of item boxes wasn't as important as item management. Despite the game's item management mechanics being limited, I can still recommend this game for those who are looking to play through the series with a unique partner system that blends well throughout the game.

I really want to like this game, I really truly do, but it just has so many glaring issues that it's hard to like it.

First of all, starting with the positives: The game's atmosphere is beautiful. From the art design to the music, every aspect of the game is unnerving but gorgeous, and the train is easily one of the most unique areas in a Resident Evil game ever. Secondly, Billy and Rebecca have some good chemistry and are relatively well developed characters, with the Mystery Man being a fun antagonist as well. And lastly, the enemy designs are brilliant and creepy as they should be.

But, here come the negatives unfortunately.
Starting off strong, the inventory management in this game is abysmal. There's no item box, and instead you have to leave items on the ground; which, in theory sounds like it could work given you're working with two characters' inventories. But due to the sheer amount of items that you'll be picking up, (and some that take up multiple slots), you'll be constantly running back and forth through tedious and at times infuriatingly long door animations just to get back to that one room that you left everything in, and in cases you'll have to make that trek several times. Secondly, the difficulty curve from normal to hard is insanity. Due to the enemy spam this game likes to do at times paired with the somewhat clunky controls, it makes it almost impossible to reach the end of the game with nearly enough heals or ammo to beat the final boss unless you've routed the game perfectly and know exactly what you're doing. And lastly, not only does the game kind of slog near the end, but you can also get softlocked multiple times throughout the game, INCLUDING near the end. I know lots of Resident Evil games have them, but this game is probably one of the more notorious ones aside from Code Veronica.

Overall, I truly want to love this game for what it sets out to do, but I cannot in good faith recommend it given its glaring flaws. I would personally wait for a remake. Overall a 5.5/10 game for me. (And yes, it says I have 40 hours on this game at the time of this review. This was my third attempt at beating the game before I finally did it).

[b]Resident Evil 0 is a good game and I'm tired of pretending it's not.[/b] 

It's a unique experience within the world of RE as instead of one character, you control two characters at the same time throughout the whole experience. This adds a whole new layer of strategy to the survival horror, who will go to this room, who will fight this specific boss, and who gets what. Rebecca is weak but has the ability to combine herbs, whereas Billy is a powerhouse but can't combine his own herbs. I tend to have my characters fan out and explore, before convening in a designated hub area to drop off loot and this play style made for such a wondrous experience. 

However it's not perfect, as many have stated there are no item boxes in this game meaning if you drop an item it stays at that point in the map. If you're not smart about "muling" your items to new designated locations then it can be a pain to backtrack, I didn't mind this and the game always allows backtracking through well placed shortcuts throughout the game. Narrative wise it's RE camp as you've come to expect, but it's a fun semi-important (not super important) piece of the massive narrative and features Rebecca so what's not to love.

My BIGGEST detractor of the game is the annoyance of the Eliminator enemy type and the lack of creativity when it comes to most of the boss fights, which comprises mainly of BIG ANIMAL. This doesn't really drag it down too much but still, kind of sad when RE has some crazy enemy designs under its belt.

Overall, I don't understand the hate for the game. You do have to play differently from other RE's but it provides a interesting new experience that no other RE game has replicated. Sure it's tricky to get that balance of inventory management right, but get creative with it. OH and slight spoilers but [spoiler]keep that hookshot with you until past the lab :)[/spoiler].

I'm one of those old farts who played the original Resident Evil games back in the late 90s, and I have to say it's quite painful to go back to that gameplay and overall jankiness. Games back then had heart and soul, but the controls, UI, and some core design aspects feel very raw and primitive today.

Resident Evil 0 could be a good game, it has most of the essential ingredients of the series, but some parts of it are simply painful and frustrating. Basic stuff like navigating the inventory, controlling the character, aiming, or even picking up items often feels like a chore. Add to that the 10second door opening animations, and having to control two characters simultaneously while fighting bosses with fixed camera angles constantly switching every few meters… it’s just not a very engaging or fun experience.

That said, I was actually enjoying myself during the first 8 hours or so. The train and mansion sections are easily the best parts of the game. But as it went on, it started to feel like a burden more than anything else. It really took some dedication to finish it.

The best thing about the game is definitely the pre-rendered backgrounds, they’re amazing pieces of art and basically carry the whole experience. Also, a very positive note for the puzzles. I’d say they hold up well even compared to more modern RE games. The animal statues puzzle, for example, felt genuinely challenging.

Overall, this is a mixed review. Not a bad game, but I finished it more with a sense of relief than satisfaction, mostly just ready to move on and play something else.

Serinin kökenine dönmek fikri güzel ama Resident Evil 0, bunu yaparken bazı konularda oyuncuyu zorlayabiliyor. Oyun, klasik Resident Evil formülünü koruyor: sabit kamera açıları, sınırlı kaynaklar, bulmacalar ve ağır ilerleyen bir tempo. Atmosfer tarafı güçlü; özellikle tren bölümü oyunun en akılda kalan kısmı. Gerilim hissi başarılı şekilde veriliyor. Ama bu oyunu farklı yapan şey, iki karakteri aynı anda yönetme sistemi. Rebecca ve Billy arasında geçiş yapıyorsun, hatta istersen ayrı ayrı kontrol edebiliyorsun. Kağıt üstünde güzel bir fikir ama pratikte bazen yorucu olabiliyor. Özellikle karakterler arası eşya taşıma işleri gereksiz mikro yönetim hissi yaratıyor.

Zaten oyunun en tartışmalı kısmı envanter sistemi. Klasik sandık sistemi yok. Eşyaları yere bırakıyorsun ve sonra geri gelip alıyorsun. Bu da özellikle ilerleyen bölümlerde ciddi bir backtracking (geri dönme) yükü oluşturuyor. Bazen korkudan çok “eşyam neredeydi?” diye düşünüyorsun. Ancak, item box modu kurup oynayabiliyorsunuz. Şahsen ben öyle yaptım ve oyundan çok daha fazla zevk aldım. İtem box sız bu oyun çekilmez, ıstıraba dönüşür. 

Düşman çeşitliliği fena değil ama bazı düşmanlar (özellikle leech/zombi varyasyonları) sinir bozucu olabiliyor. Kontroller ise serinin eski oyunları gibi: alışınca sorun yok ama yeni oyuncular için sert gelebilir. Hikaye tarafı fena değil, serinin olaylarına giriş niteliğinde. Rebecca karakterini daha iyi tanıma fırsatı veriyor ama anlatım çok güçlü sayılmaz. Teknik olarak remaster versiyonu temiz. Arka planlar güzel, karakter modelleri güncellenmiş. Ama oynanış hâlâ eski kafada ve bu herkesin hoşuna gitmeyebilir. 8.1/10

🧟‍♂️🚂 Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster Review 🚂🧟‍♂️

🕹 Length: 10–15 hours (main story) | 15–20 with exploration
💰 Price vs. Content: Good value, especially for fans of classic survival horror
⚙ Optimization: Excellent; smooth performance on modern systems
🎮 Difficulty: Moderate; can feel challenging due to classic mechanics

🎮 Gameplay

Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is a prequel to the original Resident Evil, following Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen as they uncover the origins of the mansion incident. It stays true to the classic survival horror formula, with fixed camera angles, limited resources, and a strong focus on puzzle-solving and backtracking.

One of its unique mechanics is the character-switching system, allowing you to control both Rebecca and Billy, each with different strengths. This adds a layer of strategy, as you’ll need to manage inventory, positioning, and cooperation between the two characters.

However, unlike other classic entries, the game removes the traditional item box system, forcing players to drop items on the ground and backtrack to retrieve them. While innovative, this can become tedious and is often seen as one of the game’s biggest drawbacks.

For players not used to old-school survival horror design, the experience can feel slow, rigid, and even frustrating at first. But once you adapt, the tension, resource management, and atmosphere start to shine.

✅ The Good:
✔ Classic survival horror atmosphere
✔ Unique dual-character system
✔ Strong puzzles and level design
✔ Great visual upgrade in the HD remaster

RESIDENT EVIL 0
4/10. Disappointing, tedious, boring, annoying, long, frustrating and pointless. 

Over these past couple of months I have been slowly making my way through the Resident Evil series. So far I have beat (in this order): RE2make, RE3make, RE4make, RE1make, and RE9 Requiem. My favorite so far has been RE1make. I absolutely loved the atmosphere, the story, the gameplay, puzzles and exploration of the Spencer Mansion. After RE1make wrapped up, I started RE0- being that 0 is a direct prequel taking place one day before, and has the same style of gameplay and engine. Or so I thought! This is the first one I really disliked.

RE0 plays completely differently as it centers around a gameplay gimmick of controlling two characters simultaneously- STARS Rookie Rebecca Chambers and runaway convict Billy Coen. This odd-couple premise was exciting at first, and the opening sequence on the Train is easily the high point of the game. The environment is exciting, moody, and claustrophobic, and there is a fun back and forth exploration of the train cars. Then the game separates the two, and you have to switch between them to solve puzzles and progress. Pretty cool! Exciting start! The controls are a little clunky but the AI partner handles the opening fairly well.

Unfortunately after the Train sequence, the game quickly plummets in quality and enjoyment. When I first arrived at this new mansion, I was excited to explore it and brave the survival horror and face all of those Resident Evils inside. Sadly, this mansion doesn’t hold a candle to the Spencer Estate, and many of the rooms blended together and were mostly unremarkable. This mansion belongs to another founder of Umbrella and it has been turned into a Umbrella Training Facility? For soldiers and/or scientists? It’s sort of unclear and they don’t really make the most of that theming despite it’s potential. It would have been cool to see what the company culture was like, or see the training Umbrella Corps go through in handling BOWs. It’s here where the lack of Item Boxes, and the dearth of Healing supplies rears it’s ugly mutated head. 

In total, Steam said my total playtime was 16.8 hours and upon completion my final game time was 8 HOURS AND 59 MINUTES. That means I died SO many times that I essentially played the game twice, and so so so SO much of that was dealing with these awful inventory screens. In RE1make, I did Easy Jill and Medium Chris playthroughs and felt nicely challenged with both runs. Here I just died and died and died, and more often than not I felt that it was no fault of my own. The game will throw hordes of enemies at you that stunlock you, or grab you into an insta-kill. You can almost never rely on your AI partner to help you in combat, they’ll just stand there or take aim and never fire. Sometimes you’ll be alone in a room with one other Leechman enemy and you take aim with a molotov bottle and SOMEHOW YOU MISS and the character throws the bottle in the complete opposite direction. Whipped across the room, dead. And because of the ink-ribbon save system, every little item pick up interaction or trade-off between separated protagonists becomes tortuous and an exercise in patience. You repeat this again and again and again, going through the same handful of doors over and over. There are moments in the game when you get into a groove of exploration, you forget all that and it gets really fun. Then you get to the bosses and it just completely kills the momentum.

Very underwhelming bosses. Giant Scorpion, Giant Centipede, Giant Bat, uhhh leeches. Lots of Leeches. Other RE games always make it an event when a boss monster shows up, and they always have a little bit of fun lore to contextualize them. Here they aren’t given any context whatsoever. They were just being experimented on I guess. That goes for the enemies too. We got your typical zombies, zombie dogs (in one scene in the opening), zombie monkeys that leap all around the room and stun-lock you, giant locusts, giant frogs that can insta-kill grab you while your AI partner stares and watches, Leechmen that have a whip attack, explode on death and can only die to Molotovs, and Hunters. Later on stronger zombies show up but they behave the same way just with more health. Real disappointing stuff. 

– SPOILERS —

The story is awful. The two characters, Rebecca and Billy are set up to have friction, being that they are on opposite sides of the law, but they really do nothing with it outside the first hour. These characters have absolutely nothing to say about the going-ons in the Mansion and attached areas (which I’m confused as to how they are all connected geographically by Elevator but whatever) beyond saying “This place is weird.” They don’t really have any banter during gameplay, and explore almost entirely in silence, and in cutscenes Rebecca acts so lovely-dovey and affectionate towards him (despite being charged with the murder of 23 people?). The big reveal of the game is that when Billy was stationed in Africa, he, along with the rest of his platoon, gunned down a tribe of innocent villagers based on bad intel. Or he didn’t? The game isn’t really clear if he participated in it and has a guilty conscience or he spoke out and was framed for the incident. Either way this reveal doesn’t really pay off in any way, nor does it have ANY THING to do with the events of this game.

These characters are here solely by circumstance, and any hopes that this prequel would shed new light into RE1 is quickly dashed. Our heroes are watched by the villains the entire time via security camera, so half the cutscenes are of people in other rooms just watching us explore. When our heroes finally meet the big bad for the first time at the very end of the game they ask, “WHO ARE YOU? WHY ARE YOU DOING THIS?” So he explains: Wesker and Birkin are getting ready to do the Spencer Mansion incident and begin collecting their STARS Bravo Team combat data when… an Opera Singer on a cliff summons a horde of leeches to attack a train? This throws their plan into chaos… for some reason? So they split up and Birkin says he will go activate the self-destruct. Why does he have to do it himself? I don’t know. Turns out the Leech-Man was a co-founder of Umbrella who discovered the Progenitor Virus (which led to the T and G Viruses) and was betrayed by the other two. The Leeches revived him? Cloned him? Bonded with him?

Our heroes kill him and go their separate ways. Rebecca will say Billy died in the Train crash, and goes to investigate the Spencer Mansion. The End. Wow, what a waste of my time. The only thing that keeps this from being a 0/10 is the beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds, and the opening train sequence is great. Otherwise, you can skip it.

Resident Evil 0 is a survival horror game that’s a prequel to Resident Evil, where it follows an S.T.A.R.S. officer, Rebecca Chambers, who’s after Billy Coen over something that he’s on the run for. They work together when surrounded by zombies and explore the mystery of where it all comes from. Out of all the Resident Evil games that are the main series, this is one of the more divisive efforts that tries something completely different, which the fanbase is mixed on. It made some creative choices to make it intentionally difficult and harder than the first game that started it all. For me, the results of these creative choices have some highs and some lows.

The graphics looked better than in the first game, with smoother character movement and more textures, and the cutscenes looked solid as well. There are some moments in the cutscenes that looked dated, but nothing that took me out of it that much. The gameplay is still one of the highlights, and I appreciate it creating a partner mechanic that not only has decent AI but also feels refreshing, leading to interesting pathways and puzzles. The game got the location down with such interesting designs to explore that I was curious about where each room takes me that’s different. The story isn’t too bad, which gives some interesting background to Wesker and William Birkin while showing how it all started. Granted, the lore of this game probably could’ve been an email, but I appreciate the attempt here. The fixed camera is better here than in the first game, where it’s not nearly as annoying to deal with, which gave so much space for the characters to go to where they need to go while also not go too crazy on the camera frame. The bosses were fun, although the bat boss was incredibly annoying, as it just flew really fast all over the place.

Now, when it comes to the changes, I like the partner mechanic, but the others? Less so. I don’t mind the concept of not having loot boxes that you have to drop items if you’re too full, but the limited inventory spaces made it very tedious to deal with, considering the amount of backtracking. You have the same amount of spaces as Chris Redfield in Resident Evil, and the amount of backtracking makes the first game feel like a cakewalk. It’s generally annoying when you have to go back to the one place, which will take you minutes, grab the stuff that you need, and go back to where you were. It happens more often than you think. Raising the difficulty is one thing, repetition is another. Grabbing the items can also be a pain in the ass because the controls are surprisingly worse than the first game. It feels like you have to be almost precise about where you need to grab the item, and half the time, you have to move again. It’s incredibly slippery that the first game was better at keeping it mostly tight. The voice acting and some of the dialogue are even clunkier than the first game, which just sounds bad to the point of being unintentionally funny. I could’ve used more of the character development for Rebecca Chambers, but I’m glad that Billy Coen has enough characterization. Resident Evil 0 is an all right game that I still had enough fun with, regardless of the amount of frustrations I had with it.

[h1]Resident Evil 0 Review[/h1]
[h2]Hard Mode | ~13 Hours[/h2]

After about 13 hours on hard, I can say this game was pretty much as bland as I expected.

This isn’t really a survival horror game to me. It feels more like a [b]puzzle game with occasional zombie killing[/b], and the true horror is the [b]inventory system[/b].

You only get [b]6 inventory slots per character[/b]. Weapons take up space even when equipped, larger weapons take up [b]2 slots[/b], and ammo, healing items, and key items all fight for what little room you have left. Yes, you control two characters, so technically you have 12 slots total, but all that really means is you spend even more time micromanaging junk and swapping between characters. I probably spent a disgusting amount of my playtime just dealing with inventory nonsense.

[h2]Hard Mode Isn't Hard, It's Just Annoying[/h2]

Hard mode doesn’t feel meaningfully harder. Enemies just get more health, ammo feels more scarce, and everything turns into a bullet sponge. That’s not real difficulty. That’s just tedium.

Honestly, unless you’re a completionist or trying to prove something to yourself, I’d recommend playing on [b]Normal[/b] or even [b]Easy[/b]. Apparently Easy even gives you more inventory space, and had I known that, I probably would’ve picked it just to make this game less miserable to manage.

[h2]What Dragged It Down[/h2]

[list]
[*]Terrible inventory management
[*]Constant character swapping
[*]Puzzles that are more tedious than clever
[*]Frequent loading screens for every door, ladder, and stairway
[*]Ink Ribbon save system that does not respect your time
[/list]

The loading screens are classic old-school Resident Evil, sure, but that doesn’t make them any less annoying. Exploration feels clunky, and the game just constantly interrupts itself.

[h2]Story / Characters[/h2]

The story is cheesy. The dialogue is cheesy. The voice acting is cheesy. I never really got attached to anybody.

That said, I can still appreciate this game as a prequel to [i]Resident Evil 1[/i]. It was cool seeing some of the setup for the T-virus and Wesker’s earlier role in all of this. That part had value for me, especially because I mainly played this to better understand the story before replaying the older games I grew up watching my parents play.

[h2]Extra Content[/h2]

You do unlock extra stuff, like [b]Leech Hunter mode[/b], and there’s a sort of NG+ bonus where Rebecca gets an alternate Umbrella-style outfit and Billy is replaced by Wesker with special abilities.

That sounds cool in theory.

In practice? By the time I finished the main game, I was so burnt out that I couldn’t bring myself to care. I loaded it up, looked at it, and immediately realized I had absolutely no desire to keep playing this game any longer.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

[b]I can’t really recommend Resident Evil 0 unless you already know you enjoy this kind of old-school RE design or you’re here strictly for the lore.[/b]

If you’re just curious about the story, I’d honestly say [b]watch a YouTube recap instead[/b]. The game itself feels dated, tedious, and weirdly hostile to your time.

The scariest thing in Resident Evil 0 isn’t the zombies.

It’s the inventory screen.

[spoiler]I am excited to move on to Resident Evil 1, though.[/spoiler]

Mimicry marcus is a genuine pain to deal with unless you have molotovs, in one instance i didn't have enough to kill him and had to use flame rounds on the grenade launcher which took him 10 shots to die, 10 SHOTS. Now the eliminators on the other hand might be the single worst enemy in the mainline games, they can stunlock you in groups of 3 where you can do nothing but sit there and die. The bosses are nothing special, the scorpion is alright, the centipede is ok but its less of a boss and more of a damage check where if you don't do enough rebecca will die, the bat is the second worst boss in the game, it spawns upto 16 smaller bats to attack you during the fight which make aiming at the actual boss harder than it needs to be especially since it's flying. The tyrant is the only good boss with the only flaw being it doesn't take damage when in it's staggered state. And then there's the queen leech, and oh boy is it bad. Firstly the runback from the closest typewriter is 2 minutes which might not seem like a lot but will add up when you see how cheap it is. This game just isn’t for me. I didn’t enjoy most of it—and that’s coming from someone who’s played every Resident Evil on Steam, with Resident Evil 1 being my favourite.

Starting with the positives: it does capture that classic feeling in certain areas. The train section is easily the best part of the game—great atmosphere, classic pacing. Unfortunately, it only lasts about an hour if you don’t know what you’re doing. The treatment plant is also pretty solid.

The character-switching system is another highlight. Swapping between Billy and Rebecca to solve puzzles is a cool idea and actually fun to use.

Now for the negatives… and there are a lot.

First: no item box. This completely drags the game down. Instead of proper inventory management, you’re just dumping items on the floor and hoping you remember where everything is. If you’re playing blind and forget something important like the hook shot, enjoy 30–40 minutes of backtracking. It’s not challenging—it’s just annoying.

The puzzles can also feel more tedious than clever, and some moments are straight-up frustrating. The section where Rebecca is about to fall and you have to rush to her as Billy is a good example—if you don’t know the basement layout (which you probably don’t at that point), you’re just guessing and likely failing. Then it’s back to your last save.

Enemies don’t help either. Hunters can one-shot you way too often, and while they’re always dangerous in this series, here they feel cheap—like they’re placed specifically to catch you out. Same with the frog enemy that can instantly kill you with almost no warning. Again: back to your last save.

I get that the game is old and autosave wasn’t standard, but that makes these design choices feel even worse, not better.

And the bat boss? Easily one of the worst in the franchise. Trying to hit a fast-moving target with tank controls (even using analog) is just painful. Only saving grace is the save room right before it.

I know this sounds harsh, but I just didn’t enjoy this game and I don’t see myself ever replaying it.

Resident Evil 0 is one of the more experimental entries in the classic survival horror era of the Resident Evil franchise. Originally released for the Nintendo GameCube, it acts as a prequel to the first game and follows Rebecca Chambers and escaped convict Billy Coen.

Story & Atmosphere

Set just before the events of the original Resident Evil, the game dives into the origins of the T-virus outbreak. You explore eerie locations like a derailed train and an abandoned training facility.

The tone is classic survival horror—tense, claustrophobic, and dripping with mystery. The story adds non essential backstory, inconsequential to the main plot and a lot of lore padding, it can feel a bit convoluted, especially with its more theatrical villain moments.

Gameplay

The biggest twist here is the partner system. You control both Rebecca and Billy, switching between them or directing the AI partner.

What works:
	•	Cooperative puzzle-solving (even in single-player)
	•	Unique character abilities (Rebecca mixes chemicals; Billy is stronger)

What doesn’t:
	•	The AI partner can be unreliable at times
	•	Inventory management is notoriously frustrating

Instead of item boxes, the game uses a drop system, where you leave items on the ground. It sounds realistic, but in practice it leads to lots of backtracking and micromanagement.

Graphics & Presentation

For its time, the game looked fantastic. The pre-rendered backgrounds are detailed and atmospheric, especially on the train.

The HD remaster improves textures and lighting, making it still visually appealing today—though the fixed camera angles may feel dated to newcomers.

Sound & Music

The soundtrack leans heavily into eerie ambience rather than memorable melodies, which works well for tension. Sound design (footsteps, distant noises) enhances the feeling of dread.

Voice acting is… classic early-2000s Resident Evil—a mix of charm and awkwardness.

Pros
	•	Unique dual-character system
	•	Strong survival horror atmosphere
	•	Beautiful environments

Cons
	•	Clunky inventory system (no item boxes!)
	•	AI partner can be frustrating
	•	Story is inconsequential to the main lore
	•	Controls and camera may feel dated

Final Verdict

Resident Evil 0 is a bold but flawed experiment. It sticks closely to the classic formula while trying new ideas—some of which work, others don’t.

If you enjoy old-school survival horror and don’t mind some frustration, it’s absolutely worth playing. But if you prefer smoother, modern gameplay, it might feel a bit rough.

I went back to Resident Evil 0 to finally finish everything, including all the achievements, and in the end my impressions were pretty mixed.
On one hand, the game really captures the atmosphere of classic entries in the series. Fixed camera angles, tension, and limited resources all work great. The locations are very atmospheric, especially the train at the beginning, which sets the tone perfectly and pulls you in right away.
On the other hand, there are some things that seriously hurt the experience. The biggest issue is the inventory system. There are no traditional item boxes, so you have to drop items on the ground. It sounds fine in theory, but in practice it turns into constant backtracking and a mess where you forget where you left things.
The partner system also feels better on paper than in reality. Controlling two characters sounds interesting, but it doesn’t always work smoothly. Sometimes the AI feels dumb, and other times you’re just forced to constantly switch between them, which becomes more annoying than engaging.
The story is decent for a prequel, but I wouldn’t say it’s particularly memorable. There are some interesting moments, but overall it feels more like background than a driving force.
As for the achievements, I didn’t actually spend that much time on them, but honestly, it felt exhausting. At some point I realized I wasn’t enjoying the game at all anymore. It started to feel like a chore, and there were moments where it was just genuinely unpleasant to play.
In the end, it’s a game mainly for fans of classic Resident Evil. It has its own vibe and strong atmosphere, but some gameplay decisions feel outdated or just inconvenient. If you enjoy the old-school style, you might like it, but otherwise it can get frustrating pretty quickly.

Keep in mind that, although I have played every single RE game, my memory is not the best and it's been years, sometimes decades, since I last played some of them. I'm currently in the middle of a marathon so RE1DC for PS1 is my most recently played game.
This is a very flawed game that would really benefit from either a "Definitive Edition" mod or a remake, and while the latter is thankfully in the works, it's a big shame that the modding scene for this game is pretty much dead aside from the two mods I mentioned because this original version is GORGEOUS visually. Playing it in 4K and it legit looks like a modern videogame at times.
Now, onto the (other) flaws that the remake should fix. Unlike the older RE games, this one is clearly not made with tank controls and fixed camera angles in mind, the enemies are much faster, violent, and most notoriously, tanky than they are in RE1DC. They expect you to react and shoot faster than the game allows you to, with the sole exception of the basic zombies (which are pretty much absent in this game). This part isn't helped by how the grenade launcher and shotgun have seemingly been nerfed to high heaven, while a single shotgun shot would've been enough to headshot a zombie in past games, here it only serves to...hit harder than the standard handgun, same thing with the GL. Little to no knockback, much lower damage, they make the handgun look great in comparison.
It's genuinely strange how this is the game where they decided to ditch the item box and introduce leaving items on the floor, since it's also the game that introduces the biggest amount of double-slot items: The hookshot, shotgun, grenade launcher, things that took only one inventory slot in RE1DC take double that here, and while I vaguely remember some items in OG RE2/3 taking two slots, I doubt it was anything as egregious as this. I'll replay RE2 and 3 after RE1make though so we'll find out soon, but again, I doubt it'll be anywhere near as bad. Like I said before though, I have the item box mod installed, and it really alleviates most of the backtracking and slot issues...almost as if the game was made with that in mind but later removed it...
The story and characters so far are nothing special, Rebecca is seriously incompetent and needs to be saved every two minutes, but that's how she is in the other games so it fits.

This game was a bit of a mixed feeling for me at the start, especially after playing Resident Evil HD. It feels familiar, but at the same time, there’s something different about it that takes a while to get used to.
The partner system with Rebecca and Billy is probably the biggest change, and I’ll be honest, in the beginning it felt a bit overwhelming having to manage two characters at once. Switching between them, solving puzzles, keeping both alive… it can get messy. But after a few hours, it starts to click, and you begin to appreciate the extra layer of strategy it brings.
One thing I definitely noticed is that, in my opinion, the puzzles here are harder than in Resident Evil HD. They require a bit more thinking, more backtracking, and sometimes just stopping for a moment to figure things out. It can be frustrating at times, but also really satisfying when it finally makes sense.
The lack of item boxes is another thing you really feel. Dropping items on the ground and having to remember where everything is isn’t always fun, but it forces you to plan ahead and be careful with what you carry. It’s that same idea again: patience and precaution go a long way here.
Atmosphere-wise, it still delivers. The opening train section is honestly one of my favourite parts, and the game keeps that classic survival horror tension throughout. It might not hit exactly the same highs as Resident Evil HD for me, but it still has its own identity.
In the end, it’s a game that grows on you. It asks a bit more from the player, but if you give it time, it becomes a really rewarding experience. If you enjoyed Resident Evil HD, this is definitely worth playing. 8.5/10

Back in the GameCube days, I bought this around the same time as REmake, and even then it was obvious that it just wasn’t on the same level. I remember the reviews reflecting that too: REmake was treated like an instant classic, while RE0 landed more in the “pretty good, but not amazing” range. That was pretty much my experience. I played through it once, liked it, and moved on.

Coming back to it now in 2026, I feel more or less the same. It’s a solid game. It looks good, the atmosphere is strong, the train opening is memorable, and Billy and Rebecca make for a good duo. But it also feels like the weakest of the classic tank-control Resident Evil games. REmake, RE2, RE3, and Code Veronica all stand above it. And while the leads have solid chemistry, what the hell happened to Billy post RE0? He's barely mentioned again in ANY RE game going forward. It really feels like they just needed someone to assist Rebecca, and that's it. Just some random prisoner guy, here for a good time not a long time. 

And what of the rest of the story. The leech man who likes to sing opera never quite worked for me. Back in those days the series still hung onto a somewhat 'science-ish' explanation for everything that happened in its world, but suddenly you start RE0 and you got this guy just singing at you. Might as well be screaming "LEECHES COME TO ME MY DEEEEEEEARS" Billy is like "Who the hell is that?!" My thoughts exactly Billy. He was an underwhelming villain in 2002, and he sure is underwhelming in 2026.

Plus, the coop buddy system is a bit iffy here. This was the first implementation of this system in RE history, as future games, like RE4, 5, Revelations 2, etc, use a variation of this. But it is at its worse (probably; RE5 is pretty bad when played solo) here. It feels like you're constantly swapping items back and forth between your two characters. 

But the biggest problem is the item system. On paper, dropping items on the ground instead of using magical storage boxes sounds like a neat idea. The prototype of RE1 also used a system in which the storage boxes were not interlinked, and that system ended up in REmake's 'Real Survival' mode. In practice, just like in the late stages of Real Survival in REmake, it mostly turns the game into a backtracking simulator where you’re constantly retracing your steps to pick things back up. To make matters worse, the game feels much meaner about that backtracking than REmake ever was, as in REmake enemies don't respawn. But in RE0, somehow, zombies just pop up even after you've cleared a room. Capcom, I can understand zombies respawning in the train, as we see bodies everywhere. I could also understand new zombies in rooms with open windows. But in the mansion in empty closed off hallways, where are these rando zombies coming from? If at least the game implemented a system where zombies are shown opening doors, but they're not. So now you're dropping stuff on the ground, and you're constantly running into respawning zombies on the way back to your items. Is it a huge deal? Not really. But it doesn't benefit the game.

Ultimately, RE0 has good ideas, and it is a good game overall, but it never quite comes together well enough to become a game I’d strongly recommend. In 2002, it was worth playing because it was new Resident Evil. In 2026, I’m not so sure it’s worth the detour unless you’re already a big fan of the series and want to see everything. It does add a bit of context around the narrative of RE1, as it shows how the outbreak started.

⭐ A Unique and Underrated Gem in the Resident Evil Series ⭐

Resident Evil Zero is one of those games that reminds you why this franchise became legendary in the first place. The atmosphere is thick, the environments are gorgeous even years later, and the tension never lets up. From the eerie train opening to the unsettling labs, every area feels handcrafted with classic survival horror energy.

The partner zapping system is still one of the most interesting mechanics in the series. Switching between Rebecca and Billy on the fly adds a layer of strategy that keeps you thinking, planning, and adapting. It’s a refreshing twist that makes puzzles more engaging and combat more intense.

The remastered visuals look fantastic, the soundtrack hits all the right creepy notes, and the story fills in some awesome lore leading into Resident Evil 1. It’s a perfect blend of nostalgia and challenge, especially for fans who love the old-school style.

If you’re into classic survival horror, atmospheric exploration, and that signature Resident Evil charm, Zero is absolutely worth your time. It’s a standout entry that deserves way more love.

A must-play for anyone who appreciates the roots of the franchise.

Resident Evil 0 is the last of the classic‑era games with fixed camera angles and pure survival‑horror gameplay built around resource scarcity and puzzle‑box level design. As the series is known for, it features a dual‑protagonist setup, but this time it evolves the idea: you can switch between Rebecca and Billy on the fly. This leads to some clever puzzles and tense moments where you have to swap back and forth quickly. I really enjoyed this mechanic.

The game introduces some cool new enemy types, and the boss fights are solid. Visually, it still looks great. The pre‑rendered backgrounds, animations, and character models hold up surprisingly well today. I also love the opening area; without spoilers, it’s one of the best locations in the entire Resident Evil series.

The latter half of the game isn’t as strong, but that’s a common pattern throughout the franchise. My only real complaint is the lack of item boxes. I understand that the developers likely wanted to encourage managing two inventories and swapping items between characters, and while that idea isn’t bad in theory, it doesn’t work well in practice. I ended up with a huge pile of weapons, ammo, and miscellaneous items scattered all over the floor.

Overall, RE0 is a solid 8/10. It’s absolutely worth the price.

I was excited to play a Resident Evil game for the first time. Going into Resident Evil 0, I expected tension, atmosphere, and an immersive survival horror experience. Instead, I encountered a frustrating test of endurance rather than an enjoyable game.

The main problem is the game mechanics. It's not just difficult, it feels unnecessarily punishing. The inventory system quickly becomes a chore. Constantly dropping and returning to items doesn't create tension; it just wastes your time. Furthermore, the co op system, which looks interesting on paper, becomes clunky and awkward in practice.

The controls are truly awful. The movements are stiff and unresponsive, turning even the simplest actions into a struggle. I can understand that hardcore fans or those who played in the 2000s might still appreciate it out of nostalgia. But playing this in 2026 and actually enjoying it? Honestly, it feels like this should have been your first video game.

And despite being a remake, the design choices raise even more questions. For example, the door opening animations might have been acceptable decades ago, but here they just derail the game's pace. Instead of adding tension, they completely ruin the game's tempo. After spending hours with this game, I reached a point where I didn't want to open another door—or even look at one—for a long time.

I can see how longtime fans of the series might appreciate certain aspects, especially if they’re used to this style of gameplay. But as a first time experience, this was rough. Really rough.

The only part I genuinely liked was the opening set on the train. It added a unique atmosphere. The train sequences themselves were actually decent and, at times, even enjoyable. The voice acting was also surprisingly solid, which helped carry those moments a bit. But honestly, that’s about it. Those few positives aren’t nearly enough to save the overall experience hence the 2/10 score.

Resident Evil 0, overall, I think it’s a good game. Not one of the absolute best in the series, and definitely not flawless, but still good. I had fun playing it, and as someone who knows this series very well, I can say RE0 is one of those games that has some really strong ideas, mixed with some very obvious design mistakes that hold it back from being greater than it could’ve been.

On my first playthrough, I played it fully modless, the intended way. And yes, I enjoyed it, but I also felt the game fighting me more than it should. On my second playthrough, I used the item box mod, and that improved the experince a lot. Not a little, a lot. It made the game flow better, reduced the pointless backtracking, and let me focus more on the survival horror itself instead of babysitting dropped items all over the map like I was running a storage company.

One thing that really surprised me was the graphics. The game actually looks fantastic in a lot of places. The pre-rendered backgrounds mixed with the 3D animated elements attached to them looked way better than I expected. Honestly, I think it looks better than RE1 Remake. And yeah, I said it. RE1 Remake is the better game overall, no question, but some of its backgrounds can be so messy and over-detailed that sometimes I dont even know what the hell I’m looking at. RE0, on the other hand, often looks cleaner while still being beautiful, and that really worked in its favor.

Another thing I liked was the new enemies. And this is coming from someone who, most of the time, only really cares about zombies and Tyrants in Resident Evil. Usually when the series starts throwing in weird creatures, I lose intrest fast. But RE0 actually did a pretty good job here. I found its enemies more memorable and more fitting than the enemies introduced in RE7 and RE8. I know that might sound harsh, but that’s honestly how I feel. RE0’s creatures still felt like they belonged in that older, dirtier, more unsettling version of Resident Evil.

Now the two-character system is one of those mechanics that I respect a lot, even if I also got tired of it. At first, it was a genuinely good idea. It gave RE0 its own identity instead of just being “more classic RE.” Swapping between Billy and Rebecca, combining their abilities, solving things together, it was fresh. But then the game starts using it too much for tiny inconveninces, and that’s where the problem starts. Instead of feeling smart, it starts feeling like the game is forcing separation just because that’s its gimmick.

The hookshot is probably the best example of that, and I hated that thing. I really hated it. It feels like a bad mechanic that mostly exists to force the two-character structure and split them apart when the game wants it. It takes up two inventory slots, which is insane in a game with already limited inventory space. So if you’re carrying a pistol and ammo, congrats, now you’ve only got two slots left for healing, key items, or loot. That is just bad design. And worst of all, the hookshot stays in the game way longer than its welcome. Every time I thought I was finally done with it, the game was like “nope, carry this garbage again.” It stopped being interesting very fast.

And of course, the lack of item boxes is one of the game’s biggest flaws. I understand the idea behind it, but in practice it creates the same kind of issue that Code Veronica had, where you can end up with your best weapons or important supplies on the wrong character. That’s not tension, that’s just the game being annoying. The item box mod proved this to me even more, because once I used it, the game became much more enjoyable without losing what makes Resident Evil feel like Resident Evil.

As for the characters, this is another weak point. Billy and Rebecca are not terrible, but compared to other Resident Evil protagonists, they feel weak. I never really got attached to them the way I do with the series’ stronger leads. There were even moments where I cringed a bit, which is saying something because I can tolerate a lot of RE nonsense if the characters are likable enough. Rebecca in RE1 feels more interesting just by association with the mansion incident than she does in her own prequel, and Billy never fully clicked with me either. They’re servicable, but they dont carry the game the way Leon, Jill, Claire, or even Chris can.

Puzzle-wise, this game is mixed. Some puzzles are fine, some are classic RE stuff, but some of them are explained terribly. The animal statue puzzle is a great example. It really needed a better hint or clearer explanation, because the logic behind it is so vague that I was just sitting there asking myself what exactly the game wanted from me. Am I supposed to light them from weakest to strongest? Strong and weak based on what exactly? Physical strength? Predatory rank? Which animal beats which? A snake is weak against some things but its venom can kill a human, so what are we even measuring here? Do I divide them into two groups? Three groups? The puzzle is not clever when the player can’t even understand the logic the game expects him to follow.

And there was another puzzle or sequence, which I won’t spoil directly, where the game puts you under pressure with a timed event, meaning if you waste too much time, you lose. That by itself is fine. The problem is the game does not properly guide you to the correct path. In fact, it gives what feels like a wrong hint, which led me to go the wrong way and lose a lot of progress because I hadn’t saved. That’s not good puzzle design. That’s not the player failing to understand a fair clue, that’s the game misleading the player during a stressful section. It would’ve been much better if they had simply said less, or gave a proper hint, instead of pushing you toward the wrong room and wasting your time.

Story-wise, I also have issues with it. If I’m remembering correctly, RE0 creates a weird inconsistency with RE1 regarding the lab area. In RE0, the facility under the training center basically gives you a NEST-style underground lab setup, while in RE1 the big underground lab is under the Spencer Mansion. Maybe there’s a lore explanation and maybe I’m not wording it perfectly, but it still feels messy when you put both games side by side. That’s one of the classic problems with prequels. They try to add more, but sometimes they make the older story feel less clean instead of richer.

So yeah, that’s basically how I see Resident Evil 0. It’s a good game. I had fun with it. It looks way better than I expected, the enemies were surprisingly strong, and the two-character idea was genuinely cool at first. But the game also has weak protagonists, badly explained puzzles, an annoying inventory system, and one of the most obnoxious tools in the series with that stupid hookshot.

It’s a game I’m glad I played, and as a Resident Evil fan, I do think it’s worth experiencing. But it also feels like one of those games where you can clearly see the line between good ideas and bad execution. RE0 had the ingredients to be something truly great, but too often it chose annoyance over elegance.

Very weird game to recommend. I enjoyed it for the most part, but this game really does test your patience at times. No item box, as everyone under the sun has probably stated, still a decision that I don't quite understand, especially with how linear this game felt. Sure you circle around a few areas and get access to old locations to pick up your pile of supplies, but once you get access to a new location, you're pretty much done with the old one. 
The story is weird. It's RE though, so I don't think anyone's expecting much of a grounded story. It does feel weird to see Rebecca explore all these areas with Hunters and other monsters when she was portrayed as someone who could barely defend herself in RE1 and even RE1Remake. A couple other weird story quirks and a sudden somewhat anticlimactic ending make it hard to recommend if you just want to play the mainline games, because this barely counts as one given the lack of nearly every character since.
I will say though, the buddy system had some really cool mechanics. It had its small quirks, especially when trying to get your partner to follow you in elevators or to specific locations, but when the puzzles were made for the system they really shine. Plenty of puzzles that require separating the two, often with one blocked off for a good portion of the area. I was expecting the game to control like RE1Remake given they are often paired, but there isn't even an option to change it to that control scheme. It's still the fixed camera and generally plays the same, but the buttons to check the map, run, and open the menu are all juggled around.
Also enjoyed the first "mansion" location, similar to the classic RE1 mansion but different enough to stand out a bit. Unfortunately though the later areas get really boring and a bit annoying, especially since it felt like the game was ready to end 3 hours earlier. 
Overall, a weakish but still enjoyable entry. If you REALLY want to play all the numbered still canon games in the series, go for it. At the very least the first 2-3 hours are fun.

Where do I begin with this game. I really wanted to like this game or at least try and give it a fair shake. However,  after playing it in full and getting a handle on it's mechanics, I can say without a shadow of a doubt that this is the absolute WORST mainline Resident Evil game that I have played. Yes other entries in the series like RE6, RE3 Remake, and Code Veronica have their issues, but there are moments in those games that can be fun and somewhat enjoyable. RE0 is the complete opposite of fun and has a massive amount of issues that make it a chore to play through.

For starters, WHY ARE THERE NO ITEM BOXES??? You can leave items on the floor and check where you last placed them on the map, but not having an item box in a classic RE game is like not having a shotgun in Doom. It just feels unnecessary to remove them. Both characters only have 6 item slots EACH with some items like the shotgun, taking up two of them despite that not being the case in previous entries. Most of your gameplay will just be the status screen where you exchange items between Billy and Rebecca or running all over the map just to get a specific item for a section that you didn't know that you need it for. While RE1 remake had this issue (especially as Chris), the level design was tightly condensed and locations were memorable so it made it difficult to get lost (ntm having ITEM BOXES). In this game, everything looks the exact same and encounters are so poorly designed that running past enemies to conserve ammo or using the environment to your advantage is almost impossible. 

Next, the controls...dear lord the controls are horrific. I decided to play on controller and picked Control option E and while I got used to it after a while, there was always this level of awkwardness that plagued my experience when I would try to pull up the status screen by instinctually pressing Y (like RE1R) which would then pull up the map instead where as the status screen button was on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ right trigger. It just feels messy and an unresponsive at times which is one of the biggest ways to turn me off from a game. 

Finally, the story. Barely ANYTHING happens in this story. It's a prequel to the rest of the games but there's nothing interesting that's revealed about this game that couldn't have been summarized in a movie or novel instead. We don't learn that much more about Bravo Team that we didn't already know and this sucks because this was Rebecca's time to shine in her own mainline game that completely wasted her. Billy is a plank of wood who has no other character than "GRRRR I HAVE A MULLET, TATOOS, AND PTSD GRRR" (also why does he just have on handcuff on the whole game when he could have CLEARLY taken it off anytime going by the ending cutscene of the game). Marcus is also a terrible villain that is just there to be evil for evil's sake and despite his connections to Wesker, Birkin, Spencer, and Umbrella as a whole, we don't really get anything that entertaining or interesting from him at all. Things just happen in this game and despite the train sequence being a cool premise, it's over in about an hour. 

To be fair, the game has its bright spots with some great graphics for the time and some really good music. Not to mention, some really interesting puzzle solving using the two character system. If this game just had some form of co-op as well as item boxes, it would at least be tolerable but that can only help so much  (yes I know there are mods for those things but you can only polish a turd so much before you realize it's just a shiny turd). 

Overall, this game is REALLY BAD and you should not play it even if you are a casual fan and ESPECIALLY NOT if you are trying to get into the series. Anybody who says this game is "good" or "just okay" are just coping in my eyes because fundamentally, this game is extremely flawed with little to no factors that anyone will enjoy. ♥♥♥♥ this game and get it out of my sight

I am doing a playthrough of all the resident evil games and this game is definitely a low point in the series. I am not saying this because I don't like tank controls,  I like them and I loved them in RE 1 remake. Resident Evil 0 is gameplay wise one of the worse. Annoying puzzles, terrible inventory system, insanely strong enemies, poorly explained story, and to top it off this is one of the games in the series where you can get soft-locked if you don't save properly and use up your resources due to the insanely strong enemies. 

The puzzles are poorly designed because they're poorly explained in the game. There is a puzzle in the basement level where there is a circle of animal statues with unlit torches beneath them where the player is tasked to light each one from bottom to top of the food chain. The issue is that the food chain is not what you think it is and the player wouldn't have anything to help them figure it out. Not even a file that gives you a hint. In other puzzles, there are puzzle pieces that literally blend in the map and the player wouldn't know what to do with unless they are told or reading the text of every little interactable thing. 

The inventory is infamous for being the worst in the franchise. The game makes a bold move to remove the item box as a way to shake things up in the franchise. It's a risk and it is something that could have been done well. Unfortunately, it's poorly executed. There is two playable characters in this game that have their own separate inventory. 16 inventory slots in total. There is no inventory upgrades that allow the characters to get any more. Any item can be dropped into almost any room but this can become a real hassle when the game will decide to progress to a new area and you have to take each dropped item to the location one by one. You can't just drop a bunch of items in one room and call it a day because there will eventually be a limit to the amount you can drop. This all creates for a miserable inventory system. 

The enemies can get super strong early into the game. The common zombie isn't the issue. It's the other monsters the game presents to you, such as a cricket which has a very quick wind up attack that can insta-kill. The game will also hit you with a multitude of these in one location and sometimes its for a room with little to none importance. Just a waste bullets.  This brings up another point, the enemies are tanky and can waste so many bullets which will lead to disaster later in the road. 

The story is some of the most forgettable in the series. The game advertises itself to explore the origins of Umbrella and the creation of the wretched T-Virus. This is true but all the story with Umbrella is scattered away in files that aren't fun to read and eventually just feel like it is saying nothing. The story given in the cutscene stuff is very little and honestly felt like it could've also just been a small file that says nothing. The protagonist are such nothing characters. Billy is a death row inmate that escaped after his transfer vehicle got attacked by zombies. The reason he is in death row is because he was commanded to kill around 20 people in the Cold War. This is all pretty interesting stuff, right? Well it gets rarely explored in the game and barely connects to the story at all. Rebecca is a members of the elite cop squad, STARS. This will give the player the impression that she can handle herself pretty well. This is all flipped on their heads when the player throughout the game has to save Rebecca a multitude of times in the game with them screaming "BILLY HELP". They get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ turning cranks and need alpha dark edgelord Billy to crank that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ knob. Her character is also not explored at all and the dynamics between her and Billy is just buddy buddy with little discourse at all. The final piece of this train-wreck of the story is the boring villain. I honestly think Zeno from RE9 is a more interesting villain than James Marcus. This villain just watches the protagonists through cameras while spouting his monologues about taking revenge on the Umbrella Corporation but this is barely explained on how he plans to do this or actions he has taken against the corporation. His origin is he was some edgy recluse that was invited to be work with Spencer. Their teamwork made the T-Virus but both wanted to keep the virus to themselves so Spencer acted first and killed James Marcus. James rises from the dead, all thanks to his main project he has been working on which are just some weird leeches that are probably explained in some file. The villain is very forgettable because he does nothing, only interacts with the protagonists in the end. 

All in all, this game makes for a horrendous experience that can be skipped because it gives nothing to the entire resident evil story as a whole.
