[b]Resident Evil 0 is going to be one of those love-it-of-hate-it titles for survival horror fans. How far you get really is a coin-flip. Either the mechanics and atmosphere will click, and you'll grit-your-teeth through the most egregious parts. Or each encounter will whittle-away your patience until you call it quits.[/b]

In many ways, RE0 is like they took all the parts of RE1R which were later simplified -- and made those parts more complex. And for some, that is going to work, and others, not so much. The story is particularly bad when compared to most games, but not far from the cringiness that the Resident Evil series is known for. Inventory management is also a challenge -- requiring you to prepare for each outing. With two parties to manage, this only compounds in complexity. 

My introduction to Resident Evil was the GameCube remake. So for me, RE0 layered on that RE1-style thick. It oozed the art direction, sound design, and gameplay that I so adored. And for that reason, the parts which frustrated most players were tolerable.

It isn't all praise, though. The enemies are the weakest no matter how you look at it. It's too easy to be stun-locked into death (particularly, with the Eliminators.) And throwing molotovs to kills the Leeches is not easy with tank-controls. Playing two characters at once can also be clunky for a genre which requires manoeuvrability and avoiding fights where possible. Similarly, the game can be particularly punishing if you don't team-up.

If you loved RE1, you'll likely make it through. If your introduction were the latter titles, particularly RE4 onwards, RE0 is going to feel like an unfair clunky mess. But then again, that's what Steam refunds are for.

The partner system remains fresh today and retains that classic Resident Evil feel (dark, disturbing, slightly insane).

Resident Evil Zero also has its quirks that make it a whole lot of fun to play. Vamos por partes...
Gráficos:
Visualmente es un juego que ha envejecido muy bien. Para la estética que busca y lo que propone, mantiene bastante encanto incluso hoy en día.

Jugabilidad:
Los controles son lo que son: controles tipo tanque con cámaras fijas en distintas zonas. Es algo muy propio de los inicios de la saga, así que hay que aceptarlo desde el principio. Aun así, puede resultar difícil de digerir si vienes de jugar entregas más modernas.

Aquí viene mi mayor problema con este título: la gestión de inventario.
Sinceramente, me parece una decisión terrible haber eliminado las clásicas cajas de objetos que ya eran un sello de identidad en entregas anteriores.
El juego asume que, como puedes controlar a dos personajes (con 6 espacios cada uno), eso compensa… pero en la práctica no es así.

Terminas teniendo que cargar con:
- Munición
- Varias armas
- Objetos de curación
- Objetos clave para avanzar
- El infernal gancho

Todo esto provoca una cantidad absurda de backtracking. Si además cometes el “error” de jugar en dificultad Difícil, es bastante probable que acabes abandonando el juego en las primeras horas por pura frustración.

Recomendación:
Si quieres jugarlo, mi consejo es hacerlo en la dificultad más baja y centrarte en disfrutar de la atmósfera, los puzzles y las cinemáticas entre Rebecca y Billy, que son dos personajes con bastante química.

En dificultades superiores el juego puede volverse bastante infumable, así que cada uno que proceda bajo su propio riesgo.

Conclusión:
Un título recomendable principalmente para fans muy acérrimos de la saga que quieran vivir una experiencia clásica.
Eso sí, no esperes un antecesor de RE4 ni algo al nivel del remake de RE1, porque no lo es.

Resident Evil 0 is a game that suffers the fate most experimental entries in long-running franchise's do: An extremely unearned negative reputation.

Short review: Ignore everything you've ever read online about this game and go into it with an open mind. The story is one of the most solid of the classic games, the characters have a well written relationship, and the graphics are breathtaking to this day. If you engage with it properly you will have fun.

LONGGGGG review: Resident Evil 0 is one of my favorite games ever made, with an unearned internet reputation that I think stems from a lot of people's refusal to adapt when game's try and break the patterns they're used to. What the game does well it does near perfectly. What it doesn't it still does pretty well. 

Gameplay- This is what the game's most talked about for so it's what I'll cover first. Resident Evil 0 does away with the series' traditional item boxes, in favor of being able to drop items wherever you'd please as you explore. This is an interesting change on a number of levels. Yes, it's hard to adapt to at first, but when properly engaged with it makes the game feel extremely smooth. The ability to swap out your inventory on the go is freeing, and means you can adapt to whatever situation you're in with little friction, especially considering the game gives you two characters' worth of inventory. Which leads to the next thing Resident Evil 0 does uniquely. Most of the 'Classic' RE games contain both a male and female lead, but the way they handle it is different on a case by case basis. Resident Evil 1 contains two very similar campaigns for Chris and Jill, Re2 contains two tightly interconnected campaigns for Leon and Claire that change depending on the order they're played in, Re3 is near entirely Jill's game outside of a section as Carlos, and Code Veronica starts off as Claire's game and ends as Chris' (in a way that can feel kind of insulting to Claire's character). Resident Evil 0 sets itself apart by giving you equal control of both leads at the same time. Rebecca and Billy work as a team, and you're free to utilize them however you wish, and swap between them freely. Rebecca is a slightly frailer character with better medic capabilities, and Billy is a more combat oriented character who's better on the front line, but you'll need to grow proficient at both of them to do well in 0. The way Zero handles the two character system is borderline genius, the game does force you to progress as one character alone at some points, but for the majority of exploration you're free to do as you please. Do you want to split them up and cover two areas individually to cover ground quicker? Or do you want to stick as a unit, moving slower but sharing more inventory space and being able to cover each other better for safer clears. Who carries what high powered weaponry? Is Billy injured? Rebecca can backtrack for a first aid spray while he sits safe where he is, meaning he's not at risk of dying. The character swap system works incredibly in Zero, if you're willing to take the time to learn to use it to the fullest you can pull off things you could only dream of in other RE's. Like the item mechanic, there is a learning curve, but once you master it you can play in a way that none of the other games can quite scratch the itch of, as much as I love them. For the things it does more similarly to other titles, the area design's very well done, the train gets a lot of rightful praise for it's uniqueness and gameplay loop, the training facility gets compared to the Spencer Mansion often, but in practice it plays out very differently and can feel much more ominous visually. The enemy design's an interesting change of pace, the main unique ones are many mutated animals, umbrella's animal testing subjects let loose, which feels fitting for a prequel, and they often end up feeling fun to fight and well executed. Eliminators however are possibly one of the series most evil enemy designs. Resident Evil Zero is not trying to be an easy game, in fact out of the classic games it's easily considered the hardest. The game is extremely stingy on healing items, it has some extremely tough enemy designs, and spawns them frequently in very mean places. This game is not trying to be breezed through, it is a story of two people's uphill battle for survival against impossible odds, and it is determined to make you feel that.

Visual identity: This is still one of the most visually striking games I've ever played. The train in particular is still my favorite Resident Evil area to date in terms of both gameplay and how beautiful it is to explore. The training facility, while it may at first appear similar to the spencer mansion, feels much more dark in color pallet and execution. While the spencer mansion of Resident Evil (2002) opts for a gothic horror, haunted house identity of eerie beauty, the Umbrella Training Facility goes full in on the creepy clinical torture building aesthetic. The walls are covered in chipped paint that's peeling down, there's signs of the place degrading everywhere. Candlelight feels like the main thing keeping the building lit, and where it isn't the fluorescent lights feel off-putting and uncomfortable.  The Training Facility's visual design is incredibly good at creating tension, there are rooms that make me uncomfortable no matter how many times I've played and while the Spencer Mansion can feel almost comfy at times, the Training Facility never fails at making me feel unwelcome. The Water Treatment plant is also a well designed area, it's a solid place with some very beautiful and striking uses of water (duh) and some GORGEOUS fixed camera shots.

Plot - Prequels can be a very hard thing to pull off. All too often they can feel messy, like they weirdly fit into pre-established canon and in some fans' eyes they ruin what was there before. Resident Evil Zero manages to avoid almost all of these pitfalls. Resident Evil Zero is about a lot of things, but it's beauty is what it says about optimism during tragedy. 
Rebecca Chambers is an 18 year old college graduate, and rookie member of S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team. She's a relatively recent addition, and Resident Evil Zero is about her first ill-fated mission with the team, and what happened in the 24 hours before Alpha Team arrived at the Spencer Mansion in Resident Evil. We see Rebecca start as a (rightfully) scared girl who has to team up with a wanted fugitive to survive, but over the course of the game grow into a strong, resilient person who can overcome every obstacle in her path. Rebecca and Billy's relationship is the crux of the narrative and while they start as mutually wary partners, over the course of the night they grow into one of the tightest pairs in the series, and grow as people alongside each other, which highlights the game's real strength. Rebecca, despite the horror she finds herself in, stays upbeat and positive against impossible odds, she learns to trust Billy and begins placing his best interests at heart, even ahead of her own, because she learns the kind of person he is through his actions. No matter how dark things get, she aims to do her best and stay positive. Horrible things happen to her and around her, but through it all, in Zero and 1, Rebecca is a light in the dark. Rebecca Chambers is one of my favorite fictional characters ever, and there was a time period this game gave me a great deal of hope at my absolute lowest. In Resident Evil 1, Rebecca's theme is called "The One Who Survives", and Zero shows you exactly why she is. Please, do yourself a favor and give this game a chance, it's one of the few I'd consider near perfect.

This is a rough one in my opinion. On one hand, you have an incredibly fun story, two engaging protagonists and a unique multi character system. On the other hand, you have outdated mechanics, frogs that can kill you in a single attack, hunters that can stun lock you and the total lack of an item box. The enemies in this game are also extremely tanky, often taking multiple shotgun shots to even take down. 

With that being said, I do still believe that this game has plenty of charm. It has amazing level design that feels natural to explore. The puzzles, which have never been hard in resi, are actually challenging in this game. The mechanic where you switch between the two playable characters at will gives you plenty of cool ways to explore the environment and solve puzzles. 

I do believe that under the rough exterior, there is a pretty great game hidden. Unfortunately to truly enjoy it, one must either get over the frustration or download a few QOL mods to help bring this game up to the modern standard.

The few positives I have to give this game is that the areas themselves and puzzles are serviceable. They fit into the classic RE formula and in that sense the game is good. Same with the music.

The glaring problem comes with the story, enemies and the resource management.

First of all the story is really a nothing burger. You get to know that there's a progenitor T-virus (this has always stood for "testosterone virus" and you can't convince me otherwise!) but there's really not much else added to the overarching story than that. Some guy made it, got killed, got resurrectade by it, and then you exterminate it boohoo. If anything it causes issues as Rebecca should know a great deal about wth is going on in RE1 from these encounters but she doesn't. The progenitor T-virus and Billy are also never brought up again IIRC (granted I haven't played Code Veronica or Revelations)  so whatever happened here really doesn't matter, not like the narrative was all that engaging to begin with. The information about the progenitor T-virus is incredibly sparse and so is the appearance of the antagonist. I know more that he's a great singer than who he is and what he did, at least from this game alone.

I will keep it short with the enemies, some are way too hard to hit, some are way too tanky and there's too many of them, at least in tight spaces.

The prior point with the tight spaces is relevant for the resource management. So in this game, as opposed to all the RE games I know of, there are no item boxes... And you only have 6 item slots... AND some things take up two slots. What a TERRIFIC combo! They tried to mitigate this by giving you two characters with 6 slots each but there are several times in the game where you HAVE to split them up which causes issues. You can leave items on the ground and pick them up later but that requires backtracking (more than in the other games) which is annoying. So realistically you only have 2 or 3 slots open at any given time as you generally have a two handed gun equipped, and you should have extra ammo on you as some enemies are sponges, and some healing just in case... The rest are for key items which there are a lot of. Sometimes you have to drop something despite having "a lot" of slots open.

Overall a frustrating and lackluster experience where I should have saved my time by looking up a playthrough but oh well, here we are.

Resident Evil Zero has all the vibes, music and worldbuilding of a good RE game. However there are too many things that pull it down to the point where i cant recommend playing it.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The game works with stationary 3th person camera's, and with this limitation its done decently well. The angles mostly give the overview you need without hiding too much. However this also means your controls are translated from WASD (up,left,down,right) towards diagonal movements and this is done very clunky. The characters often dont walk in the right direction or stop responding to imput. And when you transition, camera movement is often not maintained and because of camera angles the inputs change based on that angle. Where you might have a camera aiming where you want to go in one screen upwards, then it might swap the another direction once you hit a camera change location where you walk downwards. Meaning the direction you walk towards all of a sudden does a 180, and your character controls get inverted. This would be fine if movement is maintained, so you can hold down the buttons you were pressing to keep going in the same direction.... however this is inconsistent where it sometimes does that and other times you walk back towards the previous camera.

Because of camera angles, it can be hard to select the hitbox of items and doors. They could have made the hitboxes of those bigger and more forgiving, but they are pixel perfect instead. This makes fighting for controls a thing you will have to deal with most of the game.

[h3]Combat[/h3]
You aim with shift and attack with spacebar, this would work fine normaly however...
The direction you walk towards is not the direction your character faces when pressing shift, this seems to be mostly random or camera based. So you will have to stop first, press shift, adjust your aim and then you can attack. This is very clunky and slows down the combat hugely.
This is an issue since a lot of enemies move freely and fast, require hitting weakspots, or have Area attacks that you cant dodge unless you quickly attack and then disengage.
This makes some normal monsters harder to fight that boss fights, and can be extremely frustrating to the point where you have to skip (run past) certain monsters and ignore them.

[h3]Worldbuilding and Resources[/h3]
The artstyle and worldbuilding looks amazing, better than modern Resident Evil games.
You transition through multiple maps with each their role in the story and gameplay, and each map has multiple levels and rooms.
There is an insane amount of backtracking, because of locked areas being in places you have been to already and key items being given on opposite sides of the map. This extends the gameplay without adding anything meaninful to the story or gameplay loop. Characters have 6 inventory slots that cant be expanded, and some items take up multiple slots or require multiple parts that need to be put together. There is a huge part of the game where you have to drop things on the ground and get them again at a later point.
Resources are given very infrequent, you can have one room with more healing items and ammo than you can carry one moment... then later on dont get a single heal but fight after fight that drains your resources. The balance in resources in the world is done in a terrible way that will probably lock a lot of players out of finishing the game.

[h3]UI, Menu's and transitions[/h3]
Every screen has loading pages and transitions, loading a game up requires you to go through the following screens; Start menu, load content, load game, warning for autosave message, select savefile, load game, promt to continue, black screen with text message that slowly gets filled in.
Between these screens, menu's and transitions there are multiple times you have to select to continue. Dying in the game feels horrible since you have to do this over and over again, because you get returned to the main menu.
The amount of menu's and transitions seems done deliberate in order to make the game longer, and it takes away from the game hugely.
I would have rather played a shorter game having a good experience, than spending 80% of my time in menu's and transitions.

[h3]Bugs and Crashes[/h3]
The game has crashed multiple times on me, and im currently hardlocked behind a bug that makes the game non responsive after reaching a key area required to continue. Making me unable to finish the game due to this bug.

[b]Recommendation;[/b]
Hard no. This game is only worth it for free if you are a hardcore Resident Evil fan and the current price is 20euros. The vibes of RE0 are amazing, but the gameplay is so bad and buggy that its just not worth spending money on. Play RE2 and RE3 instead.

I have completed this game multiple times since its initial release on the Nintendo GameCube.

There are some minor annoyances in this game.

1. Terrible AI partner logic. This can be mitigated by simply leaving the partner on idle or leaving them in a safe room while exploring with the other character.

2. The inventory mechanic by which items can be dropped in any room and the absence of inventory boxes resulting in greater than usual back tracking and inventory shuffling. This unfortunately cannot be mitigated until the player is familiar with the map allowing for planning. However, one tip I can offer is to touch but not pick up, or pick up and immediately drop every item, this marks the items on your map for future pickup when needed. This is especially helpful during the section on the Ecliptic Express. Any item you have marked on the map will automatically be transferred to the following section of the game and can be retrieved after clearing that first room the player is dropped in. Another tip is to never carry health items with you unless entering a boss encounter. It is far easier and can reduce back tracking to shuffle inventory if you just mark them on the map then return to use them when needed.

Despite the two point above I very much enjoy this game. It is the last classic Resident Evil game and the last game in the franchise, titled Resident Evil, to feel like a Resident Evil game and not just trading on a known IP for brand recognition.

Following this, Resident Evil 4 turned the franchise into an action series. Every game in the franchise after RE0 has been an action entrée with a horror garnish. RE2 Remake has come the closest to reclaiming the feel but even that was only able to better balance the action and horror it did not commit completely to horror as the classics did.

After finishing the game casually on Normal difficulty, I can confidently say that it is an excellent installment. There is often criticism directed at Resident Evil Zero Remastered, but in my opinion, some of it is exaggerated. Maybe they have skill issuses, but who am I to judge.

As a prequel to Resident Evil 1, the game does a great job of explaining WHY and HOW everything began. It gives meaningful background to the events that unfold in the first game and adds depth to the overall story.

The graphics are impressive as well. I was genuinely stunned by the visuals, especially in the train section during the first hour or so. It shares same engine with Resident Evil 1 Remastered

The gameplay mechanics are almost the same as in Resident Evil 1 Remastered, with one major difference — the removal of the traditional item box system. Instead of using shared storage boxes, you must carefully think about which items to carry and which ones to leave behind throughout the entire playthrough. Items are constantly crucial in many situations, and inventory management becomes a key part of the experience. On top of that, you still need Ink Ribbons to save your progress, which naturally increases tension.

Why was it designed this way? Obviously, to maintain suspense and survival pressure.

However, the game compensates for this change in a different way — you control two characters at once (with AI taking over when necessary) and must manage and split the inventory between them. This creates a unique strategic layer compared to other entries in the series.

Another minor drawback I noticed is the animations for various doors and ladders, which can feel unnecessarily long. Fortunately, a fix for this has been shared through the Steam community.

I really enjoy the fixed camera angles, although sometimes they can get in the way. Still, in my opinion, they are placed in generally appropriate locations, adding to the tension and atmosphere.

[h1][b]Resident Evil 0 (HD Remaster)[/b][/h1]
[b]Genre:[/b] Survival Horror
[b]Perspective:[/b] 3rd Person (Fixed Camera-Angles)
[b]My Rating:[/b]⭐⭐⭐⭐🔹

[h3][b]The Positives[/b][/h3]
[list][*]Resident Evil 0 kept exactly the same style as the first main-entry: Beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds, fixed camera-angles and gloomy lighting. The atmosphere is very well done as the musical tunes really underline the creepiness of the places we play through. When encountering certain enemies the dramatic music underlines the urgency, I love it!
[*]I really love having Rebecca and Billy be a team here constantly instead of having two different scenarios apart from each other. There are instances and puzzles where you need to use both characters together to solve them and others where you need to decide which one of them to send forward for the task - it will never be the “wrong” choice per say or you can’t get stuck but depending on who you sent it will be easy or difficult. Billy is more tanky and shoots faster with some guns but he can’t mix herbs or chemicals - also he throws the fire-bottles really slow. Rebecca is really weak but she can throw fire-bottles faster and she can mix herbs and chemicals.
[*]I know he is sadly forgotten and Capcom threw him into the void like so many other characters but I love Billy. His story is interesting and sad but I really enjoy how he interacts with Rebecca and how they slowly build up trust. And I love his voice, even if it’s old I enjoyed his VA! This isn’t really a spoiler anymore at this point as the game has been out for so long but I have to say that I will always believe he and Rebecca remained in contact somehow even after the game-events!
[*]This game also offers both the original tank- and new modern-controls. Both work really well but honest to gawd, use the tank-controls. This game was made with them in mind, it is really disorienting with the modern controls and you need to readjust your character constantly after the camera-angle changes. The tank controls are very smooth and imo way more precise and easy to use (and I’m not just saying this because I am used to them!)
[*]I personally loved the way this game makes progression more difficult compared to RE1. In RE0 once you finish the game you unlock a bonus-level called “Leech Hunter” which you can play to get rewards like the rocketlauncher or infinite ammo for every weapon for the main-game. However Leech-Hunter’s difficulty and these rewards are tied to the difficulty you played the main-game on so you can’t just cheese through the easy mode then use the rocketlauncher for hard mode. You need to play through the main-game on the difficulty you want to unlock the rewards for through Leech-Hunter.
[*]Albert Wesker is my favorite character throughout the entire RE-series so the Wesker-Mode is absolutely my favorite thing ever! The mode is automatically on normal difficulty but using Wesker’s stare and dash is insanely fun! It’s a funny “fudge around” mode! (And let’s not pretend we don’t get the fun meme Capcom did with this as we RE-fans all know about the Rebecca photo in his office and the ongoing joke throughout the RE-fandom about Wesker and Rebecca and whatever was going on with these two! It’s really hilarious Capcom decided to add a Wesker-Mode to this game with Rebecca and her wearing the Wesker-Costume gives us a “Team Wesker” title)
[/list]
[h3][b]The “Not So Goods”[/b][/h3]
[list][*]The item-system was an interesting idea but it was really awful at times. You do not have an item box in RE0, you have to manage the items entirely though the characters’ inventory alone. You can drop stuff in the rooms and pick it back up later but every room has only a limited amount of items you can drop there. If you do not know this game yet and play through without a guide you will get overwhelmed fast and it will not be rare that you have to run back ten rooms and entire areas to grab an item you didn’t think you needed but do now or you couldn’t take it because Billy and Rebecca weren’t having any space anymore.
[/list]
[h3][b]Would I recommend it?[/b][/h3]
[i]Yes![/i] ❤️
[i]Resident Evil 0 isn’t as great as Resident Evil 1 was, it’s a bit more tedious and slow to go through and the story isn’t adding much to what transpired to its sequel but I really enjoy the old charm of the old classics so I can only recommend it!

My recommendation on whether or not you should pick up RE0 depends on a few things: those being your patience, how much of a fan you are of the Resident Evil series, and if you want additional lore to the franchise. Ultimately, I enjoyed it enough as a fan of the series, but it still has its issues. If you're not a patient person or you don't like the fixed camera angles and tank controls (though an alternate scheme exists, I still played in the original tank layout), then I wouldn't recommend this RE game. Out of all of the classic RE games, RE0 is probably the most tedious and monotonous entry thanks to one of its biggest gameplay changes. 

Anyway, the story begins one day before the events of the original game and you're playing as Rebecca Chambers. She appears in Chris' story in the first game and supports him throughout, so this game gives you more of her story. A day before the events of the first game, the STARS Bravo team is sent in to investigate murders within the Arklay Mountains. After their helicopter crashes, Rebecca explores the Ecliptic Express where she meets Billy Coen and the nightmare begins once the train is put into motion. The game revolves around Rebecca and Billy cooperating to survive the nightmare and investigate what is going on, and this entry in particular explores the origin of the Umbrella Corporation and the T-Virus. 

Without any spoilers, I like the story enough. It's not perfect and there are moments in it where I feel that it is a little silly or something feels shoved in and unnatural in its presentation, but it does give you some history about Umbrella and the T-Virus: if you don't care about that kind of lore, then you probably won't care much for the story. If you're looking for some of the big names like Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, you won't find them here -- the Alpha team's adventure is the day after (and the next game). The tone and sense of horror also isn't as strong in this game because many of the enemy designs are uninspired or outright silly. I can't say that the leeches were particularly horrifying, and some of the other enemies you'll encounter are just giant versions of animals/insects. Still, RE0 has its moments of tension and a creepy atmosphere and I think they're worth experiencing. 

The gameplay and the design of this game are where my biggest criticisms are. As it plays like a classic Resident Evil game, I really have no gripes about its controls or how you actually play this game. Resident Evil 0 is very fun for its first half until we get to inventory management. Inventory management has been there since the first game, but this game's take on inventory management falls apart after the first playable area. The new idea Capcom ran with for RE0 was to remove item boxes and instead allow you to drop items from your inventory onto the floor. This was a pretty interesting idea and I like it... for the first playable area of the game.

See, this system works best for the Ecliptic Express because it's already a small map with only a few cars, so backtracking to get certain items or managing them is not too laborious or tedious. However, this isn't the only area you play in the game, and as you collect more items, you'll move on to new areas. With no item boxes, the only way you can move all those items is to manually pick them up and drop them to a new area. Every. Time. Moving items can take literal minutes just to make sure that you don't leave important or useful items behind in an area you have completed. It also doesn't help that you will be spending a lot of time in the inventory screen and menu which will further slow down the pace. 

If you don't care for the characters, the lore, are not a fan of the series, or otherwise impatient, I find it hard to recommend this game to other people. If you want to get into the series, start with the original game or its 2002 remake. It's a good starting point and if you want more of the same classic experience, play the original RE2, RE3, and Code Veronica. If you like a more modernized approach, the remakes of RE1-4 are all there as well. Ultimately, I write this review as a fan of the series, and I will recommend it to others who are fans of the series but may not have played RE0 or to people who like classic survival horror experiences. Those who are patient might actually really enjoy RE0 as well; I personally like it enough, but I think it is still the weakest of the classic games. That's not to say that RE0 is a bad game that isn't worth playing, but it is worth experiencing and making your own judgment on.

RE0 is not a bad game. I've seen a couple of negative reviews calling it horrible. It's pretty good actually. It has some issues, sure. Mostly with the gameplay. The controls and the camera could be a little frustrating at times, and some bosses are annoying and awkward to fight. Inventory management is also a little undercooked as you constantly need to drop items and go back and forth for the said items due to the fact that you only get 6 slots per character with no way to increase that number, and the lack of a container where the said items can be stored. Story is also a nothing burger as nothing important or major happens throughout, apart from world building and context. However, despite the poor and inconsistent voice acting, I really liked Rebecca and Billy as protagonists, and I actually really enjoyed the way you play as both of them simultaneously to get through puzzles, which on their own were very well designed and interesting to solve. The atmosphere that RE0 brings to the table is phenomenal as well. At the end of the day, RE0 isn't a must play as you won't miss much if you skip it, but there is still plenty of fun to be had here. Definitely exited for the speculated Remake!

I'm writing this as I've been going through some of the Resident Evil titles and completing all the achievements for them. As of writing this, I have completed 0, 1, 2 Remake, and 3 Remake. Bias warning, this is my favorite franchise of all time.

I would say I recommend this game only to those that are very interested in the franchise already and love its faults and hiccups. I would say I am one such person. I grew up with resident evil and was always told this was the black sheep of the franchise more so than 6 and the like. I would say that's accurate but I would like to add that its not AS bad as I think most online searches of the game have you believe. This is not me saying this is an amazing game, but if you're a fan of the franchise I think you can find some things to enjoy here. 

I want to start with the first bad choice, as everyone knows, the item system. I think this design choice was interesting and although it gives you the option to freely drop things unlike other resident evil titles it was not a good choice as most people know. The issue arises when you get to understand that the item box was a learning curve in the games and you had to use it well. You couldn't and shouldn't bring everything with you since you would end up in rooms with key items with a full inventory and would have to back track to an item box, potentially putting you in danger with whatever threat may be lurking around and wasting ammo or more importantly health. Resident Evil 0 puts the learning curve in a direction which is worse, a knowledge check. If you come into this game blind, hard mode? You're gonna hate it because you dont know the optimal strats and what items to bring to the next section of the game, youre gonna find yourself backtracking to areas you thought were done and werent even important. Im looking at you hook shot. Enemies respawn and harder enemies appear when backtracking to certain areas. A lot of the enemies as well should be avoided as much as possible unless absolutely necessary to fight. The positions of Rebecca and Billy are extremely important and you can absolutely skip a lot of dangers in rooms by knowing that as long as one isnt in combat, even if across the room, the other will spawn with you if you travel with a door. There is such a HUGE learning curve to this game that isnt explicitly taught, more so than any other resident evil title before it.

That being said, once you overcome those knowledge checks, I think this game is pretty alright! I think Billy and Rebecca are cool protagonists and compliment each other pretty well and this game rewards you for having good knowledge of how to pilot the characters. The addition of having a partner to help you out is awesome in combat and reminds me a bit of RE: Outbreak. I think the huge issue with the game is just how punishing it is for not knowing all the things that you know once you complete the game twice. Scorpion can be easily knifed to death by anyone as all you have to do is stand still and knife down near the car door. Bat boss being a huge annoyance before knowing that you can stunlock it with 5 flame rounds. The hookshot being brought by you to 3 key points of the game makes navigating the maps much less of an issue. Billy should be classified as a BOW with how much damage he can tank as well.

Like I said at the beginning, I think this is a game that needs quite a bit patience before seeing where it shines that I feel only those who are already fans of the franchise will give it. Although it doesn't shine the brightest in the franchise, I don't think this game is abysmal garbage that should never be touched. I would give this game a 5/10. Lots of room for improvement but enjoyable once I got used to the mechanics.

No item boxes and constant backtracking can turn simple puzzles into frustrating chores. The story is also a bit over-the-top even by Resident Evil standards. That said, if you enjoy old-school survival horror and can tolerate some outdated design choices, Resident Evil 0 is absolutely worth playing—especially as a prequel to the original game.

RE0 builds on RE1 with some solid QoL improvements, but also doubles the complexity with two fully operable characters—even at the same time. That adds another learning curve to overcome—especially if you’re new to RE1—but it’s one meant to be mastered, not avoided, imo.

The complexity pays off with more involved puzzles and a lot of control over each character on the fly. Backtracking and traveling can get tedious though—almost the whole traversable map is interconnected, and you really need to plan your routes before saves, or you’ll end up doing extra work (no item boxes like RE1). But that’s the loop, and it works once you get it.

I figure it’s tougher to jump into than newer REs, but if you’re willing to engage with the systems, it’s a genuinely unique entry. Not perfect, not for everyone—but definitely worth trying.

I peer into the cauldron and see another Capcom Concoction gone wrong. Items all over the place, an anime villain, a journal entry about how backtracking isn’t padding but immersion, and simultaneous playable characters in a single-player game. I turn the heat up and dive in.

Zero is admirable for its ambition towards creating a more believable game space, but more often than not it shoots itself in the foot. No item boxes is haphazardly implemented; belongings spread everywhere both brings unneeded attention to the previous magic of the storage system, and kills momentum as the menu UI gets burned into your monitor. It’s extremely tedious, and drags the entire game down. 
Puzzles are barely reliant on intelligence, the dual character system should open up a whole realm of possibilities but the end result is disappointingly dull.

Other than that, game is sick. The first third especially: from the zombie-ridden locomotive to the ethically haunted training facility, every step of the way drips with atmosphere and dread. The balancing of items themselves — despite over-management — is the most taut it’s been out of any of the games. I spent the entire playthrough just barely scraping by. Perfect.

Rebecca (pre-RE1-nerf) and Billy (post-African-adventure) are fun protagonists, their differences entertaining enough in cutscenes. There’s actually a decent arc for these two to be found here, and despite the convoluted plot they shined through much more than I expected. There’s a few other characters and lore tidbits, mostly serving as connective tissue to the rest of the series, but it’s rather superfluous. I’m just glad this backstory had a backstory — the world still feels like it exists outside of what’s on-screen. It’s definitely convoluted, but that’s just the natural state of any long-running Japanese series. Tell me I’m wrong.

This is an experiment begging for a remake. I only say this because that’s kind of their thing in the last 10 years. Every flaw here can be easily done away with; homogenise the broth, just a little, and let the more interesting parts rise to the surface. It won’t stop you adding other spices, just keep the core ingredients, give it a swirl; hell, even make it for two people. That’d be a meal I could stomach.

Resident Evil 0 is a fascinating but frustrating entry in the franchise, especially when played today. The static camera angles constantly fight the player, turning combat into blind guesswork and making basic actions like picking up items far more cumbersome than they should be. The partner system helps slightly — mostly as an early warning system for off-screen enemies — but it can’t fully compensate for how dated the core design feels in 2026.

The game’s biggest misstep is its inventory management. Removing item boxes in favor of dropping items sounds bold, but in practice it creates constant anxiety, especially when certain enemies like the Leech Men practically require you to always carry molotov cocktails. Combined with slow door-loading animations, limited saves via ink ribbons, and inconsistent item usage, the moment-to-moment experience often feels more punishing than tense.

That said, despite its flaws, Resident Evil 0 still succeeds as a survival horror experience at its core. The atmosphere is thick, the sound design is excellent, and there are moments where the tension genuinely shines through. While the story adds little to the overall Resident Evil mythology and the dialogue is rough, I’m ultimately glad I played it — if only to better appreciate how far the series would evolve starting with the original game.

This is not the worst game I have ever played. However, it is, by a very large margin, the most annoying and irritating game I have ever played.

I do not believe this game was created by actual human beings. Whatever entities formulated this piece of media into existence did not playtest it, or have anyone test it to see if the game was actually an enjoyable experience. Otherwise it would have never seen the light of day, and the world would have been a better place. 

Having two characters was novel, I'll give it that. However, it quickly became very annoying to have to constantly switch back and forth between characters. Rebecca having far less health was a pain. I genuinely believe that this game would have been easier if it were not for a second character. The first stage of the final boss would have been far easier if I only had to worry about my own character, but alass, I had to worry about the other character, who cannot dodge attacks but only follow the character I'm using around, making them die very quickly. There were some puzzles that were cool to have two characters, but the general gameplay experience was not enjoyable. 

The enemy design is some of the most abominable I have ever seen in any videogame. Who designed the tentacle monsters? Who hurt you? Why are they almost exclusively placed in tight hallways, where it is nearly impossible to dodge? Why do they attack so quickly? Why are they nearly impossible to kill without taking damage? Why do they later spawn leaches that cost a bunch of handgun ammo to disperse? These are all questions I asked myself, but I found no reasonable answer other than to irritate the player, of course.

More enemy design was baffling. Why do the monkeys exist? Why would you have them not only attack quickly, but stick up to 4 in one room, that all attack at the same time, stunlocking the player? Again, who hurt you? Why would you do this? It caused a great deal of suffering on my part.

Thankfully, the other enemies were not so bad. Zombies are easy, of course. Frogs were easy. Hunters not very plentiful, and grasshoppers can be ran around.

The boss design, on the other hand, is an abomination. The bosses in Resident Evil 1 are fantastic. Not only can you skip some of them with game knowledge, but once you "solve" them, they become much easier and you can finish them much more efficiently. At no point in the first game did I ever feel like a boss was unfair, poorly designed, or limited my ability to clear them more efficiently without the use of bonus weapons. That is not the case for Resident Evil Zero. The centipede boss is fine. However, the bat boss is horrible. Why? Why? To make the fight tolerable, I had to camp in a corner. The final boss felt like it was engineered to be as annoying as humanly possible. Why stick a proto-tyrant in a narrow room? 

Why are there so few health items in this game? It felt like I was walking on eggshells for over half the game because there were simply no health items compared to how much damage I felt like I was being forced to take. It gets much easier in the last section of the game, but in most of the game, there is just not enough health items. 

The plot is awful. Terrible. Just not good. Characters, on the other hand, Rebecca and Billy are great. Very likeable.

The maps themselves I actually liked. The facility I thought was really cool, the train as well, lab design was great, and the treatment plant was also really cool. However, the placement of safe zones was confusing at times.

God, I really wish this game had item boxes. This game would be so much simpler with a simple item box. There's so many design choices in this game that I feel like the intent was to irritate the player in as many ways as humanly possible. I genuinely have not had a gaming experience this irritating in a very long time. I struggle to understand the sheer malice, and evil intent that went into designing this game. If they ever remake it, massive changes need to be made.

I also do like the fact that both characters have unique mechanics (Billy being the stronger character and more proficient with weapons, while Rebecca is weaker but has the ability to combine herbs and chemicals for various puzzles). I'd recommend this game. And if you're on the fence from other reviewers talking about being stuck on sections, make sure to keep a back up save, this game is about survival after all, and sometimes we make mistakes. But we learn, adapt and overcome. And I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

A Symphony of Survival – A Review of Resident Evil 0

Overall Rating: 8.5/10

Resident Evil 0 serves as a deliberate and atmospheric prologue to the series, stripping away familiarity to expose survival horror at its most vulnerable. Set aboard the doomed Ecliptic Express and later expanding into other areas, the game leans heavily into classic Resident Evil tension—limited resources, oppressive environments, and the constant feeling that danger is always one misstep away. Rather than reinventing the formula, Resident Evil 0 refines it with restraint, offering a slower, more methodical descent into bio-organic horror.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 9/10
Atmosphere is one of Resident Evil 0’s strongest achievements. Pre-rendered backgrounds are rich with detail, using shadow, decay, and gothic architecture to create environments that feel both beautiful and hostile. The Ecliptic Express remains one of the series’ most memorable settings—an elegant space corrupted by violence and infection. Lighting is used masterfully to obscure threats and heighten unease, while camera angles reinforce vulnerability, often denying players full visibility of what lies ahead.

Story and Narrative: 8/10
The narrative explores the origins of the T-Virus outbreak through dual protagonists Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen. Storytelling is more direct than later entries but still grounded in classic Resident Evil ambiguity, delivered through documents, environmental clues, and brief character interactions. While the plot occasionally leans into familiar franchise excess, it effectively frames the tragedy and inevitability of the outbreak. The dual-character dynamic adds emotional texture, emphasizing trust, survival, and moral ambiguity without overwhelming the core horror.

Gameplay and Tension: 8.5/10
Resident Evil 0 introduces the partner system, allowing players to switch between Rebecca and Billy at will. This mechanic adds strategic depth, encouraging thoughtful positioning, resource sharing, and problem-solving. However, it also amplifies tension—mistakes feel costly, and poor planning can quickly spiral into danger. Combat remains intentionally clunky, reinforcing vulnerability, while enemies are resilient enough to make every encounter a calculated decision rather than an impulse reaction.

Sound Design and Music: 8.5/10
Sound design plays a crucial role in sustaining dread. The creak of train cars, distant growls, and sudden environmental noises keep players constantly on edge. Musical cues are used sparingly, allowing silence to dominate exploration and making moments of danger feel sharper when they arrive. The audio design complements the visual restraint, ensuring tension is sustained rather than overstated.

Immersion and Replayability: 8.5/10
The Steam remastered version of Resident Evil 0 enhances immersion through improved resolution, cleaner visuals, and smoother performance, allowing the game’s pre-rendered environments and lighting to shine more clearly than ever. The absence of a traditional item box, however, fundamentally reshapes the experience. Instead of relying on safe storage, players must physically manage their inventory, dropping items in the environment and remembering their locations. This design choice deepens immersion and reinforces realism, but it also increases friction—backtracking becomes more frequent, and poor inventory planning can disrupt pacing. For some, this adds meaningful tension; for others, it may feel unnecessarily punishing. Replayability remains solid, particularly for players who enjoy mastering routes and optimizing item placement.

Conclusion: 8.5/10
Resident Evil 0 stands as a bold and atmospheric prequel that embraces constraint as a core design philosophy. The Steam remaster elevates the experience visually and sonically, with an outstanding musical score that perfectly underscores moments of dread, tragedy, and discovery. The lack of an item box is both the game’s most distinctive mechanic and its most divisive—heightening tension and immersion while demanding patience and precision. While not without its frustrations, Resident Evil 0 remains a thoughtfully crafted survival horror experience that rewards careful planning and deliberate play.

Final Verdict:
A haunting and methodical entry in the Resident Evil series, Resident Evil 0 uses limitation as its greatest weapon. Through its unforgettable music, oppressive atmosphere, and uncompromising inventory system, it forces players to think ahead and live with their decisions—proving that true survival horror isn’t about power, but about endurance.

After coming from the REmake, this was such a massive and frustrating dissapointment, and funnily enough, for a such a small reasons that make such a huge impact. I'll go in a little more detail for this one, level by level. This might go all over the place, beware lmao

I will start with the positives, backdrops are amazing and detailed, playing and switching with 2 characters is actually well done, soundtrack is good and creepy. That's pretty much it. Lets start off area by area, because it's not really a long game anyways:

Train - Honestly the best part of the game, and such a strong start! As you make it through, you will meet up with Billy, your 2nd playable character. Both of you have 12 total inventory slots, which seems big, but it's actually not, because there are so many items in this game. Here you will get Hookshot (item required to climb few sections throughout the game), you will meet your new enemy Leech man, boss fight etc. It's really well made starting area, packed with bunch of narrow hallways and zombies. Which brings me to first issue: Leech man. That thing, like most enemies in this game, sucks, but this one is the worst. Bullet sponge, moves and hits way fast for tank controls and slow animations of your characters. I hate it and pass it every time I see it. Second issue: boss fights suuuuuuuuuuuuck! Mechanicaly and design wise (big scorpion, how creative). Overall, great first level with some minor issues!

Training Facility - Basically Spencer's mansion from Temu. Longest area in the game, filled with bunch of crap and annoyances. This is where the game starts to go downhill, only because of one big reason: lack of inventory box. What an asinine and idiotic decision to remove the inventory box. This time your characters can drop items anywhere, but you'll have so many items to carry that you will be backtracking a lot to get the other stuff and move to next areas. And yeah, you have limit how many items can you drop in each section. And yeah, big weapons like shotgun, grenade launcher, hunter rifle, hookshot etc take 2 inventory slots. Why?! So many bizzare decisions that makes the game only more annoying, it becomes inventory management game. Also, ALSO, whenever you enter your inventory, it takes like a half a second fade to black screen to get you in and out of it. It seems like a non issue, but trust me, when you are constantly switch through menus, it will drive you nuts. Maybe it's my ADHD, but REmake had like instant switch to inventory screen when you press it. And both games came out the same year??? While I'm at it, the characters movement feels "floaty", if you get what I'm saying. Control scheme is using the old school RE controls, which coming from REmake will take some time to get used to it (game of course doesn't allow you to change them to REmake controls). In this area we have another new boss and new types of enemies: boss being the huge centipede, which sucks and poses zero challenge, it just crawls around and you shoot it. New enemies are Hunters, which are challenging but ok to deal with, Plague Crawler which are basically big bugs, annoying but not much of a challenge. But by far, 2nd worst enemy in the game are the Eliminators (btw these names sound intimidating, but then you see them and they are like real life animals lol). Monkeys that are super fast, jump at you and hit you almost constantly. If you end up with 2 or more of them on you, you're pretty much stunlocked and done. THANKFULLY they appear in like 2 rooms in the entire game, with 1 room being mandatory to clear. This area has its moments, but yeah it gets worse from here.

Laboratory - Right from the start, this one has one of the worst bosses in RE history: Giant Bat (you can guess what it looks like). It's horrible, even though I cheesed it, it still sucks. He will ocassionaly grab you and fly you around and then drop you. When you deal some damage to it, "2nd" phase will start and bunch of small bats will attack you. It's so annoying because you can't autoaim the big one, so you character will constantly aim the small ones, while big one will harass you. After that crap, you go to laboratory and for most of the area, your characters will be split up, and you need to solve some puzzles and send items over to each other. In the end, you meet up at the tram, which takes you to next area. Area is nothing special, and it doesn't overstay its welcome like the mansion. 

Factory - Honestly, this would be my number 1 area if it wasn't for the one tiny reason. This might sound dumb to you, but if there weren't those 2 hunters that pop up after you get the keys, it would be perfect. In this area, you are split with Billy and you play as Rebecca only, and the backdrops are AMAZING! You are totally alone, you can feel that something is off, there are no enemies, no zombies, nada. It builds tension perfectly to the boss of this area, the Tyrant. His design is best in the game, but he's sadly not hard at all, you'll have magnum which, on easy, can take it out in 4 hits. He walks slowly and only has 1 charge attack. Like I said, if it weren't for those 2 random hunters that spawn, area would be perfect. Also minor thing, but it's kinda dissapointing that it ends super fast, you can finish it in literally 5 minutes if you know where to go. Also, cool little detail, when you reenter the last area where you leave dead Tyrant,   you will actually see that it's not dead.

Treatment Plant - I'm gonna go out of the limb and say this is the worst area. It starts off ok, but then you meet up with Billy and you are again playing as 2, you have like 1 major puzzle that involves moving boxes, which is slow and kills the pace. Bunch of zombies, leech man, you fight later on Tyrant again (which is this time harder, only because you are in more narrow room), but has no new mechanics or anything. You have a kinda new enemy (depends on RNG if it will spawn), Lurker. Big ass frog that has a 1 shot mechanic if you are not careful and aware of its behaviour. Which sucks if you're doing the no save run. Area looks so bland and boring. After all that, you are finally at the last boss. Now let me first say that these complaints about bosses are mostly because of playing on Hard difficulty. Which by the way, lets talk a little about difficulty and reward items system. You know in other games when you get an S rank, you get infinite weapons and you can use them on your next runs? Yeah, in this one you get S rank if you complete the game under 3.5 hours, AND you only get those weapons for THAT difficulty you completed it on. For example, to use weapons on Hard, I first need to complete it under 3.5 hours on hard and then I can use those weapons on that difficulty only. Which sucks, why would I want to do it again after I've already done it? I can't use them even on easy after. Idiotic. On to the last boss of the game, Queen Leech. Absolute cancer of a boss. Moves fast, has a grab mechanic that dashes forward to you (takes almost all hp with 1 grab), hits both of you with tentacles, bullet sponge, camera angles in that room are cancer where you won't even see it unless its literally next to you. If you didn't conserve decent amount of ammo for various weapons, you'll soft lock yourself. 2nd phase is even worse, it will constantly do aoe acid damage, hit you with tail, and it's unkillable here, you basically need to survive, while Rebecca opens up valves. Which bring me to the point of how AI is garbage. You'll see when you play it. After you finally defeat it, you get a nice cinematic and game ends with Rebecca coming to Spencer mansion, which is the beginning of the first game.

Let me end the review with the most dumbest, pointless, stupidest gimmick item, that if you don't know at all, can cost you nerves and make you rage quit probably. I can't write anymore, review is too long, but.... Hookshot.

Resident Evil Zero is mainly held back by its gameplay mechanics. The item system, with no proper item box and the need to drop items in rooms, is simply frustrating and artificially drags out the game. Instead of tension, you spend way too much time managing inventory.

These issues become even more obvious when you’ve played the other Resident Evil games, especially the Resident Evil 1 Remake. Everything in this game feels slow. Text can’t be skipped or sped up, saving takes forever, and even basic interactions require you to stand in exactly the right spot. It constantly breaks the flow and makes the game feel exhausting to play.

The opening train section is actually great and easily the strongest part of the game. Unfortunately, that’s pretty much where it peaks. After that, the whole experience feels more like a small side story with some very strange design decisions. A Tyrant suddenly appearing without any buildup isn’t exciting, it’s just random. The final fight feels odd as well, and the final boss comes across as forced, like they just needed something to end the game.

In the end, Resident Evil Zero has a strong start, but is weighed down by clunky mechanics and questionable choices that make it hard to fully enjoy.

Not only did RE0 age very poorly but also this remaster is full or very frustrating aspects that should've been fixed but instead they haven't and they will drive you crazy.

2. The controls are counterintuitive, I always forget which button does what. Left trigger (switch character) and right trigger (open inventory) or Y (switch character) and X (open inventory)? - I can't even tell which of these two is worse.
3. Most of your characters' deaths will be caused by either aiming in the wrong direction, or the "switch target" button not working properly, or you being unable to dodge the enemy due to the aforementioned camera issues.
4. There're only 6 slots in your inventory. The main issue though is that there's no item box which means there's gonna be a LOT of backtracking due the need to get some item that you left in some safe room 2 hours ago.
5. A million loading screens that cannot be skipped.
6. Each time when you load a save file, for ~5-7 seconds, you'll be looking at the black screen with some dumb-ass text like "there's still evil in this place...blah blah...".

[h1] Fantastic Mechanics, Idiot Plot [/h1]

Resident Evil 0 was very close to the forbidden fruit of my childhood: RE1 Remake—the game I drooled over in Club Nintendo magazine while my empty shelf screamed “no GameCube for you.” Twenty years later I finally got my hands on it thanks to a bundle with the RE1 Remake, which is very clearly the real prize here. After all that buildup? The final verdict is a long, tired, deeply conflicted “meh.”

The gameplay is the one thing holding this circus together. Ditching item boxes and forcing you to drop equipment on the floor like a survival-hoarder with commitment issues is actually a bold move. You have to remember where your junk is, backtrack constantly, and make real decisions about what you carry. It fits the old-school RE design like a glove and genuinely creates tension. I even abandoned weapons just to solve puzzles. That’s not bad design—that’s commitment.

The dual-character system is another solid idea. Splitting Billy and Rebecca to solve puzzles in parallel is clever, occasionally brain-scratching, and honestly something the RE1 Remake should’ve stolen. Neither character feels useless, and swapping between them stays engaging throughout.

Combat? Enemies are bullet sponges with attitude, some new creature designs are cool, but several bosses fall flat. The giant bat is annoying, the Proto Tyrant is embarrassing, and neither manages to be truly scary—just loud and in the way.

Now the narrative? Disaster. It desperately tries to glue together RE1 and RE2 by waving Wesker and Birkin at you like jingling keys. The villain is a walking anime stereotype, his reveal lands with a thud, and the payoff collapses instantly. Rebecca solos a Proto Tyrant here, yet shows up useless in RE1. What happened—plot-induced amnesia?

You reach the edge of the Umbrella lab from RE2, stare straight into the conspiracy, and just walk away. Enrico then marches off clueless to his doom. Spectacular.

They even resurrect the Proto Tyrant just to kill him again. He still sucks.

RE0 can absolutely be fun if you love tank controls, tight inventory management, smart puzzles, and backtracking. Mechanically, it deserves respect. Narratively, it deserves detention. It’s uneven, forgettable, and I’ll only replay it to 100% it because I hate myself a little.

Good thing it comes bundled with RE1. If that’s how you get it, fine—try it. Do not buy this alone. Its value is dangerously close to its title.

Why would you ever think removing the item box would be a good idea? Why?! Yes you now have two characters to hold items but they can't hold everything which means leaving items on the ground. Except rooms have a maximum amount they can hold too so now you have items strewn across multiple rooms and trying to pick them back up again is its own hell. And when you need to move to the next area, well now you gotta start transporting everything slowly. And when the 2 characters have to split up that just exacerbates the issue.

I'm not dealing with infinitely spawning bats while a giant bat throws me around a room with limited resources. The horrible camera angles are not on your side either.

The good stuff is that the game looks great. The starting sequence on the train is genuinely fun and I didn't start having a bad time until I had moved onto the mansion. Rebecca is a cool protagonist, not constantly falling on her ass like Resident Evil 1 Jill. Controlling 2 characters is a novel experience even if it's not always fun (oftentimes better to just leave one at the save point and there aren't enough puzzle uses to warrant a second). The game expands on the lore which is interesting if you're following the series (though you could just read/watch a summary).

[h1]Review[/h1] 
I’ve been told it’s the worst mainline resident evil. After playing it, I see why. Is it still a bad game? Far from it.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
The gameplay is almost the same as the first resident evil remake. The main difference is that you almost always have a character following you. You either play as Rebecca or an escaped convict named Billy. Throughout the game, you never have any reason aside when you rarely split up to play any other than billy. He has more HP, shoots faster and has better knife attacks. Rebecca can get a lift and crawl or climb into places with his help. Also, she can mix herbs. Which you do and promptly switch to Billy again.
Sadly, you cannot play this coop as it would have made a good coop experience. This way you have an AI partner constantly following you. You can let them wait, but often have to switch or get the character back again for puzzles or carry space. You can control the movement of the other character and decide if they attack or not and weirdly control their movement with the right stick which is often necessary for boss fights.

The usually gameplay is the same, collect items, find keys, kill or run from zombies, solve “puzzles”. The map also shows where items you couldn’t take or dropped are. Yes, now you can drop items. This is not only useful but necessary as the item box is gone. Which cause you to drop all your stuff in the main area, just to backtrack to grab a weapon or item you need. This increases the backtracking significantly. It’s to an excessive amount.

The other negative aspect is a single boss fight which is so awful that I cannot believe it made it into this game. It’s like the RE 3 original shower boss fight. It’s a flying giant bat that is hard to it due to the camera, plus flying small enemies. If you didn’t need much healing and ammo, you will use up a lot. The only way to beat it is to shoot and leave the area before the small bats surround you. Its so terrible I wanted to rage quit the game multiple times.
If you can overlook those two very terrible design choices, I enjoyed my playthrough. Its still classic horror survival gameplay.

[u]Story[/u]
Story before RE0. Less mysterious than 1, but not as weird as code veronica. It’s okay. Not as scary as RE1 but it has its moments.

[u]Sound[/u]
RE 0 is just like every RE game except 6 fantastic in the OST department. Voice acting is cheesy, but not like the OG. Shotgun is punchy and zombies make creepy sounds.

[u]Graphics[/u]
It uses the same style like the first remake, having mostly grey and dark as an aesthethic. Although it mixes things up a bit, starting in a moving train which is such a unique concept and location for a horror game.  There are also more enemy types and various cool fire effects.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
I understand why people call it the worst resident evil. For me it has a lot of good moments and unique ideas. It changes the RE1 formula up enough to be much different than 2 and 3 ever could be but without straying away from the OG RE1 gameplay. There are the issues with the one awful boss design and removal of the box that increase backtracking. Otherwise, all good points including a few new interesting ones make a good classic horror survival game.

Resident Evil 0 Inventory – an inventory management pain in an otherwise great game that gives the backstory on RE 1, 2, and 3.

As always, I have to state up front that I’m not a survival horror fan and didn’t really play the original games because of the wonky graphics and controls. But I did own them on PlayStation due to my brother liking them, so I always felt that I should play them since people liked them so much.

When the remakes came out on Steam, I finally decided to play them through. They fixed all of the issues I had with the originals (primarily, the graphics and controls). I even managed to get all of the achievements because they were fun to replay with the weapon upgrades after completing the game. This one has its rough edges with camera angles and item selection/pickup/dropping, but if you can overlook those annoyances it’s a fine game.


Positive
-This game has had a great graphical upgrade in this HD version. I loved the cut scenes and the beautiful backgrounds. If only I wasn’t always in a state of hurry to get through the game quickly for the speed run bonuses (I should’ve taken it easy for the first run, as I just missed the 5h30m cutoff for the SMG, anyway) or just anxiety because it’s survival horror, I would’ve loved them even more. It’s so well done, and Capcom deserves a medal for keeping their past alive while improving only the things that need to be improved from modern technology (Square, for example, can’t seem to do with Final Fantasy what Final Fantasy Renaissance did with one person: keep the game intact while fixing some bugs and giving you new options).

-It keeps all of the RE1, 2, and 3 elements alive. I know that everyone points to 4 as a transformative title, but other than some of the issues with camera angles and picking up items and such, I think 0 works best being similar to what it’s a prequel to.

-As usual for Capcom, they give you the cathartic experience of going through hell so that you can get infinite ammo and better weapons so that you can go through the game again and destroy everything that angered you throughout the game in 1-3 shots. I don’t usually replay video games, but I replay RE games so I can kill everything quickly out of spite for the enemies that wronged me! Love this option.

-I loved that achievements were relatively reasonable. For example, S rank did not have a save limit, which I loved. I don’t want to have to pace my speed run into 30+ minute increments. If I want to save a second time after a difficult part, I can. Love it. The no-save run was the worst (because what if your game has an issue?), but since you can do it with the one-hit-kill weapons and learn where the ~5 spots that the frog can jump out and one-hit kill you, I didn’t mind as much. I was worried about playing for 2h45m only to die from the frog, but if you just go where it jumps out ready to turn back and go through/up the door/ladder you came from, you can avoid it with minimal risk of getting the one-hit kill. But practice it first so you don’t die without a save and rage quit.


Negatives
-While the inventory management is especially painful in this game, the biggest issue is the clicking precision. Good luck picking up the right item if you drop two or three in a pile, and good luck trying to pick up an item instead of selecting background that triggers descriptor text or a door that makes you enter another room. This was the most annoying part of the experience. I think the inventory management is one of those “I don’t like it, but I get it” kinds of things (it’s more realistic compared to the magical item box that RE typically has), but the inability to grab what you intend to and having to try multiple times to get it right—especially when trying to speed run the game—is miserable.

-Add onto the above that controls are inconsistent. For example, for doors that use keys, you can select the door, and it’ll use the key—going into the inventory and using the key won’t work. But with a key card, you have to go into your inventory and use it and not just click on the door or scanner to use it. This happens across the game: sometimes, you have to click on objects to make the item work, and sometimes you have to use it in the inventory. Sometimes, you have to be facing the exact right place to get it to work, so you go into the inventory, use it, it fails, and you have to exit and try again. Given these two issues, I have no idea how anyone ever completes a speedrun—not because they die from an enemy but because they mess up picking up an item that costs them valuable seconds. Glad I don’t speedrun because I would go crazy with a game with these issues (the inconsistency will mess with your muscle memory). Also, sometimes when the camera changes, your controller keeps moving you in the previous direction until you change it; other times, your direction changes when you change camera angles. That’s annoying because you’ll be running from an enemy and then turn right back into them, getting them killed. So, you have to fight the enemy and the camera angle changes at the same time. Example: In the laboratory, trying to walk onto that moving platform to climb down the ladder requires you basically to walk up where you know the camera change will occur, stop, and then continue on in the new direction—trying to do it fluidly unless you practice is near-impossible, making you run in circles whether you hold the direction down or try to change it quickly.

-Not a big fan of Billy, but they do make him into a good guy put in a bad situation so that he comes off as a bad guy. I liked Rebecca (her terrible health bar notwithstanding).

-I know that some people found this game’s puzzles to be more ambiguous than others. My advice is to play the game slowly and try to solve them, as me trying to run through the game quickly ruined that because I ended up just following instructions. So, play the game slowly and then try to get through quickly afterwards.


Overall, I liked this game. Capcom does a great job of improving the visuals of their old games—between the cut scenes and the upgraded visuals, I had a lot of fun. It took me hours to get over my nervousness with the game, though, as you know the jump-scares, instant deaths, infrequent saves (complete with reloads and backtracking), and other survival horror staples are coming. As always, the best part is beating the game, getting the bonus weapons and ammo, and destroying everything that frustrated you earlier. I like the RE 1, 2, and 3 remakes better than this, but it’s almost as good. I hear they’re possibly remaking this game in 2027 (might just be a rumor)—I don’t get why. They could literally just make the controls a little better, and it would be fine. It’s the same reason they jumped to the RE 2 and 3 remakes—the RE 1 and 0 HD remasters were all that was needed to make them great (for me who hated the PlayStation graphics and controls).

[i]Resident Evil 0[/i] is a rare case where “more Resident Evil” doesn’t mean “better Resident Evil.” It tries to evolve the classic formula with new mechanics, a gorgeous setting, and dual protagonists, but instead delivers one of the most cumbersome, poorly paced entries in the series. It’s not unplayable: just awkward, frustrating, and hollow. You can see flashes of greatness in its atmosphere, but every time it starts to work, the inventory or AI reminds you why this one’s often left in the series’ rearview mirror.

🕯️ [b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Classic survival horror atmosphere. Capcom still knew how to make a good setting. The train setting is really lovely, even beautiful, but its tight hallways are quite spooky. And those damned zombie groans.

[*] Rebecca and Billy are fine. Rebecca is endearing in her own way, and Billy… exists. Their dynamic isn’t exactly electric, but at least it’s a different pairing than the usual Jill/Chris formula.
[/list]

🧟‍♀️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] The partner system is a nightmare. You have to swap between Rebecca and Billy constantly, micromanaging two inventories and two health bars. The AI is brain-dead, often wasting ammo or blocking your path like an undead traffic cone.

[*] No item boxes. For reasons only the cruelest designer could explain, Capcom removed the series’ iconic storage boxes. Instead, you just drop items on the floor and hope you remember where you left them. It’s not “strategic.” It’s busywork and involves a LOT of backtracking.

[*] Inventory hell. Six item slots per character, including weapons and key items, makes every minute a juggling act. Please, no, why?

[*] Poor combat. Enemies soak up bullets, and since managing two characters limits your resources, fights feel like chores rather than challenges. Like, can the zombie just pause so I can switch characters or exchange ammo really quick? Pretty please?

[*] The fixed camera controls aren't as bad as the previous game, but it still isn't as smooth as I would like.

[*] Rebecca sounds and looks like. 12?
[/list]
