Resident Evil 0 is a prequel that is supposed to give insight as to why the Mansion Incident happened, and to give more insight into Umbrella's workings. It is also a bit low on most people's rankings of the series. It's not hard to see why, from first glance: there's no inventory boxes, there's those annoying monkeys, and the Hookshot being used very infrequently. It usually boils down to those criticisms, but I'd like to levy a little bit more on it. 

As a prequel, it honestly kind of sucks. It doesn't give more insight into Bravo Team, and certainly not to Rebecca who is one of the main protagonists. There is something interesting going on with Billy, who is basically put on death row for a botched military job. Not sure what angle they were going for with that one, but it's something, I guess. The two don't really bond that much, kind of just the usual "put in a terrible situation and have to work together" kind of deal. Not terrible characters, but I wish they'd done more since they never show up in any other future games. I wish they didn't explain why the Mansion Incident occurred, because now we have to contend with a leech man who can control leeches via opera singing and spread the T-Virus because we're repeating Birkin's storyline again with that one. It gives some insight as to Wesker's involvement with Umbrella, but the glances it gives are cursory at best. That's kind of the problem with this game's story, it doesn't explain anything interesting, opting for something so ridiculous it's worse than seeing Wesker acting like a superhuman maniac in Code: Veronica, worse than Alexia sprouting giant tentacles. And I'm the type of guy that likes Resident Evil 4. This is just the opposite approach of the stupid that I like though.

The gameplay can be described as a "sidegrade" of sorts. While you can reload without going into the status screen (kind of useless since it's faster and safer to reload from the status screen in a lot of cases), and you can use herbs to combine them if you run out of space, that's really kind of the only benefits it has going for it. While the prospect of leaving items is good if you only play it with the fact that you'll only ever be in one area, typical Resident Evil games do not have them take place all in just one area. The train, which is the only notable thing about 0, is so short and changing locations means that you have to go back and offload everything you had in the previous area, to the next one. It doesn't help that anything that isn't a pistol or a magnum in terms of weapons, takes two item slots, this includes the Hookshot, which has earned the ire of many players for being used so infrequently, and for being such a waste of space. One instance where it is used, is only to press a button. I found that to be ridiculous, even by Resident Evil standards of backtracking. The door skip mod almost feels essential with the amount of further backtracking you need to do. There's also a limit on how many items there can be in a room too, which doesn't help. You can at least search which items you left in the map, so it's not completely without thought in its integration. 

The integration of two playable characters has a little bit of thought into it, with some okay puzzles involved, and the ability to move them if not controlling them, but the drastic differences in Billy being able to do more damage and having more health means that you'll almost never want to use Rebecca unless you have to mix herbs or use her as a pack mule, or unless you are forced to. No way to up inventory slots means that those 6 slots will always be used up by a more powerful weapon than the pistol 99% of the times, limiting yourself to 3 slots of free space on at least one character and likely only 4 on the other one if you want to have ammo for the gun, which makes it even more weirder why they didn't just do the first game's design, where Rebecca should have had 2 extra slots to compensate, rather than just having a mixing set that's also used very infrequently for some puzzles. Good luck if you missed the Red Chemical and you didn't send Rebecca upstairs at the lab, that means you're going all the way back through those damn monkeys to get that for a puzzle. The monkeys are very annoying too, as they are able to tank a shotgun shell and being very twitchy and jumpy, where missing shots is common. It's no wonder they only show up in this one and not anything else. The feeling of needing a crucial item that becomes a pain backtracking later hits the hardest in this one, since they take the Code: Veronica approach of putting stronger enemies in after a certain point on revisited areas.

This game and OG RE3 are low on my list, not only because they do not appeal to me gameplay and story-wise, but also because you have to play a separate gamemode (not a fun one either) just to unlock Infinite Ammo. Completing the Leech Hunter mode gives SMG ammo, but you can only get that if you speedrun the game in under 5 and a half hours. But the rewards for speedrunning don't feel worth it, since the rocket and SMG takes up, you guessed it, 2 slots, whereas the Magnum Revolver you get from doing Leech Hunter (only one slot, and found very early game) done at A rank, gives you infinite ammo for everything (on the respective difficulty you initially played on though). So you do the math on which one will net you a better second run experience. Wesker mode is a fun little distraction though, being able to zip around like a madman with infinite ammo while melting enemies with a death stare, too bad the cutscenes don't change Billy's dialogue.

Overall, Resident Evil 0 is kind of disappointing. It certainly looks the best out of all of the old school Resident Evils, before the "Bioterrorism" arc (or the action approach) happens though. But a lot of design decisions may not really work well with you, unless you were able to find some fun with the no inventory boxes approach, which is fine early game as stated, but drags as you move locations later on. It's worth at least one playthrough, even if the story reveals things that were better not known, at least with the way they explain things anyways. Rebecca and Billy are decent, even if they don't have much to do, and also contradicts how Rebecca acts in the first game (that Hunter interaction most notably), but it's harder to find good prequels more than anything that accounts for things like that. If you wanted to relive the old days of fixed camera angles Resident Evil, then go ahead...just heed the warnings of so many that find problems with this game.

[h1]Resident Evil 0[/h1]
[h3][Overview][/h3]
Resident Evil 0 is a 2002 survival horror game by Capcom, released for the GameCube and later ported to PC and consoles. A prequel to Resident Evil, you play as Rebecca Chambers, a rookie of the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team, alongside fugitive Billy Coen. The two are forced to team up in order to survive against the horrors that await them upon the Ecliptic Express and beyond, while uncovering a sinister plot.

[h3][Recommended Tweaks and Tips][/h3]
- [url=https://fusionfix.io/wfp#re0]Resident Evil Zero Fusion Fix (Quality-of-life enhancements)[/url]
- Use the original 4:3 aspect ratio. The 16:9 mode zooms in, cropping details and ruining the cinematic framing.
- Use original tank controls. The alternate controls clash with the fixed camera angles, making movement clunky.
- Save across multiple slots (at least three) to avoid being stuck if you mismanage items or hit a tough spot.

[h3][Positives][/h3]
- Strong graphics. Beautiful art and architecture match the Resident Evil 1 Remake’s visual quality.
- Great atmosphere. Creepy lighting and eerie sounds enhance the game’s spooky tone.
- Solid music. Tracks like the save room theme shine, despite some less memorable ones.
- The map is very useful for tracking items you interact with or drop, easing backtracking without an item box.
- Level design improves after the train, with wider areas to roam and explore.
- The final chapter’s elevator gives a nice chance to collect any missed items from previous areas.

[h3][Mixed][/h3]
- The dual protagonist idea is unique and interesting, letting you swap between Rebecca and Billy for teamwork, but micromanaging their actions gets frustrating.
- Okay puzzles. They tie into the partner system well, but some are very simple while others are extremely specific.
- Weird control scheme. It feels clunky and inconsistent with the RE1 Remake’s smoother setup, despite similar gameplay and engine.

[h3][Negatives][/h3]
- Linear design. Some areas lack the open-ended level design the series is known for, especially the notoriously linear opening train level.
- No item box. Ditching the series’ staple item box forces you to drop items on the floor, leading to tedious backtracking and inventory micromanagement.
- The Hookshot. This mandatory item eats two inventory slots and is needed repeatedly across the game, despite its limited use. It’s a constant annoyance.
- Frustrating enemies. Lurker frogs can instantly kill you with one grab, punishing small mistakes harshly. Humanoid Leeches, while not lethal in one hit, are tedious to fight due to their relentless attacks and resistance to non-fire weapons.
- Clunky boss fights. Managing two characters during boss battles adds unnecessary complexity, especially when the AI partner gets in the way.
- Weak story. It’s a pointless prequel that retcons lore with an over-the-top plot, adding nothing meaningful to the series and featuring a weak villain.
- Excessive cutscenes (e.g., a 3-second cutscene for one line of dialogue). The pre-rendered cutscenes haven’t aged well in general.

[h3][Conclusion][/h3]
Resident Evil 0’s eerie visuals and atmosphere shine, but clunky inventory, linear levels, and brutal enemies frustrate. A decent game for fans, though it falls short of RE1 Remake’s polish.

Very enjoyable survival horror game. The story is ridiculous and adds some unnecessary continuity errors but it's not really important. The "levels" are great in this game, especially the first 2 which are probably around 70% of the playtime, only the last 5th of the game is somewhat annoying and confusing.

HOWEVER, here's the list of all the potential nonsense the game throws at you...

What CAN potentially spoil the fun:

[u] Overall jankyness of the combat: [/u]
- combat encounters are almost half of the time done by not seeing the enemy
- aiming either works or doesn't, depending on the situation
- some enemies are much faster than you (which wouldn't bother otherwise but it can lead to frustrating deaths)
- you are slow in every way (aiming, turning, reloading, shooting, running etc.)
[u] The camera: [/u]
- you have sometimes very hard to move into a direction you want to
- hard time to pick up items because of it
[u] The buddy system: [/u]
- you play with 2 characters so you need to worry both of them almost all the time
- can be disorienting
- you need to juggle inventory a lot
- (I've heard) you can soft-lock your progress by doing things "wrong way"
- you need to throw and pick up items a lot (also need to remember and care where you leave them)

Then there's probably the biggest problem..

[u] THE THINGS THE GAME DOESN'T TELL YOU BECAUSE IT'S OLD OR SMT: [/u]
Puzzles and "obstacles" aren't as obvious as they seem. There is a potential to fail them, not "get" them fast enough or you might miss a detail or smt that locks your progress until you get it. I had some luck with them and some of it came from previous experience playing RE games. I just assumed "this might be how this thing works", and usually it didn't but then it somehow worked out in the end..

There's some very obvious obstacles like "keycards goes to locked doors that have a keycard reader", or "key goes to a lock". But there's also a puzzles that you might think it works certain way but you miss some information the game doesn't tell you. it probably will fix itself by just going forward, exploring more, examining items etc. but it might not depending on what you missed. I don't want to tell an example since it would spoil the puzzle and some of them are quite clever and fun. But just as a warning it might not be fun if you miss a detail, overlook something or you just don't get it.

A common complaint about RE0 is that it has no item boxes and you're forced to drop items instead. Obviously the choice of having an item box would've been nice but it really isn't an issue.

The gameplay is a lot more unique and interesting compared to RE1 since there's around 6 different areas of the game you progress through, whereas in RE1 you're in the mansion for pretty much the entire game.

The playable characters (specifically Billy) were pretty meh and not that interesting, Rebecca was cool though. The other main characters like Wesker and William Birkin were really good and played a role in carrying this games story. Story is the only thing RE1 does better (imo).

The graphics are pretty trash and the controls are pretty outdated, but you're playing a "remaster" of a 2002 release game so you can't really expect anything too crazy. Besides, after playing with the controls a bit you really get used to the fixed camera angles which adds a scare factor to the game, and it became pretty enjoyable after a while.

Wesker Mode is an amazing mode which is really fun and completely changes how Billy (or Wesker) is played, instead of just using guns Wesker can charge his power which instantly kills zombies with his eyes, or his other power which allows him to dash across the playable area.

Re0 I feel is a pretty divisive game, it has unique mechanics that haven’t really been used again. It also has some great and unique set pieces that are cool, but I feel the way that gameplay flow combined with very linear levels hurts the overall experience with the game. The best location is the opening on the high speed train that gives you a sense of unease as so many things have gone wrong on this locomotive. Exploring more on the character of Rebecca is neat, but I feel that she could have gotten more time with Bravo team slowly being picked off as the game goes on. Instead, Bravo team basically gets wiped out almost immediately and besides a couple interactions on the train, the only person Rebecca interacts with is Enrico in a short cutscene. The other character you get to play as is Billy who is an escaped convict in the area that teams up with Rebecca for survival, and besides his quick backstory that is really all of his character. The main unique features this game offers is playing with both characters at the same time and no item box. Which means if you don’t have space for an item you leave it on the ground to be picked up later, but it will be marked where you left it on your map. Which leads to a big issue with the game as the inventory space for both characters in total is 12 with few items taking up 2 spaces including a key item that you have to drag around for most of the game. If you don’t know where certain items are can lead to frustration and a lot of back tracking to recover items that you feel you will need to progress. Once you factor in the weapons and ammo you have to carry you really only get about 6 spaces to play with as you go through the game. One thing that is neat is the amount of variation in the bosses that you will get to fight with some of them being more annoying like the bat or Queen Leech. The pacing of the game feels very off at times like you just got off the thrill ride of the train sequence now you are in a smaller mansion area similar in feel like in RE1. Linear nature of the game hurts these next areas as many areas you will only have to visit 1 time briefly with like a few areas being the main way to get to other areas of the location. This continues on throughout the next areas of game where you are forced to split up or near the end of game with the water treatment plant. These areas are barely recognizable due to being basically one time uses as you walk down the dotted line through the game to the end. Despite this game being developed at the same time as the RE1 remake, it really only uses the key item slot that the characters all have to mix up their playstyle. Only Rebecca’s item is actually good since you can mix herbs and store various chemicals to get through sections of the game, while Billy gets a lighter which you use 2 times. One is for a puzzle to open a gate and the other time is to open a door, you don’t get to burn bodies of zombies or use it in any other way. Basically, Billy is just a health tank that can shoot better than Rebecca, but don’t have him use the molotovs otherwise they will be wasted. The way the game plays and the mechanics you have to interact with really hurt the replay value of this game, on repeat playthroughs you can basically breeze through the game at breakneck pace. Re0 is a weird game because if you have never played it I would recommend it at least once, but also if you haven’t played it in many years it can be a fun experience as well. It's kind of a game that is neat to play every once in a while, but it isn’t the worst of the franchise, it just has some weird decisions that really bring down the overall experience of the game. 4.5/10

Resident Evil 0 — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Resident Evil 0.
The so-called “origin story.” A prelude to the grand opera of infection, corruption, and collapse that would follow. I remember those days well — the chaos before the order, the experiments before the refinement. Back when Umbrella still pretended to have ethics.

Let us begin where all good catastrophes start: with incompetence.

The Ecliptic Express. A train filled with death, ambition, and the scent of failure. I watched the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team stumble into it like lambs into a slaughterhouse. Their mission? Investigate mysterious murders in the Arklay Mountains. Their fate? Predictable. They were never meant to uncover truth — merely to serve as data points.

Rebecca Chambers — young, brilliant, and tragically idealistic. Barely out of training, thrust into the jaws of Umbrella’s filth. I saw potential in her — intellect, composure — but her compassion… it’s a disease. It clouds judgment, dilutes resolve. She could have been a scientist of note. Instead, she became a survivor. How tedious.

And then there’s Billy Coen — the convict. Accused of murder, condemned by circumstance, yet far more capable than half of Umbrella’s security division. A fugitive, a soldier, a pawn. Watching Rebecca partner with him was like watching an antibody cling to a virus — futile, but oddly poetic.

The true star of the show, of course, is James Marcus.
One of Umbrella’s founders — a visionary undone by vanity. His experiments with the Queen Leech were ambitious, I’ll grant him that. He sought to merge intelligence with replication, to create life that consumed life. Admirable goals… but he lacked discipline. He let emotion seep into science. He was devoured — literally — by his own creation. A fitting end.

Now, the Leech Queen herself — grotesque, elegant, and pathetically sentimental. I admired her adaptability, though she inherited her master’s melodrama. Shriek, flail, die. A shame. With proper direction, the Leech Project could have rivaled the T-Virus.

Gameplay analysis:
Resident Evil 0 is a fascinating study in design efficiency — or rather, inefficiency. The “partner system” is its central gimmick, allowing you to switch between Rebecca and Billy. In theory, it’s teamwork. In practice, it’s micromanagement. Managing two inventories, two health bars, and one functioning brain between them.
No storage boxes — a crime against logic. Items strewn across the floor like discarded experiments. Inventory Tetris taken to its maddest form.
Still, I appreciate the intent: interdependence breeds tension, and tension breeds fear.

The setting — sublime. Umbrella’s fingerprints are everywhere: laboratories hidden beneath opulence, corpses reanimated by arrogance. The visual design bleeds atmosphere. The train sequence is a masterpiece — a confined, pulsing experiment in panic. If only the rest of the operation had maintained that momentum.

By the time the mansion looms in the distance, you feel the story closing its own loop. The infection begins here, the spiral starts to turn, and the virus prepares to escape its cradle. The prequel ends where my ascension begins. How poetic.

My verdict:
Resident Evil 0 is a flawed but fascinating case study — a reflection of Umbrella’s own ethos: brilliant ideas marred by human error. It stumbles under the weight of its own ambition, yet it captures the essence of early bioterror — elegant horror born from corporate madness.

7.5 out of 10.

The most contentious feature of RE0 is the inventory system. Gone is the magical item box and instead players are required to drop items on the ground as the primary method of item storage. At its worst, this process IS mind numbingly repetitive but most of the time it isn’t as insane as public reception would have you believe. Unless you are incredibly frugal you’re mostly limited to having a couple dozen items, for example I topped out at 25 across my inventories and dropped items. Among Rebecca and Billy’s accumulative 12 inventory slots that means just two trips to ferry items from one hub to the next. Additionally there are really only two trips in which it makes sense to gather your various collectibles so there theoretically isn’t that much time wasted. If the animation of picking up and dropping items was faster and more streamlined then I would consider this system a near non issue. And the concept of dropping items itself isn’t without merit. In fact the option opens avenues to strategic drops as opposed to standard RE in which dropping an item meant losing it forever. I think the system overall could absolutely use some adjustments but the design philosophy here is solid. Unfortunately there is another feature of the game that I find deal breaking and that lies, sadly, with the enemy design of the game. 

The holdovers from Resident Evil HD are good/fine but the new additions are frankly frustrating. The giant cockroaches add literally nothing to the experience of the game and would’ve been better replaced with regular zombies. Monkeys are exceedingly grating in the sense that they are incredibly mobile and difficult to evade and will often stunlock you if you make a bad move. They’re easy enough to dispatch but having it feel like a necessity downgrades the experience. The plant men are laughably easy to evade and discourage any interaction since dispatching them takes far more effort. The lurkers in the last level also don’t need to be engaged at all, though if you mess up pathing they result in certain death if the ensnared player is unassisted. IMO the best enemies in the Resident Evil franchise are a masterclass in strong risk vs reward systems. None of these new adversaries come even close to that. The bosses in this game are somehow more offensive and I count them among the worst in the entire franchise's. Every boss feels like it's centered on some goofy gimmick that is often RNG based, slapped on top of an absurdly high health pool. As a result bosses are either exceedingly excruciating to deal with or mind numbingly boring. I’ve opted out of replaying the game for achievements primarily because the enemy/boss designs are so terrible and it's a real shame because other features of the game deserve some praise.

For example the other major feature of the game, the dual protagonists, is done much better. I was skeptical at first but the overall design philosophy here is excellent. It adds an extra layer of complexity when deciding who gets to pursue what task and when, where to position partners, who gets to hold what items, etc etc. It really opens up additional possibilities for puzzle and level design and the ones they had in the game were quite satisfying. Some of my favorite strategies include: using Rebecca to lure enemies away from a door entrance that Billy was waiting behind, bringing characters together for additional firepower, and lowering backtracking by having Rebecca save while Billy waits before a treacherous segment( compared to a standard RE which your one character has to save, traverse some hallways, and then reach the treacherous segment). My only complaint here is that the character imbalance is tragic since Billy is better at literally everything and Rebecca’s only strength is combining herbs which is a skill that rarely comes into play with decision making. The game would have been much better even if they had just settled to use Chris and Jill’s strengths from RE1.

The practical level design here is pretty solid too though it fails to reach the heights of the series’ best. Like the other games RE0 challenges players with traversing a world filled with locked doors, treacherous hallways, limited resources, and uncertainty around every corner. Enemy frustrations aside, there was a good sense of pacing and discovery regarding item locations, room unlocks, and enemy encounters. The game starts out with a strong sense of danger and flow though sadly later levels lose a bit of the edge by opting for generally more linear paths, straightforward paths and significantly less dangerous rooms. Additionally the last couple levels can feature some extremely unbelievable backtracking if you didn’t catch some easily missable key items. In my first run which was just under 5 hours I spent a little over 30 minutes on these specific backtracking mishaps. Regardless, I'm overall satisfied with the game’s level design.

Thankfully the levels fare better in the visual department. Again, the first levels are stronger but I think the overall vibes and eeriness are extremely indicative of Resident Evil. Some of the camera angles fail to capture quite the sense of discomfort as the older Resident Evils but I still think they are quite good, maybe only half a grade below. The areas are iconic, even if some of them are redundant but the visuals here are parts of the game I enjoyed.

The plot and voice acting here is somewhat forgettable and oftentimes borders on goofy but this is par for the course for the series. Sound design remains on par with the older games.

Overall RE0 could’ve been counted amongst the best Resident Evil has to offer, though sadly enemy variety and level design quirks prevent it from rising to the level of the more hallowed entries. I do think its worth one playthrough but consider some mods to help streamline the experience.

[h1]This Game Scores Closer to Zero[/h1]

[i]Before the mansion, before the destruction of Raccoon City, there was Resident Evil 0. Now remastered with improved visuals and sounds, as well as the all-new Wesker Mode, there's never been a better time to experience the origins of the Resident Evil story.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Resident Evil Zero is a prequel to the original series, following Rebecca Chambers and fugitive Billy Coen as they survive a T-virus outbreak on a train and uncover Umbrella Corporation’s dark experiments in an abandoned mansion. As they face monsters and deadly traps, the two form a fragile alliance while discovering the origins of the virus and the sinister actions of Umbrella’s scientists.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil Zero is a survival horror game. The character is controlled from a third-person perspective using fixed camera angles and tank controls.

Gameplay is largely similar to previous entries, but you now control two protagonists: police officer and medic Rebecca Chambers, and former Force Recon officer Billy Coen. You can switch between them, have the AI control one, or split them up to explore separately. Each character has unique abilities—Rebecca can mix herbs and chemicals but is defensively weak, while Billy can move heavy objects, use a lighter, and has higher defense but cannot mix herbs. The partner system is key to solving many of the game’s puzzles.

Characters can run and perform quick 180-degree turns to evade danger. You can examine objects, doors, other characters, and items to find clues, and some objects can be pushed or climbed to reach higher areas. Items can be examined in the inventory, equipped, or combined to create more effective tools or replenish ammo. When Rebecca and Billy are nearby, they can exchange items. Unlike previous games, Resident Evil Zero removes fixed item boxes, instead allowing you to drop items on the floor to free inventory space until retrieved later. This design choice was meant to make the game harder and feel closer to Sweet Home (1989).

There’s also a mode where you can play through the game as the overpowered Albert Wesker.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
Resident Evil Zero features a variety of enemies, from classic zombies to terrifying mutated creatures. Zombies are slow but deadly in groups. Zombie dogs are fast and agile, often attacking in packs, while Hunters are lethal, reptilian humanoids capable of long leaps and heavy damage. Spiders can ambush you by crawling on walls and ceilings. These are just a few examples of all the threats. The game also includes several bosses, which I won’t spoil.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The environments are full of locked doors, hidden items, and puzzles, encouraging exploration. Enemies are strategically placed to create suspense, ambushes, and scares.

The game opens on the Ecliptic Express, a slow-moving train where Rebecca and Billy first encounter the outbreak. Tight corridors and small rooms make combat claustrophobic and force strategic movement. 

After the train incident, you reach an abandoned mansion/research lab, a precursor to the mansion from the first Resident Evil. The mansion includes laboratories, offices, and storage rooms, with environmental storytelling showing the results of Umbrella’s experiments.

There are more areas to explore, including outdoor segments like courtyards and gardens, which offer brief relief from the indoor tension.

The game features an automap to help you navigate the different areas of the game. Additionally, you can find and pick up maps of certain sections to reveal unexplored areas. The locations of dropped items are displayed on the game map.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
Zombies and monsters are gruesome and disturbing, with visual cues for infection and mutation. Bloodstains, torn clothing, and abandoned equipment show the aftermath of Umbrella’s experiments. Lab rooms have scientific instruments, containment tanks, and hazard symbols.

Zombies and monsters produce distinctive growls, screeches, and snarls, alerting you to their presence even off-screen. The audio cues often precede visual contact, increasing tension and forcing you to react carefully.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
The fixed camera angles and tank controls feel awkward at first and take some time to get used to.

The story is bland and fails to provide an engaging backstory to the events leading up to the Spencer Mansion. Characters are poorly written and unlikable. The voice acting is some of the worst I’ve heard in a video game, combined with stupid cutscenes.

The overuse of two-slot items and the removal of storage boxes undermine inventory management. While the game lets you drop items on the ground to retrieve later, there’s a limit to how many items can be placed in a room—no matter how large. I really hate this change. It doesn’t make the game harder—just more frustrating.

The game isn’t scary at all—most enemies look cartoony and absolutely ridiculous, with mutated bugs dominating encounters. Many enemies are more annoying than frightening and feel out of place, like the monkeys. Some enemy placements are unfair, and a few bosses are poorly designed, like the Giant Bat.

The puzzles are boring, poorly designed, and far less engaging than those in the first game.

The environments are uninspired and are not nearly as good when it comes to atmosphere and horror, not even the mansion.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil Zero is mostly bad. The unique partner system is good, and it provides some tense survival moments with limited resources. The remastered visuals and updated sound design do enhance the atmosphere, and the inclusion of Wesker Mode adds a fun twist of the game.

However, these positives are overshadowed by several critical flaws. The story is underwhelming and poorly executed, with flat characters and awkward voice acting that fail to engage. The removal of item boxes and limited inventory management end up feeling more frustrating than challenging. Many environments and puzzles are uninspired, and enemy design often leans toward annoyance rather than fear, with some encounters feeling unfair or out of place.

Ultimately, Resident Evil Zero struggles to deliver the tight, terrifying experience as the first game excelled in. While some mechanics and visuals shine, the game’s inconsistencies in story, design, and horror impact prevent it from standing out as a true classic.

RE0 is an odd game, lacking the finesse and compelling story I'd come to expect from the earlier games in this series.  All told, it is only a few tweaks away from being up to par with the original RE and RE2 games, beloved by fans, and myself.

RE0 revisits the timeline just before the events of the series namesake.  The mechanics are mostly familiar.  Gun play is good, the general atmosphere is amazing, and the puzzles are all what you would expect from one of the better RE games.  However, the story itself is completely throwaway.  The lack of character development for Rebecca is a major flaw in this game, as is the overall lack of banter between the two main characters, both of whom, one would think, would be trauma bonding over this hellish experience they are having together.  Nope, instead Billy gives her the occasional boost to reach an item or has to save the damsel in distress, which happens a few times throughout the game.  But then they just sorta move on from it without really growing as a team in any noticeable way.  So much lost potential in storytelling.

Likely the game's greatest flaw is its lack of item boxes.  It was custom in older RE main series titles to provide a global item box that followed you from one "safe room" to another.  This game stripped that feature out entirely, making it so that you have to manage limited inventory of six spaces on each of your two characters, who by the way get split up periodically throughout the game.  The loading screens are a nice tension-builder, right up until you have to proceed ten screens back to pickup an item you had to drop earlier, just so you can then return to what you were doing.  Not having item boxes easily adds hours to your playtime, not to mention the reloading/redoing of segments you were unprepared to deal with as characters are split up.  Rebecca needs the grenade launcher for this solo segment?   Too bad you gave it to Billy or left it on the floor three rooms back.  This ground my gears to no end and I was content just to complete the game with the "C" Rank, which is basically what I would give this game on its report card. 

RE0 would be a much better game if it didn't double-down on an already outdated inventory management system in a game that is otherwise quite good at challenging the player with puzzles and combat encounters.  Any good baked into this game is lost due to the bad taste left by all the unnecessary features or those simply not included.  The game's title foretold how much fun I would genuinely have with this game, which was close to 0.

TLDR: A graphically improved version of a lesser entry in the Resident Evil franchise. The game is good DESPITE its main features: controlling 2 characters at once, and being able to drop items on the ground (instead of destroying them up like other RE titles). It's old school RE; prerendered backgrounds, tank controls, poor story and limited resources. 
What happened to me was that I enjoyed the new system early on, namely in the train. Both mechanics actually worked well there. But after that? It just kept getting worse.

Story: Enter Bravo team, sent to investigate the same events that Alpha Team will later deal with in RE 1. Much like RE 1 everything goes to sh!t. Rebecca will investigate a choo-choo train, where she will meet Billy Coen, our second protagonist, a murderer (allegedly) being transported for execution. Billy Coen had real potential to have a more extended upon background, but we pretty much only get a 30 seconds FMV and some banter for it. Missed opportunity methinks, at least he's got a big arm tattoo so it's fine cuz tattoos make everything better. The antagonist also took a massive leave on being both present and being taken seriously as we rarely see him apart from giggling at camera feeds. Nah seriously the story tends to tie in nicely with RE1 but... not much else. The main enemies are the usual, but we also now have... slugs, or leeches. dunno. Oh and another main enemy is the inventory system.

Gameplay: It's the good old fashioned tank controls with prerendered graphics, but no item box.
Ammo and health are extremely rare, enough so that some players are likely to want to restart midway due to a lack of resources.
The item box from other RE titles is gone. Now? You’re just dropping stuff on the floor. It saves its position permanently — but it's clunky, tedious, and makes backtracking worse than ever. Oh, and each room has a max amount of items.
Puzzles are frequent, but nothing too complicated and they often fit snugly into the natural progression of the game, especially compared to the complete lack of an item box.
Item management is truly a chore. I cannot stress this enough.
As mentioned before (apart from the LACK OF ITEM BOX WTF?!?!), you have 2 characters to control. Controlling the 2nd character is easy, but I could never bother to think about it. Often, you will want to scout ahead with Billy, and have Rebecca bring the rear as she has a lot less health. You can easily swap between each character with a button press, and when the other character is on follow, simply moving the right joystick will have them move in the direction you're... pushing, obviously. It can be useful when they throw themselves at a zombie's nibblers. God I need to think before I start writing, or talking for that matter... Oh, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I'm still writing.
Oh right!!! The item box is gone!??!
There are a couple of enemies that are overly bothersome to deal with. While one can deal stupid amount of damage over too great a distance, the other can pretty much stun lock you. On a side note, I was also slowly eaten by a frog and my ''partner'' did absolutely nothing about it, it just watched me slowly get swallowed whole. Thanks AI. At least the AI agrees that the item box should be in the game.
Speaking of partners, Rebecca can mix herbs and use her chemical set for some puzzles, while Billy has a bigger health pool, can move heavy objects and can use a lighter, again for some puzzles. Often, the game will split your characters up and you will have to come back with another character (or both) to be able to progress. 
It has happened a few times that when the AI was following, they wouldn't follow through a door, so just keep it in mind if suddenly you're all on your lonesome.
Did I mention the item box? It's missing. Must be a bug.

Graphics: The original game was released in 2002 on Gamecube while this port in 2016... I have to say that apart from the FMV, the game looks solid, even in 2025. Just missing a doodad called an item box.

Audio: The cheesy voice overs are there, in all their glory, but I can sadly only remember how irritated I was at my messes on the floor... Grenade Launcher here, First Aid spray there, a dozen herb over there... where did I leave that crank?  OH YEAH, NOT IN THE ITEM BOX.

Capcom's Resident Evil Zero remains a controversial game in the Resident Evil franchise, so it's only natural that such a controversial game was subject to a very rough development cycle. Originally being developed for the Nintendo 64, Zero's development was completely restarted for the GameCube when it became abundantly clear that the N64's storage constraints were insurmountable and the 64DD add-on sold too poorly to justify development for it. Director Koji Oda made a point to differentiate Zero from previous games, partly due to hardware constraints and partly due to wanting to innovate on the survival horror formula. These departures have received a variety of reactions, some praising them for shaking up the formula and some criticizing them for being unintuitive. I'd say I generally lean more positive than most, but I'd still argue the game has some glaring flaws.

The original screenplay was written by Noboru Sugimura, writer of Resident Evil 2, before being significantly retooled post-reboot by Hiromichi Nakamoto and Junichi Miyashita. Resident Evil Zero serves as a prequel to the original Resident Evil. You play as Rebecca Chambers, the rookie medic from the first game, investigating the strange murders occurring within the Arklay Mountains with the rest of the STARS Bravo Team. After a dangerous helicopter crash and increasingly hostile weather conditions, she is separated from her team and boards the Ecliptic Express, an abandoned luxury train now populated by the living dead. On the train, she meets escaped death-row inmate Billy Coen, with whom she forms an uneasy alliance. Together, they must survive the horrors that lurk beyond.

Zero's story is a mixed bag, to say the least, suffering from often ridiculous tonal shifts and a general lack of focus. The biggest problem with the narrative is the antagonist, a mysterious man who controls an army of shapeshifting leeches, which he controls by singing opera. This feels entirely out of place and only gets more ridiculous when his true nature is revealed. Another issue I had with the story was its connection to the rest of the series. Despite being a prequel, Zero does very little to expand on the first game in a meaningful way, only really delving into what Rebecca had been up to before it. Characters from previous games like Albert Wesker, William Birkin, and Enrico Marini appear very briefly simply to remind you that this is a prequel, and their inclusion feels like hollow fanservice as a result. Like previous Resident Evil games, most of the narrative is told through memos that can be found in the environment, and these memos do wonders fleshing out Zero's story. However, previous RE games told you their stories with both memos and more traditional cutscenes, but Zero seems content to stick to the former. Because of this, the game lacks narrative flow, and it's hard to stay invested when the writers themselves seemingly aren't. You need to have a balance between the two, and Zero simply fails to achieve this. It's not all leeches and zombies though, there is one narrative aspect that Zero's writing succeeds in, and that is the relationship between Rebecca and Billy. Initially hostile, they eventually become blood brothers on the battlefield. The scene where Billy opens up to Rebecca about his PTSD from his service in Africa, reminiscing on how his squad was ordered to fire upon unarmed civilians, is genuinely emotional and you can hear the pain in his voice. The two feel like a real pair by the end of the game and it's heartwarming when Rebecca, despite her orders to capture Billy, decides to falsely report him as a casualty instead of turning him in. It's the only element of this story that actually works and I wish it were part of a much more engaging narrative.

Zero's most controversial element was its gameplay, originally designed by the legendary Hideki Kamiya before being iterated upon by a myriad of other designers. The biggest change is the partner system. RE2 had the "zapping system" which showed that Leon and Claire were working together, though in actuality it was a thinly veiled illusion. Zero, however, gives you control of both Rebecca and Billy simultaneously. Although this has proved controversial as all elements of Zero have, I found it to be a refreshing innovation in the Resident Evil formula, especially after Code Veronica had done so little to change it. It fundamentally changes how you strategize and divide resources, after all, now you have two mouths to feed. This forces you to think a lot more carefully than you would in a comparatively easier game like RE2. The puzzles designed around this mechanic were generally quite fun, too, minus a particularly repetitive box puzzle in the late game. The partner AI is pretty decent, and you can even give it commands if you don't want it wasting ammo on every zombie in sight. You can also leave them behind in a safe room if they've taken too much damage. It's surprisingly very intuitive for a mechanic often described as "cumbersome". The lack of item boxes, on the other hand, I am not fond of. I don't think it makes the game "unplayable" as some reviews have stated, far from it, but it doesn't really add any new strategy to the game either. Any seasoned RE player will just dump all of their nonessential items in the main hall, where nothing will attack them, and just leave them there until necessary. It trivializes any potential difficulty or strategy that the mechanic could have brought since I don't have to worry about backtracking to some potentially dangerous location to find ink ribbons, I can just go back to the always enemy-free main hall. Since the new inventory system doesn't really add anything, Capcom should have just stuck with the traditional item box system, which would have at least made some of the backtracking less tedious. That's another problem this game has: the backtracking. Backtracking is just an inherent part of survival horror and isn't necessarily a bad thing, but in Zero it feels a tad excessive. For the most part, it's a little uneven, but generally fine. However, in the final stage of the game, every single puzzle is spread out so far from the rest that it becomes an act of herculean willpower to actually get through it. The game's difficulty balancing is also fairly unrefined. I played on hard mode, as I want survival horror games to push me to my limits, but Zero goes too far at points. Despite having two health bars to tend to, the game only gives you barely enough to maintain one. The game's new enemies are also ridiculously frustrating at points. The mimicry marcuses aren't too bad, they are the "elite mook" of the game similar to the hunters and lickers in the previous games respectively. The threat they represent is genuinely terrifying. The problem is, the game has two more elite mooks in the form of the hunters and eliminators, so a good amount of the game's enemies can really put the hurt on you. It feels excessive and leads to many frustrating encounters.

When you complete Zero, you unlock an extra game mode called Leech Hunter. In this mode, you have to collect as many crystal leeches as you can throughout the training facility. Essentially, this is Zero's battle/mercenaries mode. Each leech is either blue or green, and each color can only be picked up by one of the characters respectively. I only gave Leech Hunter a brief spin, as it did not hold my interest for too long, but I found it to be an interesting little minigame. The most interesting part is how it doesn't have any timer whatsoever. You can explore the facility collecting leeches to your heart's content, leaving whenever you feel you've got enough. This does mean the mode lacks the tension of The Mercenaries, but I can imagine spending more time on it at a later date. It's decent for what it is.

Resident Evil 0 is both a return to the roots and an experiment within the series. As a prequel to the original game, it unveils the events that led to the mansion incident. It combines classic survival horror with new ideas for its time, giving it a unique charm.

Pros:
✔Graphics — impressive for its release era, with detailed models, atmospheric lighting, and carefully crafted environments that still hold up stylistically.
✔Dual characters (Rebecca and Billy) with the ability to switch between them — a fresh and engaging mechanic that adds depth to the gameplay.
✔Atmosphere — music, sound design, and visuals create strong tension and immersion.
✔Varied locations — from a night-bound train to mansions and laboratories, each environment has its own mood and style.
✔Gameplay design — the absence of storage boxes forces players to manage inventory carefully, dropping items on the floor and planning ahead.
✔Save system — the classic typewriter with ink ribbons adds to the tension and sense of risk.

Cons:
➖Inventory management — limited space often forces tough (and sometimes frustrating) decisions about what to carry.
➖Controls — the tank-style system designed for early 2000s consoles feels outdated and clunky today.
➖Pacing — frequent backtracking to pick up items left behind can artificially stretch the gameplay.
➖Story elements — the main antagonist, with his over-the-top operatic style, divided fan opinion.
➖Co-op potential — the partner system is interesting, but having no real multiplayer co-op feels like a missed opportunity.

Verdict:
Resident Evil 0 isn’t just an experimental entry but an important piece of the Resident Evil puzzle. It shows the events before the original game, introduces bold new mechanics, and challenges players with scarce resources and constant choices. The game is short but dense, and even today it retains its value — for fans of the franchise and for those who want a taste of old-school survival horror.

👉 Rating: 7.5/10 — atmospheric and important, though not without flaws that have become more noticeable with age.

Fun Facts:
Originally developed for the Nintendo 64, but later moved to GameCube due to hardware limitations.
It was the last Resident Evil to use static backgrounds and tank controls.
First game in the series to feature dual-character switching mechanics.
Its unusual decision to remove item boxes significantly altered the pacing and strategy.
Billy Coen remains one of the few protagonists in the franchise who never returned in later games.
It's not one of the best entries in the series, but even so, it is a great game.

[h1][b]100% Completion Review[/b][/h1]

Holy molly, I really want to give this game a negative review after getting all the achievements. But honestly, that wouldn't be fair. Completionists like me are a niche audience, and we’re clearly not the target demographic for how this game was designed.

That said, the 100% journey is padded with a lot of unnecessary and frustrating extra playthroughs due to poorly thought-out achievement requirements.

For example, in Leech Hunter mode, there's one achievement for collecting half the leeches and then ending the mini-game. But then you also need to do another run to get the achievement for collecting all the leeches. Why? Why not just make the first one pop when you hit 50 green or blue leeches in a single playthrough? Forcing multiple runs of a fairly slow side mode just feels like artificial padding.

Then there’s the achievement that requires attaching custom gun parts to both Rebecca’s and Billy’s handguns. But you can only do it to one handgun per playthrough, meaning, again, another run just for a small, arbitrary requirement. It’s tedious for no good reason.

I understand the need to add replayability to a game, especially in survival horror, where resource management and route optimization can make repeat playthroughs interesting. But some of these design choices feel forced, adding artificial replay value rather than meaningful content. Instead of encouraging players to revisit the game out of enjoyment or curiosity, it often results in burnout. You’re not replaying because the game is fun, you’re doing it because you missed a single achievement or need to hit a specific, scripted requirement. That’s not engaging; it’s exhausting.

And the worst offender? The damn insta-kill frogs. Those things are pure evil, especially when you're doing no-save or speedrun attempts. Nothing feels worse than having a good run ruined by a surprise one-hit kill that you can't really counter if you're unlucky.

Despite all that, I do think Resident Evil 0 is a solid game. I respect Capcom for experimenting. The partner system, while clunky and not the best thing to come out of the series, isn’t unplayable. It's flawed but ambitious, and I’ll always give points for trying something new.

Just be warned: if you’re going for 100%, prepare for a grind, and not the satisfying kind.

Something to bare in mind for newcomers to the franchise or people who have only played the later games/remakes, this is when the games where extremely trial and error and you had to be very resource mindful. You are not (nor do you need to) supposed to kill every enemy you see or rush through the game. There are some fundamental things you must understand about the legacy games before you play them as I have listed below:

These games are not meant to be beaten in 1 sitting as fast as you can. Take your time, make notes of things and take breaks.

Adding onto what I said above, keep a notepad be it virtual or an actual notepad with you. Maybe even have a print out or digital version of the in game map. Write down what enemies are weak to when you discover it, write down where you found things, the answers to puzzles and where tricky enemies are. Pay attention to what enemies you NEED to kill and which ones you can simply avoid. Information is key to beating resident evil. 

Don't be afraid to load up a save or die. Make multiple saves (you have 10 slots so use them) but don't over save since you have limited ink ribbons to do so. Take a risk like I mentioned above, the game is very trial and error so you are bound to make mistakes or even soft lock yourself on the first playthrough. So BE SURE to use all your slots up instead of saving over 1 slot. Don't take death as another set back but instead treat it like a lesson. What did you learn from your death? did you discover where some useful items where? did you find out the location of enemies that are important? did you solve a tricky puzzle? Death is common in this game, if you view it as just a set back then your going to keep failing. Use and write down all the info you learned and try again using your new knowledge.

NEVER JUST DROP SOMETHING! Seriously there is an unwritten rule with these games I see almost nobody mention. The game has an interesting mechanic few people seem to either pick up on or mention to newcomers. Whenever you pick up and use a key item be it an actual key or some piece of equipment, you will be asked "this item is useless now, would you like to discard it?" this means you no longer need it and so you are safe to throw it away. The other instance of this is automatic discarding meaning you use an item and the game disposes of it without your permission. HOWEVER! if you have a piece of equipment and the game doesn't auto discard it or ask you if you wish for it to be removed.....that means you shouldn't abandon it! For example everyone likes to mention the hookshot being an item that can set you back. What they fail to realise is its because the hookshot is to be used the entire game. It never discards it for you and it never asks for it to be discarded. This means the games wants you to keep it for something later. Other RE games have similar items like code veronicas fire extinguisher. The tricky part is this game has no item box, so be prepared to juggle items around, but DON'T abandon them. 

Use your characters wisely. For some reason I keep seeing people primarily (or only) use Rebecca. The issue is they keep dying or using up all their ammo failing to realise what the game warns you of at the start. Billy is the combat guy, he tanks more damage, deals more damage and can solve puzzles that involve moving heavy objects. Rebecca can mix herbs and uses a mixing tool which is very useful for a puzzle later in the game. Rebecca however is very weak to damage and not the best at combat. So stop using Rebecca as the primary combat role when that belongs to Billy. Both have their places in this game so use them accordingly. Also their weapons also have unique abilities with Billy's pistol being slower but more powerful in overhaul damage, but Rebecca's pistol is faster and has higher chance of critical hits (headshots). A little extra tip is use your inventory to reload! seriously it saves you precious moments in game. The in game reload animation can let enemies get dangerously close to you and risk you getting attacked. Simply bring up your inventory and combine the ammo with your gun. It's slow in terms of real time pacing but fast in terms of not getting hit. You should also switch to your knife when safe to do so and finish zombies on the floor. Don't waste precious ammo on shooting the zombie an extra 3 times on the floor, instead equip your knife and stab em. 

Lastly READ! seriously the amount of playthroughs I have seen or forum posts of people not being able to solve puzzles or getting lost simply because they refuse to read is infuriating. This game has notes scattered all over the place and many of them contain clear answers to what your supposed to do. You can tell this too because many people don't read the tutorial notes that explain characters abilities and how to use certain items hence my previous post about people not using Billy correctly. Once you have done your first playthrough you shouldn't need the notes, then you can speedrun to your hearts content. But don't skip them then complain your stuck. 

If you can bare all this in mind you should have a lot of fun with the game. I'm not saying its perfect and it certainly has flaws like removal of the storage box, poor AI for the teammate, annoying enemies that are either just bullet sponges or poorly made and LOTS of backtracking. But you can certainly help yourself by following some of the tips above and not treating it like RE4 onwards where you rush in, gun everything down and move on.

Really mixed bag, this one. Got too much to say about it. I think it's best to think of it as a caricature of its counterpart in the REmake, especially considering they were released the same year, play and look the same and respectively represent a high point and median of the awkward early gen 6 console years after Code Veronica and before 4. The core gameplay loop is of course quintessential resident evil and I have little in the way of criticism for this since it would kind of apply to the entire series. 
This of course immediately segues into a problem unique to 0: the inventory management is just suboptimal. I don't think it's, like, egregious, but when you have the superior example of storage boxes not just in future installments, but its own twin game, it's almost on the nose how backwards it feels, especially on a first playthrough before you learn what to prioritize. I think all the griping about it is completely valid even if it's not something I think upends the whole game on its own. It's clear it was an earnest attempt at something different meant to go along with the partner mechanic, and the ability to drop things whenever wherever and have the map clearly spell out where and what offers some much needed brevity, but it ultimately plays as a misguided attempt at improving realism/co-op which fundamentally turns into pure tedium, replete with backtracking and forcing you to use one of the PCs as a key mule half the time. Backtracking is something endemic to the series, but this is on a different level, and more pertinently is made all the more painful by the other, and my opinion, far more crucial outstanding flaw: the gratuitous loading screens. Every time you go through a door, you have to sit through an unskippable animation. I figure this was windowdressing for needed circumvention to allow for rendering advanced graphics at a time when ROM hardware was still in its adolescence, but it's strictly annoying for something running on any and all modern hardware. The animations are fine and occasionally do a good job building tension, as I'm sure was the intention of doing a bespoke animation and door creak instead of a black screen with a swirling logo in the corner, but after two or three agonizing 5 second waits between every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ room it leaves you begging on your knees for the simplicity of an industry standard split second splash screen. Considering this HD port came out in the mid 2010s you really think they would have bothered to patch in some kind of circumvention for this, and the fact they didn't makes it all the more insulting. Occasional instant death noob traps and long walks back to items you didn't think you needed anymore (looking at you, hookshot) with a solid level of difficulty to boot pile on to this. Put these issues in a formula that already precludes punishing runaround and you have completely crossed the line from immersive and challenging to annoying and stupid. 
I think these are the hard negatives, though, and otherwise would say everything else unique to this game - the partner mechanic, characters, setting and lore - are neutral or decent. The graphics in this remake are polished - I don't care what anyone says, for nothing more than a fresh coat of paint on a game from 2002, everything within the actual played experience looks great. This of course makes the less well aged CGI cutscenes look even less well aged in comparison, but I feel they hold up fine. The voice direction in this one is rough, however, and another thing that makes it look really bad in comparison to the contemporaneous REmake (which wasn't great or anything but a deliberate and successful improvement on the original game, which this one is closer to in quality.) The music is honestly weirdly good in this one, too, and one of the best scores in the series imo, right up there with OG 2 and 4 while at the same sounding a lot more serious and professional. I have no issues with the fixed camera angles even though they still cause jelly fingers around corners, because in the absence of the god awful tank controls that plagued the first four installments, it's actually fairly easy to adapt to it and move through the world with enough fluidity the cinematic edge the fixed angles offer isn't lost to tedium and panic. Lorewise this one is a bit of an awkward fit as a direct precedent to the REmake, especially considering Rebecca and Enrico being at the ensuing Mansion incident without a word to say or a wink of sleep between the two represents a bit of a retcon, it's pretty minor and kind of made up for by the bit of scope it helps add to Umbrella's presence and history in the canonically subsequent installments, namely with facility and Wesker and Birkin sort of running the show together. Removed from the inventory management issues, I think the partner system is well done for a single-player experience and really wish the ability to separately position and control the characters was something you could do solo in 5 and 6, but the intended experience is kind of fundamentally different and does just kind of work here. That said, it's also kind of superfluous and doesn't change anything intrinsic about the gameplay, assuming you're playing smart and just locking Billy in a closet when you don't need him to carry keys or push something for you. The setting itself is kind of just a dull reflection of the far more inspired mansion and RE2 settings but isn't inherently bad, still succesfully capturing the mazelike dinginess the older RE games are really supposed to. Using a train for the first act is kind of stupid, though. Sounds fine on paper but when trying to work it into the broader setting a private train for Umbrella executives going between two facilities that are apparently within walking distance of each other is really dumb when thought about for more than a second. Billy is also stupid. Weirdly written character with weird tension with Rebecca who has both no impact or connection with the story at hand and less than none on the series as a whole. The second player really should have been Enrico, an established and likable character with a direct connection to Rebecca and the STARS, and I'm baffled they not only didn't go with him, but made up a complete write-in with no real substance who ♥♥♥♥♥ off to the woods to live as fugitive before probably being eaten by dogs or blown up with the city offscreen five minutes after the game ends. Rebecca on the other hand is of course an intrepid and charming wunderkind and we should all love her and be grateful there aren't too many less than tasteful shots or framing of her like we typically expect with Jill, so I'd say our core duo breaks even on quality here. The enemies are fine, too, but unfortunately other than James Marcus there isn't anything standout or nasty in this one - just assorted creepy-crawlies and Yet Another Tyrant. I'd dare say, easy and subjective as it is, this one really isn't scary. It's atmospheric and definitely has very tense moments, but this is driven more by score and the central loop's natural sense of tension rather than these elements successfully enmeshed with the grotesque or genuinely suspenseful. 
Overall, I'd say this is a typical Resident Evil game marred by earnest tedium and a plot, setting and characters that don't do nearly enough to overcome the more basic technical issues. It plays off as frivolous and annoying very quickly and I wouldn't recommend it to people unless they, like me, are in it for completionism. You're much better off just sticking to the REmake, as it is essentially the same game without any critical issues and a far more engaging throughline.

Resident Evil 0 is not a particularly good Resident Evil game. Compared to its other numbered peers in the PSOne/Gamecube era, it seems to struggle with what kind of story it wants to tell. It is neither as steeped in survival horror as its peers; nor has it quite hit upon the 'action horror' vibes that Capcom would later fully develop in Devil May Cry and eventually Resident Evil 4; which is still held up as a great example of a game hitting all the right action and horror notes very well.

Resident Evil 0's rooms tend to be cramped and action-heavy. There are many more enemies to had -- various event flags will trigger previously cleared rooms to populate with more enemies fairly steadily. The fixed camera angles usually discourage attempts to juke enemies or avoid combat. But there are also a lot more weapons and ammunition to be found for applying combat.

The two-character system isn't a lot of fun to actually play with. Most of the puzzles which require you to make use of both of them working together involve splitting them up to move to different rooms, effectively doubling the amount of backtracking you have to do from room to room in order to proceed. This backtracking issue is further exacerbated by the new inventory system, wherein the 'magic box' of the previous titles is done away with and replaced with a more 'realistic' system of having to leave items on the floor of the room you've left them in, and then having to go back to retrieve it when needed.

Most often, this results in a careful player simply designating a room as a 'drop' room and leaving all of your things in there. Essentially deconstructing the 'magic box' into something much more annoying and tedious. And you need to manage inventory a lot in this game because even spread among the two playable characters inventory space is at a premium with some items taking up two slots.

The enemy and boss design is lackluster and uninspired. The story is oddly toned; the Queen Leech looking more like a character that stepped out of a jRPG than a survival horror game.

Why the upvote, then? Because even through all the criticism, I can see that the design and development was trying to innovate and do different things with the formula. I think Capcom was trying not to fall into the Mega Man formula of simply releasing the same game every few years with a new coat of paint. Two playable characters going through the scenario together was new and different. The inventory management was new and different. Ramping down the survival horror a couple notches and raising the action and combat up a couple notches was something new and different. And it is through innovating and experimenting with formulas that greater ideas are formed.

A flawed game, but no less a labor of love. I can see the cracks but also the creative intensity. A game like Resident Evil 0 has to crawl so that Resident Evil 4 can run. I probably won't ever replay it. But I did enjoy having seen it through.

The atmosphere was creepy in the best way, and the partner system between Rebecca and Billy made the gameplay super fun and strategic. Loved the puzzles, the story, and the classic survival horror vibe.

[h2]Greetings, friends! Today we're diving into the archives of old-school Capcom to talk about a prototype that eventually became one of the most atmospheric horror titles in the series: Resident Evil Zero.[/h2]

[b]While many people first experienced the game on the GameCube, its story actually dates back to the 1990s. The project was originally planned as an exclusive for the Nintendo 64, and not on regular cartridges either, but for a planned peripheral that used compact discs. However, it quickly became clear that 64 megabytes of storage simply wasn't enough to realise the developers' ambitions. Hardware limitations were suffocating the project. Capcom ran into several issues. Nintendo cartridges were not only limited in capacity, but also extremely expensive to produce. The more ROM space or advanced chipsets a cartridge had, the more expensive it became. At the same time, competitors like Sony and Sega were releasing games on CDs, which were far cheaper to manufacture. This was one of the reasons why N64 games could cost 75 dollars or more, and releasing Resident Evil Zero on multiple cartridges would have killed any chance of commercial success. Until 1999, Capcom didn't even officially confirm that Resident Evil Zero existed. It was only thanks to producer Yoshiki Okamoto that fans learned the game was still in development, and initially still intended for the N64. However, market conditions made it clear that a shift was needed. All previous Resident Evil titles had come out on PlayStation 1, and moving the game to the GameCube turned out to be the right call. It allowed Capcom to ditch expensive cartridges, improve the design, and optimise loading times.[/b]

Resident Evil Zero is a prequel to the original Resident Evil from 1996. The story follows the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team and their trials in the Arklay Mountains. As with classic entries in the series, this is survival horror with an emphasis on resource management and puzzles. Combat takes a back seat here. The focus is on thinking ahead, planning, and making every bullet and healing item count. One of the game's key features is its two-character system. You control Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen, switching between them as needed. This adds depth to the gameplay: you can use one character to carry extra items and free up space. Items can now be dropped on the ground too, replacing the old magic storage boxes. It's convenient, but be prepared for some serious backtracking if you forget something important in another wing of the facility. The save system has also become harsher. To save your progress, you need an ink ribbon. There are no autosaves. This adds tension and forces you to think carefully before moving forward. Each character has unique abilities. Rebecca can mix herbs and chemicals but is physically weaker. Billy, on the other hand, can move heavy objects, use a lighter, and take more damage, but he can't mix healing items.

[i]The original script was partially rewritten to fit the new platform, but the overall atmosphere remained. Everything we love about classic Resident Evil is here: the dark interiors, limited resources, tense music, and that signature fear of what's waiting around the next corner.[/i]

The game is decent, although definitely worse than RE1R. The gameplay requires quite a bit of time to get used to because of the missing item box and the more combat-focused gameplay. Exploration is still decent but definitely worse than RE1R because of the lack of visibility of what rooms are completed. Most puzzles are quite boring and sluggish.

There are two real points that differentiate this game from its predecessor. Two characters and the new storage system.

The new storage system could have been a great addition to this game, being able to drop items wherever you want is great. Unfortunately, they decided to remove the storage boxes. Making half the gameplay just managing these items by continuously picking them up and dropping them. Most players will still want their items to be together, so you will just have a few rooms used as item boxes, which defeats the whole point. It also makes going to a new area a pain since you need to move all your stuff to it.

The second new thing is the two new characters you play at the same time. This was an enjoyable change of pace. Being able to instantly transition between them was pretty cool. There were also a few decent puzzles that used the two characters.

The environments are visually quite nice and aged well. The map design did not, there is a lot of backtracking, and I mean a lot. The game also loves to spawn enemies back in rooms that were completed, so if you decide to drop items in certain finished rooms (which I thought was the whole point), the game will punish you for it. Additionally, there are numerous instances in which the game abruptly splits the two characters, which can lead to "softlock" situations where you are forced to either reload a save or force through a section you are not ready to handle. This almost also means you have to backtrack. Some people like this way of making the game more difficult, I do not.

Bosses and enemy designs are mediocre, as expected since this is a prequel. The story is laughably bad, which does make it enjoyable in some way.

In conclusion, the game is still passable, but it is brought down by the numerous bad gameplay design decisions and laughable writing that could definitely benefit from a complete rewrite and overhaul.

Would only recommend for people that love Resident Evil and want more. And don't mind janky, frustrating gameplay and a lot of backtracking and door animations.

As much as I love the Resident Evil franchise, Resident Evil Zero ended up being one of the most miserable gaming experiences I’ve had.

I’ll admit, the beginning showed promise. The character-switching mechanic was responsive and brought something fresh to the series, which I appreciated. Unfortunately, that’s where the positives end.

I played on medium difficulty, and personally, I found the experience frustrating. Exploration felt more like a chore than engaging gameplay—mostly backtracking to find a key to unlock another area. The puzzles were tedious, often dragging on far too long (spending hours locating three obscure items isn't my idea of fun).

The combat didn’t help either. I know the series uses fixed cameras, but the gunplay felt clunky. Enemies soaked up bullets, turning every encounter into a resource-draining hassle. Healing items were sparse, and staying alive felt more about luck than skill—especially when paired with the overly powerful enemies.

Managing your inventory also came with many challenges. With no item box, I was constantly dropping and shuffling gear just to progress. Instead of adding tension, it became a repetitive and irritating burden.

As for the story, it's the usual corny RE fare—nothing particularly new or compelling there.

And lastly… those door animations. Have fun with them.

In the end, what started as a promising experience became a slog. I wanted to like RE0, but it just wasn’t for me.

Resident Evil 0 is infamous for being one of the most tedious games in the Resident Evil series. That said, this game is aesthetically amongst the best the franchise has to offer and experiments with some extremely unique mechanics.

The visuals and framing of Resident Evil 0 are unarguably amazing. From the moody train area to the grimy and health-violationy laboratory, this game is equal parts beautiful and haunting. My only gripe with the game's visuals are the often bland monster designs. Like RE1, I found that too many creatures were just a bigger version of a normal animal. Where I could look past that in the first entry of a novel franchise, it definitely feels like this game could have done a lot more to make its enemies stand out.

Where most people, myself included, take issue with the game is the item management system. Instead of space-time violating item boxes that allow for convenient storage and retrieval, RE0 makes you manually drop and move everything you collect. This change can lead to frustrating situations where significant backtracking is demanded. Another issue I had with the game was the sheer tedium of many enemies. There are micro stunlock monkeys, instakill frogs, and an absolute bullet sponge of a final boss. My issues with enemy design are also compounded by the fact that you are accompanied by a less than intelligent AI partner during many of these encounters leading to wasted resources and bogus game overs. That said, the puzzles built around this two player system are among the most interesting in the series and I can appreciate what CAPCOM tried to do.

I think this game has two failures that really hold it back from being amazing. The first, is that it punishes inexperience as opposed to rewarding experience. If you know what items you have to lug around and which enemies to avoid, the game feels a lot more balanced. I had previously watched a youtube playthrough of the game and found that the tricks I remembered from that really helped me avoid some absolute frustrations. If someone was going into this blind, I can definitely see needlessly annoying situations that could be avoided with some extra knowledge or better game design. 

Finally, my biggest problem with the game is that I found the first area to be significantly better than the rest of the game. The train is so unique in its setting and fits the game's mechanics perfectly. Its small enough to easily backtrack to dropped items, makes full usage of its verticality, as well as the two character system. This issue is compounded by the second area of the game being a complete opposite of the train. Its huge which demands more backtracking for items. The enemies in the mansion almost punish you for bringing your incompetent AI partner along. Worst of all, it greatly overstays its welcome and kills the pacing of the game.

Overall, I still enjoyed my time playing the game because of my previous knowledge and love of the franchise. It took me ten hours to complete on normal and I got it relatively cheap off humble bundle. If you are new to Resident Evil do not start with this game and play the first resident evil instead. Even then, I recommend searching up major tips for the game or completing it on the easiest difficulty to allow full enjoyment of its superb aesthetics and vibes.
