I enjoyed my time with Resident Evil 0, but it’s definitely not my favorite in the series.

First off, I really liked the aesthetic and atmosphere of the game. It has that classic RE charm with beautifully detailed backgrounds and a dark, gritty tone. Also, I really enjoyed playing as Rebecca, she’s an underrated character in the franchise and has a cool dynamic with Billy, who brings a more mysterious edge to the story.

That said… this game is not very intuitive. At all. Out of all the RE games I’ve played, this one felt like the most confusing. There are no clear objectives, no markers, no real guidance, you’re just thrown in and expected to figure it all out. That might appeal to purists, but for a first-time playthrough, it can feel like you're constantly wandering in circles, unsure of what you missed.

The enemy design is also a bit bland for my taste. Nothing too memorable, and while the idea of the leeches had potential, it never really hits the mark. The Tyrant fight was cool though, definitely a highlight.

This was my first time playing a classic fixed-camera RE, and at first the controls were a bit frustrating, but I got used to them surprisingly fast. There’s a certain charm to that old-school style, even if it comes with a bit of awkwardness.

Overall, it was a good discovery, but one I’d recommend mainly to longtime fans of the franchise who are interested in the lore. If you're more into fast-paced, action-oriented RE games, I think titles like RE2 Remake, RE3, RE4, RE5, or Village will be a better fit for you.

First of all, I’ll say this game doesn’t live up to any of today’s standards. It’s clunky, inconvenient, and at times, genuinely frustrating (I’ll explain below). its not for everyone.
But as long as you remember that this is a 2002 game and that it's only been updated in graphics and sound quality, you can just accept the problems and enjoy the game. I mean You're not playing an old game and expecting it to be like a new one.
In short: the game is excellent. The gameplay (most of it), puzzles, atmosphere, bosses, sound design, and environments are all excellent.

Now the issues:

1. Camera angles
Hands down the most frustrating part of the game. For most of the time, the camera is pointing at you towards the direction you're standing, and if there are monsters in front of or around a corner from you, you just can't spot them. So you walk forward thinking it's clear, and boom — you run into a zombie.
if you're trying to move backwards and the camera angle has changed, the direction of your walking has too. so if you want to keep going you need to switch keys but because you are holding S you are going backwards but this time towards the enemy and crash head first into it. And if the enemy leaves the screen due to the angle shift, you're either blind-firing or awkwardly waiting for it to walk into frame.

2. Some enemies feel lazy and uninspired
Most enemies are great, but some feel completely pointless — like the frog, which is just uncreative and dull. Same goes for the crows, bats, and monkeys. I get the idea, infected animals, but they are boring and not scary.
And even worse, their hp is unbalanced. crows die in one or two handgun shot, but dogs and monkeys take way too many bullets from way stronger weapons, and they’re fast, unpredictable, and often show up in groups and because of the terrible aiming mechanics, it is so hard to deal with them.

3. Leech Zombies (or whatever their name is)
These deserve their own category. They’re fast, tanky, have ranged attacks, and explode unless you kill them with fire or explosives. Overall, they’re an amazing enemy.
The problem? You can barely dodge them. Their ranged attack hits 90% of the time, and unless you have the right weapon, you either waste a ton of ammo or die trying.
the only way to dodge is to hide behind a corner or move to another room. Moving to a different room is inconvenient and when you hide behind a corner they come at you so fast that you can barely react. They always say it's better to dodge them, but that's hardly possible because they attack from a distance and if they're standing at the entrance to a passage that you have to go through a few times, you're just screwed.

4. No map labels or names
Areas on the map have neither names nor markings and in really big places like the training facility or the Factory and the Treatment Plant when you get an item in one place and to use it you have to go 3 floors down on the way to the other end of the map it takes so long and you forget the location of things which makes you do exhausting detours.

5. Item management is a nightmare
No item box. You just drop things wherever you want (usually in front of a typewriter). But when you change to another area, trying to get those items either means taking an insanely long walk. or losing them forever.
Because of that, I finished the last 3 areas of the game without the grenade launcher — even though I had 40 grenades on me. It's a system that seriously hurts the game.

Despite all of that and all the times when I got completely frustrated it's still an incredible game.
Yes, it's hard. Yes, it's outdated. But my experience with it was wonderful, and I do recommend it.

Resident Evil 0 serves as a narrative precursor to the iconic original Resident Evil, diving deeper into the origins of the T-virus and the early days of the STARS team. Released initially for the Nintendo GameCube and later ported to multiple platforms, it’s a visually impressive entry in the series that blends classic survival horror mechanics with some bold—if uneven—gameplay innovations.

The game follows rookie officer Rebecca Chambers and fugitive ex-soldier Billy Coen as they investigate a derailed train and a mysterious training facility, encountering grotesque biological experiments along the way. The story adds texture to the overarching Resident Evil mythos, though it doesn’t quite reach the narrative intrigue or character depth of later titles like Resident Evil 2 or Code: Veronica.

The environments are a standout. The Ecliptic Express, in particular, is one of the most atmospheric settings in the series, packed with claustrophobic tension and rich detail. The eerie silence, subtle music cues, and unsettling creature designs all contribute to a classic survival horror feel.

Resident Evil 0 introduces a unique partner system that allows players to switch between Rebecca and Billy on the fly. While this adds a new layer of strategy—encouraging cooperation for puzzles and resource management—it can also lead to frustration. The AI partner isn’t always reliable, and the system can feel cumbersome in tense combat scenarios.

One of the most divisive changes is the removal of the traditional item box. Instead, players drop and pick up items in the environment. This increases realism and forces more careful planning, but it also results in excessive backtracking and inventory micromanagement that can kill momentum.

Even decades after its original release, Resident Evil 0 remains visually striking. The pre-rendered backgrounds and character models hold up well, especially in HD remasters. The lighting is moody and deliberate, and the attention to detail enhances immersion. The voice acting is serviceable, though some lines suffer from awkward delivery—a staple of early Resident Evil games.

Resident Evil 0 is a flawed but fascinating installment in the franchise. It offers a rewarding challenge for longtime fans and deepens the lore in meaningful ways. However, its experimental mechanics and some outdated design choices might alienate newcomers or players accustomed to the more refined systems of later entries.

It’s not the strongest chapter in the Resident Evil saga, but it’s an atmospheric and memorable ride worth revisiting—especially for those curious about how the nightmare began.

I still remember playing this on the GameCube — jaw on the floor from how good the train looked, creeping through the dark with Rebecca, wondering who this random ex-con Billy was, and getting absolutely wrecked by zombie monkeys. Resident Evil 0 might be one of the more divisive entries, but there’s something special about it — and this HD Remaster gives it a second chance to shine.

Visually, it still holds up incredibly well. The pre-rendered backgrounds have been touched up nicely, the lighting is moody and immersive, and the audio work (from eerie ambiance to monster shrieks) brings the tension. It feels like classic RE — in the best way.

Gameplay-wise, this one sticks close to the survival horror roots, with fixed cameras, limited saves, and carefully managed resources. The partner zapping system (switching between Rebecca and Billy in real time) was ahead of its time and still leads to some really cool puzzle-solving and tense split-up moments. Yeah, it can be clunky at times — especially with no item boxes — but it adds a layer of strategy that’s grown on me over the years.

And here’s the best part: mods exist to make it better.
Want item boxes added in, or inventory tweaks? There are quality-of-life mods out there that smooth out some of the rougher mechanics without taking away the challenge. You can make it feel closer to REmake, or keep it classic — your choice.

The story leans into the campy side (leeches and operatic villains, anyone?), but it's all part of the charm. It's a prequel with cool lore bits and gives Rebecca the spotlight she never really got elsewhere in the series.

If you’re a fan of classic survival horror and you’ve already played REmake, this is a great companion piece. It’s a bit weirder, a bit less polished, but still a genuinely atmospheric, fun, and tense ride — especially with a few modern tweaks.

Underrated, stylish, and worth revisiting — this one deserves more love.

RE0 has several cheap 'gotcha!' moments which cannot be prepared for unless you are lucky, super paranoid, or read about them beforehand, e.g. the train brake sequence, or Centurion boss fight. I'm in the third camp. The game is fun only on subsequent playthroughs when you already know all of the cheap moments and are better at item management, and/or use the item box mod.

Tips for a first playthrough:
Swallow your pride and play on Easy. RE0 is childishly simple on this difficulty as it showers you with ammo and health items, while enemies have low health and deal minimal damage. It makes inventory management worse when it comes to overabundance of herbs, but ammo stacks to ridiculous levels so it’s of no concern. In any case, I was very glad I played it on Easy as I would have been frustrated to no end otherwise. Believe me, it’s better for you to experience it being too easy than whatever-the-f*ck Normal and Hard are on first playthrough.

Be prepared for cheap moments. I will try to avoid spoilers, but still add the tag just in case:[spoiler][olist]
[*]At the end of the train level there’s a timed sequence, so save regularly.
[*]There are two sections where Billy has to save Rebecca. Make sure he has a good weapon on him at all times.
[*]Before completing the Observatory tablet puzzle move all of your important stuff into the Observatory itself, especially the Hookshot.
[*]Seriously, do NOT forget about the Hookshot!
[/olist][/spoiler]
There's a few more, but on Easy they shouldn't much of a problem.

Leech Hunter side mode is boring, methodical extermination of enemies throughout the mansion, then picking up all Leech Charms and finally walking out the door. Congrats, you unlocked infinite Magnum.
Wesker Mode is a gimmicky and a bit half-assed mode added to the HD Remaster. Billy's model is swapped with RE5 Wesker, but all of his voice lines, aside from pain sounds and switching between solo and team modes, so during cutscenes it's Billy talking with the appearance of Wesker. His Death Stare attack is fairly cool, though useful only against zombies as it takes a while to charge.

Other issues I have is that RE0 early on ditches the interesting and fairly novel train setting for another mansion which is inferior to the Spencer Mansion in every conceivable way. Also, very narrow corridors making juking zombies nearly impossible unlike in RE1R. At least the static backgrounds are beautiful, similarly to Resident Evil Remake. Music is still great too.

Overall, without the item box mod the fun factor is around 3/10. With the mod it's around 6/10. Only for die hard Resident Evil fans. If you're not one of them, skip it.

The best thing I can say about this re-release is that the preservation of art, even bad art, is a good thing.

And believe me, this is BAD ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ art. 

Everything you've grown accustom to, is now harder. Not more punishing, not more reliant on skill or forethought, but the core mechanics harder to actually execute. It's a chore. A slog. You'll spend the entire game bogged down by additions and changes that serve no actual purpose other than change for changes sake. The control schemes are hampered and warped by the addition of multiple new buttons to make the partner-zapping system work.

Items are now a gargantuan task to manage if you do not already know the optimal path through the game. Every task you do will be accompanied by the fear of "Does my partner have enough items if the game arbitrarily decides that one of the two characters is now rendered unplayable by a puzzle or scripted boss". Every enemy provides a new opportunity for your partner to waste ammo because you forgot to take their gun away from them, or to get hit because despite all the dodging and weaving you can eek out of the movement, they'll get walloped/grabbed/monkey'd in your place. When an optimal strategy is "Leave your partner at the door, and just give them all the ♥♥♥♥ you don't want to carry", you'll be thinking whatever happened to the good 'ol days when item boxes were the norm.

Within all these mechanics is one throughline - they're all support structures. Resident Evil (2002) had such tight and form fitting interplay between mechanics and level design, that the desire to add something as jarring to that experience as a second player means everything else had been uprooted and shoddily replanted as a result. Once you realise this, it's hard to avoid. Every frustration, every pain point, every gnarled root jutting from hastily shovelled dirt is either a result of, or in service to that second player. 

The story could have only been written by someone with cliff-notes of the original game, because it succeeds in being both a terrible prequel, and a nonsensical narrative in it's own right. Don't worry, magic exists now for some inexplicable reason. Rebecca just didn't feel like bringing any of this up during the Spencer Mansion's plot and Billy died on the way back to his own planet.

If you're a new Resi fan, go into this game prepared. It isn't a good game. It's not irredeemable, it's just stagnant. By this point in the franchise, RE had become rusted, tired old playground. You remember when it used to be good, hell it used to be the shining, pastel bastion of your Saturday afternoons and all the diminutive thrills that gave you so much joy. 

You could go back, you're a year or two older sure, but what's stopping you? The swings still swing, the slides still slide, but not only have you grown just a little, the paint has chipped and the chains started to corrode. Adding a new, bigger slide won't fix that, and a lick of paint will only last as long as the last; It was time for an upgrade, Capcom knew it, the fans knew it, and the pundits knew it. It was time to scrap the old, returf the park and head for Spain.

Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is an updated version of an old-style survival horror game. The game has better graphics now, but most of the gameplay stays the same as before. Movement can be hard because of the control system, and aiming at enemies is not easy. The player needs to go back and forth a lot because there is not much space to carry items. These older game systems might not be good for people used to newer games.

The game gives players different places to explore and many types of enemies. There are also some puzzles to solve, and you play as two different characters. The player can try different game modes after finishing once, which gives more things to do. But during the main game, picking up items and fighting enemies can sometimes be hard because the controls do not always work well.

The graphics are much better than before, with sharp details and good lighting. Sounds in the game also help to make a scary mood. Voice acting is okay for the main characters but not great for the others. If someone can manage old game problems, this remaster still gives a complete horror game experience with many parts to explore and replay. I played most of the game in offline mode due to network issues, so the achievements haven't been unlocked.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster may not be the best choice for new players who have only played the latest games and not in order. The slow controls, limited item space, and backtracking can be hard to get used to. But for those willing to try an older game style, it still gives a full horror experience with improved graphics and sound.

Note: Even though Resident Evil 0 has small spoilers for Resident Evil 1, I played it first because I saw many reviews and articles saying the game has some problems. It's also set before RE1 in the story, so I thought it was better to play it first, even though I usually like playing games in the order they were released. I figured it was better to get through RE0 first and save RE1, which is generally more polished and better paced, for afterward. I usually like to play games in release order, but in this case, I thought it made more sense to play the harder and more flawed game first before moving on to the better one.

Review:

After playing through the entirety of Resident Evil Zero, I was surprised at how much I genuinely enjoyed it. The combat takes a bit of adjusting—especially if you're coming from the smoother mechanics of the Resident Evil 2, 3, or 4 remakes—but once you get the feel for tank controls and fixed camera angles, it becomes part of the charm.

Where this game really stands out is in its puzzles. They’re clever, layered, and at times absolutely brutal if you’re going in blind. If you’ve never played a classic Resident Evil game before, you’ll probably want to have a guide nearby—some of the logic is pretty old-school, and there were definitely moments where I hit a wall (especially during a long session). That said, the satisfaction of figuring them out is top-tier.

The partner system, unique to this game, is also a fun twist. You switch between Rebecca and Billy in real time, and the game uses that to create some really engaging puzzle and resource-management scenarios. No item boxes here—you’re dropping things on the ground and managing what you can carry, which adds tension and strategy.

My only real complaint comes toward the end. Rebecca’s chemical mixing kit lets you create multiple solutions, but I accidentally made the wrong one and got stuck. I had to consult a guide to figure out how to discard it and make the battery acid I needed. It was a minor roadblock but felt unnecessary that late in the game.

That aside, I loved the story. It adds meaningful depth to the Resident Evil lore and gives us a closer look at Umbrella’s early bio-weapon experiments. Rebecca was always a favorite of mine growing up, so seeing her in a leading role was awesome. And Billy? Honestly, he grew on me. Kind of a shame he disappears from the series after this.

Final Thoughts:
Resident Evil Zero is a hidden gem in the franchise. It’s atmospheric, puzzle-heavy, and totally worth playing if you're a fan of survival horror. If you're up for a little challenge and don’t mind the classic style, this one delivers. I can’t wait to dive into Wesker Mode next.

First of all, I must say that I really liked the idea of a Resident Evil featured in a train. Being in a closed environment enhances the claustrophobic feelings that should exist in a horror game, along with the fear that the train may derail. However the game abandons the idea early and for what? To take the characters back to a mansion and tread familiar ground. I like fanservice but I hate that they abandoned a good idea for a lame callback to the original game.
Secondly, resource management...this game abandons the boxes that were in the original to allow the characters to just leave stuff on the floor. While it makes sense, this creates two problems: the first problem is that to take back the item you have to be exactly above it TO THE PIXEL. So, have fun if you have left an item anywhere close to an area transition. The second problem that I can see, is that if you want something, you have to backtrack.
The third thing that they did, was that this game has two characters that you can switch through freely during gameplay. I will give them credit for this. It's a very nice idea and could create some good ideas for puzzles. However, they ruined this as well by adding softlocks. For example, there is this centipede boss that captures Rebecca, so have fun playing with Billy and what he had in hand (I actually ran out of Billy's bullets and had to finish the thing with a knife). If you didn't know you were changing characters at a point (and unless you were playing with a guide at another tab you couldn't know it), you might as well just reload. I hope you saved recently.
And for the first time in the series you can see why fixed camera angles can be problematic...there was this humanoid slimy thing (don't know what it's called) that was actually hitting me from beyond the camera. If you want to make a fixed camera angle game, either don't feature ranged enemies or have a way to close the distance without taking damage.

TL;DR: Unless you are someone who wants to see every Resident Evil game, I suggest you skip this (and even if you want every RE game, get this on discount). The train was a cool idea that was abandoned too early and it has a lot of stuff that can annoy you. I'll give it a 5/10.

Resident Evil 0 : By Triple F

"Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster" brings the 2002 GameCube prequel to modern platforms with updated visuals, improved sound design, and minor quality-of-life enhancements. As a prequel to the original Resident Evil, this entry explores the origins of the T-virus outbreak and the downfall of the Umbrella Corporation’s research team. While the game successfully retains its classic survival horror essence with fixed camera angles, intricate puzzles, and limited resources, it also carries over some of the original's gameplay quirks, which may divide players.

One of "Resident Evil 0’s" most unique features is its partner-zapping system, which allows players to switch between rookie S.T.A.R.S. officer Rebecca Chambers and escaped convict Billy Coen at any time. This mechanic replaces the traditional item storage boxes, forcing players to carefully manage inventory by dropping items in accessible locations. While this adds an extra layer of strategy, it can also lead to frustrating backtracking, especially in areas where enemies respawn. The AI partner mechanics are functional but not flawless, with occasional pathfinding issues and a tendency for the AI-controlled character to take unnecessary damage.

Visually speaking, the HD Remaster does an excellent job of modernizing the game’s pre-rendered backgrounds, character models, and lighting effects. The environments, ranging from the eerie, blood stained Ecliptic Express to the decrepit Umbrella training facility are brimming with atmospheric detail. Capcom preserved the game’s tense ambiance while improving texture resolution and character animations. However, since the game was originally designed for standard definition, some background elements appear slightly blurred when played in widescreen HD. The addition of modern controls alongside the classic tank controls gives players more flexibility in movement, though the game remains firmly rooted in its old-school design philosophy.

The game’s sound design remains a highlight, reinforcing the horror atmosphere with eerie ambient noises, unsettling enemy groans, and a tense orchestral score. The voice acting and dialogue are campy, in line with the franchise’s classic charm, but some performances, especially Rebecca’s can feel a bit stilted. The remaster includes an improved sound mix, ensuring that everything from distant thunderclaps to the guttural growls of leech zombies is crisp and immersive.

Combat and enemy variety are both strong, though some aspects of the gameplay feel a bit dated. Standard zombies, monstrous insects, and the grotesque Leech Man provide a solid range of threats, but enemy encounters can feel repetitive due to limited weapon options and awkward partner AI. The boss fights, particularly against the mutated centipede and the final leech-infested antagonist, are well-designed but sometimes suffer from rigid movement mechanics that make dodging attacks frustrating. The limited inventory system forces players to make tough decisions about which weapons and healing items to carry, heightening the tension.

As a prequel, "Resident Evil 0" delivers an engaging story that sheds light on the origins of the series’ lore, but its pacing can be inconsistent. While Billy and Rebecca’s dynamic is interesting, Billy’s character arc ultimately feels unresolved, as he disappears from the series after this game. Some plot points, such as the villainous Dr. Marcus and his army of leeches, verge on the absurd, but they fit well within the franchise’s signature blend of science fiction and horror. Longtime fans will appreciate the additional background on Umbrella’s sinister experiments, even if the narrative lacks the depth of later entries.

Ultimately, "Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster" is a faithful modernization of a divisive yet fascinating entry in the franchise. It excels in atmosphere, presentation, and classic survival horror mechanics while retaining some of the original game’s clunkier design choices. Players who appreciate old-school Resident Evil gameplay will find a lot to enjoy, while newcomers might struggle with its punishing inventory system and rigid mechanics. Despite its flaws, the remaster preserves a crucial piece of Resident Evil history, making it a worthwhile experience for fans of the series.

Resident Evil 0 is nowhere close to the best title in the series . It's not the worst... that belongs to 6. But it's not great. The item system is frustrating, vastly limiting you to what you can hold, while also requiring you to carry around large items throughout the entire game. You can drop them wherever you want, but this leads to backtracking if you want them.. And of course... the game wants you to have them. They'll often leave you ammo for weapons you've long dropped leading you to try to figure out just where exactly you left them.

The story is also nothing to write about. It's a prequel game meaning anything this title will throw at you is inconsequential. It adds a little bit o' lore to Spencer and Marcus as well as a few scenes that show Wesker... and Birkin in a more sinister tone. Which while Birkin has never been portrayed as a good person or father, he's never came across as just plain evil like he does in here.

One thing this game excels at is the graphics and Set/Level design. Being originally released on the Gamecube, the character models don't look the best, However the backgrounds are created by HQ photo imaging slapped on static joined 3d models leading to the game looking really really nice for a RE title even at the time on the GC. And the Rooms are all pretty memorable and flow nicely together as you're solving the mansions puzzles. 

In the end, this game is frustrating and skippable but a solid Survival horror title. If you need to scratch that itch of S/H,this game is for you. If you're a massive RE fan and want to consume every bit of RE Games and lore, this game is for you. If you're somewhat interested in the story or more casually consume RE media, You probably won't be missing much a 5 minute youtube video can't recap.

The true "Evil" in this game are its level designers and mostly the one who brought up the idea of its item box limitation. if you like suffering a lot then this is your game.

(First review among the canon resident evil Series based off their story, gameplay, mechanics, puzzles, atmosphere, and overall design)

Story - Fairly simple bridging the incidents that occur between the first three resident evil games. Adds some context to characters like Birkin and Wesker by showing their prior cooperation during the ensuing downfall of umbrella. The Progenitor virus doesn't really make much sense and capcom must agree considering how it never really shows up again in the canon story line. Rebecca and Billy are a decent duo with not a whole lot of chemistry but it is early capcom dialogue so that is what's to be expected. 

Gameplay/Mechanics - Tank Controls were never my favorite in games so I am a little bias in that regard, but even in despite of that I've enjoyed games with asymmetric cameras and tank movement, however this is not one of them. The camera placements are easily one of the hardest challenges in the game, struggling to keep an affixed point of view on what you're aiming at in the often confined little slices of room you have access to see. Crits happen very few and very far in between which also added to the games difficulty in a not super fun way. Even after acquiring the upgrade to increase the handgun's chances i only made a total of 6 crits throughout the entire playthrough. This is mostly due to the fact that most of the enemies fought in RE:0 aren't normal zombies. but animal zombies of many varieties. Bugs, roaches, birds, bats, monkies, hunters. The game is chock full of annoying little bastards that make me wish i could point the ingame shotgun at myself. The resource management is typical and fairly fun and well thought out surprisingly and makes for a fun variety of difficulty in the game, however due to the other unnecessary factors that increase the game's difficulty it can often feel tedious and even infuriating, especially when paired with the fact that inventory increases do not happen. Instead you are supposed to juggle your items between both Billy and Rebecca who each only have 6 slots. Fortunately though you're able to drop things and pick them back up :D leading to a metric ♥♥♥♥ load of backtracking that rivals any game I've ever played. an item that is used once in the first chapter will become seemingly useless, and due to the incredibly limited inventory space the item is typically left behind, and only after 2 whole chapters of the game does that item become required, and now it's time to walk aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaall the way back to where you dropped it. Also i didn't preface this enough but the monkies are the worst enemy in gaming history those little ♥♥♥♥ balls are too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fast and have no stun potential unless they die after like 5 shotgun blasts. Overall the gameplay is sloppy and infuriating with so many unnecessary factors to artificially increase the game's length and difficulty. 
 
Puzzles - Most of the puzzles are decently crafted, however they leave a lot of the solving up to interpretation, to the point of some puzzles only being solved after throwing attempt after blind attempt at it until the answer accidentally happens. Many of the puzzles require items that get left far behind due to the limited inventory system so the amount of backtracking for them is wild. Overall I feel like the puzzles in this RE game detract from the overall experience and don't achieve what they were set out to do.
Atmosphere - Incredible and breathtaking. Even after all this time the game looks utterly incredible. The use of lighting and shadows in every area is so intricately made to cause tension and unease, while saverooms often feel warm and inviting. The graphical fidelity of individual rooms can be downright incredible, the chess room in the training facility stands out particularly in my mind, along with the cable car room under the church. The music is also very well done, and while sometimes it can be a bit overbearing especially whenever a leech monster shows up. It overall is a great part of the game and most of the reason that I stomached through the entire experience. 

Final Thoughts: If I had played this game on gamecube when it first came out I'd probably have much higher to say about this title, but the unfortunate truth is that it simply doesn't age very well. The gameplay and its mechanics especially, falling incredibly short of the RE experience I am fond of. The most positive things i can say about the game is that is still looks very good and has incredible sound and level design in terms of atmosphere, and it's not super long.

Honestly, this game is incredibly underrated in my opinion. The story is interesting, the puzzles are not too dificult but not too easy either, the weapons all have their own feel to them. The only criticism I have is that the voice acting is a bit silly but it just adds to the game's cheezy charm. Highly recommended.

As a Resident Evil Veteran, I have long put off playing RE0 as many people have criticized it over the years, be it for its story that adds very little to the overall lore, or the gameplay issues.

I, for one, see myself vindicated in having put off this game. I find it incredibly frustrating to play and I am going to probably put it down.

Let us start off: There is no storage boxes in this game, this makes inventory management a NIGHTMARE. You have to drop items in a safe spot (But not too many or else the game will yell at you for it because the game room can only have so many items in it apparently).

Then on top of that, there are already 2 parts where I was forced into a Game Over, the first one happens on the train where you enter a room and it will start a timed sequence in which you have to run across the entire train, past respawned enemies and then solve 2 (!) puzzles before the timer runs out, or get a game over.

The other one was me activating an item in the Mansion and then being forced into a bossfight despite not carrying any ammo on me. This lead to one of my partners being "In danger" as I had to slowly run back to the lobby because I ran out of ammo, grab some, then re-enter the room to finish off the boss while my partner was still being pummeled by it.

Then on top of that: I have to constantly babysit an AI that I cannot control well. It is either constantly shooting at something and wasting ammo, or I have to set it to idle where it will freely have a Zombie munch on it... The only workaround for not having to deal with Partner AI is to leave them in a safe spot, which then leaves me with 6 less inventory slots and relegates them to a glorified storage box, until the game forces me to bring them somewhere for a coop puzzle.

The pacing is just terrible, if I take ammo and healing items with me I don't have any space for the several amounts of key items the game throws at me, and if I don't take ammo or healing items with me, I risk one of my two characters dying and forcing me to replay a chunk of the game again (Which has just happened, so you could see this as a ragepost or a skill issue, or whatever...)

This game is just such a step down from REmake, in REmake all of your deaths ARE at least your own fault, inventory management is your own fault. But in this, inventory management is a chore as you spend more time organizing your inventory than actually playing the game and exploring the world...

This game would have absolutely benefitted from a Online COOP mode of some kind...

Maybe I'll stick with it, maybe not. But man do I wish I was playing REmake instead right now...

Pros:
+ Runs on 120 Hz refresh rate
+ Killing enemies feels satisfying, especially headshots (although scoring them is painfully rare).
+ Fair diversity in environments
+ Environments have a decent design, puzzles are reasonable (even if a bit too easy)
+ Sound design is good. Music is fitting and builds ambience
+ Allows to use mouse when navigating inventory and files
+ Two protagonists is an interesting idea. It's fairly well executed, too: you need to use both characters to advance and solve puzzles.

Cons:
- Story is surface-level. There's basically just one major plot twist.
- Characters are flat. There could be more nuance - for example, Billy and Rebecca could've had different comments on the environment and objects. It doesnt matter if you play Billy or Becca - they always give similar comments on everything when exploring.
- After [spoiler] rescuing Rebecca the second time [/spoiler], she kind of gets this stigma of "Damsel in Distress". It doesn't help either that when she finds Billy in [spoiler] the water treatment plan [/spoiler], she really doesn't save his life - doing that would've been a good example of mutual teamwork, and how both need each other, both being as dependent on the other person. Despite the ending [spoiler] kind of leaning towards Rebecca helping Billy [/spoiler], she's the one needing help most of the time.
- Gunplay is janky. Aiming is too slow. Shooting animations lock your character on place for too long (shotgun...)
- Camera angles are horrible. Switching from angle to another, it's hard to keep moving since the controls become reversed. I hated this. It'd be nice if you could keep moving in the same direction by holding down the key and without other keys resetting your angle.
- Inventory management is very bad. In a way, having to choose where to leave stuff is an interesting idea on paper, but it doesn't work with such small inventory size. There should be more slots, and separate slots for different ammo types.
- Too much running back and forth. The game suffers from lack of transitional spaces to reduce the need to run around same rooms again and again.
- The F*CKING doors! Jesus Christ, I don't want to spend such large amount of playtime watching some stupid doors open! This is the WORST DESIGN CHOICE I have EVER encountered in a video game. This single design choice ALONE forces me to give this game a negative review. The door animations build some atmosphere, yes, but the execution is SO BAD. The doors should have an opening animation only the FIRST TIME you open them. It's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid that the player must watch the same animation when entering some old, explored room for the hundredth time......
- I appreciate difficulty in video games, but the horrible camera angles and accidentally not having molotovs in my inventory etc. led to so many useless deaths. I played the game for 15hrs, but the save file had about 9 hrs total when finishing the game. 6 hours went into reloading saves because of bad gameplay experience. The game felt like a damn chore, not an experience (let alone an enjoyable one).
- Molotovs are too hard to throw. The aiming is horrible and the throwing animation is janky and painfully slow, considering how fast the mimics move and hit.

4.5/10. With gameplay improvements and redesigning the doors the game would've been enjoyable (while the story also needs more depth). However, I cannot recommend the game like this. I wanted to like this, but there are too many barriers making it unenjoyable an experience. In fact, I think this game would've been better as a big DLC for RE1. The story is so bland that it's hard to see this as a separate game, but instead as a tie-in for the events of RE1. There simply isn't enough to the story to make it seem like an individual gaming experience.

The prototype for Resident Evil 5.

Many feel mixed on RE0, and I tend to lean more towards liking it over disliking it. I think it has enough charm to it that it deserves some love, and it did take some risks with the gameplay - some of which paid off, and some didn't. 

I think one of the better ideas to come out of RE0 was the item-dropping system. Unlike previous REs and their interconnected storage boxes, RE0 let's you drop items literally anywhere. 

This does of course come at a cost of having fewer inventory slots, which is kinda where the problems start rearing their head. Unlike previous REs, 0 felt it was a good idea to make items like the shotgun and other longer weapons take up two inventory slots as opposed to just one. This doesn't sound too bad until you realize you only have six slots per both characters.... yeah.... lots of inventory management in this game.

If RE0 were to have a subtitle, it would be Inventory Management: The Game. When I said this was a prototype for RE5, I wasn't kidding. In RE5, where you are limited to 9 slots and will spend a lot of time in between areas managing what weapons and healing items you have, 0 was doing the same in 2002. 

And speaking of RE5, how about that partner system? Interestingly enough, I feel 0 did a hell of a lot better job with having an AI controlled character with you. You can instruct the AI character to wait in certain areas and even switch to them to double up your efforts of exploring. This is something that I think RE5 massively failed with when it comes to its AI. Not being able to switch between Chris and Sheva and not being able to command them to wait in one area really kinda screwed that game's systems. Just kinda seems like Capcom isn't playing their own games because I don't know how you can design a game in 2002 with this AI system, and then in 2009, go "Yup, this system we're making now is totally better than anything we've had before. Totally."

So, a better AI system than what came after, and an inventory dropping mechanic that can work with the right items as long as the items aren't two-slotted and aren't that dreaded Hookshot item: If you are brand spanking new to this game, don't leave the Hookshot behind. The game actually punishes you for doing so by having you deal with the Eliminators...

...the Eliminators. When people talk about RE0 being the black-sheep of the RE family, I can't help but feel that the Eliminators are one of the reasons why. They are zombified monkeys/chimps that are smaller than the player, jump around a lot, and as a result are hard to shoot. And they have a tendency to stun lock you. Just the perfect enemy, y'know. In a game where you are using tank-controls, and most other enemies are shambling, slow, or rarely ever get in your face unless you let them, the Eliminators are the caveat to all that. They will get close to you and they will hit you. So make sure you got a shotgun or grenade launcher handy because that rinky dink pistol ain't gonna cut it. 

Then there's the story. As with any RE game, the story is... eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeh. I think RE0's is on the weaker side, especially when you consider that this is supposed to be the tale of how Rebecca ended up in the RE1 Mansion to begin with. Her attitude in RE1 just simply doesn't make sense regarding all the crap she goes through here. And the character of Billy is just another Capcom-Throwaway. Kind of a shame too because of the two characters, I find Billy's backstory to be way more interesting - they could make a prequel to this game to tell his story. Call it RE-1. 
The villian in this game... well, to put it simply, Wesker he is not. Saddler he is not. Alexia he is not. He's extremely underwhelming and forgettable. 

So all this game really has to rely on is its gameplay, and if you have played the RE1 Remake or the original RE1, 2, or 3, you'll fall in line with what's going on here even with the changes in inventory management. It offers a solid RE experience albeit with some quirks that will either make or break your experience. I wouldn't recommend this game to brand new players of the RE series. Try out RE1 first then come to this game. 

It does offer its own exclusive side-game as most RE games of the time did: Leech Hunter mode. Again, most people seem mixed on this mode. I find it to be the better experience than the main campaign. (Again, to draw another comparison to RE5, I found its Mercs mode much better than its campaign). Basically, imagine if you could explore the RE1 Mansion with most doors already being opened, and all you have to do is just pick up some special items in each room to win. The catch being: there are enemies in each room, and the special items you find cannot be dropped once you pick them up. I think most players when they play this for the first time make the mistake of picking up the Leeches as they find them, and as such, lose out on inventory space - that's not how to play Leech Hunter. You want to go around and basically be the Exterminator of the Training Facility and just kill every single enemy in every single room before you start collecting any Leeches. It's fun to do it this way because you can start experimenting with which weapons would be best to take with you into certain rooms. 

But that's RE0 for ya - a polarizing addition to the franchise that I think does more good than bad (unlike another polarizing entry *cough* RE6 *cough*). It took some risks with inventory management and AI, and I think most of them worked. I think if this game were to be remade, most of the gameplay wonkiness could be fixed and therefore could be seen as a highlight of the franchise (especially if they fix the story weirdness between this and RE1. Maybe don't make Rebecca the main character? Maybe Enrico instead. Would explain how he knew someone was a traitor and how he ended up in the cave in the first game - imagine if you knew he went through all this crap prior to getting there.)

[b]I'll give you the TLDR version before the main post: I gotta say that RE0 is a maaaaajor downgrade from RE1/2/3 (the OG versions). Capcom had interesting ideas for RE0, but they were poorly implemented. And somehow they picked what was awesome about RE1 Remake and did the complete opposite in RE0, which is baffling, considering both remakes came out in the same year. This is the only game that I've ever played in my life that was actively trying to annoy me. Last, but not least, this is also the first time that I have given a game an in-depth negative review. It's that bad. (I kinda feel like AVGN now lol)[/b]

Fortunately, RE0 Remaster is on its way, as far as I know!

---

Lemme preface the post with this: different people like different things, right? Cool. But there's no way you've played the classics and enjoyed this one. (I guess?) If you actually enjoyed it, I kindly ask you to explain why.

With that out of the way, I wanna let you know that I went into RE0 completely blindfolded. Didn't read a single positive or negative review about it, didn't watch any sort of gameplay on YouTube, nothing. I just got done with RE1 HD after 5 back-to-back playthroughs (which was a blast), downloaded RE0, installed a few QoL mods and pressed "New Game".

Okay, moving on! I'll start with the pros, alright?

First, I really liked the soundtrack. The theme for the Save Room is soothing, the BGM that plays during more intense parts is spot on. Bravo, Capcom. The pre-rendered backgrounds are STUNNING, and don't look dated at all, even in 2025. The in-game textures are a bit better than the ones in RE1 HD, I think. The menus/UI/fonts as well. I also liked how you can upgrade the starter handgun, it was definitely a welcome addition. And, that's it.

Like I said, I couldn't bring myself to finish the game, and I promise you that I tried to like it: on top of having a few QoL mods enabled, I changed from Normal to Easy mid gameplay because I was on the verge of soft-locking myself. I played it wearing headphones in the evening, lights out, I took my time to go through the rooms and soak in the atmosphere, the whole package. Unfortunately, I stopped after the giant bat fight (ugh ... so annoying) and dropped it like a hot potato. Fortunately, after that terrible experience, I was relieved that I didn't need to backtrack to get the Hookshot because I decided to uninstall this sum b*tch.

Now, onto the major issues and then I'll move to the lesser ones:

1) Inventory management and backtracking are a drag, Good Lord. In RE1 you have item boxes + typewriters placed in convenient locations, dropping and grabbing stuff is seamless and takes you like 15 seconds at most. In RE0, I found myself taking easily 1+ minutes to drop and exchange stuff from Billy to Rebecca and vice versa. And you NEED to manage your inventory way too often for my taste. Those 1+ minutes add up quite fast. Bigger items like the Shotgun/Grenade Launcher/Hookshot take up 2 inventory slots. May I ask why, Capcom?

2) Regarding enemies and combat/gameplay: the zombies are okay, I liked the narrow corridors in the train with them. Eliminators are a pain in the ass, they move too fast for a game with the classic RE formula/mechanics, and unless the AI miraculously decides to shoot them down along with your character, you're better off unequipping your weapon and trying to run past them. Boss fights are BORINGGGGGG, they're basically giant versions of animals (wow, how creative!). Proto Tyrant seems to be okay, Tyrants are cool. The bats fight is so infuriating, I can't even put it into words. For some reason, blasting enemies doesn't feel satisfying at all, even when you get a critical shot. It's hard to explain. All in all, it feels like playing a running + item management simulator instead of a proper survival horror game. Also, I miss the defensive items like the dagger or hand grenade, they were a cool addition to the gameplay in RE1.

3) The plot and characters and weak, boring, uninspired. Young James Marcus singing opera for leeches wearing a night-gown, what?! There's a huge plot regarding Rebecca (you know what I mean). William Birkin, Wesker and James Marcus barely interact with the main characters. Bravo Team is nowhere to be seen, the game gives us NOTHING about them, even though they're firmly tied to the RE1 plot and play an important role there, and SHOULD have played an important role in RE0. But no, it's all about a Final Fantasy-esque so-called villain and his leeches, and other nonsensical stuff. The plot is superficial and a missed opportunity to tell us more about Umbrella's background. Billy Coen shouldn't even exist, he doesn't play an important role in the franchise AT ALL. His background is dumb and his interactions with Rebecca are bland. (although I must say that the: "You've killed 23 people? I won't judge you." line is quite something)

4) Difficulty: Normal is way too hard for a casual gameplay, I had to change to Easy which ended up being too easy, but that's ok. At least I had ammo to spare to obliterate all of those annoying apes. Relying on your partner to help you fight enemies is a no-go and makes the game harder than it needs to be. You're better off leaving Rebecca in a safe room as a moving item box, which kills the point of having the tag system in the first place. The thing is: there are scripted parts of the game where you HAVE to play with either Rebecca or Billy, so if for some reason one of them are not carrying a decent gun and ammo you'll have to reset. Pretty cool huh?

5) Controls: janky, unresponsive. Baiting zombie attacks feels so weird and stiff. If they did it right in RE1, why couldn't they replicate the controls in RE0? Changing directions while walking or running feels wrong and wonky, the character stops for half a second every time you change directions. The layouts are completely different from RE1, and they're awkward to use. The animations are rather slow, for whatever reason.

6) Voice acting: RE1 had good-ish voice acting in general, some cutscenes are a bit silly though, that's alright. But in RE0 the voice acting is so much weaker, like the actors are not trying AT ALL. They sound defeated and bored. It really kills the atmosphere and hinders the non-existent storytelling aspect of the game.

7) The scenario/maps: the train is the best part of the game, hands down. Like I said, I truly enjoyed engaging the zombies in the train section. The Training Facility feels like a cheap version of the Spencer Mansion, that's very blatant. It feels like more of the same, but somehow worse.

8) Atmosphere: doesn't feel creepy at all, except for the train part. It felt like I was playing a more action-oriented game than a survival horror one. Again, RE1 does it masterfully, the ambiance is there.

Again, if you liked RE0, more power to you! But saying that RE0 is objectively a good RE game is preposterous, unless you've never played a classic RE before. I'm a big fan of the franchise and have played almost all of the classics + a couple of the newer ones, so I can confidently say that RE0 is a terrible RE game.

Thanks for reading!

I know that RE Zero is not everyone's favorite game, but to be honest, I liked this game, very much and enjoyed my time with it.  Yes, I missed the itemboxes and removing them for this game was a mistake, but by doing so the game differentiates itself from other games in the franchise and allows for different types of scenarios with different types of decision making throughout.  Being able to play as two characters at the same time was, in my opinion, a brilliant idea and the core gimmick that makes this game different and good.  This is something that I would definitely like to see again in some form in a future RE title.

Is this game as good as RE 1?  No, but it's good enough and most of the game's drawbacks can actually become its strengths if you approach them under a different light.  My advice to any person that hasn't played this game yet is not to think about RE 1 Remake and how *that* game did things and instead embrace Zero for its differences.  If you can do that you will find yourself loving it for its uniqueness.

Also, do not play this game for the first time on Hard Mode (take it from someone that learned that lesson the hard way).  Play it on Easy or Normal first, learn the mechanics, read guides if necessary (some guides in the Steam community are very useful and helped me a lot) and only *then* try the game on Hard.  Playing it on Hard is an interesting and highly rewarding experience, but if you approach it without understanding the game first then it might become frustrating more than challenging and fun so play the game first on an easier difficulty and if you liked it enough and want to challenge yourself further then tackle the Hard Mode.

Resident Evil 0 serves as a prequel to the iconic survival horror series, shedding light on the events that led to the infamous Spencer Mansion incident. 
Originally released in 2002 and later remastered in HD, the game introduces new mechanics and a fresh narrative while maintaining the series' signature tension and atmosphere.
The story follows rookie S.T.A.R.S. officer Rebecca Chambers and escaped convict Billy Coen as they team up to survive a nightmare involving mutant creatures and the twisted origins of the Umbrella Corporation. 
The dynamic between the two characters is engaging, with their contrasting backgrounds adding depth to the narrative.
What sets Resident Evil 0 apart is the introduction of the "partner zapping" system, which allows you to switch between Rebecca and Billy at will. 
This mechanic adds a layer of strategy, as each character has unique abilities, Rebecca can mix herbs, while Billy is stronger and immune to certain status effects. 
However, managing two characters can sometimes feel cumbersome, especially during tense combat situations or intricate puzzles.
The remastered visuals are stunning, with enhanced textures, lighting, and detail that breathe new life into the atmospheric environments. 
From the eerie confines of a doomed train to the sprawling Umbrella Training Facility, the settings are as hauntingly beautiful as they are deadly.
While Resident Evil 0 offers plenty of the franchise’s signature scares and challenging puzzles, it’s not without its flaws. 
The decision to forgo the traditional item box system in favor of dropping items anywhere can lead to frustrating inventory management, especially when backtracking becomes necessary.
Despite its quirks, Resident Evil 0 is a worthy addition to the series. 
It expands the lore, delivers plenty of heart-pounding moments, and introduces mechanics that, while divisive, offer a unique twist on the classic formula.
Not quite as iconic as its predecessors, but still a chilling and atmospheric journey for fans of survival horror.

By far the worst of the Resident Evil games in my eyes, not just in terms of the classic formula, but within the series overall. You can say whatever you want about RE3make being too short and cutting off a lot from the original, but at least it's a game that isn't designed to irritate and annoy you.

It has an interesting idea behind the premise of two protagonists that have to work together to solve puzzles, but God, it botches it so badly, it's not even funny. How about starting with the inventory, yeah? Both Billy and Rebecca have only six inventory slots, like Chris in RE1, but there are no item boxes, so when your inventory runs out, you gotta drop stuff on the floor and if you need it later, come back to that same room. The problems start arising when items like the Shotgun, Grenade Launcher and the Grappling Hook take up TWO slots, it was already bad enough having only six slots, but the backtracking these three items force on you is insane and highly irritating.

Then there's the problems with combat, the difficulty curve feels all over the place: enemies feel a lot more spongy this time, maybe because they were designed with the two player characters attacking at the same time, but you can't even avoid them easily as the crammed corridor design (which does work great in the RE1make) completely screws everything over because you're walking around as two characters instead of just one which makes you a larger, easier target with no room to maneuver yourselves and as a result you or your AI controlled partner get hit; speaking of which, the partner AI is simple but at least works well enough I guess, there's only two modes: Attack and Idle, so there's not much to ♥♥♥♥ up there, but you still gotta manage their items and inventory, which does add to the annoyance and tedium.

The Voice Acting is bad, but not in the funny bad way that the RE series has, more in the... uninteresting and dull kinda way, there's a few standout performances, like Marcus towards the end of the game, but even he is absent in any real capacity for most of it.

That leads me nicely into the story, it's a cool idea: discovering the exact moment that will trigger a chain reaction and cause the entire series to happen, but it's handled in such a boring way, there's nothing to hold on to. Oh sure, the files and dossiers you find across the game tell stuff that would be interesting to see, but even then, it's written so plainly that I don't care.

Rebecca and Billy have zero character as well, hell, Rebecca's presence here creates a plot hole in RE1, where she can handle stuff like a giant bat, a couple Tyrants and, more importantly, several Hunters, but then in RE1 Chris has to save her from a single Hunter (I know you could argue it's because she was tired from the events of this game, but that would hinge on her at least trying to defend herself in RE1 instead of helplessly waiting for Chris)

Billy is completely unmemorable, he starts and ends the game as the same character, there's nothing about him to hold on to: He doesn't have an arc where he learns to trust and work with Rebecca because he's the one that instantly suggests it and neither of them have any issues with it, and his whole thing about killing innocents while on a military mission is also completely pointless because there's no arc where he comes to grips with it or fight some kind of self-delusion, because he already knows he did nothing wrong and is fully aware with it. There's a very brief moment towards the end of the game where he's shown to have some kind of PTSD after seeing dead bodies piled up, but even then it's completely skipped over. Billy himself never appears in any future game after this one either afaik, so he's completely pointless.

The story accomplishes nothing and just exists as an excuse for the game's setting and very dumb villain (but again, not dumb in the flamboyant and entertaining way this series' villains are, just in the very terrible and boring villain way). 

The ending was supposed to make me feel sad that these two characters were saying goodbye after what was supposed to be a harrowing experience that brought them closer, but the only catharsis I got was that I could finally move on from this game and never touch it again. The worst RE by far, to me.

[h1]Ruh Roh Raggy – we need to go back for that hookshot-gun-thingy [b]again[/b]![/h1] 
[b]RE0 was an interesting novelty, but due to its core design complications, it’s hard to recommend it to someone who has not at least enjoyed the remake of the first game. The story and its settings are great, mechanics are curious, but at the same time the game is filled with backtracking, and it punishes uninformed, wrong decisions.[/b]

As part of the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo team, field medic Rebecca Chambers investigates the string of grisly murders in Arklay Mountains near Raccoon City. The team stumbles upon an abandoned train and a truck with dead soldiers who were moving a convicted murderer to serve his sentence. When Rebecca goes forth to look for the killer, she gets ambushed by the various horrors unleashed from the nearby mansion. In the meantime, the killer finds her first – and lowers his gun.



While I wouldn’t call the story new and surprising, it is a nice setup of a person being forced to cooperate with a supposed enemy. Billy and Rebecca fight off the horrors together, they discuss the truth behind the killings and grow closer to each other. It is just a really nice story. 
On top of that, the game explains the origins of the Raccoon City incident – what happened at Umbrella and what [strike]crustacean[/strike] monsters lurk beyond the veil. 
Also, while the train area is a pain to avoid zombies in, it’s a really atmospheric place – the game has cool settings. 



Now, we have two main characters in the game. Unlike in RE1 they don’t get their own campaigns/story routes – rather you control both of them at the same time. They have separate inventories and their own specializations. Becky can mix herbs and other stuff, throw molotovs quicker, but she dies faster too. Billy has better gun skills (bigger chance to instantly kill a zombie), has more health and a lighter which you use the whole 2 times in the entire game! 

You can tell your partner to stay where they are or follow you, as well as tell them to attack if necessary or idle to conserve ammo. That lets you choose from many different tactics – you can use the other character as a backpack, or human bait, or an additional gun or whatever. 
Sometimes, however, you need to bring both characters somewhere, either to solve a puzzle or to move to the next area together. That’s all fine and dandy, until the game decides to separate the characters. Sometimes it gives you a nice option to choose - “Who will stay behind?”, “Who will go upstairs to do that dangerous thing?” - you have a chance to trade inventory. But, then there are times when you don’t have an option. Here we arrive at the problem of uninformed, bad decisions. 

Imagine you have all the weapons on Billy – he's tankier, it is obvious he should fight for the most part. You are about to enter the transit system. Bam, cutscene, Billy’s gone, you are now stuck with whatever Rebecca had when this happened. It’s fine on subsequent playthroughs, you can plan your moves - but on the first one it’s just horseshi.t. 

The inventory management is also different than in RE1R. There is no Item Box, but you can leave items on the ground – there is a cap for each room. Yes, you technically have two inventories, but it’s still not enough to carry everything necessary. So, what you end up doing is hoard items in the main room of an area and do multiple trips through enemies to carry all this stuff throughout the game. On top of that you need to carry this stupid Hookshot key item for most of the game, which takes [b]two[/b] inventory slots (similarly to the shotgun and GL in this game) and you can’t even use it as a weapon. These things cause a lot of backtracking and if you don’t know what you’re doing (bcs how would you?) there is [b]even more[/b] backtracking. Dropping items is cool, but why not keep the Item Box? 

Other than that, it’s pretty much like RE1 – collecting and mixing herbs, looking for ammo, and running past foes when you can – even though I feel like evading enemies is somewhat harder than in RE0. There are rewards and achievements for different playthroughs. What’s cringe though is that a lot of costumes are paid as DLC. 

Enemies are cool for the most part, but the monkeys can be stun-locking sons of bit.ches. They also buffed the Tyrant, and I feel like Zombies take more shots to put down. The poison mechanic feels almost non-existent, even though there are blue herbs. Over my multiple rounds for platinum, I got poisoned only once – had to google if they even implemented it. 
The game features Leech Hunter mode available after completing the game for the first time. If you complete the mode well, you unlock unlimited ammo and better guns, which pretty much make 100%ing this game a breeze. There is also Wesker mode – it changes the models of the characters and gives Wesker (who replaces Billy) some OP moves to mop the floor with enemies. 



As with the REmake, the game looks good because of the HD jpegs as environments. The prerendered cutscenes maybe aged a little, but they add to the atmosphere. Cool monster designs and as said earlier, aesthetics of the settings. 
Good sound design – RE1 save theme was better, but this one does the job. Ambient is sometimes repetitive, but quiet and subtle which makes it alright. 

[h1]The door to safety is shut. There is no going back...[/h1]
Overall, although it was probably the least pleasant RE game I’ve played, I think it will appeal to the veterans of the classic formula – its core design complicates things even more, it requires even more planning, mostly to decrease backtracking. I see a lot of value here however, with a bunch of tweaks it would be a pretty fine game.

Oh, and Merry Crisis everybody.

I recommend this game, but begrudgingly so, after what amounts to 46 hours of Stockholm syndrome. I grew up with tank controls but can't stand them now-- but I love the RE series and decided to just go for it. I'm glad I played and got to experience the story (simple and campy, but works for RE), and there are definitely some really memorable moments and locations in this game. The partner aspect was also kinda interesting, though rather under utilized (only need it for a few puzzles in the game).

But dear god... the combo of the terrible inventory system + tank controls REALLY grates on you. Tank controls I at least sort of got the hang of, but you can tell that levels need to be designed a certain way to keep your movement fluid. I did find myself admiring the camera angles and cinematic feeling of several rooms/levels... but in the latter half of the game especially you can see levels that are poorly laid out and you keep running back in forth in place because of the camera switch + controls getting messed up. That, or there are enemies where you can't see them due to the camera, and they take cheap shots at you. It was times like these that made me realize the cinematic angles weren't worth it if it meant a hit to the gameplay.

The inventory system is absolutely obnoxious any way you slice it. You have less slots than a normal RE and there's no save inventory box. Couple this with huge stupid items like the hookshot and you end up spending a ridiculous amount of time just moving and ferrying items across the map. I love the old RE door loading screens but after the 50th time of just moving items from one room to the next, I hated it. The system did nothing but be incredibly annoying and added tedium in lieu of meaningful challenge or complexity (which is honestly a fault of many older games).

Again, in spite of all that, I'm still glad I played, anyone who is a fan should at least play through it on Easy mode with a guide. And the good news is that getting infinite ammo from Leech Hunter and then playing through with an infinite magnum is awesome. For anyone who wants achievements, here are tips I wish I knew beforehand:

* DON'T play Easy, play through on Normal (some achievements can only be gotten on Normal+, and NewGame+ defaults to the difficulty you beat it on)
* DO play Leech Hunter and get S rank for infinite ammo
* DON'T pick up Leech Charms til after you've cleared out enemies, and then pick up the charms from rooms that respawn enemies first (unless you're going for the enemy clearing achievement). BTW there are stupid zombies playing dead in the moose head room, so make sure you kill them
* Do your no save run on Wesker Mode
* Do your S rank speedrun with infinite ammo. I managed to do the no heal achievements on this too
* For your Hard run, just take your time, have a plan, and take damage/dodge instead of using ammo. Hoard everything and ferry items to convenient spots especially before doing the basement of the Training Facility

1. Don't give Rebecca all your best weapons. There are multiple critical moments where she is unplayable, and whatever she's holding becomes inaccessible.
2. When you reach the observatory (a round room on the map), before you do anything here, bring all the items you think you need that are lying around the map and dump them here - [b]especially[/b] the grappling hook. Otherwise, you'll find yourself backtracking through rooms newly filled with tough monsters that will waste a lot of health and ammo.

Besides that, save often and keep multiple saves on your first playthrough. It's a fun enough game, but definitely one of the weaker in the series. If you're new to Resident Evil, I'd recommend playing the remakes of the first two games, then come back to this if you're still interested.

A bit frustrating this time around with less emphasis on exploration and clearing out rooms akin to RE1 - rather, this is a squad-based game that centers its mechanics around that.  Overall it's a bit harder than the pure survival horror games in the franchise because of this.  You must manage 2 inventories and 2 health bars.  

---GAMEPLAY---
That being said, the execution of the 2 characters was very well done and especially scary when needing to split up.  The enemies, however, are not very good and very-bullet spongey.  Though one can argue that that adds to the survival horror gameplay, I think it cheapens a lot of the gameplay especially when they corner and stunlock both Billy and Rebecca, leaving you helpless until one of you die.  The ability to leave things in rooms, though it makes sense, makes management cumbersome especially since weapons and items need to be physically brought in the face of the gangs of bullet sponge unstunnable enemies (I'm looking at you, hookshot) instead of retrieving them from a traditional item box.  Exploration is also cumbersome since the map doesn't tell you what rooms are "clear."

---EXPERIENCE---
The addition of more animations and cutscenes add to the experience though the story is not as fleshed-out or in-depth or have much impact on the timeline with 1-time protagonists and antagonists like Rebecca and Billy and Marcus.  That being said, it was a delight to see Birkin and Wesker behind the scenes during the Arklay mountains incident.  I do hope that the protagonists, especially Rebecca, make it to some new games or at least get some screentime outside of the movies in the future.  
The sound design is beautiful just like RE1.  The foley for walking on different surfaces is truly heavenly.  So is the beautiful soft pre-rendered backgrounds that are more animated this time around.  

---SUMMARY---
Overall, I tink this is a great game with great visuals and tasty sound design, but lacks the tight gameplay, horror, and aesthetic of RE1 Remake.

I have a strong bias because RE0 was the first RE game that I ever played (way back on the GameCube). So when I say that RE0 is a great game, take that with a grain of salt. 

RE0 keeps the same fixed cameras that were used in RE1-3, so keep that in mind if you prefer third person. I personally love fixed angles. I fully believe they add to the survival horror experience (field of vision limitations, less intuitive controls), but I also won't deny that I'm nostalgic for them.

The puzzles in RE0 are well designed - challenging enough to make you feel satisfied, but not so obtuse that you can't solve them without a guide.

There are two playable characters (Rebecca and Billy) that you switch between. I really enjoy this aspect - it makes the gameplay more interesting, and it also provides more variety when it comes to puzzles. Thankfully the AI is smart enough to not make the second character a liability. 

This game sometimes gets criticized for its story. To me, campy stories are synonymous with RE, so it's honestly something I appreciate. Opera Sephiroth? Count me in!

RE0 also gets criticized for its inventory system, which differs from other RE games. There are no item boxes, which, if you've never played an RE game, allow you to store items that you can retrieve from any other box. In RE0, you have to coordinate between Billy and Rebecca's inventory or leave items behind that you can later return to. I personally enjoy this system because it adds new elements of strategy and decision making. HOWEVER, there are several parts where Billy and Rebecca separate, and if you save your game with poor inventory management, it can be very hard to progress. This won't happen with quest items, but if you don't have adequate ammo or the right weapons split between both characters, you can get yourself in trouble. This, I'd argue, is the biggest design flaw in RE0. 

Final thoughts - If you love classic survival horror, I'd strongly recommend this game!

Resident Evil 0 serves as a prequel to the original Resident Evil, offering a closer look at the events that led to the infamous outbreak at the Spencer Mansion. 

Meet your two heroes: Rebecca Chambers, the fragile medic who somehow survived Resident Evil 1, and Billy Coen, an ex-marine who looks like he walked out of a Metallica music video. Together, they form the least compatible team since oil met water. It’s like a horror-themed buddy cop movie, but instead of chasing criminals, you're fighting the undead and solving puzzles that no sane person would ever design in real life.

The “partner zapping” system lets you switch between Billy and Rebecca, but you’ll quickly find this is less about teamwork and more about the game testing how well you can juggle chaos. AI-controlled partners have a knack for standing around when they should be shooting, or worse, getting mauled by monsters while you’re busy managing inventory. You’ll soon learn that teamwork makes the dream work, but in Resident Evil 0, the dream is more of a nightmare.

Remember that inventory system from earlier Resident Evil games where you could store items in magical boxes that teleported between rooms? Yeah, that’s gone. Now, when your pockets are full, you just drop stuff on the ground like a slob and hope you can remember where you left it. Inventory management becomes a constant struggle, with key items often spread across several locations, forcing you into ridiculous backtracking. It's survival horror, but with a dash of frustration on top.

Like the classic Resident Evil games, Resident Evil 0 is full of puzzles. But instead of feeling clever when you solve them, you’ll mostly feel relieved that you can finally move on to the next section of torment. The game does feature a variety of boss fights which provide a nice break from regular encounters. The boss fights in Resident Evil 0 aren’t just hard, they’re unnecessarily hard, like trying to open a jar of pickles after an arm day at the gym.

The environments are top-notch and dripping with atmosphere. The opening train sequence sets a claustrophobic tone that carries through the entire game. From dank laboratories to creepy churches, the game nails the tension, keeping you on edge at every turn. Every camera angle is cinematic.

Resident Evil 0 is the Resident Evil game for those who think they’ve seen it all. It doesn't hold your hand; it slaps it away and tells you to figure it out on your own. Between the punishing difficulty, the partner mechanics, and the lack of item boxes, it’s easily the hardest entry in the series. If you're looking for a challenge, this game delivers. But if you're someone who values their sanity? You might want to think twice before diving into this zombie-infested nightmare.

I want to start off with the bad things and first with the most annoying one for me. The door animations.
Every single time you go to a different room you got to watch an 8 seconds animation of a door opening, it is insane how bad this ruins the pacing and slows you down for no reason. I understand that it is an old game and it needed load times in between rooms back then, but this is a REMASTER for PC, at least give me the option to skip them by pressing a button. Luckily there are mods that skips all door animations so this is solvable if you start to really hate them mid-playthrough.
There is no item box like I heard there is in other RE games, so you HAVE to keep track of items you left on the floor sometimes, leading you through 50 door animations and back to the location you were.
Your partner's AI is terrible so don't plan on leaving them taking care of the enemies for you because they will die, specially on boss fights. You basically have to control two characters at once for them to stay alive.
When you die, there is no "continue", you are back to the main menu, where you can choose to load a save file, taking so long to go back to play.
Like every old game you play, of course, there is a chance it crashes every time you tab out of the game. Seems like it's the norm not to fix this before selling "remasters".
So why am I giving this game a thumbs up after I mentioned all this things? I just personally really enjoyed it.
You can solve most of this issues with either patience or a couple mods, and it is a good game after all.

There are some bonus modes and minigames so it has great replayability if you aim to get all achievements.

Do you enjoy experiencing frustration? Do you enjoy playing the same part over and over?  This game is for you.

Things I liked:
1) I was able to change the characters outfits. 

2)  I don’t mind the fixed perspective because the earlier RE games all have this and it never bothered me.  It’s part of the game nostalgia. 

3) I like that it takes place on a train.  

4) Rebecca is such a wholesome bean, annoying with her do gooder and follow the rule book attitude sometimes, but she is someone I could see being friends with anyway.  Friends like these keep me from getting arrested IRL.
