1) I needed an ink tape thing in order to save at the typewriter. It made it difficult when one character found them all, but then a period of time happened where you needed the other character to save at the typewriter but they had nothing.  I have played the other RE games so I am used to a ‘safe room’ or a ‘save at a typewriter when you see one’ style, but this feature seemed a bit overkill.  3 times I redid a 40ish minute stretch because right before I was able to save, I died. 

2) I think I have a permanent eye twitch now. 

3) The male character/partner that Rebecca is paired with is not the brightest and does not live up to any of the other RE males you see in the universe.  I’m glad you don’t see him again.  Maybe because he dies at the end?  That’s not a spoiler though because I have no idea if he does or not since I will not be finishing the game. But all us RE nerds know that just because a character dies doesn’t mean they stay dead, which brings me back to the fact that I’m glad we don’t see him again.

Gameplay and Atmosphere

Resident Evil 0’s gameplay is quintessential old-school survival horror, with limited ammo, save ribbons, and a focus on inventory management. The game’s pacing is deliberate and slow-burning, building tension as you navigate the Umbrella Corporation’s sinister training facility. The atmosphere is creepy and foreboding, with creaking doors, flickering lights, and an unsettling soundtrack.

Story and Characters

The story, while convoluted and occasionally laughable, provides a fascinating glimpse into the Resident Evil universe’s early days. Rebecca Chambers, a rookie S.T.A.R.S. member, and Billy Coen, a former Marine, form an unlikely duo as they investigate a mysterious train and uncover the dark secrets of Umbrella. The characters’ interactions and banter add a touch of humanity to the game’s horror.

Visuals and Sound

The HD remaster’s visuals are impressive, particularly considering the game’s age. The updated graphics and widescreen support enhance the game’s already eerie environments. The sound design, including the creepy ambient noises and unsettling sound effects, is equally effective in creating a sense of unease.

Conclusion

Resident Evil 0 is an acquired taste, but fans of the series and survival horror enthusiasts will find much to appreciate. While it may not reach the heights of its predecessors, the game’s unique setting, atmospheric tension, and challenging gameplay make it a worthwhile revisit. If you’re looking for a nostalgic dose of old-school Resident Evil, or simply want to experience a lesser-known entry in the series, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is a solid choice.

For fans of the Resident Evil series, survival horror enthusiasts, and those looking for a nostalgic gaming experience.

Overall the game was fine but feels like a step down from RE1. The dual character idea is interesting but clunky. Trying to constantly navigate through the menu to check inventories, drop items, or exchange items becomes a chore. Lining yourself up to pick an item off the ground can take as long as 20 seconds due to the pinpoint targeting making you jiggle around on top of the item desperately trying to find the angle where the game realizes you want to interact with said item. Some enemies in this game have 'mini enemies' along side themselves. These mini enemies will constantly force you to lock onto them instead of the main enemy or will chase and attack you, disrupting your attack on the main enemy and making a 5 second fight take 30 seconds or more.

At its core it's still a Resident Evil game with the fixed camera and tank controls, you're still killing zombies and solving puzzles, and for that alone I say give it at least one playthrough if you're interested at all in the franchise. But I would suggest playing on easy so that you can blast through enemies and never run out of ammo or herbs. The charm of the RE environment, story, and characters will suck you in enough for one playthrough, but afterwards you'll mostly likely just want to continue on to the next game in the franchise.

Graphics and Atmosphere: This game’s got more atmosphere than a foggy graveyard. The pre-rendered backgrounds? Still holding up like a champ. You’ll see wine bottles waltzing on that train – classy, right? And the lighting? So good, it could make a zombie tear up. 🌌

Controls and Combat: Now, let’s talk moves. Rebecca and Billy? They’ve got the coordination of a synchronized swimming duo. But hey, it’s 2002 – cut 'em some slack. Combat? Well, it’s like trying to salsa with a chainsaw. Not ideal, but memorable! 💃

Story and Pacing: Hold onto your ink ribbons! The plot? A mix of bad acting, bad writing, and more clichés than a rom-com marathon. But somehow, it works. It’s like watching a B-movie with a side of brain-eating. The pacing? Steady, like a zombie on a treadmill. 🎬

Inventory Juggling Act: Remember Tetris? Well, this game’s inventory system is the expert level. You’ll swap herbs, bullets, and keys like a pro. It’s tedious, but hey, survival ain’t easy. 🎮

Verdict: Resident Evil 0 is like that quirky dance partner who steps on your toes but still makes you smile. It’s not perfect, but it’s got charm – like a zombie doing the moonwalk. If you’re up for a spooky tango, grab your controller and join the undead soirée. 💀🕺

Disclaimer: No real zombies were harmed during this review. But my sanity? Yeah, that’s a different story.

Resident Evil 0 tries some interesting things but ultimately fails in innovating on the old entrees. You now control 2 characters at once rather than having specific scenarios for each one. This isn't a bad idea, but the execution is messy since your A.I. partner is either deadweight when evading zombies or is literally dumping precious resources into every zombie on the map when set to combat mode. The only instance where I would think your partner would be useful is during boss fights, but more often than not you still fight boss monsters with one character rather than both due to how the game structures these encounters.

This game also has the most annoying enemies in the series. The eliminators especially are quick, tanky, and are bound to frustrate you in every instance you have to fight them. There is also a bat boss fight which is horribly difficult in the worst way possible. As you damage the big bat it will summon smaller bats to attack you as well but the real threat is how they will snatch up your auto-aim making it near impossible to shoot the boss without wrangling the controls off of the trash mobs.

My last major complaint is that there are no item boxes in this game. If you never played a RE game before, item boxes were interconnected storage spaces that let you stash extra supplies in between safe rooms. Because you have limited inventory, these boxes meant you had a place to put key items or ammo without having to backtrack later. This game gets rid of the item box and instead keeps your items wherever you drop them, which means you will have to backtrack often and it is likely you will suffer for it.

There are things to appreciate about RE0. The visuals are great, I like a lot of the puzzles, and it shares a lot of the strengths that made this franchise great. It can be fun, but these critical flaws really make it hard to recommend. Buy it if its on sale, and at least have Resident Evil remake under your belt before you tackle this one.

This game is fun, but flawed. First timers will definitely have a rough go of it. There are a few traps and potential soft locked situations I feel could be easily avoided due to some changes in the design. I hope to keep others from falling in some of these traps.

The main tips I have are as follows (Light Spoilers from here on out):

- After the Leech Zombie intro cutscene, go right back down the stairs. You'll save ammo and initiate the next cutscene faster.

- Billy can't mix herbs, so explore with Rebecca if you can. While it can still be worthwhile to have Billy with you as backup, this way you won't have to do as much backtracking in the long run.

- When possible, fight bosses with Billy. Dude is a tank, and while the game mostly doesn't tell you when a boss is coming, you can have an easier go at first if you (Trying to be light on spoilers):

1. Send Rebecca to the top of the train after it starts moving. 

2. Send Billy in the Church to Save.

3. Treatment Plant B7 <-> B9 Small Elevator. Maaaaybe take control of Rebecca w/ Billy following here after you get to B9 so you can move her out of the way after the cutscene ends. 

4. Any other Boss you fight will be determined for you by the game.

- If you don't interact with an item before the Train segment is over (The end is clearly telegraphed), you will miss out on that item. You don't have to pick the item up and drop it, just interact with it.

- After you get the Shotgun, dump Rebecca's Handgun wherever and never think about it again. Give her Billy's Gun because it is stronger, and give Billy the Shotgun. There is an optional Handgun upgrade you can get that increases critical hit chance. Still try to save Shotgun Shells where you can. 

- After you deactivate the steam, be sure to head towards/past that area after the cutscene ends. (BILLY HELP!)

- You need the HookShot a total of 3 times. First is the Train, Second is the start of the Laboratory, Third is the end of the Laboratory.

- There's no Item Box in this game, instead you just dump what you don't need. To mitigate difficulty where you can, dump your stuff on the first and second floors of the Training Facility Main Hall. If you need, you can also dump stuff right outside the Main Entrance and/or the 2nd floor Meeting Room adjacent to the Main Hall.

- If you use Molotovs, have Rebecca throw them. Billy has a large af arc of a throw for some reason, and will either overstep right in to claws of an enemy, or overshoot the enemy altogether. 

- Related to last tip: If you play on Normal or Easy, feel free to use your Molotovs/Fire Grenades on the Leech Zombies. Guys soak up ammo otherwise. If you play on Hard (Bless You), avoid the Leech Zambos altogether. The guys take so much damage, I can guarantee you will not have enough ammo for the Final Boss if you pursue conflict with them. Instead, use your Molotovs on whatever else. I recommend Normal Zombies only, as there are other enemies too fast/durable to rely on Molotov usage for.

In case non first-timers read this: I wouldn't recommend a knife only run unless you are seriously about that.

Resident Evil 0 is the prequel to the original Resident Evil which tells the story of rookie S.T.A.R.S. member Rebecca Chambers.

[h1]I Like[/h1]

[b]Fanservice[/b]. There's fanservice throughout both the main game beyond (see "reply value" section).

[b]Replay value[/b]. As per any Resident Evil game, there's replay value for those who wish to try their hand at the unlockables, in this case a mini game and an alternative playthrough.

I liked the [b]games length[/b]. It's a very short condensed Resident Evil experience in a collection of very small areas however... 

[h1]Gameplay Dislikes[/h1]

I disliked the [b]bloat[/b]. Modern games may have spoiled me as I've discovered that I no longer have patience waiting for door animations to end. It's not necessarily the door animations end of, it's the clear constant reminder that everything takes that extra little bit of time, even the simplest of tasks all add up. An example of what I mean is that Rebecca can mix herbs but Billy cannot, that's fine, so in order to mix those herbs you have to select Rebecca and swap inventory. Once that's done, you combine the herbs and then swap your inventory back (this example is based on Billy having originally picked up the herbs). Why can't the system simply allow players to combined herbs when both characters are together, why the persistent to you, to me, to you, to me, to you, to me item management mini game.

I also dislike how [b]item management[/b] is handled in this title in comparison to other Resident Evil games. Gone is the item box and now... there's... the floor. I despised having to backtrack to previous areas because I didn't know I needed an item such as the [spoiler] grappling hook[/spoiler]. I despised that feeling I got when I entered a new area and found the new save room because it was at that point that I knew I'd have to backtrack for all the ammo, guns, health items etc that I wasn't carrying.

[h1]Story Dislikes[/h1]

The [b]plot[/b] is to put bluntly, awful. Characters have zero depth of personality. The two main characters Rebecca and Billy barley interact and when they do Billy's voice actor is just dreadful (particularly during the end). The main villain has zero charisma, looks like he's in the wrong game and overall gives off the vibe that he'd bombard you with unhinged argumentative private messages on X (formally Twitter) for simply stating what your favourite snack is. He just seems weak and pathetic.

Regarding the plot as a whole, there's no real reason for this quarter of a story to be told. It's completely forgettable and has no real impact on the Resident Evil series as a whole. Are players genuinely supposed to believe Rebecca goes through all the obstacles in RE0 then meets Chris in RE but never mentions [b]anything[/b]? suspension of belief only goes so far.

Some may/could argue that we learn a little about what [spoiler]Albert Wesker[/spoiler] and [spoiler]William Birkin[/spoiler] was like before their respective title appearances but seriously, who really didn't know that they've always been evil scientist bad guys?

It's the utter lack of realisation that makes the [b]writing[/b] so amateurish, here's an example:

"You're under arrest" informs Rebecca.
"No thanks dollface" Billy replies, rising his left arm to punctuate further his retort, "I've already worn handcuffs".

Billy... he's still wearing them. The cuffs are literally hanging off of his wrist, the very wrist that he lifts up. "Worn" is a word used to describe past tense. Billy throughout the entire game minus the end cutscene wears handcuffs.

The entirety of this games plot and dialogue is littered with mistakes and much worse.

[h1]Last Thoughts[/h1]

I bought this game (on console) when it originally came out. I turned it off and never returned to it in the first area. Years later I bought it again with the same result. There was just something about it that just never caught my attention or my imagination. Now with third time being a charm (or not in this case) I bought it on Steam and completed it only to find that it's utterly lacking.

I'm certain many do and will love Resident Evil 0 and ultimately I'd say to those that do like it, I can understand why. The appeal of a game that at times does a decent job at capturing that original Resident Evil sentiment is a strong one but for myself the gameplay is more often frustrating than not and the story is not worth paying attention to.

Resident Evil 0 serves as the prequel to the original Resident Evil and tells the story of rookie S.T.A.R.S. officer Rebecca Chambers discovering the origins of Umbrella's T-Virus project. You'll also work in tandem with Billy Coen, an escaped criminal who allegedly murdered over 20 people. Swapping between this tag-team and working together will be key to solving puzzles and escaping this nightmare alive.

Summary over, I want to talk about why this is a negative review, because I even gave Resident Evil 5, a notoriously clunky and absurd game, a positive review. What makes Resident Evil 0 not that great? There's a few things.

The mechanic of swapping between Rebecca and Billy is interesting in some parts. Working as a duo to solve puzzles is cool and each character having their own strengths and weaknesses is cool, but the system has its drawbacks. For one, Rebecca is able to combine herbs to create stronger medicines, but Billy can't, meaning portions of the game where you can only play as Billy can be rough since you may need full heals from green and red herbs but can't actually make them despite having both in your inventory. Billy gets access to a lighter in a free inventory slot, but I can't remember actually using it outside of puzzles where it was required. While you do get the luxury of having twice as much inventory space due to controlling two characters, Resident Evil 0 lacks an item box entirely, meaning any items you don't need at the moment have to be just left on the ground for you to come pick back up later. You better hope you left the item in a convenient spot too, because making the trek back and forth to transport a key item or powerful weapon to a new location can be a royal pain. It feels like I'm playing an old Dark Souls game with how bad some of this game's runbacks are.

The special enemies in Resident Evil 0 suck major balls, to put it bluntly. The most notorious is the Leech, a fleshy leech-human form that tanks a lot of damage and has a long-ranged whip attack that often hits you outside of your fixed camera angle. They're weak to fire damage, but fire grenade rounds are hard to come by and molotovs are cumbersome to find ingredients for and carry around. The little monkeys that get introduced halfway through the game are obnoxious as hell, constantly jumping around and taking a lot more damage than you would think a fairly common, mobile enemy would. They also have a habit of showing up in pairs and stun-locking you in a corner of a room until you die. The final boss also comes to mind as being particularly annoying, where the mechanic of actually defeating the boss isn't available until you burn half your ammo on it, at which point after it becomes a battle of navigating around its gigantic hitbox and hoping A.I. Rebecca doesn't get absolutely crushed.

Finally, the story just does not resonate at all. There's very minimal cutscenes throughout the game, meaning you don't get a chance to really experience any depth of personality from most of the characters. Rebecca and Billy barely get to truly interact and when they do it comes off as just flat-out strange. The main villain lacks any sort of sauce whatsoever, just completely no charisma, almost no backstory, very little about him is truly menacing and most everything about him is incredibly forgettable. And speaking of forgettable, the story as a whole lacks any sort of real impact on the Resident Evil series. When I finished the game, I couldn't help but think "okay, how does any of this actually matter?" Sure we uncover how Umbrella gets its hands on the T-Virus project but ultimately the story has zero genuine influence on Resident Evil 1 or any other future games. We even see lore of Wesker and Birkin before the events of Resident Evil 1 but in both cases the lore can be summarized as "oh they've both always been kind of evil and messed up", which doesn't actually add much of anything to the story. 

At the end of the day I just can't say that Resident Evil 0 is worth the time spent playing it. When the gameplay is more often frustrating than not and the story is barely worth paying attention, I can't help but think my time would have been better spent re-playing a different Resident Evil that I like more.

Resident Evil 0 is a game that many people who have played the other games in the series find frustrating - so if you're someone who isn't used to old RE design, then this game might kill your interest in playing the rest if you don't have a lot of patience. What's interesting is that RE0 has purposeful obnoxious design compared to the other games in the series, since there are fewer item slots, a two-character system with terrible partner AI, and no item box which means you have to backtrack an awful lot.

However, if you give the game some time and get used to its difficult and archaic design - you might end up having fun like me. It's a game that makes you explore every single part of its locations, offers little explanation, and punishes you for not thinking ahead of things. You can't waste ammo, but if you don't, then there is a decent amount of it available to beat the game in Normal mode. Saving is limited, but you don't really run out of ribbons if you keep collecting them - even if you like to save often like me.

The first half of the game is a bit torturous for a newbie to old survival horror design, but it also hardens you for other, far better games that use similar inventory management and gameplay. The second half is fortunately slightly more linear and quicker. Just remember to move the hookshot with you to every new location (or close to it so you can pick it up again), and don't leave your partner too far behind as the game randomly spawns enemy in the way as a penalty.

For RE fans, I'd say it's a must-play since it's not a bad game. It's a challenge and you'll feel good after beating it. For new RE players who want to start at '0' because it comes before RE1, well, it's quite a skippable game if you don't like frustrating game design. So, up to you to decide.

[h1]A great game hampered by one major issue.[/h1]


Resident Evil 0 is underrated. There, I said it. It doesn't deserve the negativity it receives. This is an excellent survival horror game with some great qualities.....and one huge flaw.

[b]Positives:[/b]

+ Beautiful visuals. Somehow it's even prettier than RE1 thanks to sharper textures and more complex environments, with an even more impressive seamless integration between the prerendered environments and the 3D character geometry. RE1R still has the edge in art design, though.

+ Perhaps the best puzzles in the entire RE series. People often create a divide in the RE games between 0/1/2/3 as survival horror and then 4/5/6 as action games, but I think that's wrong. 0 and 1 are in their own category. They are far more puzzle-oriented than RE3R or even RE2R. RE1R was the gold standard for RE puzzles, but I think RE0 may very well have beaten it, with an excellent assortment of puzzles throughout the game.

[b]Mixed:[/b]

* Enemies are a mixed bag. The leeches and monkeys are a pain, but most of the other enemies are classic RE. The boss fights aren't great but aren't terrible, either.

* The environments are consistently good but never great. Nothing comes close to the Spencer Mansion or RPD, but I enjoyed all of these environments more than RE2R's sewers, for example.

* The Rebecca/Billy dynamic is fun. The acting is bad, but it has a charm to it. And the player switching works surprisingly well. I hated it at first, but as I learned it better, I grew to enjoy it. Most people loved the beginning train sequence and view the rest of the game as a step down, but I was the opposite because I spent most of the train sequence still figuring out how the character switching worked, so I didn't really enjoy it. But eventually it just clicked and I started to really enjoy the game.

[b]Negatives:[/b]

- Items boxes. You knew this was coming. This was by far the weakest part of the game. Every time you moved to a new 'home base' area, you had to go back and haul all your stuff with you, which was a real chore. If this game had item boxes, it would have been a really solid game. Still not as good as RE1R, but not too far behind.

- The story is garbage. Even by RE standards, this story made no sense. Rebecca's continuity with RE1R doesn't work and the Queen Leech stuff was just bad.

- The controls are very different from RE1R and can't be changed, which I found confusing. Also, I wish the Map would actually show you when an area is cleared, like it does in RE1R. The fact that that's missing is absolutely baffling.


Overall, I must say, I enjoyed RE0 quite a bit. It's difficult, item management can be a pain, there are some annoying enemies, the story is awful, and the environments and music are merely good but not great, and yet I really enjoyed the game thanks to the beautiful visuals and the excellent puzzles, which are Resident Evil's real bread and butter.

This is definitely one of the more difficult RE games and I died several times, but I still managed to complete the game in about 11 hours of in-game time, which felt like a good length for this type of game. In total, it took me a couple hours longer, but 11 hours excludes the times I died and lost progress. My total Steam time was about 17.5 hours.

[h2] GOOD [/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b] Gorgeous Visuals [/b]  
Resident Evil 0 (2016) impresses with beautifully rendered backgrounds and crisp character models that bring the early days of the outbreak to life.

[*][b] Outstanding Music and Sound [/b]  
Atmospheric audio and a tense soundtrack crank up the dread, making you think twice about turning every corner.

[*][b] Immersive Atmosphere [/b]  
Every inch of the game oozes mood and unease—you’ll regularly wish you were anywhere but this hellish train or mansion.  
[/list]

[h2] BAD [/h2]
[list]
[*][b] Tedious Inventory Management [/b]  
Item juggling is a chore. Dropping and backtracking eats up time and patience—why not just let us use a magic chest and have an achievement for skipping it?

[*][b] Tank Controls Return [/b]  
Classic tank controls are alive and well… and still clunky. If you hated them before, nothing’s changed here.

[*][b] Loose Narrative Threads [/b]  
Major plot points—like Billy’s fate—are never resolved, leaving frustrating gaps and unanswered questions in the story.
[/list]

[h2] Final Thought [/h2]  
RE0 is a visual treat and a solid entry for the hardcore Resident Evil fan. The drawbacks are real, but if you can live with some old-school frustrations, it’s worth adding to your collection. Give it a chance—you might be surprised.

Let's start by giving a brief context of this game: This is a prequel to the original RE trilogy. Being a survival-horror game it shares certain core characteristic with those games such as limited items and inventory. This game was originally made in 2002 and this is the 2016 face-lift of it. Despite being chronologically set before trilogy events, it should be played after the trilogy. That being said the RE story is very far from being a literary masterpiece, ultimately you should feel free to play in any order you desire. However, I would still recommend playing the trilogy first, mainly because they are just better and worth your time more. As for the game itself, after mentioning that I got these impressions from one playthrough under normal difficulty, I will start with the positives:

Pros:
-I didn't like early areas of this game too much but I enjoyed the latter areas. My primary complaint about these last areas is that there are too many long empty halls between places, which needlessly drags down game's pace.
-Dual protagonist mechanic is interesting and overall well designed. You are controlling your character and have the AI companion following you, you can change between which character you control, and which character is AI. However, the game is designed as such that the two protagonists will need to split up from time to time to solve traversal puzzles, or one of them will be put out of action and the other will need to rescue them. Some of these split periods can be long. Most of these periods are good, some less so but it is still one of the saving graces of the game. It helps a lot to rejuvenate the pace of the game, making it less dull.
-Controls, while I wouldn't call them fully modern or amazing, are much better than the original trilogy. This remaster did a better job with modern controls than the RE1 one.

Neutral:
-Enemy variety isn't very high, but the game doesn't really need it so I am not actively complaining.
-Puzzles are mostly alright. Enjoyed some didn't care much about most of them. There is one puzzle however I felt that it was particularly badly designed.
-While I like the partner system there are times their AI could be better. There were a few cases where I felt like my partner wasn't doing enough when I was grabbed, despite being instructed to attack. AI is serviceable and far from the worst, but it could have used extra work.

Cons:
-This game has no item chests. You have a total item slots of 12(some items taking double space) split evenly between the two protagonists. The way you deal with a full inventory is to drop excess items to the ground and they stay there until you pick them up. Sounds simple? No. In practice this results in horrendous amount of backtracking, quite often across large swaths of the map. This needlessly pads out your game time and is a pretty awful experience overall. It's intriguing why they chose to insist on this design decision, I don't believe that the devs seriously thought "Yep, it sure is fun to go back all the way from the final area to the first facility in order to get a single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ herb" as they were testing the game internally.
-Bad writing. Not the ironically entertaining "Jill sandwich" corny bad, just miserable. I am seeing some of the other reviews mentioning how they liked it and how it is just like the other games but I respectfully disagree. I found no charm in it. Some of the most egregious examples are the bad handling of one of the protagonists' PTSD, it is so bland and cliché I was laughing through the supposedly sad and traumatic cut scene. And again despite my laughter I am not talking about "Jill sandwich" kind of good bad. And also the main villain sucks. He is genuinely just so lame, no redeeming quality whatsoever. The story gives some background info about some of the other RE villains, which is I think the only part of the story of this game that somewhat interested me.
-Soulless aping of original trilogy. I think the devs tried to "make recreations of and draw parallels with" parts of the original trilogy to "provide cool references to the fans". Which by itself is not a seriously bad thing and can be cool. But here the execution is very uninspired and dull. To me these references just come off as uninspired and lazy design. Just to be clear, I am not making a cynical accusation here, I am not sure whether they deliberately tried to use these references as a cover for lazy design but regardless of their intent their output feels like a soulless copy of the parts of the trilogy they are borrowing from. Having a boss fight be largely a blatant copy of a trilogy boss fight with minor differences isn't a nostalgia trip to me, it's lame.
-Speaking of boss fights, they are meh. Especially the mutated animal ones.
-I don't want to derail this review so I saved this for the last and especially since other reviews mentioned it before but I would like to take this opportunity to mention that I do not appreciate Capcom retroactively adding DRM to games I already purchased from them. I don't think this game has it(yet?), but other Capcom games in my library have it. Worrisome situation.

Overall if you played other RE games and really itching for more, I would say go for it with. But I wouldn't recommend this game to most people. One last heads-up for the Linux crowd. This game needs proton-ge to display cut scenes. Get your hands on it if you do not want to see broken cut scenes. After that the game works fine except for a light rendering bug that draw a few green lines on the screen. It's not super annoying but a bit immersion breaking for sure. However, it only happens in some parts of the first train area of the game and the elevator rides of the late game(said rides take seconds and you only ride it a few times). Whether this is a playable experience is up to you, I just wanted to warn before you purchase.

I will admit right off the bat: nostalgia definitely factors into my recommendation of this game. This game has plenty of faults, but despite this I can’t help but love it. I have very fond memories of beating this when it first came out on GameCube, and this is coming from someone who chickened out of playing OG Resident Evil - I could only bear to watch my friends beat it back in the day. In a weird way I think this difference came down to the fact that you play as two characters in this game: Billy and Rebecca. Having two characters (for the most part) cooperating and navigating the game together somehow made the game less scary in my mind (compared to the usual Resident Evil approach of “hey let's split up”). Back in the day I thought Billy was the coolest, and Rebecca is great in the game too. It is neat getting her backstory and the setup of her introduction into Resident Evil, even if it is not the most consistent with the established lore. The partner system in 0 does allow for some great puzzles often requiring you to navigate both characters independently. And I absolutely love the train setting for the first part of the game (it honestly should have been more of the game as the following environments are passable, but not nearly as memorable).

But now the bad: 0 still kept the robotic tank controls and didn’t really try to change anything with character handling from their main installment. Inventory management in this game is absolutely PAINFUL. There is no item storage and each character only gets six slots to hold items. Items you put down do persist in the environment, so theoretically you could return to a room you dropped an item in at any point and pick it back up if you need it (and the map will even flag the item types and locations if you have interacted with them). But it is a chore to move the items around in the inventory. More often than not Rebecca will have an item that Billy needs, or Billy will have ammo for a gun that Rebecca has and you will have to spend time readjusting everything. During boss fights you won’t be able to exchange items so if the wrong character has the ammo it gets very clunky. One character will have to put the ammo down, the other runs over to it, but they probably have a full inventory already so they will have to put another item down, pick up the ammo and reload it, then pick up the other item you dropped to make room for the ammo. This is way too many steps for simply reloading a gun. The UI does allow you to open the inventory and swap characters there so you theoretically have access to both characters inventories, but it is so slow switching between the two that I honestly think it is faster backing out of the screen, pressing the swap character button, and then opening the inventory again with the second character.

But man I just love this game. Like the pizza quote: even mediocre Resident Evil is still Resident Evil. So while I have come to appreciate the brilliance of the original, and in hindsight RE0 is nowhere near the highs of that game, you still have the fundamentals of that here - even if it is not as polished.

This game has terrible balance. Let me explain. I played all the games in the Resident Evil series and always did it on maximum difficulty, which did not prevent me from completing them without any problems. In Resident Evil 0, I very often found myself in situations where I didn’t have a single cartridge in my inventory, and there was an enemy ahead that I had to kill to get a plot item. I had to load old saves and run away from enemies to save ammo to fight an enemy that was impossible to avoid. It was very annoying. Simply put, this game has too little ammo and health kits and too many enemies. To avoid repeating my mistakes, in most cases you need to avoid battles and simply run away from enemies using various tricks. For example, quickly enter the door between game locations at the moment of receiving a hit from a zombie in order to avoid damage. Dude, I want to kill zombies not abuse the mechanics of loading between locations to complete the game!

The second problem with this game is the inventory. The character has only 6 inventory slots and the game does not allow you to increase the size of your inventory (as can be done in other games in the series). Imagine that you need to carry at least one heavy weapon (2 slots) and one light weapon (1 slot). You need 1 slot for a first aid kit, 1-2 slots for plot items. That's it: you're out of slots. There are no boxes in the game to store your items in, so you have to throw your items on the floor and then run back and forth between locations to pick up the item you need. All these manipulations with inventory take up at least a third of the game time! This is incredibly annoying! I know that in their subsequent games the developers abandoned this idea, but what stopped them from solving the problem of the original game in the remaster? All these manipulations with inventory which take a lot of time artificially lengthen the game. A sneaky trick!

If you ignore these two problems then this is a great game for fans of the series.

In my area this game costs about $20, but I don't recommend buying it at full price. If you can get this game at a 50+% discount, it will give you good value for money.

Which leads me to the real reason this game sucks: its mechanics. Firstly, it tries doing this new two-person party system which controls really clunky. Having a partner is also pointless since you don't want them to use your ammo since you're trying to preserve the finite amount of it, which leads to them just being extra inventory slots and a second health bar to waste healing items on. However, this becomes the worst when the game splits you and your partner apart. What a fantastic experience for my October game.  As a teenager, I played a Resident Evil title (1, 2, 3 or 4) every October to celebrate the spooky season.  I decided to revive that tradition this year with Resident Evil 0.  I was not disappointed.

Graphically, the game is dated.  Each area is a "scene" with no real option to adjust the camera.  This can make playing the game, particularly during combat, difficult at times, but the graphics are solid compared to some other titles from this era.  The iteration I played and reviewed seems to be a port from the original GameCube title from the early 2000s.  Graphics could've been better, but they're fairly decent for the era. (6/10)

The controls are also somewhat dated.  It took me about an hour to get comfortable with the control scheme.  I haven't played a Resident Evil title in over a decade, so I felt like a fish out of water at first.  I used a DualShock 4 for this game, as I do with most of my games.  Making minor adjustments as I went seemed to help, but ultimately, the default scheme worked fine for my purposes.  (6/10)

The sound really shines here.  In an otherwise dated game, the guttural moans of zombies, the bang of the weapons, and the screams of Billy and Rebecca pulled it together.  Music is minimal, but high quality where presented.  The atmospheres blend quite well with the overall experience.  (9/10)

Resident Evil 0 offers a compelling story that fans of the series will definitely appreciate. The game's lore is rich, making it a must-play for dedicated enthusiasts. The enemy design is impressive, and the overall atmosphere is engaging. 

However, the game does feel quite dated, and several aspects can detract from the experience. For instance, the animations for opening doors, the shooting angles, and the fixed camera perspectives can evoke nostalgia but also add to the game's challenges.

[h1]The Gameplay: [/h1]
Resident Evil has always been known for its tank controls, and this game adds a twist by letting you control two characters at once. On paper, it sounds like a cool co-op mechanic, but in practice, it can be clunky and frustrating. Managing two characters during boss fights can be a nightmare, and some areas aren't designed for this dual-wielding style of play. The camera can get wonky, turning tense moments into controller-chucking tantrums. That said, the alternate movement mode does offer more fluid control, and the ability to share and drop items adds a strategic layer to the gameplay. It's not as convenient as the classic item chests, but it can be used to your advantage.

[h1]The Story:[/h1]
If you thought Resident Evil's story was cheesy, this game takes it to a whole new level of B-movie badness. Sure, there's some world-building here and there, but it's mostly window dressing for a parade of uninteresting, cartoonish villains. The main antagonist is particularly cringe-worthy, making you question if the actors were held hostage during filming.

[h1]The Visuals:[/h1]
The graphics in this game are surprisingly good, especially for its time. The environments are beautifully detailed, with a timeless art style that still holds up today. Despite the terrible writing, the game does manage to create a decent atmosphere. The environments are well-designed, and the level designers deserve a round of applause for their work. They even managed to modernize Rebecca Chambers without turning her into a generic action hero, which is a rare feat these days.

[h1]The Sound:[/h1]
The ambient music is the real star of the show here. It's so good that you often forget it's even there, perfectly setting the mood for each scene. The rest of the sound design is mostly recycled from previous games, but it's still effective for the most part. The zombie groans are particularly well-done, giving you that classic Resident Evil chills. Unfortunately, the voice acting is not so good. The lines themselves are often cringe-worthy, and the delivery is even worse. It's hard to say whether it's the writing or the actors' fault, but the end result is some truly bad voice acting.


[h1]The Experience:[/h1]
This is a mixed bag of a game. It has some good things going for it, like the visuals and the atmosphere, but it's ultimately held back by a bad story, clunky controls, and some truly awful voice acting. If you're looking for a classic Resident Evil experience, you're better off playing one of the other games. But if you're a completionist or just curious to see what this game is all about, then go for it. Just don't expect to be blown away. This is a Resident Evil game that you could honestly skip. I wouldn't mind seeing Capcom remake it someday with a stronger narrative and better controls. Until then, I can only really recommend this to the most die-hard Resident Evil fans. That said, I still deem it a good game, just not a very good one.

Resident Evil Zero is definitely the weakest of the franchise's Gamecube era. The concept of playing as two characters simultaneously is a solid idea for a ResE adventure, I feel. However, execution falters due to one factor: the inventory system. Unlike in the entries from Resident Evil 1 to REmake 1, there's no item box, meaning that you have to exchange items between Rebecca Chambers (returning from REmake) and Billy Coen (a new character for this adventure). 

And weapons like shotguns and grenade launchers take TWO slots of your inventory.
Eeyeah, starting to see why this game isn't as fondly remembered as its older and younger brothers Resident Evil Remake and Resident Evil 4, yet? Although it's nowhere near as tedious as the anime/action dark ages of 5 & 6 (the game is still deliberately paced and survival horror, and thank god for that), it is still frustrating to have to leave certain items scattered around the environment, and having to backtrack to pick the up and or only pick up one green herb due to you carrying one two-space weapon. It's arguably the worst inventory system of the bunch. And it only gets worse when you die after a large portion of gameplay where you forgot to save.

HOWEVER, despite being a weaker game, Resident Evil Zero is still a damn solid effort. 
Like I said earlier, the game is still a true Resident Evil game with deliberate pacing of the action and suspense, so playing it doesn't feel like a burden. Writing and voice acting-wise, it's a solid companion piece to REmake, the game it acts as a direct prequel to, with the plot being a fun exploration of the ResE universe that provides solid answers to lingering questions from that game, and the voice actors doing a good job once again. And scare-wise, it has a fantastic atmosphere and some truly morbid monster designs and setpieces that I genuinely think will catch you, the first-time player, off-guard.

So ultimately, despite being one of the weaker main entries, this is easily the lesser of the bad main entries IMO. It doesn't sell out the series to become a generic mediocre action shooter whilst indulging in ridiculous shark jumping setpieces and action movie cliches (6) and Mother Miranda doesn't reveal Rose Winters to be Eveline's successor thus rendering the entire franchise pointless just to make Alice a reality in the games (Village), plus it's genuinely good and fun despite its crippling flaw, so I'd happily take this over those other three games any day of the week.

"Resident Evil Zero HD" is the remastered edition of the prequel to the original "Resident Evil" game, and it's a title that offers a unique experience within the Resident Evil franchise. Here's an extensive review that highlights why gamers should consider playing "Resident Evil Zero HD."

Narrative and Setting:
"Resident Evil Zero HD" takes players back to the events before the infamous mansion incident. It provides crucial backstory to the series' lore, introducing players to Rebecca Chambers and convict Billy Coen. As they uncover the sinister plots of the Umbrella Corporation, the game weaves an intricate tale that enhances the overall narrative of the Resident Evil universe. The setting transitions from a mysterious train to creepy mansions and underground labs, maintaining the series' hallmark of suspenseful locations.

Dual-Character Mechanic:
One of the game's standout features is its "partner zapping" system, which allows players to switch between Rebecca and Billy at the press of a button. This mechanic isn't just for storytelling; it's integrated into the puzzles and combat. Each character has unique abilities and limitations, and players must strategically use both to navigate through the game's challenges. This system adds a layer of depth and complexity to the gameplay that is distinct within the series.

HD Graphics and Atmospheric Enhancements:
The HD remaster brings significant improvements to the game's visuals, with high-definition textures, improved lighting, and updated character models that make the eerie environments more immersive. TL;DR RE0 isn't a bad game so much as it is a tedious one - I'd say only get it on sale if you have nothing better to play. If you're new to the series and just coming from and getting used to RE1, this game will demand that you get used to it too; it is very different than the other classic REs as there are no item boxes, and this fact alone changes everything. If you thought to yourself "Hey, why can't I just drop this item for now and come back for it later?", this game will grant your wish on paper, but in practice, this leads to an absurd amount of backtracking (possibly through rooms of enemies) that will make you regret asking the question. Specifically in the late game, you'll have to make constant and long treks through previous areas to much later ones in order to transport all of your resources to where you are in the game, and should you choose not to, those resources may as well be counted as permanently lost. And if you care about the plot, don't worry - skipping this one won't make you miss out, believe me. It adds nothing at best, and at worst tends to clash with events in RE1.

As someone who was brand new to the series until fairly recently (2 years ago), I actually enjoyed my first playthrough of RE0. When I first played RE1, I personally hated item boxes and found myself wondering why I couldn't just drop some of the things I didn't need and come back for them later instead of going to a special room with a special box. This game answered my prayers, and I for one found it pretty refreshing. I technically had 12 inventory slots instead of 6-8, after all! At the time, I thought I liked this game more than RE1. 

Flash forward two years later as someone who has played every mainline title, I installed it again and tried to give it another playthrough. I uninstalled it again after 30 minutes. The pain of having to physically transport every item you own through every area of the game is a level of tedium so great that you'll probably feel like a zombie yourself by the time the credits roll, assuming you're crazy enough to make it that far. But like I said, you have 12 inventory slots (6 between each character), so surely it can't be [i]that[/i] bad, right? 

Not quite - the shotgun and grenade launcher (two very important weapons obviously) take up 2 slots. So assuming you want to carry one or both of those around at all times, that's 2-4 slots in permanent use, and as resources stack up, you'll find yourself weighing the pros and cons of just straight up abandoning a few of them to spare yourself some backtracking. You might think the zombies and other enemies in this game are the main threat, but the greatest threat is actually this game's inventory "management."

In all other classic REs, the term "inventory management" referred to only bringing what you thought you really needed with you, and saving the rest of your stuff for later so you could have slots available to pick up new things should the want or need arise. In RE0, you "manage" your inventory the same way a manager may "manage" who gets laid off from the company, and as the game goes on, it's highly likely you'll reach a point where you become such good management material that you can put it on your resume, get hired in a real life managerial position, and do the same thing you did to your resources in this game to real human beings: Abandoning them not because they weren't useful, but because they were too much effort to keep around.

If you think you can live with the aforementioned aspects, I'll point out a few other things one should be mindful of. Firstly, RE isn't a game you play for the plot, but this one's is entirely irrelevant (and extra nonsensical), so don't be afraid to skip it. In many ways, it clashes with the continuity of 1, and while I can't say why without spoiling anything, just know that this game adds nothing to the canon. Secondly, if you do play this game, don't even think about letting Rebecca stay at or below Caution (orange) health, as she will 100% die to something and make you reload, mostly because of my third point: This game has a couple of particularly annoying enemies that are both nimble and hit hard, and in a classic RE game where you can't conventionally aim, you can probably see why this would be a problem. They're called Eliminators, and when/if you meet them, good luck hitting them with anything that isn't a point blank, downward angled grenade launcher round or maybe shotgun. 

But RE0 isn't all bad. I like this game's partner mechanic, where you must switch between Billy and Rebecca to do different things. At times, you have to solve puzzles using this mechanic, and it feels good to do so. And aside from the painful lack of item boxes, this game is the classic RE experience in every other way with puzzle solving, limited resources and saving, and all the other things you like if you liked RE1. It's just a shame that the removal of the item box makes the game collapse under the weight of its own tedium.

What I would say is: Try this game at your own risk. Get it on sale if you do. And I'd challenge those who've played this game once and liked it to try returning to it again, and see if their minds change. Because I can say with certainty that I'll personally never play it or return to it again, and I still find myself baffled as to how I completed my first playthrough and walked away with a feeling of enjoyment.

It doesn't space the door/stair/elevator loading transitions far enough to account for the extra space being traversed by to characters if they ever need to regroup across long distances, and even though this is meant to build tension for the next area you're going to, it quickly loses all meaning when you have billy on the other floor across the map fetching an item to run all the way back to rebecca where the loading screens might waste around 15 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes of your time. [h1] Resident Evil Zero Remaster: A Welcome Throwback to 2002 [/h1]

Resident Evil Zero kicks off on an intriguing note, aboard a moving train in the Arklay Mountains. We're reacquainted with the world of cheesy yet strangely effective horror storytelling. The story might be a little murky, but it's an enjoyable journey while it lasts.

The game presents us with Rebecca and Billy, an oddball duo with a unique dynamic. Rebecca handles item combining, while Billy is your tough guy who can withstand more punishment and move heavy objects. It's a familiar concept, but the "zap" partner system adds a layer of tactical flexibility. Having both characters on-screen at once, with the ability to control your partner's actions, is a welcome twist.

The game brilliantly uses this concept to diversify its pacing. Rebecca and Billy might be separated in one area, exchanging key items through special devices, or they might collaborate to solve puzzles. It's a refreshing change from the conventional Resident Evil formula.

One significant departure in Resident Evil Zero is item management. Unlike previous titles where magical storage boxes held your excess gear, here you can drop items anywhere on the map. It's a more challenging system, as you can't rely on an infinite box. The game doesn't hold your hand - sometimes you'll have to run through hordes of enemies to retrieve a crucial item. It's slightly tedious but helps shape the game's unique identity.

Resident Evil Zero stays true to the survival horror roots of the series, emphasizing limited ammo, save ribbons, and inventory management. The zapping system adds complexity, ensuring both characters are well-equipped to deal with any scenario.

The "Remaster" delivers visual and control updates, along with the addition of a modern control scheme. It's a faithful upgrade, retaining the charm of the original game. But what truly sets it apart is the Wesker mode, injecting a delightful dose of silliness into the experience. Wesker, with his superhuman abilities, takes the place of Billy as Rebecca's partner, adding a fresh layer to the game.

The game also offers a variety of unlocks, including costumes, weapons, and the Leech Hunter mini-game, providing an additional layer of challenge for series veterans. I was a toddler in 2002, so having the experience to play this game in this age is just a lovely thing to bed able to do. Say what you want about remakes but they truly allow new generations to experience classic games on hardware that may be hard to come by or heck... doesn't even exist anymore.

While Resident Evil Zero isn't my top pick in the series, this remaster's careful attention to detail is winning me over. It's another excellent addition to the growing list of Resident Evil remasters. If you haven't experienced it yet, consider getting both Resident Evil Zero and Resident Evil HD Remaster. 

You won't regret it!

 - Story is bottom of the barrel. The main villain is an emo opera singing leech man. This is like a b-tier villain in an anime.

[b]Rating[/b]: 2/10; why am I even wasting my time venting
[b]Verdict[/b]: I loved the fixed camera angles and the scarcity of resources in RE1. While these two aspects remain the same in RE0, the other changes RE0 made to the core mechanisms brought out the worst in the two.

[b]Positives[/b]:
[list]
    [*] Switching between controlling two characters on the fly is fun! Well, for the most part anyway. Giving the two playable characters each unique traits so that many puzzle-solving actions can only be performed by one specific character adds an extra layer to the puzzle aspect of the game, and while the puzzles themselves are very similar to RE1's, which I found mediocre, switching between characters to solve these mediocre puzzles made it more enjoyable for me by a surprising amount.
[/list]
[b]Negatives[/b]:
[list]
    [*] The most frustrating part of RE0 for me is some of the enemy designs. Some of the enemies really belong to an action game rather than a game with such limited maneuverability. Some examples:
    [list][*] The [spoiler] Giant Bat [/spoiler]. It's simply not fun to fight an enemy that literally flies in circles around the character when the game features fixed camera angles and scarce ammo, not to mention the swarm of smaller [spoiler] bats [/spoiler] thrown in for good measure to make the already miserable aiming controls even worse.
    [*] The [spoiler] Queen Leech [/spoiler]. The AI for the player-controlled characters does a terrible job of self-preservation, but I honestly find it serviceable throughout the game—until this fight. To have this enemy's attacks focus on the AI-controlled character who happens to have to stand for extended periods of time while relying on the other character to distract the enemy, while also making said enemy not reliably distracted every time the player-controlled character shoots at it (Did I mention how scarce the ammo is?), is simply a recipe for disaster. I had to take a week-long hiatus from gaming altogether because I was burnt out by the frustration.[/list]
    [*] RE0 managed to mess up many core mechanisms that worked ok in RE1. Some examples:
    [list][*] Inventory and saving. I can almost accept the change where heavier weapons take up two out of the six precious inventory slots, but the removal of Item Boxes does far more damage than good. Now whenever you want to retrieve an item, instead of the easily navigable UI of the Item Box, you have to try to make the character stand at juuuuust the right spot facing the item and pick it up from the ground, not to mention that it's possible for an item to not be visible from any of the fixed camera angles.
    [*] Saving. Thanks to the removal of the Item Boxes, the players no longer have easy access to the Ink Ribbons next to each Typewriter. Instead, there are three obvious choices:
    [list][*] waste an inventory slot to always carry the Ribbons, which is utterly useless except on a Typewriter,
    [*]backtrack to where you left the Ribbons previously each time you want to save, or
    [*]ignore the Ribbons left on the ground earlier, which isn't even always an available option, since you may not have acquired new Ribbons yet.[/list][/list]

    [*]The overall writing is marginally better than RE1, but it's in the same ballpark. The idea of having two characters to control is interesting. Being able to switch between Rebecca and Billy on a whim is seamless, but it starts to fall apart when both of them are in the same room together. Conserving resources becomes all the more difficult when trying to dodge zombies while your partner is following behind, because they're either going to start shooting or get caught by an enemy, forcing you to waste ammo to break them out. This can be remedied by taking each character through some rooms alone, one by one, but this just ends becoming more of a hassle, than actual engaging gameplay. However if I'm gonna be honest, it does feel very satisfying to go guns blazing on a room full of zombies with your partner, every now and then. 

The best sections of the game are when Rebecca and Billy are seperated and you have to solve puzzles by sending items between both of them through item elevators and have each character deal with their own routes. Reuniting afterwards does give a nice sense of satisfaction. But that just makes me wish the game had more sections like these. I like both Rebecca and Billy, but they're probably the least interesting protagonists in the mainline games. This game also has some weird continuity with RE1, since Rebecca becomes a total badass by the end of RE0, but acts very differently in the mansion. And as far as I know, Billy is never brought up again, so his impact on the series is very minimal. This game is also home to some of my least favorite enemy types. To be honest, if they removed the leech men and the monkeys, I'd probably recommend the game more.

Anyways, to end on a more positive note, the game has great atmosphere, it's incredibly gorgeous to look at it, the train section is fantastic, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. There's a great game hidden here somewhere, but finding it is as difficult as the game is frustrating.

A criminally slept on title in the Resident Evil franchise. 
While it may be difficult for those new to the franchise, or those used to the action oriented titles, it's absolutely worth giving it a spin. If you aren't used to tank controls, it might be quite jarring at first, but I assure you it's worth it. For me, the biggest strength of the game is absolutely the duo of protagonists you get to control, Billy and Rebecca. I like that each one has a different set of stats and abilities, and they're both likable characters that aren't seen often in the rest of the series.

A classic RE game with none of the charm or smart design.
As a prequel, this is a failure, the plot here is lite, never gets referenced again and if you play it before 1 & 2, you're just spoiling plot elements of those games, and the plot that is established here is one that I would argue lessens the impact those games can have.

As a game, the defining feature of this is that you control two characters throughout the single campaign instead of just one.
This is a cool idea in concept, it means that you don't have to replay the same game as an alternative character, and that you can witness a good pairing of characters and their personalities... if only they had personalities.

Both of these leads are so incredibly dull, with one of them plucked straight from RE1, and she doesn't really have much more of a personality here sadly.
The other one is just a very boring gruff and edgy lad whose only notable features are that he can take double damage and push things.

Onto the game design, what makes it not work are a couple things.
Puzzles that could've been solved just as easily with one character instead of two, and the removal of item boxes in favour of two inventories to ferry things across the map.

A lot of puzzles end up being as basic as "There's an elevator, but the switch to operate it is not on the elevator", so you have to get one person up the elevator and unlock an alternative route, it's basic in concept but one thing that makes it not just boring, but awful, is how this will basically double the amount of door loading transitions you'd normally have, since you'll need to backtrack with your alternative character.
All these co-op puzzles were not only easy, but just boring and a waste of time.

As for the items complaint, both these characters have 6 inventory slots, but most weapons take up two by default, not to mention the ammo needed for them. This means you are ALWAYS struggling with inventory spaces.
The games lets you drop items which admittedly is a nice feature, but all this means is that if you want to bring items with you, some of which are mandatory, you will most likely find a room to dump things in, but if it has too many interactables in said room, you may find yourself having trouble picking up what you left.
Furthermore, item boxes no longer exist, if you find that you want to go back and bring a weapon you left behind, or need a plot important item, you need to backtrack back to where you left it, pick it up, and go back to where you were, this increases the amount of backtracking you need to do by a ton. With the door opening animations being more frequent since you have your characters split up on occasion, you really feel the length of these animations build up, awful.

One other thing I should note about the level design, not only are there so many pointless hallways that don't need to exist, especially towards the end, but they keep respawning trash mob zombies as you progress throughout the campaign.
With how tight these corridors are, and how some of these are positioned, you may find yourself either taking cheap hits, wasting ammo or continually but annoying baiting and manoeuvring past them, which with a partner is incredibly unlikely.
It's just tedious, and not as interesting as the respawn mechanics from the original RE1.

Finally, the bosses aswell are all just terrible.
The vast majority are solo bosses, which I am thankful for, but it does waste the duo potential the game had.
But most of these bosses are just bad, the first one has issues with the camera unless you choose to be aggressive, but it's the first boss so I won't blame you if you're not.
The second is a damage sponge with no interesting mechanics.
The third is the worst in the game with perspective issues, respawning trash mobs which mess with your lock-on and comes at such an awkward time if you need to backtrack, which you most likely will after said boss is done.
The next few aren't even worth mentioning, they're just boring, but the last one in particular makes terrible use of the duo mechanics.

Resident Evil 0 is one of the most nothing burger games I've ever played in my life. It isn't outright horrible, but it doesn't really have enough good qualities going for it to be either worth a play-through if you're only a casual RE fan, or a game worth getting mad over. Resident Evil 0 does look very good, because it reuses the graphics and engine from REmake. Still though, visuals are incredible. The level design is a mixed bag throughout the game. The opening train sequence is really cool because it's a small area but it has a lot of classic RE design going for it. The next area the training facility is very bland, it can be boiled down a diet Spencer mansion that is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stingy with health items for some reason. The labs are okay, and the final area, the waterworks is actually my favorite area in the game. 

The gameplay is very eh. I've already mentioned the level design being mixed, but the general exploration just isn't really fun because of it. Inventory management is at an all time low for several reasons. First, there is no item box in this game, meaning you just have to leave items in areas and backtrack for them later if you end up needing them. 2nd, both characters can only carry 6 item slots, this wouldn't be a hassle except for point 3. 2 handed weapons take up 2 item slots for some reason despite having never done that in previous games, so it just makes the game arbitrarily padded because really one of your characters is only going to have 4 inventory slots to work with at any given time. Another aspect to mention are the bosses and how completely uninspired they are, frustrating in the case of the giant bat, and actually fairly good with the final boss. Most of the bosses in this game are some generic giant horror monster that require no strategy to beat them. Classic RE has admittedly never been GREAT with bosses for the most part but at least they were inspired

Then there's the story with is one of the most nothing burger stories in the history of Resident Evil. This game is a prequel to RE1 / REmake. That ultimately doesn't amount to much in the grand scheme of things though. There's some scenes with Wesker and Birkin conversing which is a nice bit of fan service but I don't think we needed RE0 to know that these 2 interacted in the past knowing that both of them were key players at umbrella thanks to knowledge of previous games. The villain is super forgettable, he hardly shows up throughout the game so he leaves no impact in the few cases where he actually does show up, his boss fight is kinda cool I guess though. The only worthwhile thing about the story is that I do like Rebecca and Billy's interactions. I like how these 2 grow more comfortable around each other throughout the game and the ending between the two of them is really sweet. But that's honestly all I can say about the story, there truly is nothing terrible or amazing going for it.

What RE0 ultimately boils down to is that it is not a game worth your time. Either as a fan of Resident Evil, or Horror games in general. Your money (and more importantly time) is better spent elsewhere, rather it be playing the other Resident Evil games, or different horror games. Although it is not a terrible game RE0's good aspects simply aren't in abundance to the point where the bad stuff can be mitigated, but then again it's not like the bad stuff makes this some terrible abomination. No, RE0 is just thoroughly "okay" and that's just not enough for me when it comes to this series. I honestly think 0 is best skipped, even if it is cannon it really doesn't add a ton to the lore and the gameplay isn't spectacular either.

[h1]Where It All Begins...[/h1]
Resident Evil Zero is a prequel to Resident Evil (1996), covering the ordeals experienced in the Arklay Mountains by a special police force unit, the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team. The story follows officer Rebecca Chambers and convict Billy Coen as they explore an abandoned training facility for employees of the pharmaceutical company Umbrella. Throughout the game, you will take control of both Rebecca and Billy, at times switching between both characters in order to proceed. Learning the advantages of each character is the key to solving puzzles and surviving the nightmares that lie ahead.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/ATReviews]Follow My Review Group Here![/url]

💾Graphics - RE0 has the best pre-rendered background in the franchise no question. At first I thought the game was fully 3D but nope, which really shocked me. This game aged so perfectly. The backgrounds are sharp and so perfectly designed. I wish the RE1 remake had this much sharpness in the backgrounds for the remake (granted it’s an older remake but still). The atmosphere and locations are just impressive as h*ll! Every location hives a feeling of dread and keeps you on your toes. I can talk about the graphics for hours! It’s just so perfect on what they were going for here. Big props to Capcom!

🎮Gameplay - Resident Evil 0 plays just like your most survival horror games from this time. Solving puzzles, tank controls, conserving ammo/healing items, and trying to get key resources so you can survive and find a way to escape. It’s fairly simple, well sorta. RE0 has some unique mechanics not found in any other Resident Evil game that I have played (for the most part). You play as Rebecca Chambers, and Billy Coen. In RE0, you have to control both characters at the same time. Now this works actually really well. The zapping system (switching from each character) is really smooth and works wonderfully. You can literally be across the map from each other and the transition is nearly flawless. You can order your partner to stop, follow, not shoot, or help you fight other enemies (but will use ammo). Many rooms require keys and some sort of puzzle to get into, giving you a feeling of interest and curiosity to see what's on the other side of that room. The game does this very well for the most part, because every room feels so unique and interesting to check out. Also many rooms reward you with ammo and healing items (even key puzzle items to move forward). The flow for the most part is good. The problems lead to severe backtracking. Since this game doesn’t have an item box, you will be going back many times to grab items you left from past locations. This is absolutely annoying and can ruin the pacing for me. It doesn’t help that later into the game that some enemies become more present, making this games backtracking much more painful and annoying. Speaking of annoying, some of the enemies are just trash. I don’t want to spoil anything, but certain enemies that become much more common in certain sections will stun lock you, reach you from insane distance and will wreck you like no tomorrow. The boss fights are just lazy and uninteresting (also borderline annoying). I won’t spoil too much, but I’d say that RE0 has some of the lamest boss fights in the Resident Evil franchise. This is a Resident Evil game, so do expect some unlockables that may be challenging to achieve. You also have some extra game modes once completing the game which is a nice touch.

📜Story - The story is a mess. Let’s talk about the leeches. I never really understood why the leeches are controlled by Opera. I didn’t really find them scary, or interesting to be honest. From turning to a liquid, to transforming to a zombie with all of the detail (including their uniform) just doesn’t make much sense. Also the main villain is just flat out lame and boring. RE1 Origins was much more interesting and felt more realistic than this game. Spoilers: [spoiler]Even Rebecca Chambers can just wreck hunters and tyrants, but gets scared and cornered in RE1 by a Hunter! It’s just some annoying plot holes that makes it hard for me to take this story seriously and overall feels like an afterthought.[/spoiler]

🕛Playtime - The games length is around 7+ hours to complete. You do have extra game modes and unlockables to achieve that will grant much more playtime.

🎧Sound - The sound design is flawless! The music is so creepy, and incredibly well made. The enemies sound terrifying (including the ambiance). The voice acting is pretty subpar. It’s not horrible, but pretty average in many areas.

❗Bugs❗- I only had crashes if I Alt+Tab but that may be some bug in the game. Besides that I don’t really have any issues.

🔅Performance - The performance is great! Solid 60fps on max settings felt really good. No stutters or frame rate issues. The game is really well optimized.

✔️Pro’s✔️
[list]
[*]Terrifying atmosphere
[*]Good enemy variety
[*]Amazing soundtrack
[*]Great survival horror elements
[*]Extra game modes and unlockables
[*]Fantastic cosmetic outfits (with DLC’s)
[*]Best pre-rendered backgrounds in the franchise
[*]Two partner system (Unique mechanic in the RE franchise)
[/list]

❌Con’s❌
[list]
[*]Horrible boss fights
[*]Can crash if you Alt+Tab too much
[*]Certain enemies feel so unbalanced
[*]Some plot holes that connect to RE1
[*]No item box (this promotes tedious back tracking)
[/list]
        
🏆Rating - 7/10
Buy this game on sale for around 50% or more.

🔗Conclusion - Resident Evil 0 may not be perfect or great, but I’d say overall it’s a good game and pretty fun (especially if you are a RE fan). If you can get over the janky mechanics and some annoying enemies, then you will have a good time. I wish they had the item box, and some balance tweaks, but it’s workable with some practice and patience. If you love a challenging survival game or a huge RE fan, then grab this without question. If you are new to this genre, than I’d try RE1 or maybe even the remakes sense this is one of the harder RE games out there.

In "Resident Evil 0," A prequel  to resident evil you play as Rebecca Chambers, a member of the Special Tactics and Rescue Service (STARS), finds herself aboard a runaway train en route to investigate mysterious murders in Raccoon City. She encounters Billy Coen, an escaped convict, and they join forces to survive. Together, they uncover a dangerous bio-weapon experiment orchestrated by the sinister Umbrella Corporation. Exploring an abandoned training facility and underground labs, they face mutated creatures and solve puzzles to expose the corporation's dark secrets. Along the way, they unravel the origins of the T-virus and its devastating effects on humanity, leading to a climactic battle against a powerful Tyrant. With teamwork and courage, they survive the ordeal, vowing to bring Umbrella to justice and prevent further bio-hazardous outbreaks.

Prepare yourself for a heart-pounding, spine-chilling adventure like no other as we delve into the macabre masterpiece known as Resident Evil 0. Brace yourself for a rollercoaster ride of fear, tension, and awe as we explore the eerie halls of the Umbrella Corporation's nightmarish facility. This is not your average positive review; it is an homage to the terror that lurks within the depths of this game, blending horror and positivity in a unique, unforgettable way.

From the moment the game begins, you find yourself immersed in a foreboding atmosphere, haunted by the desolation of the Raccoon City outskirts and the eerie silence that hangs in the air. The visuals are nothing short of breathtaking, with every inch of the game's environments meticulously designed to send shivers down your spine. The attention to detail is exceptional, from the hauntingly dilapidated hallways to the grotesque monstrosities that await around every corner.

Resident Evil 0 introduces us to a truly terrifying and gripping storyline, delving deep into the origins of the Umbrella Corporation's sinister experiments. We witness the plight of two unlikely allies, Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen, forced to confront their worst fears and fight for survival against hordes of grotesque creatures. The narrative is beautifully woven, presenting us with a dark tale of conspiracy, betrayal, and the limits of human resilience.

The gameplay mechanics in Resident Evil 0 are nothing short of brilliant. The unique "partner zapping" system allows you to switch between Rebecca and Billy at will, enabling strategic puzzle-solving and intense combat scenarios. The challenge lies in managing your inventory and resources, forcing you to make difficult decisions that could spell life or death. This dynamic adds an extra layer of tension and excitement to an already heart-racing experience.

Resident Evil 0 introduces a new auto-targeting feature and modern controls that greatly enhance the gameplay experience. This addition revolutionizes the way players engage with enemies and navigate the game world, making it even more accessible and enjoyable.

The auto-targeting feature in Resident Evil 0 automatically locks onto enemies when aiming, providing a seamless and intuitive combat experience. This feature alleviates the need for precise manual aiming, allowing players to focus more on strategizing and conserving ammunition. It ensures that encounters remain intense and challenging while reducing potential frustrations.
