Many consider RE6 to be the low point of the franchise, where it was unfun, cliche, trope-filling action-over-horror before properly returning to horror in RE7. In a similar way, RE0 is another low point where it's as clunky and uncomfortable as it ever got before the breath of fresh air that was RE4.

PROS
+The protagonists are rather fun. Rebecca really gives off 18-year-old cop vibes, and Billy was far more interesting of a character than I expected given what I knew of the game beforehand.
+The soundtrack is phenomenal at setting the mood for each given scene. It genuinely filled me with a sense of unease.
+The graphics are a fantastic upgrade from the original GameCube version!
+Difficulty scaling is specifically intended to train you for the next difficulty. Hard mode only increases the health of the enemies and reduces your resources available, instead of also increasing the damage and number of enemies available like other entries later down the line.
+The prologue is one of the best in Resident Evil. It has a great environment, does a good job setting the stage for the story to come, and trains the player on the various gameplay mechanics like juggling two characters and item management.
+Instead of needing to use the classic RE tank controls, the HD release allows you to move based on the camera's orientation. Useful accessibility option for those who can't compute the tank controls.
+Credit where it's due: whenever there were multiple items on the ground close to each other and I pressed the pick-up button, the game always grabbed the one item I wanted from the jumbled pile!
+Many people say that the puzzles in this make no sense. For me, the puzzles were at the perfect difficulty level. I can't say how ecstatic I was when I solved the animal puzzle in the basement without needing a guide, as I'd heard that it was rather rough.
+On paper, the antagonist is a fascinating idea. Thematically, he serves well as the inhumane side of Umbrella, as opposed to [spoiler] Spencer, who serves as the human greed side to Umbrella's evil. [/spoiler]

+I don't like using leeches as the next big bad BOW in theory, but they make for an interesting change in practice. In particular, Mimicry Marcuses are a pain-in-the-ass enemy who I enjoyed having to struggle against.
+Each boss fight in this game is different from the others in a way that kept them all challenging and fun.
+The post-game Leech Hunter mode is a fairly fun gamemode which felt similar to The 4th Survivor from RE2, but having to find the good weapons made it feel uniquely fun. 
+Wesker Mode allows you to have a power trip playing through the game as Wesker instead of Billy. It's stupid and fun!
+DLC: Speaking of stupid fun, the costumes are fantastic. Some are actually pretty cool, but there's nothing like running around in those dumb prisoner and nurse outfits with a rocket launcher and a SMG gunning down everything you see!

CONS
-This game meets so many Resident Evil tropes that it makes me sick. You go from an initially dangerous situation into a 1910s-era building which houses a high-technology secret location. You go through the secret location, find out that there's something evil going on there, and after you shoot the final boss a self-destruct timer starts. Once you think you're free, the final boss comes back, but oh no! he's mutated! Then you kill him and roll credits. So much of this game was just playing Classic-RE Bingo, and it's so forgettable because of it.
-While the antagonist is interesting on paper, in practice he's emblematic of the worst video game villains from the mid-late 2000s. Dude looks like a Great Value version of a Final Fantasy antagonist, talks like he huffs his own farts, and spends so much time whining about his problems that I wanted to kill him out of irritation more than anything else.
-Moreover, the framing device of cutting from the story to [spoiler] Marcus whining at Birkin and Wesker through the cameras [/spoiler] every 20 minutes got old really fast. I know it's difficult to tell the story they had without doing something like that, but it really took me out of Rebecca's and Billy's story.
-Honestly, Rebecca's and Billy's rapport was fantastic. But there's so little of it to make room for the framing device listed above, and it really hurts the game because of it!
-The training facility was clearly designed to invoke nostalgia for the Arklay Mansion, and instead of making me feel anything, it just irritates me because it's so much worse.
-Speaking of RE-Bingo, [spoiler] one of the boss fights is a prototype Tyrant. The idea and design is neat, but it feels like the developers just wanted to put a Tyrant in because "we need to prove that Rebecca's every bit as good as Chris or Jill!" [/spoiler]
-Managing two characters is a funish gimmick at first, but it quickly becomes bland. Billy has almost twice as much health as Rebecca, and the only thing that Rebecca has over Billy is that she can combine herbs. In essence the best way to play is to play as Billy, using Rebecca as a mobile item box who occasionally mixes herbs when you need them. I really wish they hadn't given Billy such a significant mechanical advantage.
-Speaking of item boxes: this game has no item boxes. You need to juggle your item placement based on when you think you'll be passing by that area to grab the key you need. For my blind first-time playthrough, this was horrendously unfun. I spent about a full hour of my 11-hour playthrough just making runs of moving all of my items from one save room to another whenever I was going to advance from one chapter to the next.
-Frankly, once you get off the train, with the exception of the boss fights, the game is horribly unfun. Hunters didn't feel like a threat at all, there's no sense of danger or urgency unless you play on Hard difficulty (even when I was at low health, I never felt afraid or stressed), and instead of having to carefully plan ahead for entering a new area to advance the objective, I was able to boredly blunder my way through with whatever I had on hand so I didn't have to worry about juggling items again. I wound up being so bored that there were multiple times when I just got up and walked away from the game to watch an episode on Netflix or play something funner on my Xbox before coming back to get to a save point before closing. It wasn't a game, it was a damn chore.
-The idea of the hookshot was fantastic. It would be really fun if I had an item box to keep it in before I needed it!
-Shotguns in this game are busted. I'm used to being able to reliably aim up and, once the zombie charges, pull the trigger for a guaranteed crit. In this, the autoaim is more than happy to guide your pellets to their chest, even if your barrel is stuck in their eye sockets.
-While looking for good guns in Leech Hunter was fun, the actual Leech collecting was droll, boring, and as fun as watching paint dry, with twice the irritation when you realize you missed a room.

I would rather the hookshot have been a special item in the slot of the mixing set/lighter that you could swap between characters.

Having a 'player 2' was a very fun mechanic and made the gameplay feel fresh and have more puzzle/story opportunities. While i understand the gameplay would be vastly different and difficult to integrate, I wouldve loved to have had the ability to plug in a secondary controller.

The majority of the puzzles themselves felt alot easier and faster to solve than RE:HD; but there were alot more difficult puzzles that I had to spend more time on, google a clue, or die trying to figure out.

Boss battles were nice but I was constantly confused by them. I could never fight one without wondering, do i shoot to kill? wait out a timer? am i hurting it? The lack of context and hit registry on bosses made for alot more confusion and google searches.

Sometimes the two characters get separated and the game gets absolutely bogged down by constantly having to pass items one by one via small elevators. If there was a limit to what you can pass, it would add some strategy, but you can move stuff infinitely, so its just a matter of how much time you want to waste. Actually there is a rule: you cannot pass big items, which means if all the big guns are on one character when the separation happens.... tough luck. This also happens with some bosses that kidnap one of the characters. If your best gun was in that character, time to load your last save.

Also the game is just very annoying in general: Camera placement is insanely bad in most fights, some places have many interactables with overlapping hitboxes which make you try several times to pick something up, a lot of bulls*** "surprise" moments... the list goes on.

With all that in mind, don't play this unless you HAVE to play all RE games.

This is by no means a bad game. This is a prime example of why Steam reviews need a "neutral" option. For fans of the RE series, I definitely recommend playing through it once. For those that want to get into the series and think they should start at the prequel, maybe skip ahead to the RE1 remake (whose events begin immediately following the conclusion of RE0) and come back to this. Coming from somebody whose first experience with this series was the fantastic duo of 7 & 8, the game as a whole just feels very dated. The story is serviceable; definitely not to the level of the other games, but it could be much worse, and I actually enjoyed the dynamic between Rebecca and Billy. Playing as both characters is an interesting take on the RE formula, and while it wasn't the worst thing in the world, it definitely could have been executed better. The puzzles were fairly difficult but not frustrating, and the environment was fairly interesting from a story perspective. The big issues begin when you actually analyze the gameplay.

First off, I understand that classic RE fans have a soft-spot for the fixed camera, but as someone who never played those games all those years ago, it makes the combat and interacting with the environment incredibly frustrating. On top of that, some of the enemies are incredibly annoying to fight given their small size and the fact that they often exist in groups, so death can jump on you in an instant if you aren't incredibly careful, and that is where the biggest issue comes in: dying, and specifically where your saves are. I get that it was a symptom of the hardware limitations and storage issues, however the lack of auto-saves and limited saves in a playthrough heavily disincentivize exploration and trial and error, which is a big part of the RE series. Sure, there might be plenty of items to use to save scattered around, but on a first run, you don't know that, so you don't want to waste them. That leads to you playing very slow and careful and avoiding exploring, because dying means you could lose an hour of gameplay, and that feels very bad.

And then there is the inventory system. I respect wanting to try something different from the item boxes, but oh my goodness, the VERY limited inventory space and having to drop items feels terrible, and even worse, it leads to a ton of back-tracking. Back-tracking isn't inherently bad, as all RE games do it, but the payoff for doing so is incredibly limited, and that compounded with the save issues means running into an enemy on your way back to a key item or weapon you left behind could mean completely restarting an area. On a first playthrough, it is also entirely unavoidable, because you never know what you need and when you need it. There is a reason they didn't do this again.

All in all, the game is far from bad, but it certainly isn't great. It is just aggressively mediocre. Is it worth playing? It definitely was for me, as I want to experience the entire series from beginning to end, but by the end of the game, one playthrough was enough. Upon beating the final boss, I was just ready for it to be over. I'm happy to say that I beat it, but I can't say I'm that interested in playing it more.

Step into the nightmare world of Resident Evil 0, a prequel to the iconic survival horror series that aims to expand the lore and deliver another chilling experience. While the game retains the classic Resident Evil formula, it falls short of capturing the same magic and scares that made its predecessors so memorable.
Let's start with the positives. The graphics in Resident Evil 0 are undeniably impressive, showcasing the system's capabilities it was released on. The environments are intricately detailed, from the decrepit mansion to the eerie underground labs. The lighting effects add an extra layer of suspense, making each dark corner feel genuinely menacing.
The dual-character system is an exciting addition, allowing players to switch between Rebecca Chambers, a rookie police officer, and Billy Coen, a mysterious prisoner. This dynamic opens up new possibilities for puzzle-solving and cooperation, as both characters possess unique abilities that complement each other. It adds a fresh twist to the gameplay, providing moments of strategic decision-making.
However, despite these strengths, Resident Evil 0 stumbles in several areas. One of the significant drawbacks is the need for more clarity and storyline. The plot attempts to provide a deeper understanding of the events leading up to the original Resident Evil game, but it often becomes tangled and difficult to follow. The narrative must include cohesive and engaging storytelling in other series titles, leaving players disconnected and uninvested.
The inventory management system, a hallmark of the Resident Evil franchise, is a source of frustration in Resident Evil 0. The limited inventory slots force constant backtracking to item boxes, making progress feel tedious and repetitive. It hinders the sense of exploration and survival, instead becoming an annoyance that disrupts the game's pacing.
Another letdown is the enemy design. While the classic zombies appear, they lack the same impact and terror defined in earlier games. The variety of creatures encountered throughout the game feels uninspired, failing to evoke the same fear or surprise. This lack of memorable adversaries diminishes the overall intensity and thrill of the gameplay.
Furthermore, the puzzles in Resident Evil 0 often feel contrived and overly complex. They require complex solutions that rely heavily on trial and error rather than logical thinking. This design choice can lead to frustration and detract from the immersive experience the game strives to create.
In summary, Resident Evil 0 falls short of the high expectations set by its predecessors. While it boasts impressive graphics and introduces a new dual-character system, the convoluted storyline, frustrating inventory management, lackluster enemy design, and challenging puzzles hinder the overall enjoyment. It's a missed opportunity to deliver a compelling prequel that genuinely captures the essence of the Resident Evil series.
Die-hard fans of the franchise may enjoy exploring the origins of the Resident Evil universe, but for newcomers or those seeking a genuinely captivating horror experience, there are better entries in the series to sink your teeth into. Resident Evil 0 stands as a middling addition to the Resident Evil canon, a game that fails to live up to its own potential and leaves players longing for the haunting brilliance of its predecessors.

The limited inventory/no item chests isn't that bad. You can drop items anywhere and they'll never disappear. Turning save rooms into item storages is a good idea.
Items you do leave behind are marked on your map in a color coded list. You can "tag" items to appear on your map by checking them and leaving them if you don't have space at the time.
Don't kill the first human leech you meet on the train. Turn around and run back down the stairs.
Don't neglect molotovs (gasoline + empty bottles). They are one of the best ways to kill the human leeches.
Don't forget the handgun either. There is a lot of ammo for it in the game (at least on normal), and I found it incredibly useful during the last boss. There's an upgrade for one of them you can find that is worth seeking out.
There's no reason to keep the hunting gun once you find the shotgun, which is almost immediately in the training facility.
The hookshot is written out to make it sound like only Rebecca can use it, but it just means only one person can use it a time. You will have to use it a few times throughout the game. The last time is in the cable car station.
Make sure Rebecca has the green chemical when leaving the training facility. It's in a lab room near a chess puzzle.

Okay, hear me out: this is far from the best game (really setting the tone here), but it's a good time.

The puzzles: confusing, but you can always just google it if you get stuck.

The gameplay: not only do we have fixed camera angles and tank controls (I am not a fan), but we have a single-player partner mechanic where you can switch between the characters. Basically, the gameplay is a mixed bag. It's interesting, but the partner mechanic needs refinement.

The story: is a completely unasked for prequel, but it's a fun one. The files have some great lore, and Rebecca is a joy to play as. The game has a more classic RE story, and it's on-par with REmake. The game isn't unique but definitely worth the play.

The monsters: there's some wonderful monster designs in this. They make my skin crawl!

The music: unforgettable.

Verdict: If you're itching for more Resident Evil, it's worth the time. Particularly when it goes on-sale, Zero is well-worth the asking price. Just go in with curbed expectations, and you'll find a pleasant surprise.

Resident Evil 0 was the first time that the Resident Evil franchise began to stagnate. It would happen again somewhere in between 5 & 6. This game signaled to Shinji Mikami and Capcom that something needed to chnage.

Re 0 is not a bad game. But it's certainly not good either. I can't recommend this to anyone who isn't a Resident Evil junkie or searching for  a more obscure title. If you're starting the franchise, stay far away from this game. Even though it's a prequel to the first game, you need all the context and mechanics of the Resident Evil 1&2 down pat to enjoy this one. It's not kind to beginners both in a narrative and design sense.

There are many comparisons you can draw between REmake and Re 0. But its those minor differences that make 0 a fever dream version of the original game, A spooky mansion, a lab, some gross industrial settings return as the areas you traverse. But none of them ever feel original, just lamer versions of content we've already played. I mean the game mimics the first game, but its environments are banal, much plainer compared to the original. There's a personality to REmake that 0 just doesn't have, but desperately wants. Technically though, the graphics look amazing though even if the art direction is uninspired.

The big exception to this is the train segment, where you start the game. It's an AMAZING area of the game, personally one of my favorites. So much attention to detail, with the luggage and bodies strewn everywhere, the rain pattering on the windows, and dimly warm dining cars. But the train only takes up about a third of the game before you're whisked off to yet another mansion.

Even the enemies feel pretty uninspired. Re0 sometimes feel like you're trying to escape from a zoo, because many of the enemies are just feral animals and insects. Monkeys, spiders, centipedes, scorpions, bats, and other critters try to kill you. It feel cliche and worn out, especially after fantastic designs in the previous games. You even fight a tyrant...again! But in Re0 this tyrant is the prototype ♥♥♥♥♥♥ version even though it behaves exactly like the Re1 version. Seeing a comparison here?

But even though 0's art direction generally is uninspired, I could look past that. What really pissed me of throughout the entirety of the game was purely mechanical issues. This game removes the item box to instead feature two characters that have together have 12 total slots of inventory. In addition, items placed on the ground will stay where they are forever until they are picked up again.

I feel like this isn't a terrible idea on its own, but Re 0 doesn't handle it well. You must be thinking wow 12 slots?! That's a lot. Consider however that RE 0 doubles the amount of key items, makes nearly all weapons take up 2 slots, and each character must carry their own ammo. In addition certain puzzle items take up more than 1 slot.

Because there's no centralized storage there is so much backtracking in the game. If you want to move your items to a different area, you'll have to backtrack multiple times across a maze of similarly looking corridors. But it's not "good" backtracking. It's all just busy work, annoying you when you realize you forgot something and now have to run to the beginning of the game to get it. Or you dropped an item to make room for another and forgot about it. Now you have to search the whole damn mansion to find it again.

There's also times where the games decides to ♥♥♥♥ with you and make you backtrack on purpose. Certain items show up in the beginning and don't have another use until hours later in the game when you've forgotten about them and now must fight your way back to get them. That part doesn't feel like an epiphany where you realize what item you need, it just reminds that I have to slog back through content I finished just because there was no where to put the key item. Also the game has now filled the corridors with invincible t virus monkeys. Let's talk about that.

Re0 is the hardest game Resident Evil game I have ever played, and I played it on normal. The game requires an intense amount of micromanagement and a fair bit of luck. The non-zombie enemies are way too strong and ammo/healing is sparse, perhaps the least I've ever seen. Take the monkeys for example. They're small, fast, and if there's two of them they can easily stunlock you. They're also incredibly tanky, requiring 5-6 shotgun shells to put down. The game naturally starts throwing packs of 3 of them at you.

The inventory is so limited that you often never have room for healing items, causing quick deaths and forcing you to play perfectly between each save.

So for all this frustration, you're hoping to at least get a fun or goofy story to alleviate your stress as you navigate Re 0's clunkiness. Nope. This is by far the worst Resident Evil story, and that's really sayin something when you look at some of the other games.

Billy and Rebecca have no chemistry. 0, zilch, nada, sefr. They are two hollow blocks of wood that bump into each other on occasion. Other than that they have barely a hint of personality. We rarely see them talk to each other and when they do they contribute almost nothing. Billy also has this backstory where he's a prisoner because he refused to execute a village in Africa. It's an incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up scene that is never addressed again and feels  weird next to an anime leech man who sings to his leeches. Why did they put the massacre scene in? Why never bring it up again? What does this have to do with Umbrella or viruses or any of that. It feels like they just threw in a Nam flashback to be edgy.

The game ends with another mansion explosion, and then foreshadows the next mansion explosion. The whole game just feels like an inferior recycling of ideas.

At the end of the day this game is decent but hella annoying sometimes. If you really, I mean really, liked REmake then I would play this game.  Other than that it's not worth it. I recommend but barely.

You should neither buy nor play this.

First off, this game won't work on modern PCs. I'm on Windows 11 with an RTX 4090 and just couldn't get it to start. I fiddled for two hours with various tips in the forums and nothing worked for me. I ended up playing the Nintendo Switch version, which as far as I can tell is identical in every way. But even if you get the Windows version to work, I think it should stay on the shelf. It's a frustrating game with too few rewards. If you're interested in how the whole [I]Resident Evil[/I] saga started then you're better off watching a video playthrough of [I]Resident Evil 0[/I] instead of playing through this painful game yourself. Note, though, that even when watching someone else play it's impossible not to feel the frustration!

The game's basic DNA is closer to that of point-and-click adventures than action horror, as it's essentially about solving puzzles by finding items in the environment, using them on the environment, and sometimes combining them. There are some enemies, too, and combat follows the usual survival trope of having very limited ammo so that every bullet counts, which encourages you to consider running away instead of attacking in order to conserve ammo. So far so good, but there's a lot to keep you from enjoying this basic formula.

One major issue is the atrocious save system. Its in-story conceit is cool, but there are ridiculously few opportunities to save. And because it's too easy to die due to a silly mistake (did you waste all your ammo?), you're often sent way, way back in your progress.

And this sucks because everything about the gameplay is tedious. Your inventory is extremely constrained so that much of the game consists of dropping items, moving them between characters, going back to pick them up again, etc. There's no clever thinking involved in terms of strategy or efficiency of inventory management. It's just an arbitrary obstacle that adds nothing but annoyance.

Another annoyance is the load screens: they occur very often because the levels are so small, and they are incredibly slow. Couldn't this have been fixed for the HD remaster? Save slot loading times are very slow, too.

The final frustrating issue has to do with the fixed camera perspective. It's great for atmosphere and the remastered HD graphics do make it look majestically cinematic. However, it's a disaster for gameplay as it's very common for enemies to come at you from angles you can't see. How did this nonsense ever pass any kind of playtesting?

After the fourth time I died and had to tediously repeat the same puzzle sequences and inventory management rigamarole, I rage quit. I was not having fun. At all.

What is your reward for suffering through such poor game design? A mediocre, predictable plot conveyed via bad storytelling. Despite the rich environmental design, herein is a narrative that too often prefers to tell you rather than show you. The cutscenes are blatant exposition with the characters saying out loud exactly what they are doing and why. The writing is almost comically bad.

Relatedly, the game doesn't know how to treat its female protagonist. On the one hand it wants you to take her seriously as a capable, professional law enforcer. On the other hand it lets you to dress her in skimpy "sportswear", a cheerleader outfit, or as a sexy nurse. It's hard not to feel sorry for her.

All in all, [I]Resident Evil 0[/I]  is a disappointing entry in the franchise.

If you are looking for a sign to get into the Resident Evil series after the release of the RE4 remake, this is it.

Resident Evil 0 is a solid introduction to the franchise and doesn't require any in-depth knowledge of the universe. Despite its age, the game's visuals hold up well by today's standards.

While the plot is mostly unremarkable, Capcom set an industry standard for survival horror titles by creating an atmosphere full of tension, mystery, and suspense. The difficulty particularly comes from the scarcity of ammo, healing items, and consumable save items (ink ribbons).

Some of the mechanics are unique to RE0, such as having to control two characters at once and the lack of a storage box that can be accessed from every safe room. Since these challenges might be initially overwhelming, I would suggest following a general guide during the first playthrough to make the whole ordeal more manageable.

The bottom line is if you are willing to put up with a cheesy villain, tank controls, and some challenging mechanics, you are in for a very fulfilling treat that welcomes you to the herb-mixing and rock-punching world of Resident Evil.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[h2]Visuals and Atmosphere[/h2]
The PC version is an HD remaster version and was released in 2016 but the graphics don't look aged at all. The eerie and creepy atmosphere is enhanced with the HD upgrade. The textures look crisp. Models look modern and less jaggy. It's just like what you expected a classic RE remaster could be.

[h1]The Mixed[/h1]
[h2]Gameplay and Camera[/h2]
On the other hand, the tank control aged quite well in 2023. I was fine with it during the 90 but, but after I experienced the third-person control in RE4, I found this kind of control quite cumbersome. The game was designed with this control in mind so it worked well overall but I'm not really the fan of fixed camera angle. If you play the game with the analog stick, the game won't retain your movement direction unlike when you use the D-pad, and sometimes it makes you run straight to the enemies. That happened a lot and it was quite annoying.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[h2]Inventory System[/h2]
There's one and ONLY one aspect that I truly hate from the inside and it is the game's inventory system (or lacking thereof). Since the Buddy System is a big selling point of the game, some idiots at Capcom thought that it might be a good idea to get rid of the inventory box altogether. In this game, you need to manage your inventory manually by carrying items from one point to another. And how do you leave behind the unused items, you ask? You drop them to the ground. Crazy, right? This poses two main problems. The first is, if you forgot to carry your key items to the designated area, you need to backtrack all the way to where you left them. And because of this, the game forces you to carry unnecessary items with you because you don't know when they might be needed. For example, the Hook Shot. The f*cking Hook Shot! I can't say enough how I hate it. It takes two slots but its usage is scarce (it's only used three times during the entire game) but you need it anyway. Carrying this around the game is so tiring.

Second, did I already mention that you need to drop the unused item on the ground to free up your slots? By doing this, your item might end up behind some background items that render your item invisible entirely since this game uses fixed camera angles. Worst yet. To pick up the dropped item you must precisely maneuver your character to the specific location that can trigger the pickup command. Imagine you scattered many items in the same area and tried to pick one up. Yeah. I wasted half of my playtime trying to get back the items I dropped. Talking about unnecessary time wasting.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
This is a classic example of a great game ruined by one broken feature. I always play every RE game in more than one playthrough, but, I won't go back to play this game ever again since I don't see any reason why I should be suffered from its trashy inventory system. It still provides you with a classic RE experience which you should play it at least once. But if you are not an RE fan, watching Let's Play on Youtube might be a much better option.

[h1]Resident Evil 0: My Least Favorite of the Good Games[/h1]

[b]Introduction[/b]
Resident Evil 0 is a survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. It was originally released in 2002 for the Nintendo GameCube and later ported to other platforms. As a fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I have played through most of the games in the series, and unfortunately, I have to say that Resident Evil 0 is my least favorite of the good games, meaning those released before the franchise transitioned to a more action-oriented gameplay.

[u]Story[/u]
[h1][/h1]
The story of Resident Evil 0 takes place before the events of the first game in the series. You play as two characters, Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen, who are investigating a series of bizarre murders in the Arklay Mountains. The story tries to expand upon the lore of the series, but it ultimately feels convoluted and unnecessary. The plot jumps around between different characters and locations, and it's hard to really care about what's going on.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay mechanics of Resident Evil 0 are similar to other games in the series. You control your character from a third-person perspective and explore different areas while fighting off zombies and other monsters. One of the unique features of this game is the dual-character system, where you control both Rebecca and Billy at the same time. While it's an interesting twist on the series' formula, it can be a bit frustrating at times.

The inventory system in Resident Evil 0 is also clunky and frustrating. The lack of item boxes makes it difficult to manage your resources, and the decision to remove the traditional item chest system makes the game feel needlessly difficult at times.

[u]Graphics and Sound[/u]
The graphics and atmosphere of Resident Evil 0 are top-notch. The pre-rendered backgrounds look great, and the character models are well-designed. The sound design is also impressive, with eerie sound effects and music that add to the tension and horror of the game.

[u]Conclusion[/u]
In conclusion, Resident Evil 0 is not a bad game, but it falls short of its predecessors in many ways. The story is convoluted, the gameplay mechanics can be frustrating, and the inventory system is needlessly difficult. However, the graphics and atmosphere are top-notch

First let me point out that this is not a remake or reboot of the series, it is a HD remastered version of the original 2002 GameCube version that was limited in scope and design having been originally designed for the Nintendo 64 which began development in 1998. Due to the N64 limitations, Capcom decided to switch to the new Nintendo system, the GameCube, released in 2001. The core game concepts, mechanics, and story were carried over to the new system. 

RE0 is a prequel to the original RE. This for me carries the biggest purchase factor. The game play design in which you switch between characters is refreshing. However, the mechanics themselves are cumbersome. Graphics are mediocre at best offering a HD upgrade to the originals but in no way can compete with modern graphical fidelity. The inventory system is horrible, and will require painful planing to manage. The story while being a prequel to RE, is below average due to hardware restrictions during it's original design for the N64. They could have been innovative and modernized this HD remaster as a remake to improve game play mechanics and visuals on a new engine, instead it is just a better looking (HD) playable version for modern consoles and PC. 

Even on a sale, this is a push to recommend for me because I was disappointed in the quality delivered. Playing RE0 has been more of a compulsive desire to complete the game rather than finding anything addictive about it. I do realize that there are people whom love playing old school games and those that just want the nostalgia of replaying a game they loved back in the day. Therefore, I only recommend this game if you are a fan of the series and are looking for a prequel to the original RE game on a DDD (deep-deep discount), if you are not turned off by dated old school mechanics.

Befriend your worst enemy: Ever wanted to team up with your worst enemy? Well, now's your chance! Play as Rebecca Chambers and work alongside the infamous Bio-Organic Weapon, Billy Coen. They say keep your friends close and your enemies closer, but in this case, just make sure you have a First Aid Spray handy.

Stuck in tight spaces: Love puzzles? How about puzzles in tight, claustrophobic spaces with flesh-eating zombies on your tail? Sounds like the perfect Saturday night, if you ask me.

What's in the box?! Move over, Brad Pitt. The real mystery box is in Resident Evil Zero. You'll never know what's in store until you open it, and it might just be the key to your survival.

Customize your weapons: Who needs a gun store when you can just combine items in your inventory to create the ultimate weapon? A shotgun with a flamethrower attachment? Sure, why not!

Train your reflexes: Want to improve your reflexes and reaction time? Play Resident Evil Zero and you'll be dodging zombie attacks like a pro in no time.

It's a prequel: If you're a fan of the Resident Evil series, then you'll love that Resident Evil Zero is a prequel to the original game. Learn more about the origins of the T-Virus and the Umbrella Corporation, all while fighting for survival.

Take a trip down memory lane: Relive the classic survival horror experience with updated graphics and gameplay mechanics. It's like a trip down memory lane, but with more blood and guts.

Boss battles: Who doesn't love a good boss battle? Resident Evil Zero has plenty of them, and they're sure to get your heart racing.

It's scary as hell: Let's be real, the main reason to play Resident Evil Zero is for the scares. With its eerie atmosphere, jump scares, and creepy enemies, you'll be sleeping with the lights on for days.

I loved the RE1 remake/remaster and specifically picked this game up because it possessed some similar features and a similar gameplay style. I’m afraid this game left me with mixed feelings, though, and makes me wish there was a "neutral"  recommendation option, as with every positive, there's unfortunately a negative.

Pros:

- I love Rebecca, and am glad they gave her a moment in the spotlight.

- It has the "old school" feel of RE1 with the fixed camera angles and forced inventory management.

- It was interesting to see what happened with the Bravo Team pre-RE1.

- Graphically, it still looks pretty good, even after all this time.

Cons:

- The story wasn’t all that memorable and it feels stretched pretty thin, with there barely being enough of to match the amount of gameplay.

- Despite the fixed camera angles and similar location style, the atmosphere failed to provide the same tension and unsettling feelings that the RE1 remake did. Only on very rare occasion did I find myself feeling tense and anxious about what was to come.

- Billy himself felt kind of flat and one-note. I know that the characters in the early RE games didn’t have a lot of depth to them, so it was nice that the writers went out of their way to try and give Billy a somewhat tragic backstory. Unfortunately, however, it’s only mentioned once or twice, and doesn’t really contribute that much to his character or the game’s overall story.

- And yes, the inventory system was occasionally a pain in the butt, especially when you had to make a mental note to almost constantly carry certain key items with you, so you don’t have to backtrack all the way to the beginning of the level just to fetch it, so you can continue into the next area. This wouldn’t be as much of an issue, but there are some areas you never return to again, so...

To sum it all up: this feels like it should've been a side DLC for the RE1 remake. If you're aiming to play every game in the RE series, I'd recommend it - especially if you’re a fan of Rebecca or the fixed camera-style of RE1 - but just barely. Best to pick this one up on sale.

There are lots of reviews effectively-outlining all the issues this game has in terms of difficulty design, absolutely unfair enemies, horrible item management, etc.  I'll reiterate that all those things are true, but more so: if you think that because you've played Resident Evil 1 Remake ("REmake") that this game won't be hard to transition to, you're wrong.  

Almost everything is worse than REmake and even if you're a major fan of that game, RE0 will be incredibly-frustrating for you.  Most mechanics don't actually work the same way (even though you'd expect them to, being it's the same fixed-camera style and same development timeframe) so any advanced tactics you mastered in REmake won't apply here.  The only things better here are the graphics, and better NG+ weapons to unlock (and, the DLC cosmetics for Rebecca and Billy are cool).

This game is absolutely NOT worth a blind playthrough unless you like wasting your time and dying to unfair, horrible design.  Some bosses make no sense, one you even HAVE to use cheese tactics on because the fight is basically an awful mess of constant stunlocks.  Only play this to know the experience for yourself, and if you're just that much of a dedicated RE fan.  NEVER play this as your first experience of the fixed-camera style... go to REmake for that, and stay there, it's a much much much better game.  
Seriously all the new enemies are bad and they even managed to screw up some of the familiar enemies... it's almost a joke.  Almost.
As experienced fans say, be thankful that if you have to play this that you get to play it with modern controls because it would be nearly-impossible with tank controls.

And all of these problems and it has actually nothing redeeming to offer in terms of story- it's a "prequel" that tells you almost nothing and doesn't even tie into RE1 effectively.  So don't expect this to really explain what happened before the Mansion, think of it more as some sort of weird RE1 ripoff game made by a different team that didn't know what made things work in RE1, because that's what it feels like.  Sorry to the Capcom employees who put their passion into this, but this really wasn't a win other than the graphics, and it deserves to be ignored except for historical/series-development-tracking purposes.

OK, the back and forth is frustrating, the leech zombies suck unless you're stocked on molotovs, the character switching is a pain and the lack of an item box is just stupid. This game is not for people who played newer REs and want to try some of the older games.

All that being said I've been streaming the game with a couple of friends watching and we're having a blast. Looks good visually and the music is solid to. The story is brilliantly hokey and the villain is so bad it's good to me, there's more Wesker which is a win and it fleshes out Rebeccas character. It's old school survival horror at heart and It isn't as hard as people say, just time consuming more than anything and some trial and error is needed.

Is it the best survival horror? No. Is it the best Resident Evil? Not even close but it is a damned fun blast and a decent shift from the more modern run and gun style of more recent Survival Horrors

Resident Evil 0 introduces a unique character-switching system distinct from RE1. The gameplay experience in RE0 feels subtly more challenging, primarily attributed to the confined spaces, which are abundant throughout the game. This necessitates a more strategic allocation of resources compared to RE1.

TL;DR:
I honestly feel like this game has aged better with time. With hindsight this truly feels like a gem. There are so many unique mechanics to the game that lead to some of the most fun and interesting boss fight and puzzles that series has to offer.  However, a few missteps take it away from being potentially the best title in the resident evil franchise.

Pros:
- Train section at the beginning and the latter sections of the game really capitalize on the idea of managing two characters at once. It feels satisfying to manage two distinct characters with different abilities through the  puzzle box environments the series is known for.

Neutral:
-Managing resources, on one hand you have some cool moments you can stock pile from room to room  and just go back to main halls to reload or decide what weapon of choice you need for the occasion. On the other hand it can get a bit tedious to manage the sheer volume of resources but a lot of the time it beats having to go all the way back to a save room then go all the way to where I was to pick up an item. I would have loved to seen a mixture of both objects on the and storage box but I kind of feel like it would have been far to simple if that was the case.
-Middle section of the game is a mansion similar to re1 and if you come off the back of re1 remake it might feel like a retread but I personally was not bothered by it.
Cons:
Mixing agents and the hookshot (2 slot item), I don't want to spoil anything but if you want save yourself a lot of headache I would look up where they are useful and then you will understand. I felt like both of these key quests items were very poorly implemented.

Chambers, the rookie S.T.A.R.S. member, and Coen, the convict with a heart, create a dynamic duo that is sure to send shivers down your spine as you navigate through this world of horrors. 🕹️🧟‍♂️

Not only does Resident Evil 0 make you feel like you are in a survival-horror film, but it also demands strategic thinking. The game has a unique 'partner zapping' system that enables you to switch between characters at will, and believe me, you'll need to. The diversity in character abilities demands strategic use. For instance, Rebecca can mix herbs to create healing items, while Billy uses his brute strength to move heavy objects. The ability to use each character's skills efficiently can be the difference between life and undeath. 🎮🧟‍♀️

The game also teases your brain with intricate puzzles that require teamwork to solve. You'll find yourself trying to piece together solutions, using the unique skills of each character to progress. Add to this the impressively detailed environments, and you've got a gaming experience that is genuinely immersive. The graphics are beautiful, and the eerie sound effects coupled with the creepy background music make the game even more immersive. 🖼️🎵

But remember, my fluffy friends, Resident Evil 0 is not a walk in the park. It’s a product of Capcom’s golden era when they made challenging games that pushed the boundaries of gaming. The game is a true survival horror masterpiece. Yes, there will be times when you’ll want to howl in frustration, and yes, the fixed camera angles can be a little tricky to master, but believe me, once you get the hang of it, you'll appreciate the cinematic feel it gives the game. 📽️😱

The combat, while not the main selling point of the game, is functional. It's not Call of Duty, but it doesn't try to be. Resident Evil 0 focuses on survival, puzzle-solving, and inventory management. However, the auto-targeting system makes combat smooth and bearable, while the partner system adds an extra layer of complexity and depth to the game. The inventory system can be challenging, with the need to backtrack to pick up items you've dropped, but it adds to the survival aspect of the game and helps ramp up the tension.🔫💼

Now, let's talk about the story. As a seasoned gamer and a lover of lore, I must say that Resident Evil 0 offers an engaging narrative. It gives depth to the Resident Evil universe by introducing us to the events leading up to the original game. You'll learn about the origins of the Umbrella Corporation and the biological experiments that caused the zombie outbreak. It ties in nicely with the rest of the series, giving us a backstory that only serves to deepen our understanding and appreciation of this iconic franchise. 🧪🦠

In summary, Resident Evil 0 is a trip down the terrifying lane of survival horror, offering players a mixture of puzzle-solving, strategic gameplay, and a chilling atmosphere that'll leave you on the edge of your seat. For fans of the series and newcomers alike, it's a must-play. It's got its quirks and challenging moments, but that's what makes it such a memorable experience. It's a piece of gaming history that has been wonderfully remastered for new and old fans alike to enjoy. So grab your gamepads, brave the horror, and remember - in Resident Evil 0, survival isn't just a game, it's a necessity. 🎮👻

For this game, I have both pros and cons. I'll start with the pros:

 Resident Evil Zero is a prequel to the first game, Resident Evil. As the result of the game being a prequel, I genuinely loved getting the chance to see the true beginning of the Resident Evil franchise. Not just the order of events, but the slow and noticeable progression and evolution of the Umbrella corporation themselves. The story of Resident Evil Zero follows the inevitable development of a virus that originally functioned as a type of  natural growth hormone whenever introduced to biological materials (i.e. living beings), the mass pharmaceutical Umbrella Corp. took one look at this virus and asked themselves the same question any government would; "Okay, now can it be weaponized?" 

I personally find this concept interesting because Resident Evil is a well known zombie horror survive apocalypse style game series as a whole. While there are some zombies in Resident Evil Zero, the game puts emphasis on the fact that most of the enemies you run into in the game are results of the original viral strain that operated as a growth hormone (the "Progenitor virus"); not the typical undead monstrosities everyone today is used to as a result of the much more well known "T-virus". As a result of that one difference, all the monsters you face are failed prototypes of the more well known monsters introduced later in the game timeline. Large frogs, overgrown locusts, massive bats, and hyper aggressive apes. Even most of the more human enemies are just prototypes, while there are some zombies most of the humanoids are actually clusters of mutated leeches that had been taught to mimic a human form. There is even a monster that appears to be some kind of prototype of Nemesis from Resident Evil 3 that the game suggests was made by mixing a human with progenitor infested leeches, a failed attempt to create the eventual Tyrant virus.

 At the end of it all, they're prototypes; failed attempts to advance Umbrella Corp.'s agenda that were eventually axed and abandoned. I loved being able to see one of the earliest stages of Umbrella's evolution.

I particularly loved the saving mechanic of having to resource manage ink ribbons just so the player could save their progress. In gaming today, most games don't even give you a choice because their programmed with an auto-save feature. Resident Evil Zero gave me a sense of challenge and made me feel like my choices had a genuine consequence every time an ink ribbon had to be used. 
  
The cons are about the annoying controls and functions: 

The buttons made little sense causing me to constantly hit the wrong buttons at all the wrong times, the button I would have thought would pause the game instead caused me to jump from one character to the other. The map button was set to a button I'd normally use to aim or shoot a weapon, while the control stick I'd normally use to control the camera angle was set to move the partner character instead. 

All camera angles are fixed, causing me to accidentally turn around at the drop of a hat and go back the way I just came. I frequently got lost and forgot what I was doing simply because I got turned around while I was in a hurry. 

The puzzles were fun, but complicated to the point where I had to keep cheating by looking up what to do online. I have no idea how anybody is expected to play this game blind without any help. The map shows items general locations and even color codes them, but doesn't mark the locations of all items found or otherwise and doesn't have a map key that tells players what the item color codes mean. I eventually had to guess that green is healing items, blue is combine-able, red is weapons, orange is key items, and I ran into a yellow item but didn't understand the point of that one. 

Now, why am I recommending this game even with all these frustrating problems? Well, even though these are all problems in the games we play today, only having these problems in a game that originally released back in 2002 is a godsend. There were significantly less resources to work with back then, a time period that was riding the tail end of the gaming era where everyone was still freaking out over the exciting idea of 3-D graphics. Taking the time it was developed into account, I'm honestly surprised at how good the game still is today. Most games this old haven't aged well at all, but I think I can compare this game to something akin to a fine wine. It's meant to be savored, and remains a memory of history nobody will forget for years to come.

Resident Evil 0 (Remastered) is one of the old school RE games. Fixed camera, puzzles, inventory management, lots of backtracking. If you like RE Remake you should like RE 0. The graphics look very crisp here compared to RE Remake, you actually can select resolutions higher then FHD. The environments also look beautiful.

Not having an item box is a big change and while it is nice to be able to drop items temporarily, this means you will convert the floor of save rooms into a mess full of ammunition and herbs and this actually increases the backtracking.
My biggest complaint would be the badly balanced difficulty settings. "Easy" is basically "Story Mode" since you have more ammunition then in a CoD game, enough herbs and sprays for the whole S.T.A.R.S team and enemies are not only weaker but also fewer. On the other hand "Normal" difficulty is really tough, much harder then "Normal" difficulty in RE2 Remake, RE3 Remake or RE7/8. There should have been a difficulty setting in between (very) "Easy" and "Normal". RE Remake has a similar problem. 
What I would recommend before you start playing is that you inform yourself online about certain enemy types and how to deal with them. Also, look up the Hookshot.
Overall I would recommend Resident Evil 0. It's not perfect,  inventory management can be annoying, some cheap instant deaths, but still a very good RE game and I would actually rate it higher then RE2 and RE3 Remake.

Resident Evil Zero is a single player survival-horror game with puzzles added in. 
Since it's chronologically the first Resident Evil game, it's also my first game in the series. So I have no game to compare it to and see how future games improved or kept certain aspects. As a new player I can say the mechanics felt pretty easy to pick up.
The door cutscenes (can be modded) and changing perspectives are something you need to get used to. I personally didn't mind it after playing for a bit.

Gameplay:
You are able to control two characters, Rebecca and Billy which is different to other games of the series. 
It has it's advantages but also struggles and problems. As a new player you tend to have both characters teamed up and set to attack which can result in lots of ammo getting wasted. It was a hard lesson for newbies to learn to not waste all ammo on enemies without using your brain (since other games often highlight those gamestyles). Similar to that, the healing items and ink ribbons (used to save your progress) should also be used wisely and not just whenever you feel like it. Which, in my opinion, is a good aspect of the game. 
Having two characters can help with bosses if you know what you are doing. At the same time it can backfire very easily and get you killed when you only focus on one of them. The major advantage besides extra damage to enemies are the added 6 slots to carry more items. The limited item slots are probably the worst part about this game and can hinder the overall gameplay flow. Many times, you have to walk back to pick up items and go through multiple 3 second cutscenes every time you change rooms, just so you have your shotgun ready for a future fight or get your hookshot to be able to reach different areas and continue the story. Both of these items take up two item slots out of 6 a character can have (12 for both). You are also not able to store items anywhere, so you have to drop them on the floor and sometimes struggle to pick the right one up with them all crowed on the floor 
What I like are the different weapons that are all more or less effective against specific enemies. Leaving you to try and see what damages them the most and also if it's better to save less effective ammo for other fights. You can get around half the enemies without fighting them, just by clever movement.
The autoaim is good for rapid firing but very annoying against multiple targets, the best example is [spoiler] the Bat Boss in the church and your character rather focusing on the smaller bats instead of the big and more dangerous one. [/spoiler]
On the other hand most bosses on normal are manageable for newbies, providing you with ammo, health and checkpoints beforehand. 

The game itself is running smoothly on 60 FPS with HD graphics, either full screen or adjusted. Only some cutscenes are a bit blurry but that's fine. The characters and enemies look great. The music and sound design is awesome; The voice actors for certain characters can feel a bit goofy (*Personal opinion*). 
Enemies can allow for some small but well delivered jumpscares. And can also be quite stressful to deal with, especially Mimicry Marcus'

I loved the storyline and the setup for future games by focusing on Umbrella and major characters like Wesker and Birkin. I also wish Rebecca and Billy would appear again since the chemistry between them felt wonderful. 

I don't think the game is for everyone, I'd still highly recommend it tho, even if it's just so you played all RE games.

Game is pretty good. The pre-rendered backgrounds still look gorgeous and the gameplay is solid. Tank controls are now optional if you don't like dealing with that. Cheesy storyline and dialogue, a lot of running around and backtracking, puzzle solving, and resource management. Basically classic RE so if you enjoy this kind of game you'll like this one.

That being said, even though I very much recommend it, there are some infuriating things in this game:

- Resource management has always been a staple of the series but it is just plain annoying in this game. Very few inventory slots per characters, which is manageable till you get to the real problem: no magic storage chest (I hope I wasn't just blind but I don't think so, normal difficulty). Not having a dedicated storage is a nightmare. You have to constantly drop stuff on the floor and backtrack to where you left it when you need it while managing both characters' inventory. I beat it in about 12 hours or so and I really do feel like half of it was spent on menus and pixel hunting to pick up the right item out of the mess I left on the floor while also constantly backtracking to the room where I left my dragon's hoard. Doing this instead of progressing through the game almost killed the joy of playing it.

- Door opening cinematics, taking ages to load a game (partly my fault for installing in an hdd), and having to wait for some text to slowly scroll every time you load a game. I get it, this is the og RE experience and it does tickle my nostalgia bone but I really do think you should be able to skip those by default. You're probably gonna die a lot on your first playthrough and repeatedly going through those time wasters can really erode your sense of fun. You can probably mod that functionality in but I didn't bother, just wanted to beat it once and be done with it.

- Cheap enemies are also a staple of RE with some stun locking ones being really annoying but... Yeah, there's 2 instances that are just plain awful: A boss with adds that makes you waste a lot of precious ammo when auto aiming (I'm not skilled enough to carefully aim in such a hectic situation) and stun locks you to boot. The worst offender though is an enemy at nearly the end of the game that can just one hit kill you and lose you a lot of progress (AND you'll probably have to got through a lot of inventory management when retrying). Avoiding this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is not intuitive at all and I had to look it up.

Even though I ended up writing more negative stuff than positive, this is still classic RE and a solid game.

[b][u]PROS[/u]:[/b] This game plays out like the Resident Evil Remake, using fixed camera angles & either tank controls or stick movement.  The story is just as wonderfully camp & goofy as any of the early Resident Evil games, & leans into it with a B-movie sensibility.  The puzzles are also quite fun in this title.  There are a few extra rewards upon completing the game, both of which have plenty of fun moments (such as getting to play as Wesker).  The visuals have that edge of disaster to them, & the soundtrack can be creepy enough to unnerve as well.

[b][u]CONS[/u]:[/b] Out of all of the classic Resident Evil titles, this one has the most problems.  The biggest one is no item boxes.  Items are placed on the ground, & require the player to run back to said location to pick them back up.  Each character you control only has 6 inventory slots each, with some more powerful weapons taking up 2.  This means that unless one plans routes out in advance, backtracking becomes even more prevalent.  The second half of the game is rather uninteresting after a stellar start, which unfortunately drags the endgame down.  An odd decision was to make the game co-op with no local or online multiplayer options.  The Eliminator enemies are a chore to deal with due to their small body & rapid movement.  Worse are the Lurker enemies, which have an instant kill move that's quite difficult to avoid without your partner around.  Lastly, & this is a minor one, some key items & hookshot locations are a little too well hidden, the latter's case thankfully relieved a little due to indication on the map in whatever room one is in.

[b][u]ACHIEVEMENTS[/u]:[/b] This list is actually a little challenging.  Many achievements will be gotten through story progression, & even by complete accident.  The most difficult are the obvious full run achievements, such as S-Rank, no saving, & no healing.  Others are challenging due to the controls & mechanics, such as I Have the Touch, gotten for defeating a Mimicry Marcus using only the knife.  My suggestion is to beat the game & collect all Leaches in the extra Leach Hunter mode, as this will unlock not only infinite ammo, but also the ridiculous end game revolver right at the start, & save when going for a challenging achievement with an inventory full of healing items.

[b][u]FINAL[/u]:[/b] Resident Evil 0 is an unfortunate misstep in the main numbered titles in the Resident Evil series.  Though it does have plenty of highlights (such as the camp story), the bland second half, poor enemy design, & rather frustrating gameplay gimmick drag the entire experience down.  Even worse, for fans of Resident Evil's lore, this title does next to nothing in advancing the plot of the overarching narrative.  For the hardcore, it's worth a look, but for everyone else, one'd probably be better passing on this one.

Here are some tips I wish I knew:

Don't be afraid to restart your save if you aren't far past the train. I did this myself and you can easily complete the train in 20 mins and the mansion in another 30. I was able to catch back up to my save after fighting the centipede and having no ammo in like an hour. It didn't take long and now I have over 100 handgun ammo and the shotgun/grenade ammo is mostly unused. I'm on the bat boss now excessively kitted out. This is on normal btw. I will admit I spent a while learning and practicing beforehand but didn't watch any spoilers. I am really rusty on games like this. The train gives you a ton of stuff if you do it right!

Drop any special items in whatever main area, the middle of the train, the main hall in mansion, so on. If you can't use it immediately, drop it. Keep as much space open as you can. Even drop the ink ribbons, healing, and ammo. There will almost never be a time you need more than handgun ammo and if there is, die and backtrack. It seems excessive but trust me, it will save you so much time. 

Don't be afraid to use shotgun/grenade ammo on bosses. The only two bosses I recommend you DONT use this ammo on is the scorpion and centipede. You can kill the scorpion easily with a handgun with your back to the door and the centipede is tanky but can be killed with a handgun too.

You do not want to miss a single item. Take your time and search around, memorize the area. If you are on normal/hard, ALWAYS try and do headshots, don't try and kill the ravens, don't fight unless you have to, be ready to run at all times, and if you miss too many shots do NOT be afraid to start over on Hard. 

Google the bosses, they can be a pain sometimes.

Practice doing headshots EVERY TIME!! They may seem useless but trust me, they will save you a whole lot of ammo in the long run. Don't be afraid to use your knife only when there is 1 zombie on the ground. Knives do save ammo overtime if used! Only carry 1. 

I recommend when you first start out save and kill the zombies in the main train, practice on headshoting them at least a dozen times. It will really, really help you along the game. Learning the headshot hitbox mechanics will save you a lot of ammo in the long run. I did this myself and I am now basically walking through this game.

Do NOT bring your partner with you to rooms you aren't prepared for!!! Your partner is a liability, will waste ammo, and waste healing. Clear the enemies solo first. I seriously wish I followed this tip early on. It has caused me a massive headache after the 3rd boss

If you feel yourself getting burnt out don't be afraid to google. But for real, you wont ever have to google anything if you just really pay close attention to each room and look for the files in each room. There are a whole lot of clues and its easy to remember them if you pay attention.

Unfortunately the worst Resident Evil game I have played so far (though haven't played 6).
The two-character system seems completely unnecessary and, like many other mechanics in the game, only serves to frustrate me. It's just tedious to constantly switch between Billy and Rebecca and managing two inventories at once.

You will constantly be pacing back and forward through the environment picking up items and probably leaving key items in one room - the amount you can leave in one room is limited too. This could easily be solved with an item box, but I suppose Capcom wanted to go for 'realism' here? I suppose that's why most enemies can gank you to death after not saving for 10 mins, forcing you to repeat the same arduous task of wandering back and forward between rooms and repeating the same old door opening animations (this feature really hasn't aged well - the doors don't even look unique like in Resident Evil 1).

While the gameplay and balancing is terrible (making me 10x more frustrated than when I played Getting Over it), Capcom definitely nails the atmosphere, a hallmark of the Resident Evil series. This particularly shines on the starting train level, where you can hear every little detailed sound as if you're actually on a train with the unrelenting rain outside. Again, the gameplay alongside a weak story shatters this immersion in an instant, unlike Resident Evil where you truly feel alone for the entire game.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
The best I can describe RE0 overall – its existence seems unnecessary. It goes for a dark tone just like the original, yet a lot of elements (OST choice for leech enemies, main villain’s story and voice acting) make it into some weird silly spinoff story and underwhelming.
[h1] Story [/h1]
Events of the game start off with Bravo team – the team of STARS officers assigned to research bizarre murders, along with Rebecca Chambers. They crash land in Arklay Mountains, the same area where the Spencer Mansion will later be found. Another nearby crash scene revealed documents about Billy Coen, a criminal sentenced to death for killing numerous people. While searching the area, Rebecca comes across a train and goes in to investigate. The train is full of zombies and otherwise bizarrely mutated people. Rebecca finds Billy inside the train and from there, the two agree to team up to escape the ordeal and many more to come.
[h1] Characters & writing [/h1]
Unfortunately, Billy Coen and Dr. James Marcus (one of the people behind the discovery of the original virus) aren’t well-written characters and one of the main reasons this game falls flat. Billy’s backstory is nothing special, but it’s not connected with anything in the world of Resident Evil – whether it be with the infamous Umbrella company, its staff or just about anything that we know from the first game’s lore/world that’d further compliment him being a threat to society. This makes any bonding moments between him and Rebecca seem pointless. Marcus’ past is more relevant to canon events of later RE titles. It involves experiments with injecting the virus into leeches, which can bond into human forms. Yet we only get to see his motivations for wanting revenge on Umbrella towards the end of the game, and even then, the writing doesn’t present this character as a present/potential future threat to the wider public, silly voice acting and weird idea of singing opera attracting leeches to himself don’t make him good either. Both of these characters are such wasted potential, they could’ve made RE0 a worthy competitor of RE1. Bravo team and their personal investigations that night have no representation in gameplay or in cutscenes whatsoever, such small details could’ve enriched the story of RE of that time period.
[h1] Gameplay & negatives [/h1]
Gameplay-wise, this game takes RE1 as a base and adds new features to make it different. Now you get a prompt for instantly combining items and herbs instead of picking them up individually, 2 characters can attack groups of enemies more efficiently. Unfortunately, this is where QoL gameplay improvements end. I feel most of the new auditions were a miss.
There are no item boxes, you can leave items behind in different rooms and come back for them later. This makes item management a lot more strict and it’s a nice idea, but it makes 1st playthroughs frustrating – backtracking for items you’ve left in distant areas can be a chore, there is now a 2-slot hookshot item which is a must-use item on only 3 occasions and you don’t get notified when you'll use it again and when you can forever leave it behind.
You have 6+6 item slots, divided equally between Billy and Rebecca. Characters gameplay-wise have their own pros and cons, but ultimately the game encourages to use both characters as often as possible (getting to new places, killing groups of enemies/stronger ones easily), which makes gameplay have some decent variety. The inclusion of the hookshot greatly reduced moments of cooperation. This item not existing would’ve eliminated the frustration factor of always backtracking for it.
Designs of almost all locations aren’t as memorable or intricate as in RE1, although visuals are beautifully upscaled compared to RE1. The beginning train section is undoubtedly the best in terms of gameplay flow and design. Other locations don’t leave an impression of themselves.
Enemies is another weird aspect of this game. Most of the bosses are just big insects/animals, infected by the virus. They are not memorable either, but rather another feature which makes this game’s dark tone disappear the more you play. Besides zombies, other common enemy is a type of insect, which, again, just look weird and therefore don't feel fitting to be among common enemies in RE. Regular enemies are hunters and monkeys – fast and aggressive enemies, which can easily stunlock and kill you in one place if there is more than one in the room. Leech humans can be dealt with swiftly by using fire, but their ranged arm attack is far too long and feels unfair to deal with in a fixed-camera game.

The game’s conclusion left me feeling like this journey didn’t contribute anything to the canon. Billy is never to be seen in any media again. Bravo team are only seen once and we are shown nothing about their personal investigations. It just shows Rebecca going on some kind of adventure, trying to help a criminal escape and at the same time fight against weird mutated creatures. After you go back to playing RE1, you notice obvious continuity issues as if events of this game never occured. It's just silly.

I can definitely recommend the game if you are looking for more gorgeous REmake visuals and much greater challenges in gameplay, although artificially generated through lots of backtracking and some frustrating, aggressive enemies. But I must say this was more of a weird, at times frustrating experience, rather than an immersive, even at times relaxing one I had with RE1.

I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate this game. I actively ignored advice to play literally any other RE game first, and from what I've seen of the series, this one goes heavy on meticulous item management and pioneering single-player co-op (which, when combined with the limited saves, make for an unholy mix I hope to never see again in a triple-A game).

6 slots per character, and most good weapons need 2 slots each, and that's not counting ammo or the frequent need to lug around items required for progression. Even optimally, you're going to spend so much time backtracking for one item or another (which might even cost you health and/or ammo if you don't gather items early on) that you may as well have a walkthrough or guide open for when you inevitably get stuck.

The partner system wasn't very practical for me, playing on Hard. Combining the doubled (and often wasted) ammo usage of having your computer-controlled partner assist you in skirmishes with the inevitable healing items required when they take damage from standing still adds up very quickly and can drain whatever you might think you have, so you learn early on that the optimal method is to have them enter a room once your other character has cleared it of threats.

Even the story is pathetic, it only serves to justify another game's plot but has its own logical gaps. [spoiler]Old man brought back to life seeks revenge on former employees, proceeds to cause an epidemic that continues into RE1. Somehow his initial targets, only seen in cutscenes and assumed to be the only survivors with no explanation as to how, slip through his fingers and simply vanish halfway through the game, presumably to fulfill their roles in RE1 and RE2. Meanwhile, our dear protagonists looking for a way back to civilisation and safety accidentally gain his attention, and the game ends with him being so irked by their presence that he decides to chase and attempt to kill them. I'm not familiar with the lore, but I think the best spin on this story is that, had he survived, he intended to be the monarch of the zombie apocalypse. [/spoiler]

It wasn't as bad in the areas I expected it to be. It didn't have many "quick" enemies that seem to appear in later games, mainly Hunters and Eliminators which are only strictly unavoidable in a handful of scenarios (and still a major threat on Hard without proper prep). The knifing mechanic was also surprisingly intricate (but not without an element of chance), and saved me a ton of handgun ammo, much more than I even intended to save.

For the item management alone, I think "tedious" is a word you might see often in reviews of this game, and having stumbled through quite a few runs of it now (playing through the Leech Hunter sidegame is totally worth it for the rewards in your story run), I do agree with that assessment. I'm only putting a "recommend" on this because it clearly isn't for casual gamers (I personally never expected to find any enjoyment from it), but for hardcore RE fans who enjoy the challenge.

I was excited to pick up a classic RE game I hadn't played before, but this one kinda misses the mark. It takes a big step backwards by removing the Item Box feature, and the whole playing as 2 characters at once thing is never really used for anything interesting, it just adds an extra frustration to combat. 

The companion AI is not awful, it's not as bad as Sheva from RE 5 for example, but you still can't trust it to not die in combat. At least it reliably follows you instead of fighting when you run, though it is not smart about dodging zombies. Switching characters is a bit clunky and jarring, but you will have to do it frequently to avoid the AI costing you health or even a game over, which is yet another road bump in a game that already has pacing issues.

Outside of the 2 playable characters, everything else about the game feels pretty uninspired. It's just more of something that most of the earlier games did better. It is also really long for a classic RE game, or at least it feels that way with the lack of Item Box causing so much backtracking (not the good kind). With 8 hours of playtime I'm about 2/3 of the way through, and that's a bit too long for a classic RE game that is supposed to be short and replayable. 

Not to mention that since you play both characters at once there is not 2 different progression routes through the game, or a B side. In fact, given the lack of interconnectivity in the main mansion, I don't think there is even a whole lot of room to improve later playthroughs besides knowing when to pick up items to reduce backtracking. 

In short, RE 0 follows the classic gameplay and structure of early RE games, but does not employ either to great effect compared to earlier titles.

If you really need to complete your RE collection then this is serviceable, but if you are considering this as a place to start, don't. The gameplay is a downgrade from previous titles, and the story does not add anything noteworthy to the series either. In fact, it will make little sense to someone who has not played the original trilogy.
