Resident Evil 0 is great for an early horror title, and the remake adds a lot of quality of life improvements. Great graphics, setting, and atmosphere; with generally acceptable gameplay that can be challenging. Overall, it plays a lot like the remake of the original: exploring rooms, managing inventory, and slowly killing zombies. There's the best aspects of it in the locations, this time including a train, mansion, and factories; along with the incredibly immersive door animations for room transitions. Still love that effect, even though it mainly just covers up loading screens. The shooting is still incredibly slow, with a lot of bullet sponges, and limited ability to aim. A few less puzzles this time around, and they're easier to figure out; but sometimes way more enemies. 

In Zero, you have two characters to control simultaneously; as compared to the optional choices from the first game. Rebecca, who has slightly less health and can mix herbs or chemicals; and Billy who can move heavy objects. Being able to play as Rebecca is an immense treat, since she's the cutest character in the franchise, though Billy isn't too bad since he feels strong due to his higher health. They can either work together or solo, but since they each only have 6 inventory slots, both of them are necessary for moving items and solving combination puzzles. It opens a lot of avenues for exploration, boss fights, and challenges when you have to think about controlling each one separately. However, if one of them dies; the game is over, and the inventory problems are immensely magnified, since it's balanced around having 12 total slots. 

Most of the game involves picking up items, transporting them, putting them down, and backtracking to grab more stuff. You'll need large items like the Grenade Launcher, Shotgun, and Hookshot often, but they take up inventory necessary for keys, ammo, and health restoration; so it's a huge chore having to make sure items are available for bosses or rooms with lots of enemies. Worse, since saves are limited; you can lose a lot of progress made on puzzles, rooms, and item transport; so it was a constant annoyance. The combat itself isn't anything special either, you fight all sorts of bizarre animals, and you can't really do anything except aim and tap the button; so it's hard to return to after playing the remake for RE2 and RE3. 

Altogether, it's a decent classic; and a worthy instalment in the franchise. It's best if you can play this shortly after playing the first game so you don't get spoiled on the other HD Remakes or the games with heavy gunplay like 4. If you want to replay, it also an interesting option with Wesker mode, where you can play as the villain. Worth the price, and definitely worth it for Rebecca.

This is what "classic" resident evil should feel and play like, at least in terms of those who insist upon resident evil sticking to the archaic fixed camera angle type of horror game. I personally enjoy the 3rd person horror games a whole lot more, the change in perspective for remake 2 and 3 was a welcome addition for me, and I look forward to diving into resi 4 for the first time, but i'll be honest, the classic "tank" controls of resi 1, 2, 3, and code Veronica X are pure and utter trash, it makes the whole game feel clunky, like your controlling a big lumbering dopey rescue hero, and the fixed state of the camera and characters makes the gunplay incredibly boring because there is no variation beside point and shoot, other than move further away from the enemy and shoot again. Basically it makes all combat, including boss fights incredibly one dimensional and utterly similar, you fight everything the same way, and that no fun, it strip away any variety in the enemy types. Anyway, back to the point, its not like tank controls ruin those games, to be totally honest, when I first fired up Code Veronica X, i thought the controls alone would turn me off to the game entirely before I could even give the story a chance, but I got familiar enough with them and the rest of the game, the story, and the classic style of like metroid-vania-esqe resident evil horror totally hooked me and I loved the game. So i think that "tank" controls are totally serviceable and tolerable if the game itself is great, but that doesn't mean they are good, definitely not better than literally any other control scheme in any game made after 2000! The inclusion of a more modern movement scheme in RE0 (remake) make this game amazing, it has everything a good classic resi game should have, and it doesn't control horribly, it actually feel smooth, responsive, fluid, and natural while still being classic old-school resident evil. This game with its slight modernizations is how the classic resident evil games were supposed to be played, it feels different from what were used to, but not archaic. Therefore, it is so much more accessible to newer fans of the series than the older classics. Besides all of that, 10+ hours in and i'm enjoying every other part of the game as well, the story is intriguing, the puzzles fun, and the exploration challenging without being ridiculous. The only gripe I personally have is the no item boxes, I like that you can drop items if need be to make room for something else more important in that moment, but I absolutely hate that that simple Quality of life improvement over the older games essentially is also supposed to pull double duty and replace the item box. It feels stupid to have to back track all the way to the specific room you left something to get it rather than being able to stop in saves rooms that are naturally sprinkled along your gameplay path and having all your items. It also makes carrying over items between characters and areas more complicated cause you cant just stuff everything in the box and have it follow you no matter what.

Resident Evil takes two steps forward and one step back with each of its design decisions. Controlling two characters is novel and interesting narrative and gameplay decision that doubles your inventory and firepower; but managing two inventories becomes more of a hassle than a benefit, especially on your first play through and enemies have been turned into bullet sponges, mainly the leech monsters. Being able to drop items whenever and wherever is a relief: no more disposing of valuable items just to avoid backtracking to an item box. But, item boxes are now removed, in what I can only imagine was a misguided attempt to balance this mechanic or add to the immersion. RE0 has a lot of good elements simply by nature of being a Resident Evil game: atmosphere, beautiful environments, exciting set pieces, exploration, resource management, and puzzle solving. But it doesn't quite reach the heights of its other RE games. Mostly bogged down by odd decisions that act as nuisances, RE0 is a mixed bag. If you like Resident Evil games, this one is a worthy addition to your library. But if you're only looking for high quality, you can skip this one. Play RERemake for the same but much more refined experience.

Back when I first played RE0 on GameCube, I found no particular fault in it. Just like with my girlfriends, I guess my standards were critically low. Booting this up all these years later was initially a rude awakening:

The story is a drippy cheese sandwich. Comically bad, making the whole series somehow even goofier than it was otherwise. James Marcus is a Final Fantasy villain who forgot his dialogue, so just resorts to paper-thin placeholder cliches from every old and uninspired thing ever. "Playtime is over. I will have my revenge." I think maybe he just uses a Magic 8-ball of villain cliches when he talks.

It doesn't matter. In the early days of Resident Evil, the story was mysterious enough to maybe be cool. But the more details Capcom layered atop that mysteriousness, the more it became evident that this series is a hot mess storywise. And that's OK with me. It's a fun hot mess.

The major reason I hated my first RE0 playthrough in nearly twenty years, was the inventory management. I found it grueling, cumbersome, and uncalled for. 

Then I found the final few areas of the game completely uninspired and indistinct, leaving me with this sense of: "There is literally no reason to ever play this game again."

But... something weird happened. The next day, I felt like playing again. "What's wrong with me?" I muttered to myself. I decided to get a few more achievements. Then a few more after that. And so on.

Before I knew it, I played through the entire game about six times on easy and normal. Each playthrough was smoother than the last, until I just about had it all down to a science. Then I beat it on Wesker mode (that was fun), and whooped Leech Hunter (that was... meh). 

Now I've got 87% of the achievements, and will probably go for 100%. I mean, why stop now?

I can't really hate on a game that has kept me so engaged, and actually somehow gotten more and more fun with each playthrough, can I?

Naturally, people who weren't alive or playing video games back in the old days of Resident Evil, are going to find this weird and archaic. But to me, I find this old-fashionedness somehow comforting and enjoyable.

The first Resident Evil's GameCube remake is a top-to-bottom masterpiece, so I was psyched for Resident Evil 0. In preview coverage, it looked like everything I loved, but now with new, more advanced features. Controlling two characters at once! Leaving items anywhere, at anytime, instead of having to schlep over to a save room! A fresh, new environment!

Unfortunately, the train setting is nothing more than an introductory level, and you're soon dumped in a mostly forgettable stand-in for the classic Spencer mansion. Worse, though, is that every bullet point that seemed like it should be a quality-of-life addition just makes the game more tedious and cumbersome. Sure, there are a handful of neat puzzles that force you to thoughtfully split up your heroes, but more often you're left running back and forth to try to get the pair back in the same room or fiddling around with equipment to make sure your partner has enough ammo to keep from getting killed without burning through too many precious resources.

So, yes, I had some complaints back in 2002. I had high hopes, and Resident Evil 0 fell short. Twenty years later, though, "Just like Resident Evil but not quite as good," doesn't seem like such an unforgivable crime. They don't make games in this style anymore, and it turns out that I really, really miss this style. Moreover, Resident Evil 0 isn't merely good enough. It's good. It's an exceptionally engaging horror adventure that had the misfortune of being released just months after the best game in the genre.

Approach it with patience and realistic expectations, and you are in for a fabulous time.

---A final note:
Much of Resident Evil's appeal as a horror series comes from tension. Playing on an easier difficulty significantly reduces that tension. I found that I felt borderline invincible while playing on Easy, but because juggling items and navigating the space is more tedious here than in previous games, suddenly dying and having to make up lost progress can feel extra frustrating, which is likely why I burned out without reaching the end back in the GameCube days. Give yourself a break. Play it on Easy. Oh, and download the mod that skips door animations. It will save your life.

Giving this one a positive review only because I am a Resident Evil fan and nothing more than that - to be exact, I recommend it only to die-hard fans of RE franchise. If you never played any RE game before, don't start on this one, you won't have the will to play any RE title after this one. At least that's how I felt a bit playing this one but pushed myself forward because I knew that next one that I am going to play is Resident Evil 4.


To start off, I have to praise the idea for adding new aspects in the game. 

The first one is being able to play 2 characters and switch them whenever you want. You play either as STARS member Rebecca chambers or a convicted criminal Billy Coen. This of course has its pros and cons. The creators did this so that you can't progress on certain areas without both of the characters being in the same room, which I found quite interesting. The advantage is that now you have an AI controlling the other character and helping you fight off the zombies and monsters, and also most of the time the AI will aim better than you, often landing headshots. This comes in handy when entering a room full of enemies when dodging isn't quite effective. But, there is a flaw and that is survivability; the characters aren't the same, meaning that Rebecca has less health than Billy and often 1 or 2 hits on her would result in getting the caution status quite fast. So instead of playing as a pair, you'll probably spent more time playing solo and leaving the other character someplace safe while you explore.

The second one is that one thing you always asked yourself (did this a bunch of times when I first started playing RE) while playing the previous titles - why the hell you can't drop items in RE? And creators fulfilled our wish and the option to drop items was now enabled. Now you'll think that this innovation will remove the backtracking from RE but you are wrong. Jokes on us, the item chest doesn't exist in this game and now you can drop your items literally wherever, but every time you need them, you'll have to return to the place where you left them. And yeah, when you progress and enter a new area, you won't be able to come back where you were before meaning that all the items you left behind will be lost... Yeah, this was executed so poorly, yet it had potential to be excellent.

Some enemies are so hard to kill. Compared to previous REs, this is the only one where I had the danger status on my health more than any other. And to be fair, I always look to dodge unnecessary fights that would drain my health. I'd also use to have reserves of herbs and health sprays but here I literally had to fight for my life. 

Of course, graphically this is the best RE yet, having the most polished design. The cutscenes are also really good, the best ones so far. 

Storywise, I don't know how to feel about it. It's a prequel to the RE 1, but it really didn't answer any questions. It was fun, no doubt about it, but it was a bit cheesy if you ask me. The logic (spoiler):  [spoiler] the first director of Umbrella Corporation gets betrayed by his companions, also from Umbrella, so he seeks revenge. The only guys he goes after and fights in this game are Rebecca and Billy - the enemies of Umbrella. Doesn't make much sense really. [/spoiler] And also the ending was kinda bittersweet, it wasn't so pleasant. But, it is kinda an introduciton to some characters from RE1, so yeah, let's say it was connected. 

This game had potential to be much more better, but it was poorly executed and it crumbled. I give it 5.5-6 out of 10 because I had the same feeling that I read in one review - I just wanted to finish the game, and that isn't good at all. Most probably the weakest RE title I played so far. But as I said, if you are a die-hard RE fan, play it. Just don't get too hyped up for this one.

I would definitely not recommend it to players as an entry point to the Resident Evil series due to its difficulty. Even though the game is very generous with ammo and health on the normal difficulty, the lack of item boxes for storage across areas and the lack of inventory space (only 6 slots per character with several weapons/items that will take two slots) mean there is quite a bit of backtracking possible in the game. This can be both rewarding and frustrating, rewarding when you have good inventory management but frustrating when you make one mistake that results in 15-20 minutes of backtracking. I would recommend it to people who love the Resident Evil series and want to play an entry that will challenge them. If you are interested in this game and are not familiar with Resident Evil, I would advise getting this game in the Origin bundle with Resident Evil Remake so that you can play that entry first to gain enough experience to play this entry in the survival horror series.

A lot of people hate on this game for being very different from the first 3 resident evil games... namely introducing a buddy system involving tag-team combat and inventory/weapons management, and splitting up to tackle the environment or puzzles. Another reason they don't like it is because there is no item box. You drop an item and it stays where you left it. Each character has six blocks of storage, and two-handed weapons take up two blocks. 

Inventory management, speedrunning is made a little bit more of a challenge this way, but these are not features or characteristics that are a negative for me. If anything, it's a shakeup from the other, original Resident Evil games. People coming from RE1HD or the Third Person remakes of 2 and 3 may find this game to be troublesome for them. 

This is a barebones remaster with some changes and a single minigame added. So don't expect co-op functionality or anything of the sort. What you do get in this package is the original game and its features, ability to swap costumes on the fly, and an additional mode allowing you to play as Wesker for the duration of the original story mode. Cutscene dialogue remains unchanged in this mode, and Cinematic cutscenes still feature Billy and Rebecca in their regular costumes, which is a bit of a letdown, but this is why I think of the mode as more of a non-canon minigame than an extra "alternate timeline" mode. 

Playing these games (the original cinematic cam games, at least) with a keyboard is a pain in the rear end, though it's doable. I still prefer to use a controller, so you'll have to decide what's right for you on that. But the controls aren't terrible for a keyboard user. Whether you've played the original on gamecube and want an HD remaster this is basically the same game you love and little as changed about it aside from the costume convenience and the added Wesker mode. If you missed out on this game and want a chance to play it, it's a great game in the series, and stands out because of its features from the other games. Whether it's better than the original 1, 2, or 3 is up for debate, but it stands up on its own.

Onto the game itself if you aren't familiar, the story serves as a prequel to the events of the first Resident Evil, featuring Rebecca Chambers of S.T.A.R.S (Chris' companion from the first game) and a new character named Billy, an ex-army convict. They meet and form an unlikely partnership on board a train.

The game features multiple environments chock full of various puzzles and varying enemies, including the Train, a training facility/mansion-like building, its basement, a factory, and a water treatment plant. There are a few unique and terrifying enemies, many unique to this game, that you will face off against. 
Billy and Rebecca travel together as a team, both using their weapons to fight the monsters, and occasionally cooperating to complete puzzles. However, they will split up at times. 
Instead of choosing between a weaker female character like Jill and a stronger male character like Chris, you are given both in this partnership. Each with their strengths and weaknesses. Billy has substantially greater health and damage threshold, along with a personal lighter to solve a puzzle
Whereas Rebecca has a weaker threshold and is the only one who can mix the healing herbs and mix chemicals. 
You will at times have options (though you may be unaware of the choice being made) to send one character ahead into a specific section of the map while the other stays behind. There is some strategy involved in this, as some sections will include more difficult and challenging enemies, or perhaps puzzles that are more convenient with Rebecca present. 

It's a unique tradeoff, making the game a little more strategic than the original Resident Evil, although one could argue the replay value is reduced this way.

Regardless, this is one of the classic resident evil games and one of the only two you can access on Steam that will give you the classic, tanky, puzzle-filled gameplay.

[h1]Resident Evil 0[/h1]

Being a big time Resident Evil fan for almost 20 years now, Resident Evil 0 was the first Resident Evil game I was introduced to. As a result, it kind of holds a special place among the RE games I've played.

Playing it on and off on different consoles and ultimately buying it for the umpteenth time, I can say that Resident Evil 0 still holds its own as a great Resident Evil game, but there are a few things in this game that make it sort of a background name in the series compared to other titles.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]Resident Evil 0 takes place a day before Resident Evil 1, focusing on the events before the Mansion Incident through the perspective of Rebecca Chambers; a rookie cop assigned to S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team. Tasked with investigating the murders occurring in the Arklay Mountains, the team switches their focus to searching for Billy Coen, a military prisoner who escaped from his transport vehicle and upon her encounter with the fugitive, Rebecca realizes she has to cooperate with him to survive the night of horror.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]While this game does answer a few questions as a prequel to the first Resident Evil game, I have to admit that the Resident Evil 0 plot goes kinda weird with points like the conjuring of leeches and... well, the "big bad" in general. But other than that, the story is pretty decent by adding layers to the origins of Umbrella, even if the plot of Resident Evil 0 is relatively detached from the whole RE series timeline as a whole.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

Resident Evil 0 was the last RE game to use the classic "static camera with tank controls" mechanics that were common in the early games of Resident Evil. It can be a bit hard to get used to since you can't even see the enemy at times, but certain sound cues can give away the presence of an enemy (Zombies walking, i.e.) and tank controls are clunky but the HD Remaster was kind to have new control setups that make it a bit easier to move other than straight. If you're new to the series, it's best you use the alternate setup instead of the classic one since it's a lot easier, in my opinion.

Resident Evil 0 has the dual character system in which you have to manage both characters and ensure they both survive. Both Rebecca and Billy have unique abilities to them that help them step out: Rebecca can mix herbs and has the ability to create certain mixtures to progress through the game, Billy is more proficient in firearms and can tank more damage from enemies. This ensures usefulness to both characters and forces you to be more strategic in who to use in certain situations as monsters can cheese Rebecca (especially on Hard difficulty) and Billy's inability to mix can clunk up your inventory with herbs which can force you to drop items or even backtrack.

As part of the dual character system, the AI does really well to be your partner when you are using the other and doesn't get in your way that much. You have the option to tell your AI partner to wait if you just want to explore parts of the game by yourself or allow it to accompany you to assist you in fights. You can switch to either character (Rebecca or Billy) at any time in which they are present so you can check on them if you've separated them while exploring.

Puzzles in the game are balanced between simple and complex and are abundant. Some are unique to RE0 in that it sometimes requires the use of both characters to complete a puzzle, which are the most fun ones to go through (except for the one where [spoiler]you get gassed if you do it wrong[/spoiler]).

Aside from the game itself, Resident Evil 0 has a lot replay value in the "Leech Hunter" extra game where you can also unlock rewards that can be carried to your respective save data's main game. All of the rewards are fun to use after you've beaten the game and there's no harm in trying out Hard Mode - only your patience with Rebecca's health.

However, Resident Evil 0 isn't without its flaws and it has some noticeable ones.

Resident Evil 0 suffers from lacking an item box that were present in its predecessors. This forces you to make a item trip every now and then if you aren't the best at managing your gear and tediously drop/pick up items. The developers were most likely trying to do some kind of balancing here given that you had twelve item slots (six per character) and had the ability to drop items to grab later but I don't think the lack of an item box does well as a way to create challenge for the player, it's just tedious. Some people like it, some hate it.

At some points in the game, your characters will be forced to "separate" almost without a heads up. This would be fine, if you know that you are going to separate at a certain point of the game or if you saved at a recent spot, but for new players, this can result in you sometimes having no weapon at all to deal with the monsters before you with one of your characters because you gave all of them to the other and there's sometimes no way to exchange them.

The Hookshot.

The enemies. While Resident Evil 0 has a great amount of variety in the monsters you battle against, some of them are considered to be the most frustrating to deal with in the series. Not frustrating in that they're clever or well programmed, but frustrating in that they're just not suited for the pacing of this game. Two unique enemies in particular come to my mind:

[spoiler]The Leech Men / Mimicry Marcuses are very tough to deal with because they are mobile + long ranged, take so much punishment, and can even swell up to explode if you kill them with methods other than fire. Fire weapons are often rare to come by, with only two sources (one of them being very clunky to use). Luckily, you can usually run past most of them (might have to fight three or two times) if you know how to dodge them and they have a "passive" form in which gives you a window to lower their health or run past them before they transform into their "aggressive" form.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]The Eliminators (monkeys) are arguably even worse because these monsters are usually in a pack, highly agile, as tanky as the Hunter Alpha, and are of small stature. Without a high powered weapon, you can easily get stun locked by these things and get ganged up on. On the plus side, like with Mimicry Marcus, you will usually only get into a forced battle with these jerks once unless you backtrack to the Training Facility. Also, the Shotgun is best for these buggers.[/spoiler]

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

At the time this game came out on Gamecube, it was already one of the most visually impressive games to come out thanks to Resident Evil's use of pre-rendered backgrounds. HD Remaster boosts this game's already beautiful atmosphere to appear even better in order to suit today's visual capabilities. It's definitely a hell of a treat for the eyes. Sound effects and music are also great with the music tracks having a distinct tone of dread to them.

Despite it's flaws, Resident Evil 0 is still a decent addition to the Resident Evil series. Resident Evil 0 is (in my opinion) the weakest game of the franchise after Resident Evil 6 (excluding the non-canon spin-offs). However does that make it a bad game? No. Absolutely not.

Resident Evil 0 does exactly what Resident Evil 1 Remake did afterwards. It does a ton of world building which gives you a lot of "Ohhh!" moments if you play this game AFTER you play Resident Evil 1. Rebecca is a cool and enjoyable character, but not my type of character to follow. Perhaps I didn't like the whole "naive rookie" cliche, but she's also by no means a bad character. Billy is probably the most cliche badass character that you'll find in any 90s action movie and to be completely honest, he's kinda the only character I genuinely cared about here.

Overall, this review can be summed up in a simple way:
Do you HAVE to play this to enjoy the franchise better? No.

Play it if you want to understand the Resident Evil universe better, get more world building and some more cheesy lines the franchise is known for. 

Bosses are ultra boring here, however the visuals and general vibe of the game are absolutely on point, although this game kinda relies more on "in-your-face" type of horror than the atmospheric horror you get in RE 1, 2 and 3.

Overall, worth playing if you're a sucker for world building and game lore.

A decent survival horror, a lot of the core elements from classic Resident Evil are here, from the fixed camera angles, the great sense of atmosphere, resource management and puzzles. In general it is an ok game, but sadly the greater potential for it is lost by its main gimmicks. The first one is the 2 character gameplay, which while not terrible is annoying most of the time. From simple resources exchange to general equipment loads, it’s slow with too many steps on the menus and then sometimes the game separates the characters at random which can completely destroy any strategy that you could have planned. On the other hand there’s the other big problem, the game doesn’t have an Item Box, instead you can drop whichever item you want in whichever room. While this doesn’t seem like a big issue at first, a lot of times the game will throw at you puzzles or enemies which require a very specific item or weapon/ammo, so you have to back travel sometimes too much. So while none of these elements destroys the game, it does make it a lot more tedious and annoying than it needed to be.
So at the end while it still carries a lot of the good elements of RE, it’s honestly one of the weaker entries in the series thanks to unpublished and frustrating new elements. I give it a 6.5/10, mostly recommended for people who are already fans of the series.

For anyone else looking for a good classic survival horror experience, avoid this one and buy RE1 Remake, which looks and feels like this one but with waaaaay better level design, gameplay and rhythm.

I’m going to give this one a tenative recommendation. Firstly, the art style in this game is drop dead gorgeous, featuring easily the most richly detailed and gloriously spooky pre-rendered backgrounds in the entire series, even surpassing the RE 1 remake. Second, the puzzles in this game are actually quite good require a bit of thought, becoming some of the franchise’s better puzzles, and the partner system is well-utilized within this context. There is also quite a bit of content in this game, with it being significantly longer than I thought it would be, with a sprawling final complex to navigate. However, there are drawbacks to this game. The partner system means that double the inventory management is needed, and adds a surprising amount of difficulty to the game, feeling unfair at times. The boss and enemy design is also a little lacking, with the giant bat in particular being quite aggravating. The characters and story are completely ridiculous, but in a way that allows them to be hilarious instead of just immersion-breaking. Overall, I would say that this is worth a play for any fan of the series, but it is not nearly as polished and quality of a title as the RE 1 remake it shares so much DNA with. If you have to choose between the two, play that instead.

Originally a N64 title remade for the Gamecube and (much) later ported to other systems. Resident Evil 0, despite its old school survival horror allure, is harshly let down by its downright dismal gameplay design choices that aimed to unnecessarily reinvent the wheel.

Gloves off, dear reader. I’ve always despised this game. From its level design to its item & character management mechanics, its nonsensical story & characters, and finally its cringe falsetto-infused main theme.
I remember forcing myself through this game back in the days because it did have all the ingredients of a classic old school survival horror game (the Gamecube was my favourite system at the time as it had all the essential old school RE titles) but it executes them in such a dismal way.

Surely the dual character dynamic is a neat concept and swapping between the two on the fly sounds great on paper – it might've worked swiftly using the N64's cartridge medium – but in practice it's nothing short of tedious. It means babysitting the other character manually at all times. Unfortunately neither of them can be temporarily stuffed in a rusty dumpster like Resident Evil 4’s whats-her-face.

The scariest thing about RE0, well folks, it ain’t the Mimicry Marcus, nor the Plague Crawlers, nor the Eliminators, nor the Hunters, nor the Centurion, nor the zombies or the leeches. It’s suffering through an entire traditional survival horror single-player campaign with a secondary character by ones side, having to manage it or stomach its presence with its thick as hog excrement AI. I can live without the burden of such an immersion-breaking mechanic. Not to play with live, not to babysit as a semi-NPC. Nein danke.

For the life of me I cannot wrap my brain around this spastic desire devs/publishers/gamers harbor to force a secondary character into (what originated as) traditional survival horror games. Nobody went “Man, these games are scary… You know what would make it even scarier? Another player/character! Oh boy! That’ll really ramp up the scare factor, let me tell you.”

Here’s the memo, chief. It doesn’t. Literally nobody asked for this. Unless we’re talking about the players who aren’t the target audience for these types of games. Surely the RE4/Halo/Gears of War-crowd can get their fix elsewhere?

Moving on. Combat? That’s a hoot and a hollar. Attack animations such as firing the pump-action shotgun, throwing a molotov, etc. come with several frames of attack stun, leaving the player completely open to enemy attacks without any possibilities of defense or recovery.
As for zombie headshots with the shotgun, that’s a ton of fun too. Suppose another zombie stands behind the first one, perfectly within lethal blast radius, the first one will be decapitated, the second one not always. The decapitated zombie’s hitbox is still present as long as it doesn’t fall to the ground. Thus making the second zombie impervious to damage, having the player potentially wasting a shotgun shell into the first zombie’s invisible hitbox.

Getting rid of the magic item box in favor of dropping items anywhere anyone pleases is, once again, great on paper but in practice it's just messy, making the entire map a giant messy item box – It has been brought to my attention that a mod exists, integrating an item box into the typewriter menu. Kudos to the purist RE fans doing the devs work here.

The plot, pacing, characters, main villain, as well as the vast majority of enemies all have one thing in common; they are as forgettable, dull and ridiculous as they come. The plot ventures into anime-level territory with elements such as a gloating cute blue pendant-wearing, hime cut-sporting antagonist dressed in a deep v-neck triangles-collared Woodstock-era garb vigorously proclaiming that “he will have his revenge and that the world will burn in an inferno of hate!”
Forced maniacal laughter ensues. Who is this ridiculously childish monologue aiming to intimidate, I wonder? Anime fans? Whoever wrote the dialogues in RE0, I guarantee, came straight out of a burger-flipping gig. Not that the previous entries of the series were penned with Shakespearean eloquence, mind you, but this is truly next-level cringe.

Though RE0’s cardinal sin lies in its storytelling inconsistencies. After the events of RE0, we see Rebecca teaming up with Chris in the Spencer mansion, but she doesn’t ever mention anything of her predicament in RE0. Which happened the day before... 
Not even a “Hey Chris, the craziest thing happened to me yesterday, you’ll never believe me! I was facing off a giant mutated scorpion inside of a train full of weird leeches and infected zombies. The train crashed and we ended up inside some sort of a training facility with hidden laboratory/factory/treatment plant below. And whaddayaknow today we’re stuck in this creepy mansion full of traps, zombies, mutants and whatevs. Like, ain’t that the darnest thang, Chris?”

That’s the thing with unnecessary prequels. There was no need to tell this story. It serves no purpose, other than to muddy the core narrative. Aaand to make a quick buck on the side.

RE0 is just a total mess of neat ideas poorly executed. It looks great, sure, but this is by far the worst entry in the old school survival horror era of the series. To me, this is a mainline entry title that festers in similar effluent cesspool waters as RE4-5-6.

As for the delusional claims made by some that RE0 is “underrated”; I am beyond convinced the big 0 in its very title is the highest praise it could give itself.

4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.

- Not being able to save without Ink, and no autosave (which means if you die and didn't save, you also lost all your progress of the time being, this made me ragequit one time..)
- Small inventory, the inventory is so small and there are so many items that you need. The inventory is only 6 spaces for each character and some guns take up to 2 block of space so it makes things a little more hard.
- There's quite a bit of backtracking, going back to places to get some item and coming back etc. -
- The map is so big and I got so many times lost and confused as to where to go. 
- The enemies are more annoying than hard, for example if there's 2 hunters and they get you in a corner they just spam attack just like your little sibling in mortal kombat. Which means you can move, aim or shoot. They just spam attack you so long until you die and that is one of the most annoying things.
- Now this might be the annoying or confusing thing in the whole game. This game doesn't have an objective. It doesn't tell at all what you need/should do! When you get on the train what was the objective there? Nothing. When you go to the mansion what do you do there? Again nothing. This made the puzzles on the first run for me a lot harder since I was so confused as what to do.
- You can't save when the other character is in other room.
- The other characters AI is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dumb. Rebecca only shoots when you have shot 3 rounds she then shoots one. Also both bots really love running into the boss and not following you to the safety.
- The level design was not made well, as I said before there really wasn't any ''objective'' to know what you were doing.

- Also when you try to speedrun the game or get the S rank achievement, you cannot see the time how long you have played. Aka I had to do this with a literal timer on my own phone..
- There also isn't autosave. You can only save when you have ink ribbons (saving items) to save. So if you did a lot of progress and died, you would have to start all over again.
- Every single door/ladder/hatch is a loading screen... It is really annoying to watch the cutscene many times over and over again. There is thankfully a mod made by fans to skip the cutscene / loading screen.
- Also the shooting/aiming system is god awful. Especially to some of the bosses like the bat that just keeps you stun locked with other smaller bats.

But there were also some ok/good-ish parts:
- The story was ok but weird/confusing at some parts.
- It felt like a a new mechanic being able to switch characters in between, it was also at some parts, you guessed it annoying,

A pretty ridiculous but still fun entry in the old school (read: pre RE4) Resident Evil series. It was originally released in tandem with the Resident Evil Remake on Gamecube I think, and as such mirrors that game a lot in controls, combat, style, and so on.

It's an old-school survivor horror with static camera angles and a focus on puzzle-solving and avoiding enemies instead of blasting everything you see. The latter is especially true in this entry, as it is rather challenging even in the normal difficulty. It has some of the most annoying enemies in the series to date (I'm looking at you, zombie monkeys and leech men) and the gimmicks present in this game make things even harder.

What are these gimmicks exactly? Well the first main 'gimmick' of this game is that you play as two characters at once: Rebecca, a rookie medic from the STARS Team, and Billy, a disgraced army veteran who was freed from his prison transport during the viral outbreak. There are certain puzzles which require both characters cooperating in tandem to complete, as well boss battles which need both characters doing separate things.

The second gimmick is the item management. For whatever reason Capcom did not put traditional item boxes in this game, which means that you literally just drop stuff on the floor when you need space in your inventory. And it stays exactly where you drop it, meaning you need to backtrack to get anything important you left behind. On your first playthrough you're not going to be sure what is important and what is not, which means lots of unnecessary time spent getting attacked by respawning enemies as you try to get back to an item you need.

The co-op aspect is somewhat poorly implemented as well, as I found it much easier to just park Rebecca in a room and let Billy (who has considerably more health than her) do all the heavy lifting. There are points where you can't do this, but this strategy works for about 70% of the game.

Some might look at this review and imagine I mostly had a negative experience but this game is legitimately a lot of fun, especially if you enjoy the old school survivor horror thing, you just have to go into it with certain expectations so you don't get a nasty surprise.

If you think you can deal with managing two characters and the inventory, then I'd totally recommend it, as it gives some pretty cool (if slightly ridiculous as I mentioned before) backstory on both the Umbrella Corporation and the events that happened directly before the mansion incident in RE1.

I am glad that Capcom is really good about porting and remaking their old games, but without the nostalgia that some may have with Resident Evil 0, I can say that this game is just all right. Speaking of controls wow are they rough. I think it is always funny that whenever I play an old game I get amnesia and feel like I am discovering for the first time ever that old games NEVER controlled well, even hours into my playthrough I was still stumbling on the controls. If you think the controls will bother you, just don’t even play this, go to YouTube I am sure there is a let’s play of it on there. BUT if you are willing to willing to learn the odd controls I think you can get used to them enough to play through with only minor annoyances. In a modern game, I would easily consider this a death sentence, but the game is good enough and old enough that I give it a pass.

As far as the gameplay itself it is a pretty satisfying survival horror that the Resident Evil series is known for. Inventory management was easily the weakest part of the gameplay though they give you next to nothing and it is so annoying having to run back and forth for ammo you dropped so you can use a puzzle item that you found halfway across the game. Perhaps I am spoiled, but moving from RE4 to this was disappointing. Damn, apparently 3 years was enough to go from barely serviceable inventory management to an inventory management system that is still being emulated to this day, what a leap. The other parts of this game like puzzle-solving, combat, and navigation all were pretty fun once you understood their quirks. One of the things that the original Resident Evil was known for (its specifically angled and claustrophobic cameras) is in place here. Some people will hate that, but I love it and the way it forces you to play. Because of it I actually got jump scared at a few moments, which I could not say for RE4 which I think shows that the series has moved more into the action and less into the horror classification. I prefer the former, but it is sometimes good to experience the latter. As a last thought on gameplay though, I think this game is a perfect length if it would have been an hour or 2 longer for me I don’t think I would have been nearly as enthusiastic. This game is bite-sized (as far as story experiences go nowadays), and I think that is good. Show everything you got and then end before it gets repetitive.

As far as Resident Evil games go I found the story to be meh. I will not pretend that the series has ever had a good story, it hasn’t, but damn is it presented in such a weird way that I can’t help but find myself enjoying it. This game in particular though adds very little story (or at least interesting story) and feels weaker in its presentation than many other games. As such if you are not invested in the lore just skip this one, you’ll be fine just getting the cliff notes from a YouTube video or something.

The music and sound design are good… well… except for the line reading of course. All of the early Resident Evil games suffer from this and in this case, it is either funny or cringe depending on the scene, I didn’t see any in-between personally. Also of note, the save area music is good, like just about every other game in the series.

Graphically it is obvious that this game is old, but compared to its original release the update is quite impressive. And honestly, this game’s graphics have a charm that I really appreciate. Maybe it is pretty boomer of me, but I remember that era of gaming with prerendered art assets that were way more detailed than the characters themselves, but also way too damn shiny. I can’t explain my love for it, but it just gives me the warm fuzzies.

Overall I like Resident Evil 0. Would I play it again? Probably not. It is worth a play-through, but nothing more to me. Also if you are thinking of starting the Resident Evil series do not start with this one, you will be confused. Play 1 to get a better understanding of the story, plus this spoils at least 1 surprise for the first game as well, and honestly, if you could play 2 and 3 as well that would be best as that is closer to the way the games were released anyways. All-in-all though I was pleased with what I paid for (which was definitely its sale price which is like $5), and if you are willing to manage the quirks I think you will be as well.

There are some interesting ideas presented here, like the character switching, item disposal, and a look at what happened to Bravo Team prior to the Spencer Mansion incident. One could make the argument that the RPD from RE2 is also a throwback to the Spencer Mansion, and it admittedly is. The training facility is just a sort of revamped Spencer Mansion, but a lot less memorable.

Originally released exclusively for the Gamecube, in 2002, this prequel to the original (and HD REmake) features extra content, and a mostly enjoyable experience. However, not a prequel necessary to the plot in any way, shape, or form.

It begins as a sequel, but it becomes clear that some of the period of the game is spent outside the mansion as Chris, Jill, Barry, and Wesker are inside, and the dookie hits the fan. But the fan isn't only hit from inside the mansion. Rebecca and Billy have their own share of problems, including Billy being an alleged convict.

New enemies are introduced to the series, and unique bosses make their appearances, but aside from that there's not really a lot here, and Rebecca is far from a frequent character throughout the Resident Evil/Biohazard series. So unless you're interested in the railshooters on the Wii and the canon CG films, you're not really gonna need to connect to her. And don't even get me started on the pointlessness of Billy. He's an entirely uninteresting character, and ultimately not as important even compared Rebecca.

So what's the verdict on the game? If you think you're a hardcore fan of the franchise, then you may as well go for it. It plays exactly like the HD REmake of the original game, without the tank controls, and it's just as challenging. So if you loved the HD REmake and want to really dive into the franchise with reckless abandon, then absolutely go for it. If you have any doubts, wait for a sale. It's not THAT bad, but it's by no means a GREAT addition to the series.

As someone who loved the RE Remake from this same year, I can confidently say that overall I did not enjoy my time with this game. I played this on normal difficulty. That's not to say I didn't enjoy any of it, but the parts I didn't like absolutely overshadowed the parts I did like.

First, some positives:
I liked the whole first section on the train(for the exception of the un-creative boss fight). It had great atmosphere, was a new and fresh environment for the series, utilized the new mechanics the best out of any area, and featured the most actual zombies out of the rest of the game. The graphics are astonishing, easily the best out of any of the games from this era. Also, while the character switching idea has its own problems, the fact that they made it such a seamless function way back in 2002 is an impressive technological feat. Lastly, while I have plenty of issues with the gameplay, let me say this: when the game sticks to that classic RE formula, I would have a fun time. However, that's where my praise ends.

Now the negatives: the story and the gameplay.
The gameplay additions of removing item boxes, the two character system, and new enemy types, all combined with old elements really make the game a chore to play, and not the normal RE style of difficult but satisfying gameplay. Without item boxes, you have to transport items between areas whenever you move to another section of the world. However, with limited inventory, several rooms all separated by loading doors, and possible enemies, this makes the transportation process a long and tedious one. Then there's the character switching system, which, while a cool idea, is implemented in a very hit-or-miss way. The way that you can adjust their movement and combat behavior is quite interesting, but with two characters to keep track of, limited health even by RE standards that has to be split between two PCs, and Rebecca having the endurance of sandwich, makes it more advisable just to do most of the work with Billy. But when the game forces you to use two characters, you better hope you put the right character in the right spot with the right weapons and items. Otherwise, you're gonna have a bad time.

Then there's the enemies. Many of them are just from RE Remake, or giant bugs(very original). But there are two new ones that are both the worst things in the game, the Eliminators(mutated monkeys) and Leech Men. The Elims are fast, small, have way too much health, they stagger you when they strike, hit you multiple times in succession, stunlocking you, and there's usually at least two per area. Then there's the Leech Men. They are sturdy, deal a lot of damage, can tank several point-blank shotgun blasts, have a long range and a close range attack, and can only be killed permanently using fire, which the resources for are spread very thinly. If you don't kill them with fire, if you go through that room at any point later on, there are individual leeches that will grab onto you, lowering your health gradually. And you can't kill the individual leeches.

Lastly, there's the story. Not getting into spoilers, it's stupid. And not normal RE stupid. The villain is too ridiculous to be believed, the main characters are blander than any previous protagonist. Also, the story is practically irrelevant to the story of the first or later games, making it even less needed to play. Probably the worst offence is that it takes itself deadly seriously, yet is incredibly dumb. That makes it a lot less fun than say RE 4 or 1.

My conclusion: it is a beautiful game with a great first level that gives you more Resident Evil, but it's gameplay and story are lacking, and the difficulty is artificially hard. Unless you are a completionist, a hardcore RE fan, or a masochist, I would recommend skipping this. Now if you'll excuse me, I'm gonna go play RE Remake again to cleanse my palate.

Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is a remaster of Resident Evil 0, and like the remaster of Resident Evil 1, both games are in widescreen, have better graphics, and adds a new, easier control scheme. Gameplay-wise it is very similar to RE1, where it is played from a fixed camera perspective, focuses on inventory management-puzzle solving, and requires ink ribbons to save. It is a prequel to RE1, but it is recommended to play RE1 first because RE0 contains some spoilers, and if you can finish RE1 then RE0 is no problem for you.

However, there's a difference in combat and inventory management. There are more enemies, but they're weaker and there's also more ammo so you can kill them without worry. And for inventory management, there are no item boxes, but you can freely drop items. They won't disappear, and marked on the map. Most of the areas are still accessible even though you're on the final level, so if you dropped an item somewhere you can always backtrack. It's better to drop important items in save rooms.

In this game you play as 2 characters, medic Rebecca Chambers and escaped convict Billy Coen. With the exception of several sequences, you can switch between them freely. Some of the puzzles require switching between both characters. Rebecca is weaker but faster and can mix herbs, while Billy is stronger and can push boxes but cannot mix herbs. I recommend using Rebecca as the item carrier, and Billy as the weapon carrier.

After you finished the game once, you can access 2 extra game modes: Leech Hunter and Wesker Mode. Leech Hunter is basically a survival collecting game, where you move around the mansion collecting 100 leech charms (50 for each character) while trying not to get killed. There are no saves, and if you die your score won't count. Your score will unlock some rewards that can be used in new game from that save and Wesker Mode.

Wesker Mode is a new addition in the remaster, but it's basically the main campaign except Billy is replaced by Albert Wesker, with his powers like Death Stare which can instantly kill many enemies and Shadow Dash, a fast run. Unlike Billy, he can mix herbs, and his command lines reuse his voice lines from RE5. However, his other voice lines still use Billy's.

Many people, myself included, seem to be intimidated by the fact that there are no item boxes and may require backtracking. But honestly, it ain't so bad if you just leave items in save rooms and don't overequip your characters. Resident Evil 0 is a pretty good RE game, and in a way easier, shorter, and less stressful than RE1, so go play it.

[h1]A classic Resident Evil (RE) game 🕹️[/h1]
By that, I mean fixed camera angles, "tank" controls*, door animation transitions, ink ribbons, red-green-blue herbs, and the associated gameplay. If you played RE 1 (1996, 2002), RE 2 (1998), RE 3 (1999), or RE Code: Veronica (2000), you should have a pretty good idea of what to expect. You will be shooting, knifing, or evading enemies, solving puzzles, reading files, collecting key items, and all that good stuff, but with a twist! Well, two twists, actually. And they will probably make or break the game for you.

*If you abhor tank controls, it is your lucky day because this HD remaster version of the game features an alternate controls scheme. From what I gather, it makes the game easier due to being able to change directions abruptly, so dodging enemies is easier. I can't say much about the alternate controls scheme because I went full old skool and played with tank controls.

[h1]Twist 1: Partner system 💑[/h1]
[b]I'll go check over there 😁[/b]

For most of the game, you can control either Rebecca Chambers or Billy Coen, and switch between them at will. Your partner (the character you are not controlling) is controlled by the AI 🤖, and you can have him/her follow you or stand still. In addition, you can have him/her engage enemies or not.
Each character has a set of unique features, which, I suppose, were intended to make the game interesting in different ways depending on the character you are controlling. What it does, in practice, is coax players to only play as Billy. "Why is that? 🤔" I hear you ask. Just take a look at this:

[table noborder=1]
[tr][th]Rebecca[/th][th]Billy[/th][/tr]
[tr][td]Can mix herbs[/td][td]Has more health points[/td][/tr]
[tr][td]Can collect chemicals[/td][td]Can use the lighter[/td][/tr]
[tr][td]Throws Molotovs faster[/td][td]Has more chance of headshots[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][/td][td]Fires weapons faster[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][/td][td]Can push heavy objects[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][/td][td]Can play the piano[/td][/tr]
[/table]

I don't know if the developers thought everybody would want to play as Rebecca (since she is a S.T.A.R.S. member 👮‍♀️ and had already appeared in the first game) so they felt the need [strike]for speed[/strike] to buff Billy or whatever, the fact is that they've made playing as Rebecca a looney choice, the kind of thing that will make your parents want to disown you.
Oh, but wait! The developers came up with the [u]perfect[/u] solution: to make Billy unavailable during certain parts, thus forcing you to play as Rebecca. Wow, that's what I call an elegant solution! 👏

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2635681320

[h1]Twist 2: Items management 🗝️[/h1]
So you like those classic item boxes 📥  that are magically interconnected, huh? Well, time to forget those. In this game, instead, you can drop items basically [b]anywhere[/b]! How cool is that? Well, apparently a lot of people didn't find it cool enough. This is the #1 complaint for this game. But you know what? I really like this approach. Not only is it more realistic but also more flexible since you can drop any item pretty much anywhere.
OK, it's not entirely 100% [b]anywhere[/b] because the rooms have a limit of how many items you can store there, depending on the size of the room. Usually that's not a problem, but if you want to store [u]everything[/u] in one single room (which I don't recommend), chances are you're going to hit this limit.

Detractors will say that the absence of magical item boxes makes you backtrack. And I will ask "in which classic RE game you don't have to backtrack? 🤨". It's true that if you manage your inventory poorly, you will have to backtrack a lot, but that's not different from the other games.
And if you're wondering "how in the world will I remember where I put that key?", the answer is "you don't need to" because the developers implemented a neat feature in the map that shows what items are stored in each room 🤩. Actually, the game marks on the map any item you interact with. Just check an item once (you don't need to pick it up) and it will be shown on the map 🗺️. It's also worth mentioning that you don't lose access to areas you previously visited, so you can always go back and pick an item if you need.

[h1]The story 📜[/h1]
[b]Ah, the story 😶[/b]

I've had the pleasure of playing games with gripping, engrossing stories. And I assure you this is not one of them. To be fair, I don't think the series' forte is the story, but this one has arguably the worst story of the classic games. For me, it not only adds nothing relevant to the overall narrative but also clashes with the first game. I think it is the low point of this game.
It feels like it is only there to "justify" things the developers wanted to happen (some of them absurd, I might add).

[h1]What is new in this HD Remaster version? ⌨️[/h1]
[list]
[*]As the name implies, the textures are in high definition.
[*]Besides the 4:3 aspect ratio (original), you can play using 16:9 (wide). Bear in mind that the backgrounds are pre-rendered and made for the 4:3 aspect ratio -- when using 16:9 the screen is panned up and down to reveal the cropped area.
[*]Wesker Mode: Albert Wesker substitutes Billy as Rebecca's partner. Also, Rebecca uses a device similar to the [url=https://residentevil.fandom.com/wiki/P30]P30[/url]. Wesker has three special abilities: Shadow Dash (can run faster), Death Stare (powerful ranged blast of energy), and mixing herbs.

[h1]Verdict 🧑‍⚖️[/h1]

All in all, I found this game to be very good. The plot is lame, but the gameplay more than makes up for it. From this perspective, it's a solid entry. It has interesting locations (probably the train 🚂 is the most iconic), the puzzles are quite diverse and some have multiple solutions, it has extra game modes once you beat it once, and quite a bit of replay value (so far, I beat the game five times).
I will finish with two pieces of advice:
[olist]
[*]In your first run, I strongly recommend avoiding the hard difficulty. Unless you are a masochist 🔗, you will probably drop the game before finishing it.
[*]Always keep the Hookshot in accessible places. You wouldn't want to traverse half the game's map, probably still full of enemies, to get it when you need it.
[/olist]

The definitive version of... well, a failed experiment that helped precipitate the end an era if we are being honest with ourselves. Which certainly isn't to say that it doesn't have it's merits. Just that ditching item boxes *really* didn't work out the way that the developers must have hoped it would, and the game is less enjoyable than it otherwise could have been as a result. 

As was the case for Bio1HD, lighting has been tastefully enhanced and positional audio has been improved, but the real selling point is the rerendered HD backgrounds. The backgrounds are absolutely *stunning*, and leave you dreaming of a better world in which Capcom actually put in this sort of care and effort for Bio1HD and/or Onimusha HD.

But for some reason, it was decided that Rebecca should look like a bizarre anime alien. Mods to the rescue!

As with Bio1HD, everyone will want Fluffy Manager 5000 to install and manage their mods.

To fix Rebecca's weird busted face, i would recommend the "Rebecca REmake face" mod by Bloodyhunter, Iron Soul, and Johnny Valentine for first time players, but there are a number of other options to be found that use the same head model.

And as you would expect from the name, Bloodyhunter's Samurai Edge - Gamecube style makes Rebecca's Samurai Edge match the Gamecube version/Bio0's promotional renders. An uncontroversial change for the better in my opinion.

Other noteworthy mods include:

Bunny's Original RE0 Font (As was the case for reaccount's UI Improvements, i consider this one to be essential, but i suspect that the HD font is more readable for some, so ymmv.) [Incompatible with Alkimical's REalistic Weapon Names unless you decompile, merge, and recompile the correct files using ArcTool]

EvilLord and Zky's Rebecca STARS Vest (Given her position as a medic, Rebecca having a unique outfit never struck me as unusual in the same way that Jill's Bio1 costume did, especially since it *did* still include a bulletproof vest, but it's still nice to have options)

Johnny Valentine's Resident Evil 0 Mega Reskin Pack (Remake) Update 2019 (Includes a lovely take on the version of Rebecca's S.T.A.R.S. 2002 costume that was used in promotional renders, with alternate coloration)

Johnny Valentine's Rebecca S.T.A.R.S. N64 (A tweak of the S.T.A.R.S. Prototype costume that more closely matches the one seen in N64 footage)

teo's NGC Inventory Portraits (Much better looking than the defaults in my opinion. I prefer the 1.0 version personally.)

Alkimical's REalistic Weapon Names (As you may or may not know, up until the Bio1 GameCube remake, the series used actual real life weapon names. I am quite torn over RE0. It has some great ideas, but I don't think they are well thought out, it has an interesting story that ends up muddling further the overall narrative, and at the end of the day it ends up feeling like a game I can only recommend with severe warnings to the curious.

Let's get to the point. Having two mutually playable characters is a very interesting gameplay twist, but the game really suffers for it. You have to manage way more than usual, and combined with the lack of item boxes that will force way more trips and the crammed up level design, this just leads to a lot of tedium.
I also really dislike how you don't have an adaptive AI setting that makes them change if you're under attack, so I'd be chewed and my friend would sit doing nothing. 
The sloppy level design and significantly stretched out backtracking really hurt the game for me, which is really disappointing considering everything else is quite good. The game is still good ol' survival horror, with all the lovely quirks you'd want, and this HD remaster looks absolutely outstanding to boot, featuring some really good parts and fun puzzles to seal it.

If you REALLY like RE you likely already have played it or know about this one, and if you not, maybe consider it on an aggressive sale, knowing you might give up after the first chapter. I think it has a lot of positive qualities, and this is a very good PC port, but I am hesitant to really encourage anyone but dedicated fans of the genre and people with a significantly higher pain tolerance.

🖋️ If you browse through other reviews for this game, you will quickly understand what people complain about the most – [u]boring[/u] inventory management, [u]unfair[/u] difficulty, [u]uninspired[/u] enemy design, [u]lacklustre[/u] story – just to name a few. However, what [i]really[/i] sets my teeth on edge is the fact that when you interact with random static items you find around the world hoping to read a witty (or scary) one-sentence description – which I consider to be one of the best and most immersive features of RE games – you're mostly slapped in the face with the same sentence over, and over, and over again: [i]"There doesn't seem to be anything special about it."[/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2585598085
To me, this screams "creative writing failure". Nothing special about The Last Supper [i]cut into eight pieces?[/i] Are you kidding?.. It can at least be stained with fresh blood, or have some unsettling details not found in the original painting. Ironically, this line alone [u]perfectly[/u] encapsulates what it feels like to be playing Resident Evil 0. 

It's an okay game; truth be told, not without some serious flaws, but still playable and enjoyable. There just... [i]doesn't seem to be anything special about it.[/i] Or, to be more precise, some [u]very[/u] questionable design choices ruin the impression the developers were going for and leave a uniquely bland, boring, forgettable aftertaste. You know, like when you find a cockroach in your otherwise perfectly cooked lamb casserole the waiter has just put on your table – I doubt you'd be leaving [i]any[/i] tips that evening.

Let's begin with the cockroaches. Yes – plural 🙄

🦂 [b]The music is slightly disappointing[/b]
😒 Level of annoyance: 💢🔲🔲🔲🔲 (variable – tastes differ)

Take it with a grain of salt since it's just my opinion, but I think the majority of background music in this game falls flat and fails to produce any effect apart from slight dissatisfaction. Any other Resident Evil game I can think of has many themes I can remember and still be mesmerised by – [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5KEHOU3ChN8&list=PLmAjrkj1KHpL3nA9S31EJwp8nc0m_p9x6&index=13&ab_channel=Doomsday17died]chilling, dismal[/url] compositions that set the perfect mood for a survival horror game, or [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z1o_3yBe6Cg&ab_channel=WhoamIbutwhoareyou]warm, relaxing tunes from safe rooms[/url] that wash away the unspeakable terror of dark hallways even just for a moment. 

Enter Resident Evil 0 – not all tracks are horrible, there are a couple of [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mYRStm9UCts&list=PLEC2465FC284C427E&index=16&ab_channel=LazarusPhoenix]fairly good ones[/url], but I mostly found myself turning down the volume at first and then switching to my favourite online radio on subsequent playthroughs. Even when you first launch the game, the song that greets you sounds like it wants to rip your ears apart and scratches at your eardrums with unparallelled bloodthirstiness of one thousand rabid dogs. I mash the "Start" button to skip it harder than I mash all the other buttons while a giant mass of slimy flesh chews on Rebecca's pretty face and she's already in [b]"Danger"[/b]. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2581846496
🦂 [b]Playing this game is like walking in pudding[/b]
😒 Level of annoyance: 💢💢🔲🔲🔲 (mild)

Some things are so-o-o slow in Resident Evil 0 – even the things that have no business taking so long actually take forever. I'm not speaking of door opening animations, as these are the staple of the series and I enjoy them very much. I will also have you know that I can appreciate slow-paced gameplay and I don't need adrenaline-pumping action sequences to leave a good review. I just genuinely don't understand why I'm forced to read "THESE CONTROLS REGULATE THE SUPPLY AND DRAINAGE OF WATER IN THE TANKS AND CONTROL THE ROTATION OF THE RAILING. USE THE DEVICE?" [u]every single time[/u] I need to interact with this machine, which I needed to do a lot before I finally figured out this particular puzzle. Resident Evil 0 as a game was okay overall, however the thing that really hinders this game is the mechanics. Having the control of two characters seems fun in theory, but the way that it's executed results in much frustration and annoyance some of which I will discuss in this review.

First, inventory management : Unlike the first Resident Evil this game gives the ability to drop items, which sounds great at first, however the drawback is that there is no longer any item boxes. I like the concept of this idea, however the reality is that you have to constantly backtrack, moving items from each area as you progress. The game also ironically punishes you for backtracking by spawning enemies in places that you've already explored that it comes to the point in which I would prefer to have item boxes over dropping items. There's also the annoyance of have to constantly pass items back and forth between characters, which I inform you is only possible when they're standing right next to each other. If they aren't then you have to spend minutes on end sending items one at a time through a slow ass dumb waiter or even worse be stuck with the items because the characters are separated due to some story element.

Second, partner A.I. : So with the introduction of two controllable characters gave way to the ability to swap between each person, with the partner being controlled with an A.I. from whom you can issue commands to. This, like the dropping of items, sounds good at first, until you realize that your partner is a absolute dolt. There were many occasions in this game that I would dodge an enemy's attack only for it to hit or even kill my partner as they stood there staring blankly off into space. It would come to the point in which I would leave my partner in another room while I killed the monsters up ahead as they were more of a hindrance than helpful, sometimes even blocking me as I tried to move around.

Lastly, the enemies : There were two enemies that I found to be really annoying to deal with, those being the Leech men and the Eliminators (aka the monkeys). With the leech men you've got two options : either run past them and risk getting hit by their far range attacks or use the janky throwing mechanic to chuck molotovs to burn the thing and pray that you don't accidentally clip parts of the environment lest you want to waste grenade launcher rounds. With the Eliminators, dealing with one alone isn't too bad, however the real frustration comes when having to deal with two or three in the same room. These gremlins can attack multiple times and as a group can chain multiple attacks so that you basically get stun locked. Not to mention that these guys are resilient little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so good luck trying to kill them with a only a handgun. Luckily unlike the Leech men these guys only appear in a small portion of the game unless of course you backtrack.

In terms of tough enemies, I died a lot at the bat boss, at the part where Billy has to save Rebecca from falling down the pit and the monkeys are attacking you the whole time, and often when I had to get past one of the exploding leech monsters. As a huge RE fan I don't know why it took me so many years to play through this entry in the series. Having read the books, I knew exactly what to expect when I started it, still, it managed to surprise me in a bunch of ways.

This game is a prequel to the original Resident Evil, it takes place around the same area, the Arklay Mountains, telling us the story of Bravo Team and how Rebecca Chambers got to the Mansion. The story is straightforward; you start off as Rebecca Chambers, who is a member of S.T.A.R.S. investigating a series of brutal attacks in the region with her team. After your team finds a wrecked prison transporter, you're tasked with finding the escaped convict. Strange things begin to occur, killing some members of your team. While exploring a nearby apparently abandoned train you end up crossing paths with the escapee, Billy Coen, who's going to become your partner, setting the tone for the rest of the game. Overall, the story’s alright, it provides some solid background to the Mansion arch, it’s not as mysterious as the first one but gets the job done. Some things I found silly and corny, like Billy’s backstory or the villain’s cutscenes.

The gameplay is core classic Resident Evil, with the fixed camera and pre-rendered backdrops. You're going to be exploring, reading notes, managing your inventory (2x), gathering items and supplies, surviving the common enemies and killing the occasional bosses. I loved the creatures in this game; the mutated animals look awesome. The location's design and the color palette used this game reminded me a lot of the first RE, it looks and feels the same, although this one is a bit more “claustrophobic” with the environments. The main difference gameplay-wise is that now you’re playing with two characters at the same time and you can switch between them whenever you want (for the most part). They have their own abilities, inventory and health, bringing new challenges to the game, like, some particular actions can only be done by a certain character and in some puzzles you’ll need to position them in a specific way or with a specific item. You can give orders to the other character you’re not controlling, things like: hold your fire, fire at will, follow, stay, meaning that there are many ways you can face a situation. The levels and environments in this game are very cramped and tight. You are going to be either using a lot of ammo, a bunch of healing items or both since it’s pretty tough to avoid the enemies in the narrow halls and corridors, which is a huge problem cause the inventory space is a joke (more on that later). Like the originals, this game has no “dodge” in combat, so you either run or gun the enemy down. 

The game also features two extra game-modes that you unlock after beating the game for the first time, one called leech hunter and the other is Wesker mode. Leech hunter is basically a poor man’s raid mode, not really engaging, you unlock new guns and bonus after completing it, only worth it if you’re a completionist or would like some fun with unlimited ammo in the campaign. Wesker mode on the other hand is great, one of my favorite things in the game. You play the same main story but Albert Wesker replaces Billy Coen as your partner. I loved playing as him, his abilities are awesome, he looks great and Rebecca is a total Babe in that outfit.

	All my gripes with this game come down to one thing: the stupid inventory system.  Look, I get it, it’s part of the RE series to manage your stuff and make good use of your inventory space. In this game though, they take that to next level and ruin it, there are just too many items you have to keep, taking precious space, it seems like some of them take way too long to get used in the story. There’s a goofy ass grappling hook that takes two inventory slots and you have to carry it through almost all the levels, it serves absolutely no purpose other than moving your character a level up in a building, you can’t even use the thing as a weapon or something, couldn’t they find a better way? Maybe a quest to build a ladder? Even a simple rope would do, taking less space and making more sense. Another major issue that the inventory ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ creates is backtracking. Again, I know backtracking is a part of the classics RE, I don’t mind it at all when it makes sense. In this? It is waay too much, excessively frequent, feels forced as hell and drags the story. All because your inventory sucks and you’ll have to return to a place to get an item you couldn’t carry before. 

I really enjoyed this game and I recommend it to any classic RE fan, if you liked the originals or just want to know more of the story and some Rebecca Chambers “fan-service” [spoiler]( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)[/spoiler], you’re going to love this.  If you are new to the series, I suggest you try the original first as it makes more sense and it’s the overall better game.

Damn good game. Why?

-If you loved Resident Evil 1 Remake, I can literally guarantee that you will like this game. In graphics, length, and gameplay it is nearly identical except you get to play as two characters at once.
-The music in RE1 Remake was good, but the music in this game is PHENOMENAL. Nearly every track stands out to me in it's own way.
-Great enemy variety.
-I was initially worried that the double-dragon character feature was going to be a gimmick, but I was really delighted to see just how the game ran with the idea. You approach most situations like how you would in RE1, but also SO much differently at the same time. Do you send in Billy first to take the heat? Or do you need Rebecca for the extra firepower? You REALLY need to think these things through, and be decisive when it counts: this game is VERY unforgiving.
-People really exaggerate the loss of the Item Boxes. It sucks, but don't let the idea of inventory management drive you away; this game is great.
-The interactions and dialogue between Rebecca and Billy made the game feel less lonely, but also made it feel even worse when the two are inevitably separated.

What advice would I give to a new player?

-USE CONTROL SCHEME D! I played the first fifteen minutes of this game sick to my stomach because of the awful controls, but control scheme D is literally the RE1 controls with like two buttons changes for the partner mechanics. USE IT.
-WOW this game is hard. I played Resident Evil 1 Remake on Standard and somehow never died (I still don't know how), but this game was not the same. I think I died maybe some odd 20 or 30 times. It is HARD. Play Standard and do NOT make it any harder.
