Resident Evil 0 is an interesting addition to the series.  If you're interested in Resident Evil and are looking for a stepping on point, this is [i][b]not[/b][/i] the game for you.  That being said, the game does bring some really cool things to the table.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
-The character swap system is cool to use.  I enjoyed being able to have each character independently explore the game world and go anywhere they wanted.
-The locations in the game feel well made and are in line with what you would want from a Resident Evil title.
-The puzzles make you think, and I enjoyed them.  I didn't have any major issues with any of them.
-It is great to have a game where you play as Rebecca Chambers.  I hope they do more with her character in the future.  Billy is a cool sidekick, although he doesn't really have much of a personality until later in the game.  He shares the same fate as Sheva Alomar (RE5), a character that has potential to expand into something more interesting, but has since been seemingly forgotten about by Capcom.

[h1]Things I was mixed on:[/h1]
-The character movement in this game feels the slowest its ever felt (I played with the original tank control system  because I like them).  I can't really pinpoint what it is, but something about it just makes Rebecca and Billy feel so incredibly clunky.  At times it could be a pain.
-Some enemies attack so rapidly that you don't even have time to aim your gun in defense, or complete the quick turn animation before you are stunlocked.  That got frustrating at times.
-This port of the game is not the best.  For some reason it kept resetting my display resolution and disabling full screen when I launched the game, which got annoying.  I don't know why it wasn't saving my settings.  Strangely though, as I got towards finishing the game, this stopped happening.  The last time or two that I booted the game before I finished it, it launched in full screen with the correct resolution just fine.  Very odd.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
-Perhaps my biggest gripe with this game:  No item boxes, and really small 6 spot inventories for both Rebecca and Billy.  I cannot stress how much I disliked having to just leave things on the ground.  On top of that, you can only leave a set amount of things in a given room.  My initial idea to combat having to leave things on the floor was to put them all in one room, and have that be my inventory room.  The limit prevents you from doing that, and forces you to leave your stuff spread across several different rooms.  It feels very messy and I really didn't like it at all.  There were too many situations where I wanted something I had put down and had to trek all the way across the map to grab it, whereas if there were item boxes I could just go to one of those set locations.  Also, sometimes I would get ahead of myself and go to grab something in a rush, only to realize upon arrival that the character I chose to make the trip has a full inventory.  The characters can offload items to each other, but only if they're near each other.  There are weapons that take up 2 of your 6 slots, which is kind of inexcusable when there are puzzle pieces you are constantly having to juggle.  The entire system is just so hit or miss, and it soured a lot of moments for me.  I can see what they were going for, to make you have to chose carefully what weapons and items you decide to keep with you.  But, that was a decision you already had to make in the original games with the item box.  They just made it more tedious.
-The game's story, while containing some really cool lore stuff, feels only partially realized.  It also ends abruptly.  I was so surprised when I realized I was in the final area of the game.
-And finally, something others maybe not care about but something that really bugged me: If Rebecca and Billy become poisoned, Rebecca can store poison antidote in her medical kit and use it on herself... but not Billy.  He can't use the one Rebecca has stored because her medical mixing kit is her personal item, and the characters can't use each others personal items.  This means she can't help him at all despite literally holding the antidote in her inventory, even when standing right next to him.  In a game all about teamwork and co-operation, I found that extremely silly.  She is a medic but can't use her treatments on anyone but herself.  Clearly an oversight by the developers, I'm not sure how nobody caught that.


Overall, I would say Resident Evil 0 is a title worth playing.  I enjoyed my time with it.  It is not a horrible game by any means, it just has some glaring flaws.  It was clearly an experimental title by Capcom, but there is still fun to be had, especially if you are a fan of the original trilogy.

All these bad reviews don't understand what makes a resident evil game great. They complain of unbalanced weapons and lack of inventory.. First of all, a good player doesn't try to kill every enemy thrown in front of them in a game like this. The weapons aren't balanced because you actually have to weigh what is worth killing and expending ammo and health to kill. Because you gain nothing from killing an enemy, only lose resources.  Maneuvering around enemies is a must. But maneuvering isn't always possible and is sometimes hard... That's where the planning and genuine fear comes from in this game. The mechanics aren't set up for you to be able to snipe a zombie from 1000 yards away and breeze through the area. They also aren't set up for  you to be able to take out an entire hoard of zombies. You may not always be able to bring an entire aresenal of weapons.  This isn't that type of game. You have to plan. Pick and choose which weapons to take with you. This is a game where one enemy can cause so much fear and distress and make you actually run away as the player. If you fight a tough enemy, you will have to expend your best ammo and resources to kill them. If i can easily kill the enemies, why should i ever be afraid of them? This is where the frustration comes in for most players. We are so spoiled and so ready to easily defeat whatever is put in front of us.

All the people complaining about lack of inventory management or progression loss probably never made it past the train sequence. THAT IS ON YOU! You're fault as the player. You didn't manage which items and weapons to take and you didn't even manage your ink ribbons properly. 

With that said, RE 0 is one of my favorite in the series. Just beat it  on the GameCube and it is amazing. The puzzles are simple but fun and require you to use your notes to solve. DO NOT GOOGLE how to beat them, you will rob yourself of the experience. I love the environments and how the developers use context clues to tell a story. An example of this is in the operating room of the laboratory, with the overturned operating table and the trail of blood which leads into the next room. Inside the next room is a legless zombie in a military uniform. showing that he was the subject of  one of Marcus's experiments. There is nothing in writing or in the storyline about this zombie, but just from the context clues of the map, you could piece together a small story which makes this zombie more than just a random enemy, but a person who was taken here and experimented on.  An unobservant player will miss these details which immerse you into a much bigger world. The game is great and i recommend playing it with some patience and care. Actually think about what you're doing and you will get immersed in it.

When Capcom released REmake it was obvious they struck gold with the engine and style. It would have been a waste to use that architecture for only a single game. Resident Evil 0 was born of both that desire and its cancelled N64 counterpart. 

The first environment in the game is a luxury passenger train. Before playing I’d always wondered how the developers adapted puzzles and combat to such a cramped space. They certainly pulled it off. Though there are some more open areas with familiar structure later in the game, I think much of it shares this same claustrophobic feeling, which adds to the tension. It’s the same ornate environment design as REmake, and it creates a great atmosphere. You could realistically probably get through this train section in 10 minutes if you know what you’re doing, and I wish there was more of it. I’d love to see future RE games return to this sort of unconventional setting as opposed to exclusively sprawling mansions and castles.

This game has you controlling two characters in the forms of series favorite Rebecca Chambers and newly-introduced escaped convict Billy Coen. Both are pretty likable and I would have liked to see more character vignettes play out between them. RE Revelations was for some reason obsessed with this idea of “pairs” and never really made much clever use of it. It’s better implemented here than it is in both Revelations and RE5. Mechanically the partner system is fairly interesting and it works quite well. You’ll have to carefully manage two inventories and juggle items, made all the more difficult when Rebecca and Billy are separated. The AI is a bit useless at times but passable. I wish there were more puzzles oriented around Rebecca and Billy’s personal items (chemical set/lighter). There are only really 4 or 5 from what I can recall.

Speaking of inventory management, I find it a bit weird that you’re able to just drop items on the ground and leave them anywhere, as opposed to dropping them all into a shared inventory item box you can access elsewhere. You really have to remember where you’ve put things. At first I thought I kind of liked it, but not having items tied to a universal item box means that you may find several maps between yourself and crucial items you carelessly dropped earlier in the game. I happened to leave the grenade launcher in the lab area without realizing it and really could have used it near the endgame. I wasn’t going to make the long trek back for it, though. It can also lead to situations where you’ve placed things at an awkward angle that just makes it a pain to try and maneuver your character into the correct position to pick it up again. I noticed a lot of items are placed in positions next to examinable features of the environment (ie a painting or statue or whatever). So when you try to pick up the item you end up examining the environment instead. The fixed camera (second-person perspective?) contributes to this confusion, and can definitely act as a hindrance to general movement and battle when the enemy is out of frame. For those accustomed to the freeform camera perspectives offered by the recent third-person 2 & 3 remakes or the first-person RE7, this game may understandably be a bit of a struggle at first.

For fans of the series, this game still holds up as the first chronological entry in-universe. The love and care put into the game is clear in the lavish environments and item models. The eerie soundtrack is a standout as well (the safe room theme is among the best of its peers). It’s also got a fair bit of replayability with some cool bonuses (Wesker mode, Leech Hunter). The puzzles are well thought out, if at times a bit tedious. Overall, I definitely enjoyed it, but I can get if people are turned off by the outdated control scheme and camera. Great/10

All of that said, this game is far more tense than the more recent entries. Ammo, herbs and comfort are all limited to the point where you feel you're barely surviving more often than not, 

The majority of the puzzles are straight forward, although you might find a guide useful for the few which boarder obscure (specifically one which requires you to light fires in front of animals according to their place in the food chain, apparently a horse comes above a deer).

RE0 permanece no estilo câmera fixa, cenários mais escuros, corredores estreitos, zumbis, hunters e as mais diversas criaturas. A novidade fica por conta do sistema “coop single player”. Você pode alternar o controle entre Rebecca e Billy. Cada um tem suas características: Rebecca pode mixar as ervas e Billy aguenta mais dano dos inimigos. Algumas estratégias são necessárias, pois há momentos em que é melhor seguir com o Billy ou com a Rebecca.

Além disso, os famosos baús (onde guardávamos os itens e quase sempre estavam presentes nas salas de save) foram removidos. Agora é possível dropar os itens onde quiser (a menos que a sala já tenha atingido o número máximo de itens). Essas inovações trazem novos desafios, pois deixando um item em certo lugar, se precisarmos dele, teremos que voltar ao mesmo local. Talvez um ponto negativo disso, é que tem um item (a “arma” com corda que você precisa para subir em alguns lugares), que ocupa dois slots no inventário (tanto Rebecca quanto Billy possuem 6 slots cada) e ele é usado quase o jogo todo. Aí você precisa carregá-lo durante quase toda a campanha. 

Uma vez que você termina a campanha, em qualquer dificuldade, você habilita dois jogos extras: Wesker Mode (é igual a campanha principal, só que ao invés de Billy, temos Wesker, que tem uns poderes de raio, sei lá hahah, que mata os inimigos em volta); e o modo Leech Hunter. Esse último ocorre no Training Facility (mapa com a mansão) do jogo principal. Algumas salas são inacessíveis, o que deixa o mapa um pouco menor. Seu objetivo nesse modo, é limpar as salas dos monstros e depois coletar as sanguessugas (tipo umas pedrinhas verdes e azuis). Billy só pode pegar as azuis e Rebecca as verdes e, uma vez que você pega a tal pedrinha, não pode mais soltá-la, então cuidado! É um modo legal, mas para platinar você precisa jogá-lo algumas vezes e, depois de um tempo, ficar catando as pedrinhas é chato.

Uma coisa que não gostei é que, diferentemente de RE1 Remake, você só poderá jogar novamente uma campanha pelo mesmo save (Once Again), na mesma dificuldade. Então não adianta pensar “Vou zerar em menos de 3h e 30 min (esse é o tempo, nesse jogo, para conseguir a submachine gun e a Rocket Launcher infinita), no modo NORMAL e depois vou dar Once Again no HARD, pois estarei com a rocket infinita”. NÃO! Se você conseguir a rocket infinita no NORMAL, só terá a arma no NORMAL, pois não pode mudar a dificuldade no Once Again.

Dica: para platinar o jogo, eu joguei a primeira vez no EASY. Consegui a maioria das conquistas nessa campanha. Habilitei o Wesker Mode e Leech Hunter no EASY e fiz TODAS as conquistas relativas a esses modos.
Depois joguei a campanha no HARD em menos de 3h e 30 min, para liberar a submachine gun e a rocket launcher (e pegar as conquistas de terminar no HARD e no RANK S). NO MOMENTO DE TUNAR A PISTOLA, GRAVE qual a pistola que você está tunando (Billy ou Rebecca), pois para conseguir a conquista de obter todas as armas, você deverá tunar as duas em jogatinas diferentes pelo mesmo save. Além disso, NÃO ESQUEÇA DE PEGAR A OUTRA FACA NO TREM, a que está jogada em uma das cabines. Após terminar a campanha no HARD em menos de 3h e 30 min, eu joguei o Leech Hunter no HARD e peguei 91 sanguessugas para liberar a Magnum especial. Comecei mais uma vez a campanha no HARD (Once Again) para pegar a nova Magnum liberada (que estará em uma das cabines do trem) e tunar a outra pistola que eu não havia tunado na campanha anterior. Nesse momento a conquista de pegar todas as armas irá aparecer e você nem precisa terminar a campanha.

Resumindo: 
Joguei 1x a campanha principal no EASY. 
Joguei 2x o Leech Hunter no easy (uma para as conquistas de matar todos os inimigos, pegar todas as sanguessugas, terminar rank A e consequentemente o E, e outra para pegar apenas 50 sanguessugas com a Rebecca).
Joguei 1x o Wesker Mode (para conseguir as conquistas de não usar itens de cura, nem salvar e habilitar a roupa Wesker).
Joguei 1x no HARD (para terminar em menos de 3h e 30min e habilitar as armas extras).
Joguei 1x o Leech Hunter no HARD (para pegar pelo menos 91 sanguessugas e habilitar a Magnum especial).
Joguei no HARD pelo Once Again para pegar a Magnum e tunar a outra pistola. Uma vez que apareceu a conquista de obter todas as armas, eu nem terminei a campanha.

Considerações finais: super recomendo RE0! Eu me diverti muito com esse jogo e adorei a dinâmica entre Rebecca e Billy (tanto na mecânica quanto na interação dos personagens ao longo da história). Além disso, o jogo explora a história de um dos fundadores da Umbrella, o Dr. Marcus. Os puzzles também são bem legais, porém você não fica tão perdido no início quanto em R1 Remake. Diferentemente do RE1, onde você tem uma mansão imensa cheia de portas e chaves diferentes logo de cara, aqui as portas e locais vão aparecendo "aos poucos". Então você consegue ir resolvendo por partes, e se situando melhor nos locais.

The idea of not having a box and just having items lying there is perhaps more realistic, and could have worked if there were more inventory slots. In practice, what it does is create a lot of backtracking to go pick them up, and all the mechanics make this as slow and laborious as possible: 
- Only 6 inventory slots per character. Yeah it can make weapon and health juggling interesting, but there are so many key items that you spend a ton of time just swapping items between them, passing guns back and forth, loading them, combining items and repassing, etc. 
- Leaving items on the floor is not a bad idea, but the controls for picking them up are so clunky that you keep trying to run over them for 5 seconds. Since the game encourages you to leave them around, you can put them in a row and accidentally keep running to the wrong one. 1 second to open menu, 1 second to say no not this one, another 5 seconds to try to line up with what you actually want again, etc. 
- Sometimes items you leave on the floor are hard to see because the camera is too far upwards, trying to show you the game's 4head beautiful 2D scenery. 
- Trying to pick up items in the game is also sometimes a pain; you keep trying to pick them up but the boxes are so small that you keep clicking on the flavor text (~2 seconds to skip each time you miss)
- You have to micromanage your partner. Frequently you have to go into the menu (1 second to open), select the weapon you want them to use, then exit back (1 second), and you have to do this a lot because they will do things like waste shotgun shells on leeches and crows. You also have to move them out of the way of things, then tell them not to move (this action makes you freeze in place for 1 second). 
- Going through doors takes 5 seconds. If you forget to call your partner to come with you, that's 1 second to swap to them, another 5 to go through the door, and another 1 swap back. 
- Interacting with some things to progress in the game starts cutscenes. Some are skippable, others are not. And you often have to handle them more than once, because-
- Dying puts you back in the menu. 3 menus to get through, then a slow text crawl for a total of 30 seconds. 

All this compounds into making the game very slow and very frustrating to handle. It doesn't benefit the atmosphere when you're repeating it this many times. As John Carmack says, "UI should work in game time, not cinematic time. A transition should happen as fast as an impatient user can button mash -- a small-integer number of frames." 

Anyway, on top of that, neither the story nor characters are compelling, the atmosphere is surprisingly washed out, the writing's bad (although it is RE so), it's not scary, and there's little to the combat. Particularly silly is how to save resources you tend to just run past monsters, and then they don't follow you into any different rooms. 

If you're an RE completionist or have nostalgia, then maybe it's worth $10, but between this and RE1 I don't think old Resident Evil holds up at all. Frankly, the franchise has long surpassed it; play 7, Rev2, 4, 2, all good.

[h1] A very mixed game but still worth a shot for fans of the series [/h1]

I'll just quickly cover a few points that bothered me most and think if they would annoy you as much. If not, you may give it a shot.

[u][b]Item Management[/b][/u]
This is by far one of my biggest gripes with the game. Like most Resident Evil games you have item slots for what you can carry and this is just fine; the first issue here in Resident Evil Zero is that items that would only occupy one slot in many games, like the shotgun or the grenade launcher no occupy two. Add to it the fact that each character has very few inventory spaces and to my knowledge there’s no way to add more slots, like you can in Resident Evil 2.

[u][b]Where is the item box?[/b][/u]
This is kind of a continuation of item management but for some reason the developers decided to remove on of the most beloved features of the series: the item box. Since you can’t carry everything you find around the game with you, like you can in many games, you would put them in the box that would appears in some handy locations throughout the game making it a breeze to get that ammo you need or some healing items. That was a good mechanic, right? Well, not good enough for Resident Evil Zero because…

[u][b]Throw items on the floor[/b][/u]
Because in case your inventory is full you should drop items on the floor. Sure, there is a small positive side to it, as you can decide on what to carry at that specific moment without having to backtrack, but the deal is you will have to backtrack unless you enjoy leaving items that might be useful behind.
As the game progresses you may find your precious items (even plot specific items, mind you) laying around all over the place. What makes it even worse is that as you progress to new locations you might wonder what would you do about carrying your items? That’s it, make I don’t know how many trips back and forth to carry them from on spot to another, and you’ll have to do that on more than one occasion.

[u][b]Dialogue is atrocious[/b][/u]
Since I was talking about laughing I should mention this too, the dialogue. It starts fine but as the game goes on it keeps getting progressively worse, to the point the end of the game it was cringy.

[u][b]Conclusion[/b][/u]
I sure have my complains about Resident Evil Zero but I have to add that even with lots of complains I did have an overall good time with the game. There are many good moments here, it’s just a shame there are also a bunch of horrible decisions together with them.
I started this post comparing Resident Evil Zero with Resident Evil 6 and while the former doesn’t reach the lows of the latter, it also doesn’t reach its highs. I remember that when I finished Resident Evil 6 I was pissed (and that’s not the case here) but believe or not I still think I’d rather come back to Resident Evil 6 than Resident Evil Zero.
In the end it is among my least liked Resident Evil games but I still think it deserves a playthrough.

BIG WARNING for anyone who has played a bunch of other classic Resident Evil games using an Xbox or PlayStation controller!!! This game's button layout is based on the GameCube controller, which of course has its A, B, X, and Y buttons completely swapped compared to most other controllers. This means that you run with "B", open your inventory with "X", and so on. This is not remappable within the game and you will have to use Steam's controller remapping to fix this if you want to control in a similar way to all the other classic Resi games. It's not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, and you will likely still fumble other controls occasionally, but it's better than having to relearn something so absolutely ingrained in most Resi fans for the sake of a single game.

The level design is no where near the polish of REmake 1, but to be fair it's rather difficult to live up to that standard. Without a walkthrough to tell you which items you will and won't need at any given moment, you WILL be backtracking repeatedly to pick up items you've had to drop on the ground due to the lack of an Item Box in this game. Swapping between the protagonists is clunky, the A.I. of your partner is unreliable at best and game ruining at worst, and without a walkthrough some segments can feel a tad "Trial and Error"-ish.

Still though, despite its many flaws, this is a great game and I wholly recommend it to any Resi fans who haven't gone back and played it yet.

[i]"Billy, did you really kill twenty-three people? I'm not going to judge you."[/i]

It’s not that [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i] is bad. It’s just not really all that good. And Billy’s a tool.

But don’t worry, you’re still in a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game—and an old school [i]Resident Evil[/i] at that.

At its core, old school [i]Resident Evil[/i] is about being an amateur sleuth in a bizarre, madcap, irrational environment determined to bamboozle you to the point of death. And you know it’s [i]Resident Evil[/i] when you have a character—one who has never been subjected to the supernatural before—face off against a giant mutant scorpion and neglect to tell their partner about it.

Just, you know, whatevs.

Only [i]Resident Evil[/i] could get away with that kind of narrative incompetence. It might be one of the few consistent attributes in a series that has mutated many times, crossing genres and even mediums to tell all kinds of silly, melodramatic tales that don’t make a lick(er) of sense (the extent to which the series’ dreadful writing bothers me is directly proportionate to how much fun I’m having with the game itself).

[i]Zero’s[/i] the point in that mutation where the survival horror theme, seemingly so vital to the franchise’s identity, ended, although it would be unfair to lay the blame for that at solely at [i]Zero’s[/i] feet (if it's even a case of blame). [i]Resident Evil Remake[/i] (released the same year) was incredible, but its sales didn’t meet expectations. It also raised serious questions about the mechanics of the games themselves, which no matter how well-executed were starting to show their age.

Fixed perspectives and tank controls were not the future, so [i]Resident Evil[/i] needed to modernise. Neither [i]Remake[/i] nor [i]Zero[/i] did that.

The cooperative mechanic, which is [i]Zero’s[/i] main selling point, is a failure. I don’t mind relatively long transitions between rooms or to your inventory, but adding a third transition between characters slows the game to the point of tedium.

Equally egregious is the sheer sexism of the mechanic. Rebecca, the woman, cannot push the heavy stuff, but Billy the man, can. It’s an outdated and tiring trope—both then and now.

Good questions to ask of cooperative scenarios would be things like: does the AI partner positively contribute to the gameplay? Are they useful? Do we have to worry about them in combat, or can they handle themselves? I would argue [i]Zero[/i] is a ‘no’ in all of these cases; you're going to need to worry about whoever you aren't controlling, because they are very, very dumb. It’s often best to wander off on your own until you come across a puzzle that requires both characters’ input.

Somehow [i]Zero[/i] is able to magnify the problems with the classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] formula. I was reading a review for [i]Remake[/i] where the player had real issues in combat—they didn’t like the camera angles or the aiming system and downgraded it accordingly. I didn’t find that to be the case in [i]Remake[/i], but I did here. And yet the two aren’t very different, so what’s up? It has to be a question of design.

The absence of storage boxes is another misstep. There are some who will argue that it doesn’t matter when you can just leave your items in one spot, but that’s to ignore a couple of key points.

If an item is ‘dropped’ by the player (i.e, not placed by the designer), then picking up that object can be irritating in terms of positioning, and it also means endless back-tracking to one spot when the most player-friendly option had [i]already been found[/i] without coming at the expense of horror.

How successful was the storage box? Well, it is still with us today, and I don't think [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was any less creepy because of it.

If I was to lodge another complaint against [i]Zero[/i] (the last, I promise) it’s how quickly it reverts to type. The train set piece is a definite hook. It’s a new, fresh locale, that has the exciting benefit of being in motion. It’s too bad it serves as little more than a glorified prologue, then. I know a train is a restrictively linear space and so works against the series’ emphasis on exploration, but the bulk of the game is spent in yet another spooky mansion. And it ain’t no Spencer Mansion, either.

So, where does that leave us? Well, I did say [i]Zero[/i] wasn’t bad, and I stand by that. It’s a gorgeous game, oozing atmosphere and tension, both of which are perfectly complimented by some truly stellar sound design. And once you’re past the crap mansion, things do pick up.

It’s just a shame that by then you’re about at the end. Then again, that does mean you’ll be free of Billy, so perhaps it’s for the best. Certainly [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] was for the best, so it's hard to mourn the end of this particular era. It had its time and produced several fantastic games.

[i]Zero[/i] is not one of them.

Whoever decided to take item boxes out of a game with maps this big and item drops this many needs a good stern talking to, because in terms of its basic framework, that simple concession could have gone a long way towards making RE0 a much more manageable experience. As is, however, this game's loop is essentially trying to figure out which items need to stay in your inventory for progression's sake and how much ammo you can fit in your pockets out of the Massive Amount of Items you'll find strewn across the floor. I can see the logic behind this approach, because it could potentially make it so that there's less backtracking and wandering off looking for healing items and ammo, much like RE4 would eventually facilitate. In this game, it just means that there is backtracking, and there is wandering off looking for healing and ammo, but instead of just backtracking to the item box, you have to try and remember where you dropped the stuff last, and then navigating the zombie-crowded hallways to try and get to it (over and over and over), and god help you if you reached one end of the map thinking you're about to progress, only to figure out that you set the key item to do so down somewhere back where you came from because it didn't seem important. That is not an exercise in problem-solving, resource management, and navigation like a traditional RE game from this time. That's just tedium and some layout memorization. 

It's a shame, because in almost every other aspect, RE0 could have been a great addition to the series. Rebecca and Billy aren't the most charismatic protagonists, but all the environments you go through look great, the sound is fantastic as always, and the story, as is also typical for this era of RE, plummets into nonsense so hard and fast that it bounces back up to being good fun. It's just a shame that I couldn't enjoy the story as much as I wanted to because I had to actually play the game to get to it.

Writing this review coming off of my high of beating the main story (there's an unlockable "Leech Hunter" mode). Keep in mind that this is an HD port of a Gamecube game from 2003, using the original Resident Evil Remake (2002) as a base - which also has an HD port on Steam. As such, it has many of the same common mechanics from that release + some modern conveniences. Examples being that with the "modern" control scheme, you have the ability to switch between tank controls and full-3D rotation just by switching between using the D-pad or thumb sticks. Other than that, as far as I can tell, there are very few tweaks for balance or bugs.

Narratively-speaking, this game is a prequel to a game that already had at least 4 sequels released prior. The story takes place the day BEFORE Resident Evil 1, and as such cannot do anything particularly interesting to the plot. Albert Wesker and William Berkin both make cameo appearances, but only insofar as saying "I'm going to go do the thing I did in Resident Evil 1!" and "I can't wait to be the lead villain in Resident Evil 2!". Billy, the new playable character partnered with Rebecca, is very bland. His outfit is that 2000's-chic complete with a silly tribal tattoo. I would highly recommend changing him to his other outfit, which lets him sport a cleaner "mafia/yakuza/club" look.

In terms of mechanics, I think the gameplay was very subpar. There's a hookshot that only gets used 4 times throughout the game, and it does not notify you when it is no longer necessary (you can safely get rid of it after you have access to the train car). Controlling both characters at once (or simply leaving one behind until they are necessary) does not feel engaging, and oftentimes I found myself frustrated with the AI not aiming/shooting properly. The lack of item boxes, thus replaced with simply leaving items on the ground, feels like a step in the wrong direction. It works for RE4, because that game's inventory is much larger, and allows you to properly organize. Item boxes, in a way, allowed for a bit more freedom, because there was no need to remember pathways to each item. You could simply make your way to the nearest safe room, pick up what you need, and continue playing. I found it difficult to navigate the mansion section, but that may have been my inexperience. Eventually, the areas become more narrow, and it's easier. Some may find it better than others.

Most bugs I saw were minor, but I highly recommend rotating saves. There was at least 2 bosses in the mid-game that appears IMMEDIATELY after exiting the safe room. If your character is not equipped with enough ammo, you will be soft-locked and need to reload an earlier save. Rotating saves allows you to keep as much progress as possible, and there's 20 save slots to use for this reason. Thankfully, the game provides an ample amount of ink ribbons (the items used to save your game @ type-writers). I was able to save 39 times in one playthrough on the normal difficulty.

FYI: It's the save room in the church. You have to fight a giant bat immediately after saving. I would highly recommend using Billy, and giving him the grenade launcher. The second time is immediately after attempting to ride the train car. Billy will be pushed out of the battle, and Rebecca will have to fight on her own. I suggest you drop all of Billy's items on the floor prior to starting the fight, as they will be ENTIRELY UNAVAILABLE OTHERWISE.

This game is thought by many as one of the black sheep of the classic Resident Evil games; it came out just before RE4 and people were burned out of the old formula; still Resident Evil 0 is very well executed.

The design of the game is great, the facilities and puzzles are well thought out; It has an atmosphere that few games manage to create; the prerendered backgrounds still look good, and allow for some beautiful scenes; the environment and music have a perfect synergy that give an eerie feel. Bear in mind that if you have not played any of the classic Resident Evil games, the fixed camera angles and tank controls take some time to get used to.

The team mechanics and splitting up to solve puzzles could have been exploited more, you can play most of the game with just one character and your partner sometimes feels like a walking item box. I felt that the difficulty was higher than that of Resident Evil Remake; this game demands a little more from you, I do not recommend playing on hard in your first playthrough. I mismanaged my health items early on and had to reload a previous save to progress; also while I was never out of ammo, you do not have a significant supply until the final parts of the game, be conservative.

[h1]Review[/h1]
Resident Evil 0 is a survival horror zombie game that takes the static camera angle mechanics of Resident Evil 1 Remake and introduces some new additions like 2 controllable characters. You will play as Rebecca - a supporting character from RE1 - and Billy - a new character to the series. Rebecca is less damage resistant, but can mix herbs with her mixing set, while Billy is tougher in a fight and has a lighter used for some puzzles. The story is a prequel to the events from RE1, making this the first game in the timeline as far as I know. You will explore, collect weapons, resources and key items needed to progress through the story, all while defending yourself from zombies and monsters.

The game is very difficult with scarce resources and many dangerous enemies, demanding you to pick your battles and avoid combat wherever possible. In that respect it's one of, if not THE most demanding RE game to date, so keep that in mind if you are looking to try it.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ New mechanics fine on paper[/b]
[b]+ Classic RE game[/b]
[b]+ Second half[/b]
[b]+ Unlockable modes[/b]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- New mechanics don't work with the rest[/b]
[b]- Map design[/b]
[b]- Spawning enemies[/b]
[b]- Partner's AI[/b]
[b]- Common, dangerous enemies[/b]
[b]- Mansion[/b]

More about pros and cons below:

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ New mechanics fine on paper[/b]
There are 2 changes from RE1 remake to this:
1 - No item boxes, meaning you can't stash items and access them from any save room like in other calssic RE games, instead you can put items on the ground and they will stay there for you to pick up later.
2 - 2 characters you can switch between at will, with one being controlled by the AI while you control the other yourself. You can ask them to stay, follow, attack enemies or stay passive. Characters will often have to split to solve some puzzles or open passages that only 1 of them can use.

In practice this may not have worked out this well, but more on that in different parts of cons section.

[b]+ Classic RE game[/b]
Static camera angles ain't popular nowadays, but I still think they represent the best way of portraying a survival horror gameplay as long as they are not used to obscure enemies. Here there's some of that, but for the most part it's fine.

[b]+ Second half[/b]
After you are done with the first major area (mansion) - the game gets more focused with tighter environments and good puzzle design dependent on characters working separate, but still interacting. There's also less problem with lack of resources and much less enemy spawns from nowhere.

[b]+ Unlockable modes[/b]
There are 2 unlocked by finishing the game:
1 - Wesker mode - where you play the game normally, but Billy gets replaced with RE5's version Wesker, who sports some special moves like super-running and powerful melee attacks. Rebecca gets a new costume in this mode.
2 - Leech hunter - where you explore the mansion with the task of finding leech statues hidden all over the place, while fighting enemies and looking for items and weapons. It gives you rewards depending on your performance. It's much more fun than the typical mercenary mode seen in other games of the series (I was never a fan of time-based, kill-enemies mode).

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- New mechanics don't work with the rest[/b]
There is a problem with both new mechanics being used in this game. No item boxes is bad because of how much backtracking the game will demand from you and how much stinginess there is with ammo and healing items and spawning enemies. More about those in their respective sections.

The AI partner would be great if not for already mentioned spawning enemies and terrible lack of resources as well as AI being simply bad and unable to dodge and being useless in a fight. So let's get straight down to it.

[b]- Partner's AI[/b]
This idiot will stand in a spot and shoot at anything that comes close, but won't disengage to gain distance or really display any sense of self preservation at all. If you put AI in passive and try to run through a room, they will nearly always get hit in a process because they simply cannot dodge attacks like a player can. If you want to dodge through a room it's better to control them separately 1 by 1, which is tedious and unfun.

[b]- Common, dangerous enemies[/b]
Some enemies like the leech mimics and eliminators are very dangerous, being able to take you down from yellow health down to dead in 2 hits sometimes and that's on normal difficulty. Mimics are also very resistant to gunfire and have to be killed with fire or they will explode in your face and even then they can take 3-5 hits to go down. They appear too frequent and in areas which make them difficult to avoid and you don't get enough means to deal with them for half of the game.

[b]- Spawning enemies[/b]
During seemingly random events or exploration, new enemies will spawn in specific areas. Some of these spawns are just naughty with a dangerous leech mimic spawning just behind you if you explore a room with some resources for example. God help you if you left Rebecca in a corridor behind you at that point. That works to the game's detriment already even without mentioning how scarce ammo and health is...

[b]- Scarcity of ammo and healing[/b]
There's a serious problem with ammo and health in this game. For the most part you will have enough ammo for the pistol, but it's only really effective against weakest enemies. Eliminators and mimics are very common, as already stated. Molotovs can be wasted if you stand to close to a wall when throwing - they will hit that wall instead of being thrown forward. Also AI partner tends to waste health if left on their own. The difficulty in here being how the game requires you to memorize sections of the game in order to conserve resources properly. That with how you don't have item boxes and the map that requires backtracking is problematic...

[b]- Mansion[/b]
All of the above problems are the most noticeable in the first major area you will spend about half of your playtime in - the mansion you get to after the train (tutorial area). I don't want to spoil any more, but trust me - once you are out of this place you will start having much more fun with the game.

[h1]Lowdown[/h1]
So the train is ok, mansion is very bad, the rest of the game is good. Since mansion is the largest area you will spend the most time in, about half of the game is below average, with the rest being fun. So how on earth do you review this thing? Do you recommend it with caveat of having to slog through half of it by trial and error? Or do you not recommend with a comment that only first-ish half of it is bad?
I decided to go with a not recommended, because a player should not be expected to go through bad gameplay only to get to the good part. I can tell that RE0 will be more fun on subsequent playthroughs, especially with 2 additional modes and many unlockables, but I'd still give it a
[h1]5/10[/h1]
Average score, because of that very bad mansion level seemingly put in just because RE1 had a mansion. Do I like it? Yes. But speaking objectively this game cannot get a thumbs up. I can recommend it for a fan of the series that wants a game that will demand planning and time investment, but not for someone who just starts their adventure with classic RE games or just wants to play a good horror game. Play RE1 remake instead and if you like it - you can try this one.

This is a great game, like the RE1 remake, but it has had some major changes made to the gameplay. The main change is the addition of a partner system- you will need to keep track of two characters in this game, making sure they both have enough ammo and health to survive enemy encounters. This can create a bit of a problem where one of your characters is fully healed but the other is close to death, and if one of your characters dies, the game will end. This adds another level to the micromanagement of the game, but it is usually not a huge problem if you make sure to keep track of all the health items you come across, and this is made far easier by the new item tracker which lets you open the map to see which items are in each of the rooms you've been in. To counter this change, the item box has been completely removed from this game, meaning you will need to carry all the items you need to new areas. This does get annoying later on, especially when you pick up the new weapons that take up two slots instead of one. 

One of the changes I was glad to see in this game was a lesser amount of backtracking compared to the RE1 remake, with many interesting locations that do not to be revisited over the course of the entire game, including some areas from other games in the series that have been completely remade. Graphically, this game looks as great as the RE1 remake, with some highly detailed backgrounds and excellent visual effects for the time.

In terms of story, this game is a prequel set before the events of the first game, and it's interesting to learn more about Umbrella and more about the backstory of characters such as Wesker. Still, it is nothing groundbreaking and you shouldn't go into the game expecting a story on par with RE2 or RE7.

Overall, you should play this game if you were a fan of the RE1 remake, it is very similar but has enough changes to keep you interested. It's also a great place to start if you're new to the series.

The most interesting feature of RE0 is the requirement to alternate between 2 different characters in order to progress through the game. Managing 2 different characters adds another layer of depth to the puzzles and the combat. However, it's a shame everything else about the game is either mediocre or outright terrible. 

Before I proceed, firstly the item management aspect of the game should be addressed. There's no item boxes in RE0, you have to drop everything on the floor, where it remains until you pick it back up. This might sound convenient if you come across a key item that you need, but when you move to another area it means a hell of a lot of tedious backtracking is necessary to reacquire your old supplies. On balance, the magical item boxes of other Resident Evil games are a far more convenient (albeit unrealistic) solution to the issue of item accessibility. But at least RE0 tried something different in this respect. Anyway, onto the main reasons that I can't recommend the game...

It seems as though the developers ran out of inspiration for the game very early. Before defaulting to the usual Gothic house, the usual lab and the usual industrial area, you're first greeted with a train, which is something different at least, even though nothing particularly interesting happens on it - with the exception of the first boss encounter, which is the most interesting boss in the game, and, since it henceforth becomes a basic enemy, the most interesting new enemy in the game as well, as none of the others introduced in this title can compete with anything you've previously seen in other RE games. In fact, the new enemies introduced in RE0, with the exception of the aforementioned first boss, are invariably boring and obnoxious. One basic enemy comes to mind in particular, and one boss. I'd consider each of these to be the worst enemy and the worst boss in the series, respectively. The basic enemy that I'm referring to (if you've played the game you'll likely already know which I'm talking about) is simply too fast, and, where they occur, their numbers too numerous -  in a game with tank controls and fixed camera angles, inevitably you'll find yourself getting swarmed. The boss I've got in mind (one of three uninspired and lazy bosses of the 'giant critter' category) is intolerably aggravating for similar reasons, being too mobile and difficult to hit with the limited aiming capability that tank controls allow. 

The level design is also disappointing. The training facility, ie, the biggest area in the game, is full of dead ends. This means that often you can't plan ahead and take alternative routes to circumvent enemies like how you can in the Spencer Mansion of Resident Evil 1 Remake (which has an interconnected and labyrinthine mansion as its main area). You just have to walk from A to B, get what you need, then turn around and go back the way you came (most of the time anyway, there's a few exceptions). In Resident Evil 1 Remake, there's lots of options for routes to take through the mansion, and careful planning is rewarded, minimising enemy encounters and saving time.

There were a few things in the game which I thought were utterly ridiculous. Firstly, there's the encounters with the tyrant. Quite literally the most lazy, inexplicable, shoehorned-in tyrant encounters of any of the resident evil games. He just pop up a few times for a few boring, anticlimactic battles- it doesnt do the monster the justice it deserves, unlike in the other RE games in which he occurs. They clearly just added him in for the sake of it. Secondly, there's a particular key item that you need to obtain, which is in a high-up location. Not especially high-up; on a pillar about 10 feet off the ground. To get to it, you need to obtain a battery, to power a lift, to bring a box down on the lift, and then to push the box to the pillar so that you can climb on the box to reach it. Now, there's a different puzzle later on in the game where, to obtain an object on a shelf, you need to give your partner a boost so that they can reach it. So why can't you just give your partner a boost so that they can grab the item on top of the pillar, it's blatant that they'd be able to reach it. 

And as for the story...What can I say? I think there's more mwhahahaha-ing in this one than in all of the other Resident Evil entries combined.

[h1]“It’s going to be dangerous from here on in, why don’t we cooperate?”[/h1]

[b]YEAH GAME, WHY DON’T WE?![/b]
[i]From start to finish,[/i] Resident Evil 0 just refuses to cooperate. Let’s keep ink ribbons and Typewriters. Let’s keep low inventory slots and all the other frustrating design choices from other early Resident Evil games. Let’s change the controls to some bizarre and un-intuitive scheme that no one [b]EVER[/b] would choose on purpose. After several hours I was still hitting the triggers to shoot (they don’t, they control the map) and the aim button to open my inventory, or the inventory button to open a map… it’s terrible and the game doesn’t let you change it. Instead of a game that is fun to play and gives you an exciting and interesting survival horror experience and uses those elements to ADD to the experience… with Resident Evil Zero we’re going to throw in a barely cohesive player swapping mechanic, puzzle after puzzle after puzzle, enemies around every corner… oh but we’re going to take away storage boxes, now you have to just drop items you don’t want to carry… now you have two characters with bad AI that will get themselves in trouble… Now you have ZERO (see that? It’s the numerical title of the game!) healing items when you need them and lots of insta death situations that are in NO WAY explained to you. HEY CHESSBOARD I’m talking to YOU! You hear me FROG!?!

Okay, now that I have that out of my system. No, I don’t hate Resident Evil Zero. It’s by FAR the weakest entry in the entire series though, yeah I said it, it’s the worst, but it’s still Resident Evil. Rebecca Chambers being a likeable character in  RE 1 doesn’t make any other character in this game interesting, well written, or relevant. In fact, playing Resident Evil Zero is like watching Star Wars: Rogue One if that film were just the characters dying in an explosion and ending 30 seconds after it started. Sadly, this game takes that knowledge of these characters' fates and expands it to about 10 hours (for a first timer) and makes you slog through it room after room. 

[h1] STORY [/h1]

Who cares? Well, I do. You might. [b]SO[/b] [i]here it goes[/i]. Resident Evil Zero isn’t just a clever numerical title. It’s a prequel to the classic Resident Evil. You are Rebecca Chambers of S.T.A.R.S Alpha Team. You know, the one who helps Chris Redfield in the first game, and doesn’t seem to have any idea what’s going on. You were the first team sent in to investigate the mysterious murders that have been happening around the Racoon City forest area, which is apparently SO LARGE that several MASSIVE secret mansions and Facilities, including an entire railway system with Waystations can go unnoticed by anyone for, welp, 30+ years. ANYWAY, impossible train aside.

There are now not just zombies… but killer leech monsters too. And a bat, a frog, a scorpion, you name it, this game probably has a Virus version of it. Now they’re on a train, and so are you. You run into an escaped convict Billy Coen. This man is such a douche that even after he helps and saves Rebecca a bajillion times throughout the game, you still fully expect him to either murder or drug her by the end. With all his flat out deplorable and sexist remarks and comments I don’t understand how they ever thought this character was a good idea. This is also who you play as throughout the game. Yep, you play as both. Not in separate sections, not in different chapters, you play as both basically at the same time. When you’re playing as one character the other follows along right there with you, wasting your ammo, dying, or standing in the way of you trying to push a puzzle table around to climb up on. [i]ANYWAY, [/i] [b]STORY[/b], sorry. 
So you and Billy are then set upon by a mysterious Sephiroth lookin’ guy who can for some reason sing like Matthew James Bellamy from the band “Muse” to control these gross, slimy slug creatures… it’s just… ugh. These creatures can even take the form of the “first” uh, overseer of the facility? Dr. Marcus… and access a loud speaker system to randomly shout:

[h1]Attention! This is Dr. Marcus. Please be silent as we reflect upon our company motto: Obedience breeds discipline, discipline breeds unity, unity breeds power, power is life”[/h1]

Yeah, this guy may as well be a leech and slug infested Sith Lord. Seriously?
You venture through a train, barreling at impossible speeds through the forest, a training facility that acts as sort of a pre RE1 mansion area, a laboratory, a dam… I mean this thing just slogs on like a slimy slug. Except the slugs in this game move at loony toon speeds and leap through the air while this game just crawls, leaving a slimy and smelly mess of a trail. When you finally get a story payoff in the FINALE of the game, explaining why this mess is relevant to the series and what’s been going on… it still is irrelevant and nonsensical. I truly have no idea why this was written, except maybe to introduce us to Billy and bring back fan favorite Rebecca.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

This is the Resident Evil 1 style. Fixed Camera angles, tank controls, inventory management (but without storage boxes this time, which is a HUGE problem) typewriter save points, janky animations, poor dialogue etc… but instead of campy fun and tense atmospheres like the first game, this game is just super far out there. If Resident Evil 1 is Evil Dead or Dawn of the Dead, Resident Evil Zero is Plan 9 from Outer Space. Yeah, it’s [i]bad[/i]. Gameplay is [i]bad[/i]. Not in a Deadly Premonition [i]It’s so bad it’s actually endearing[/i] kinda way. I tried with keyboard and mouse, like the first game, this simply doesn’t work. I mean, people beat Dark Souls with a guitar and Dance Pads, so it can be done, but why the ♥♥♥♥ would you want to? Controller isn’t much better here sadly. This game is just NOT FUN to play. It honestly seems like people like this game a lot because they find Rebecca adorable and just want to stare at her all day. That really is all it has going for it.

[h1]Performance[/h1]

Much like the Resident Evil HD remake, this game runs just fine on newer systems. I had to do zero tweaking and had no issues through the game (other than the game itself) No crashes, no frame stuttering, no patches just to get it to work. It gives you the option of widescreen or 4:3 like it’s original release, which is cool but… I don’t know why anyone would choose 4:3 on purpose. Whatever.

[h1] SUMMARY [/h1]

[b]Overall Score: 4/10[/b]
[b] Why you should play it:[/b] It’s technically RE canon. So, there’s that I guess.
[b] Why you shouldn’t play it:[/b] If you care about the RE canon you can simply read a synopsis, because this game is just painful to play.

Sorry to hate on a game so many people seem to absolutely love, but man… I just couldn’t find enjoyment here. Skip this sucker and move on to the vastly superior Resident Evil HD Remake or the more modern remakes of RE2 and 3.

[h1][b]Content[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 14/20[/b]

Resident Evil 0 Remastered typically takes 12-15 hours to complete, depending on the player's familiarity with the Resident Evil franchise and chosen difficulty level. The game offers additional content, such as the Wesker Mode, where players can experience the story with Albert Wesker as a playable character, and the Leech Hunter mini-game, which provides an extra challenge to collect leech charms throughout the campaign, neither of which I found entertaining.

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 20/20[/b]

Resident Evil 0 Remaster seamlessly resurrects the classic, robot-like gameplay mechanics that, surprisingly, feel perfectly at home in the game's mysterious universe. A departure from the approach taken in the remasters of Resident Evil 2 and 3, the retention of these mechanics maintains the original presentation's core without compromising its nostalgic charm. For someone more inclined towards straightforward gameplay in other genres, delving into horror and puzzle-based experiences may seem daunting.

However, Resident Evil 0's initially complex appearance slowly reveals itself as its main appeal. Embracing fixed camera views, deliberate character movements, and rapid decision-making, the game crafts an experience that stands its ground against the more advanced gameplay of first-person or third-person survival horror titles. It's a departure that, against the odds, captivates and differentiates itself. One standout feature is the careful attention to detail in the game environment. Nearly every object you encounter, from old figurines to seemingly ordinary bottles, serves a purpose.

While the sheer volume of interactive items initially appears overwhelming, mastery of the micro-management and decision-making aspects becomes satisfying. No room remains unexplored, no object overlooked, immersing players in an engaging and extensive experience. The core gameplay centers around two characters that can be played collaboratively or independently. Navigating the game becomes a skill of knowing what, where, and when to search for specific items, especially in subsequent playthroughs. The strategic switching between characters can save valuable time, yet certain puzzles necessitate a cooperative use of both characters, adding an extra layer of complexity.

The inventory system contributes immensely to the immersive experience. Constrained to accommodate a primary weapon and a handful of essentials like herbs and ammunition, it prevents the accumulation of useless items. Constant inventory management forces players to carefully consider each item, ensuring a keen awareness of each character's possessions. The ability to leave items strategically across the map adds a layer of forethought, allowing players to retrieve them as needed - a thoughtful touch that enhances the overall gameplay dynamics.

[h1][b]Presentation[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 17/20[/b]

The Remaster release has noticeably overhauled graphics, showcasing high-quality textures and carefully detailed assets. The overall horror ambiance is excellent, leaving little room for improvement. While the absence of more advanced settings to toggle graphical effects is a minor drawback, the decision is understandable. Notably, the grain effect hides artifacts on specific objects, and the bloom effect illuminates darker corners, enhancing the visual experience. Although CAPCOM's animation system may not lead the gaming industry in this one, it achieves a convincing level of detail and polish. However, the occasional 'robotic movement' occasionally makes way for a laugh or two in an otherwise ominous ambiance. Some instances require precise character alignment to pick up items or interact with objects, impacting the fluidity of 'in-and-out' gameplay strategies.

In the realm of survival horror, few franchises hold as much sway as Resident Evil. Resident Evil 0 Remastered masterfully revives the classic survival horror experience with its spine-chilling soundtrack and immersive sound effects. Composer Seiko Kobuchi's eerie score, blending nostalgia with modern flair, intensifies the game's atmosphere. The iconic save room theme returns, offering brief solace amid the relentless terror. The sound effects, marked by 3D positional audio, elevate the suspense and guide players through the darkness. Every creak and moan becomes a potential threat, making each step a nerve-wracking decision. Resident Evil 0 Remastered's audio design successfully resurrects the fear-inducing magic of the original, proving the enduring power of the series in delivering a chilling experience that transcends time.

[h1][b]Story[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 15/20[/b]

The narrative unfolds as Officer Rebecca Chambers and convicted criminal Billy Coen explore an abandoned training facility once used by the pharmaceutical giant Umbrella. If that premise doesn't pique your interest, I'm unsure what will. Resident Evil 0, often dubbed the 'Resident Evil game with the silly story' by some franchise fans, diverges from the norm in my experience. Despite not typically finding horror narratives in video games tempting, I must admit that Resident Evil 0 strikes a balance between serious and cringeworthy moments that kept me totally entertained from start to finish. The boss fights, simultaneously tense and hilarious, owe much of their charm to the weird appearances.

At times, I found myself pausing the game, entertained by the presence and aesthetics of certain enemies, some of which boast downright comical designs. As for other content, once the core storyline ends, that's it. A few extras, like the leech mode, offer a degree of replayability. While you can replay the game and explore alternative approaches, the narrative can't be different enough to necessitate a second playthrough. However, for completionists aiming for a 100% game and all achievements, there are some intriguing challenges to pursue. Explore the descriptions of each achievement, and you'll understand what I mean.

[h1][b]Technicalities[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 16/20[/b]

The game runs smoothly across all PC hardware, performing admirably even on integrated GPUs with a playable framerate. I haven't encountered stutters or freezing during gameplay, except for occasional instances when the camera angle changes and the game stops for a split second and resumes. While noticeable, this issue isn't game-breaking. Even though the camera cuts are constantly present, it didn't detract much from the overall gameplay. The transition between actual gameplay and cutscenes is seamless. I highly recommend using the door-skip mod, as it can save valuable time for each door-opening and ladder-climbing sequence. It's a feature I wish the developers had officially implemented, at least as a toggle, as waiting for a ladder climb or a door to open becomes tiresome. Were it not for this mod, the rating score for this section would've been 12.

[h1][b]Final Verdict[/b][/h1]
[b]Rating: 82/100[/b]

I want to recommend this game SO BADLY, but I seriously can't. It's just not what I was expecting after playing through the first three games in the series.
First and foremost, this is a cooperative experience where you control Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen interchangeably. It sounds cool and it kind of is! But it becomes very tedious after a while, especially when you need to split up.
Item boxes are gone. Yeah. GONE. The way they make up for this is by allowing you to drop items which is not something you could do in previous games. Sounds cool, but it becomes a chore when you drop an item, then realize you need it later in the game and have to make the mile long journey to find it again. Top this off with enemies being able to attack you while you make the journey makes this all the more tedious. Like how hard would it have been to maybe also have a universal item box? Idk.
The story? Meh. It's a bit overhauled. It provides some clarity, but it's a bit overboard for a resident evil game. Seems too Si-Fi for me. I didn't hate it, but I didn't love it.
Finally, the special enemies in this game are an absolute NIGHTMARE. The leech people are tanky and force you to use fire weapons, which usually consist of grenade ammo, which I would rather not use on these guys. The Eliminators are just as tanky and are SUPER annoying to fight with tank controls. It just feels out of place; like the combat style does not fit with these enemy types, so I'm not to sure why they thought this enemy was a good decision. Not to mention their fast and travel in packs.
That's all I really have to say about this game. I guess try it if you want? Maybe if you're a story complentionist like me. It's definitely one of the more difficult and frustrating RE titles to date, so just keep that in mind.

GAMEPLAY:
Resident Evil Zero is a third-person survival horror video game. The gameplay remains largely the same as previous entries in the series. However, unlike controlling one sole character like the previous games, the player controls two protagonists throughout the game. The player may switch between  Rebecca Chambers and  Billy Coen. If they travel together, either one of them can be controlled while the other character is handled by the AI. Each character has unique abilities. Rebecca has a mixing kit which allows her to combine herbs and other chemicals, but she is weak defensively. In contrast, Billy can move heavy objects, use a lighter, and has higher defence, but cannot mix herbs. The partner system is central to solving many of the game's puzzles.

It is the fifth major installment in the Resident Evil series and was originally released for the GameCube in 2002. It is a prequel to Resident Evil.

[b][u] TLDR: [/u][/b] To the general person, I cannot recommend this game. Even though this remaster is very well done with beautiful graphics, high framerates and resolutions and somewhat modernized controls, the interface, controls and inventory system are still clunky and awkward which means that playing this to the end is more of a slog of an experience: trying to cope with awkward camera angles and the inventory system, rather than enjoying the horror, story, iconic locations and characters. There are multiple newer horror games on Steam that provide a good experience without the awkwardness – including Resident Evil 2 Remake and 3 Remake which I think are much more accessible ways to get that original Resident Evil feel but with modern 3rd person shooter controls.

[b][u] Conclusion: [/u][/b] This Resident Evil Zero Remaster is an excellent effort in bringing the original to the modern age though I fear it is only interesting to existing fans and people really wanting to check this historic franchise – just be aware you’ll have to be very tolerant to awkward controls and very patient with frustrating inventory management.

[b][u] More detail: [/u][/b]
I was born in '84 and was around when these games originally came out, with the original tank controls and all that. And this remaster is very well done preserving the original but modernizing graphics and the controls somewhat (free move with the analogue sticks).

However, all this can't make go away the fact that the controls and interface are still awkward and frustrating, and the overall design is just antiquated. You will spend lots of time going back and forth carrying items, weapons and ammo due to the limited inventory. I understand the limited inventory is a way to heighten the dread, but when you open a door and suddenly face a tough enemy or a boss and you don’t have everything with you because you’re saving slots because you may run into a key, a card or something like that, and end up dying, it’s more frustrating and tedious to repeat that section… Also, of course the fixed camera angles makes it so that sometimes you can’t even see what the enemies are, making combat not a very enjoyable affair. 
It’s a pity, because I feel the background story is interesting and the different locations very iconic as well. Also you can separate the two main characters which is necessary to complete some puzzles – there are sections where story events even force that – which I found make it a nice twist (though if you get caught with the wrong equipment you might have to reload to a previous save).

Resident Evil 0 was released just after my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/crateboxer/recommended/304240/]weird childhood Resident Evil obsession[/url] came to an end, so I didn't know too much going in for my modern Resi marathon. I knew it closely linked up with the start of RE1, I knew there were leeches involved, I knew it promoted antidote-fetching all-star Rebecca Chambers to a starring role, but aside from that I was a bit in the dark—not a good place to be in a horror game.

Once the credits rolled, my first impressions were... eh? Not bad. It was probably by default the worst RE game I'd played at that point (Code Veronica is great come at me), but it was still a perfectly reasonable experience Entering the Survival Horror.

There's some great elements to RE0. There are some pretty cool enemies and bosses to deal with. The artwork demonstrates a similar mastery of the nearly outdated pre-rendered background method displayed in REmake. The opening level is absolutely incredible, trapping you in cramped passenger cars packed with monsters for an all time great train level.

Part of the meh-ness comes from the fact that, incredible opening aside, a big chunk of 0 feels like a too familiar rehashing of RE1's haunted house set-up. The games following RE1 really varied up the scope and settings of the series with city streets, secret islands, Antarctica, etc. Moving back to a mansion turned secret lab—not the same mansion turn secret lab, mind you, just [i]another one right next door[/i]—feels... safe. If the rest of the game was as gutsy or fresh as the train level, RE0 would've had a lot more cachet with me.

The other bump in the road is the partner character mechanic. Like most RE games, 0 features dual protagonists. However, in 0 your characters stick together throughout, finally realizing a design-doc goal from as far back as RE1. 

This is a surprisingly sensible in-universe decision for RE protagonists, but it presents a bit of a logistics mess for the player. You end up spending a lot of time babysitting whatever character isn't under your command, or trying to octopus maneuver both with the left and right sticks simultaneously. The AI, bless its heart, does its best, but the optimal plan is usually to leave one character behind in a safe spot and run each hallway dodging gauntlet twice. It feels like the game was built for actual, human-buddy co-op just without the co-op actually implemented, so the hacked together one player two character solution didn't enhance my enjoyment all that much.

Still, it's worth a playthrough as a sort of not bad Rogue One lead-in to the much better RE1. If you're gonna play it this remaster is easily the best way to do it—your next best option is, what, the Wii version? And unlike REmake, there's actually new game content in here as well as the widescreen and alternate, newbie friendly controls. Overall RE0 is a bit weird, a bit experimental, but it's still Resident Evil. If you're already into the series it's a fun enough installment.

Unlike the strengths of a game like Alien Isolation which provide a frightening white knuckled gaming experience through level design, story and atmosphere, Resident Evil 0 offers the same thing through its mechanics. Although the game does a fine job with its soundtrack, atmosphere and visuals, the core design of the game play severely holds it back. 

Although there is often the opportunity to evade an enemy, there is little incentive for the player to actively engage in combat given the fixed camera which makes combat a chore.  Since enemies can attack you while off camera, the process of having to turn and face them in a fixed camera perspective, especially to align aiming, feels more inconvenient than it does necessary for survival. This is especially frustrating for fast paced boss fights. 

Additionally, much of Resident Evil 0's game length is substantially perpetuated by constant backtracking as a result of the limitations and inconsistencies of the inventory system. Although a limited inventory system is a welcome feature to any game, RE0 is not only limited but also inconsistent since a key and a gun take up the same space. This requires players to constantly leave behind certain items and then backtrack to reclaim them. Secondly, the save system also adds to the backtracking since not only are the save locations (a typewriter on a desk) are limited, but so are the number of times a player can use these points due to an ink printing strip. 

The game also features a bug where, upon quitting the game, it will drop the player back to a black screen. The game can only be exited properly by pressing ALT+TAB. 

While the game can be frustrating, there is a b-movie charm (through its hokey voice acting and dialogue) which adds an ironic levity to the story with its cackling villain and oversimplified characters. 

Resident Evil 0 is great to admire at times, but it hardly invites any replayability.

Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster Review

The good ol days… So much nostalgia and memories right here!

Please note that this Review may contain spoilers from the Original game 

Some key points that this Remaster offers:

1.	The original experience
2.	Remastered HD Visuals
3.	Remastered sound effects

Remastered:

You won’t say that this is the same Resident Evil 0 we played back then…  It has been totally overhauled and upgraded to offer us a brand-new HD experience.

Several of Resident Evil 0’s systems and features were reworked to offer us a more current take on the game. Some of these changes are high-resolution textures; These were created from scratch and includes 1080p support for the next-gen consoles. The screen ratio has also been overhauled. 

We still have the original 4:3 ratio or we can make use of the new 16:9 widescreen feature. I do have to note here, even though the visuals were majorly overhauled, it still offers you that same experience that the original release does, it just does so with updated visuals to make the experience so much more memorable and vivid!

Sound effects were also updated to offer 5.1 surround support and I assure you this totally changes the experience; things sound and get a whole lot creepier than it did back then. Unfortunately, voice acting remains the same; There is nothing wrong with it per se, merely that the voice acting back then was done a lot differently than it is today. The scripts and dialogue’s come across cornier than need be, but it can easily be attributed to being part of the original experience.  

This one might just be the best overhaul entirely. Control schemes were a lot different back then, however, they went and made an alternative more modern control scheme for us. We still have the option to play with the original variant or make use of the newer more modern one. The choice here would come down to personal preference on how you would like to control the gameplay. Either works perfectly in their own way!

Last but not least is the added game mode Wesker Mode, unlocked after completing the main game. Experience the remaster from the eyes of the Ultimate Resident Evil baddy… Overpowered and pretty much unstoppable… He comes packed with his own unique abilities and powers. 

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:

All things considered; the remake is a pretty amazing game. If you played the original from back in 2002, the HD Remaster is going to bring back a whole lot of memories. 
If you have never played it, or if you are new to the Resident Evil series, then you will get to experience a Zombie Horror Survival like few others.

The Resident Evil game franchise pretty much created the Horror Survival genre back in the day. Limited ammo, narrow corridors, and Zombies. As then you are in for one major memorable experience!

Resident Evil 0 is the prequel of Resident Evil (1996). The game occurs before the Mansion Incident, covering the ordeals experienced in the Arklay Mountains by special police force unit, the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team. 

[h1]Plot[/h1]
On July 23, 1998, Bravo Team (S.T.A.R.S.) was sent to investigate a series of cannibalistic murders that were happening (for quite some time) in the Arklay Mountains outside of Racoon City. On the way to the scene, its helicopter has an engine failure and crash-lands in a forest. Bravo Team survives and searches the forest only to find the corpses of dead officers, upon examing the scene they find a prisoner file, which was ordered to be transported, Bravo Team assumed the prisoner killed the guards and escaped. Resolved by this event, Bravo Team decides to search for the murder and bring him to justice, they decide to separate and Rebecca Chambers, a Rookie, wanders around and finds an Express, now motionless, and explores it, only to find the passengers and crew rushing at her, after surviving this strange event her crewmate desperately jumps inside the Express to tell her that:
