[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay remains largely the same as previous entries in the series. However, unlike the previous games, in Resident Evil 0, you control two characters at the same time, with which one having advantage and disadvantage, like Rebbeca can make herb due to her being a prodigy and graduated from college at age 18. Billy can move heavy objects and has more endurance due to him being a former Marine. 

When Rebecca and Billy are close by, they can exchange items between one another with each one having their personal inventory (6 for each one, 12 in total). The game doesn't have box storage, so the player needs to manage on their own.

The camera is not one of the best, most of the time you'll crash into walls, some times the camera won't be able to capture the whole scene, so zombies in your front and back will bite you, but It should be no problem If you got a headset on to hear them. 

[b]The aim is NOT automatic, It can fix at enemies, but ONLY at their direction[/b], you must be in their front, aim and move it manually, keep in mind that your chances to headshot enemies long rage are very slim.

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
When It comes down to difficulty the RE series won't let you down, and Resident Evil 0 push it to the limits. While playing this game for the first time I thought I had a good background on the series having encounter pretty much any type of enemies— from humanoids to an fk* frog. But, the enemies are not the problem, the real problem It's the way the remake is designed, you constantly have to worry about the enemies, the camera and your inventory. There is twice the ammo, but the enemy count is nearly triple. Base enemies are a bit squishier though. 

Playing this game for the FIRST TIME on hard mode is asking for a mental break, anyway, [b]I personally consider Resident Evil 0 the hardest game of the series[/b].

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Despite being a game from 2016, the graphics are almost the same as from the original (2002), the reason for this is that after the remaster of Resident Evil (2015), Takenaka (director), recognized that many Resident Evil fans preferred the old style of gameplay pre-Resident Evil 4, and so he reasoned that the HD remasters were to provide that same gameplay experience on modern hardware.
For the remaster, Capcom used the original 2002 models and textures from their archives. To Takenaka's surprise, the models and textures were actually designed in very high quality and then downscaled for the original release. This meant that some assets had to be redone, as items that were intentionally blurry or illegible in the original were now much more clear and did not make sense in context, such as posters or signs in the environment. The models and textures were re-touched, and then the backgrounds were re-captured.

[h1]Extra Mode[/h1]
Additional modes were added as well, including an easy mode and Wesker mode. On Wesker Mode, Albert Wesker—who replaces Billy—accompanies a P30-injected Rebecca. All of the original full-motion video sequences in the campaign remain the same, while the in-game cutscenes feature the alternate costumes. 

While playing this mode, you got two abilities, Shadow Dash - which the player will dash forwards knocking back enemies and Death Stare - which you can chop off enemies head's with Wesker's Stare. The Suitcase is unavailable in Wesker Mode. 

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Resident Evil 0 is a case of love or hatred, some love others not so much, I personally love it! But, Capcom could have done a much better job at this game, remasters are meant to be just a Ctrl-C, it's about getting the best from the original and improve it as much as you can, implementing new features, better graphics and dynamic gameplay, [b]but always being faithful to original so that it doesn't lose its essence.[/b]

What can you say, or perhaps not say, about a franchise that is knocking on the door of its third decade, whose most recent entries collapse under the weight of a polished remaster of its first entry? Resident Evil has become so bloated in its sequels and spin offs, all of them underwhelming, that revisiting Spencer Mansion for the third time is sadly a breath of fresh air. Nevertheless, it is a welcomed breath of fresh air as we now have the best Resident Evil in some years. Leave it to a polished up version of a 2002 Gamecube release, which in itself was a remake of the original 1996 release of Resident Evil's starting point, to put smiles on the faces of all the devoted old school fans who have wanted the series to return to its terrifying albeit cheesy and clunky roots. Capcom achieves greatness with making the arguably best even better by tidying up the controls, graphics, textures and sound, and letting it live and breath on current generation consoles. Those who only know modern Resident Evil, or never got to play this in 2002 entry have themselves a fantastic experience ahead of them as they explore Spencer Mansion and witness the groundbreaking horror first hand with the original core characters. This game doubles as a grocery list of what Survival Horror should be, and how the modern conveniences of gaming do not always make for the best experience. This take on Resident Evil is both familiar and curious, both comfortable and nerve racking, and both full of nostalgia and yet as challenging as a never before seen adventure. So those of you who have played the original '96 game, are still in for surprises around some corners, and challenges that will make resources vital. The dialogue, though still a bit cheesy, is multiple levels up from that of the delightfully awkward original script. It remains similar enough to bring back all the memories of the original, but separates itself enough from the past to intrigue, creating an almost parallel world experience with how similar but more thought out the new dialogue is. I found myself both listening to the new, but in my head quoting the old, making for some laughs. Once again, those first person views of doors opening, tight corridors with the moaning undead near by, and limping through halls praying for ammo and health all have your hair on end, and it is a most welcome return. The Mansion is only slightly redesigned enough to make you lull into comfort, thinking you have the situation under control before springing something new on you such as a new zombie placement, or unfamiliar room, or retelling an old experience in less predictably ways. The results are fun and frightening. The Mansion is alive with creaks and shutters, moving light and flashes of lighting, shadows and mirrors, fog and water, all pulling you in deeper than ever before. This is Resident Evil in all its Survival Horror glory. It would be impossible to rate this any lower than a perfect score, seeing as it is a better version of a past masterpiece, and then improved once again on top of that. Get lost in Spencer Mansion, and take a bloody bite out of the game that started it all, the one and only, Resident Evil.

Before this, I've only played a few Resident Evil games in the order of RE7, RE1 HD then RE2 Remake. As someone who did not have access to PlayStation or GameCube, I hated the game mechanics of RE1. The fixed camera angles and tank controls really made the game extremely frustrating for me. The game was truly way ahead of its time. The developers of RE1 had ideas that were too advanced for the technology in its day, which made the gameplay so unnecessarily hard. I completed RE1 about 4-5 times in total, trying different modes and getting as many achievements as I could. Then there is RE0, a game that after completing it once, I really have no desire to play it again.

It did not bother me that RE0 was similar to RE1 in terms of maps and general gameplay. Since I was "trained" for fixed camera angles and tank controls from my repeated gameplay of RE1, I had a much easier time for RE0. At least in the beginning. I quite enjoyed the train segment despite sharing the same negative feelings I had towards RE1. Then as the game progressed, the enemies became more difficult to handle, and more difficult, and then frustratingly difficult to the point of irritation and annoyance. At that point, the game was no longer fun. Any potential fun was sucked out from getting past these irritating enemies. The limiting controls simply require you to rely on luck in order to either defeat or evade these enemies. I get that the developers wanted to make the game better by creating more challenge for the players, but this has crossed the line to the point of being sadistic. I could go on, but in a nutshell it just isn't fun facing enemies that have no reason being this difficult due to the controls. 

Then, in the spirit of change, this game abandons the item box function and instead introduces the ability to leave things on the floor without the need to discard them. This is a great function as it was regrettably missing from RE1. It was okay during the train segment, but when it came to the rest of the game, having the need to MANUALLY transport all the items you want to the next location is a frustrating chore which may also lead to your death if you stumble upon the aforementioned overly difficult enemies. Games are supposed to be fun, but I cannot imagine anyone having fun in running back and forth long distances, going through multiple loading screens and positioning yourself perpendicularly to the item you want to pick up many times. It is extremely time consuming and not practical. Also, each room has a maximum amount of items you can leave on the floor. If you have more, you gotta leave it in another room. Even more annoying. 

Another new element introduced to this game is the ability to switch between characters and have (or not have) the other character follow you during the gameplay. This would have been a really interesting feature, if not for the fact that one of them is almost useless. I like Rebecca Chambers. I was so eager to play this game because I liked her in RE1. I wanted to kickass as Rebecca. But throughout my first playthrough of RE0, I played mostly as Billy. Rebecca is weaker and cannot do anything that is actually important to the gameplay, other than the fact that only she has the ability to mix herbs and chemicals. Also, many times I find myself just playing solo as Billy while leaving Rebecca behind at a safe spot. This is because when she tags along, the AI is stupid and either does not fire at enemies when required or does not know how to move away from approaching enemies. When she dies, game over. Gotta restart. I don't get how the AI works. In other words, the extra character is just a burden. The developers should have made her more indispensable by giving her a more important trait that can actually help in the game play and be important to have her tag along.

In summary, I think this is still a pretty good game. Great ideas and great flow of puzzles like RE1, although RE1 did it a lot better. However, the technology of its time does not do the game justice and therefore fails as an overall package. For longtime fans of the series, the problems I mentioned are probably nonexistent. However, for people who are more familiar in the modern ways of gaming, proceed with caution.

I Have a like/HATE Relationship with RE 0

First off the game is not scary, the voiceacting is awkward again not RE1 levels of bad but more like Code Veronica, the game is full of flaws, and it's just not fun to play at times especially on hard difficulty. BUT at the same time it's main characters are memorable and the game does have it's charm which is why i usually don't mind playing it.

RE0 was supposed to be a N64 game and was closer in tone and in atmosphere, with a more consistent story and design to the original RE1. The no item box mechanic with just 6 inventory slots could've worked in a smaller N64 game but it's a problem here because it forces you to drop and keep essential items (like the fuccin' hookshot) close to you up until half of the game or else... MORE backtracking is required for you to progress in a game that is already full of tedious backtracking with too many doors and too many useless rooms. 

Billy is an allround cool character and nice addition to the series, he doesn't say much, he's just cool and would make a nice couple with Rebecca. Rebecca, however... SUCKS! She is too weak and is only useful for mixing stuff, you'll have a hard time surviving with her on Hard mode. The pre-rendered backgrounds and character models in the Remaster are gorgeous and with extra costumes makes these additions a huge improvement over the original RE Remaster but no leaderboards anymore which is too bad. The music still has some of that late 90's/early 2000's Japanese horror soundtrack, some memorable, some not, but i'll admit that it's soundtrack is better than RE Remake's soundtrack. 

RE0 is probably the hardest game in the series, challenge is always nice but here it's mostly because of the horribly clunky gameplay. RE 0 also made A.I. partners a trend in the RE series which does make more sense from a story perspective partners would stick together in an unkown place not split up all the time, but this also means that the game won't be that scary and the A.I. is usually horrible, if you want to leave a room while your partner is under attack or you didn't tell them to join you, you'll have to go back in the room or switch to your partner just to move along it's tedious.

Whatever you do, DON'T play on Hard mode first! It's unbelieveably unbalanced and you'll have a hard time understanding the mechanics and horrible backtracking. Best thing to do is play on Easy or Normal first then get the unlimited ammo prize (only for handguns in hard mode) in Leech Hunter to have an easier time on Hard mode. The story ruins Rebecca in the original, RE 0 is supposed to be a prequel to RE 1 but it just doesn't fit storywise and the antagonist is so stupid and pointless none of it really matters. The antagonist uses leeches to create a replica of himself and shows up in scripted locations like Nemesis from RE3. Nemesis is a cool villain but the Leech Monster is terribly boring, hard to kill, annoying and you'll only waste ammo cause you won't get any rewards for killing him so many times!! It's just dumb, better to just avoid him. 

The enemies and bosses are not creative at all, aside from your usual zombies it's mostly just large insects and other animals like killer monkeys. Speaking of enemies, i can't see them most of the time because of the horrible camera angles, in previous RE games i didn't have too many problems with the camera or enemy placement but in this game the developers seemed to have made this intentionally bad along with the tedious backtracking. Boss fights are terrible, a large scorpion which takes a long and boring time to kill, a large centipede which takes a long and boring time to kill and a large bat which takes a horrible and painful time to kill... Why didn't they throw in a large cow as well? Prototype Tyrant was kinda interesting but overall just a WEAK nostalgia attempt since he doesn't matter to the story and the Final Boss fight is the worst i've ever faced in this series. The killer monkeys and Hunters can parry you while attacking making it impossible to escape and you can only pray you'll survive if you haven't saved your game. The giant enemy frog can instakill you if your partner just stands there and doesn't shoot it to save you. Also you can't aim while shooting, if you missed one shot and try to aim up or down while shooting the characters won't react! You'll have to stop shooting first, wait for their shooting animation to stop, THEN aim at the enemy and hope you don't miss again or get killed in the process! It's just crazy how clunky this game is after so many previous RE games got these mechanics right!!

Also a couple of nitpicks. 
- the game is not well optimised when opening doors i always get stutter
- just like in REmake, shotguns don't do headshots as often anymore, which is bad overall, but in this game it's even worse!
- Rebecca's (and most of Billy's) animations are exactly the same as Jill's from RE Remake which is lame, no personality whatsoever.

I can honestly not recommend this game to anybody other than Hardcore RE fans, i guess i'm one of them which is why i kinda like it but it's an absolute nightmare to play through.

I have some mixed feelings about this game, but I definitely lean on the more positive side.

First of all, this should not be your first Resident Evil. This game is way too hard for a newcomer unfamiliar with old RE's mechanics. Play REmake 1 instead. 

How's the gameplay? It's not bad. REmake 1's inventory mechanics are still here, but they take up so much of the gameplay that it completely removes the option to dodge/avoid most enemies. In this game, you have to kill most enemies you see, like in RE 7. The puzzles are pretty good as well, but nowhere near as good as REmake 1's puzzles. Well, all the puzzles in this game are acceptable, save for the Hook Shot. Whoever came up with that awful thing should never come up with a puzzle again.

The bossfights are... well, you know. RE has always been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible at bossfights, excluding the last ones of each game. From REmake 1 to RE 7, bossfights have always been a bad idea. There are a lot of bossfights in this game to make matters worse, but, as long as you play very strategically, most of these fights should be just annoying, not difficult. Most. Definitely not all.

The enemies are all pretty unfair or annoying, except for the zombies. The leech humanoids are ridiculously powerful, taking almost all your health upon explosion (in normal difficulty). The primates jump around the room and make it hard to aim at them. The mutated frogs are one hit kills if you're just a little too far away from them. However, even though these enemies are BS, there are just enough zombies to make the game not completely unbearable.

How's the story? It's alright. If you aren't familiar with RE, this story will be pretty lame. If you are familiar with RE, this story gives a lot of insight to other entries and builds most of the lore we know about Spencer and the beginnings of Umbrella. 

Overall, this game is pretty good. It's better than the 3rd person action games by a mile. This was one of the last dying breaths of old RE before it was revived by RE 7 and REmake 2.

There is a fine line between a challenging game and a frustratingly difficult one. [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i] triple-jumps over that line breaking both of its legs in the process. Throughout most of the game you guide two characters, manually or with the help of an AI, as they navigate the luxurious train from caboose to the locomotive and later on as they traverse Umbrella's abandoned training facility and its underground lab. The journey through those locations is a perilous one since they are swarming with some of the strongest, most resilient and toughest to handle monsters ever seen in the 'Resident Evil' series. Your means of fighting back are very limited as you are given an already noticeably small amount of ammunition that you have to split between Rebecca and Billy. Avoiding combat more often than not doesn't work due to AI-controlled character being inclined to get hit or grabbed by enemies while you run through the corridors skilfully dodging monsters' attacks. True to the game's survival horror branding, knowing that you have to enter a room with something awful in it and you've only got a few bullets left arouses a sense of dread in player, but after failing to bring down the same enemy for the fifth time that dread tends to give place to rage. Furthermore, the item management is additionally messed up by the omission of item boxes. You constantly have to leave items behind to free up space in your inventory and then backtrack when you realise that you left the key item behind. This head-scratching decision added absolutely nothing to the game, it just needlessly inflated the total playtime. [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i], however, is not without merits. Serving as the prequel to the first game, it fills you in on some important details regarding the initial t-Virus outbreak. Yes, the writing could've been bolder and twists should've been more spectacular, but this paucity of imagination is made up with interesting exposition and fantastic chemistry between the lead characters. It's easy to see why Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen quickly became fan favourites. The atmosphere in [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i] is truly horrific, created by the tense and unnerving background music, various noises and great use of light and shadows. Momentarily, you get the impression that spacious halls and tight corridors are haunted by otherworldly beings instead of man-made monstrosities. In the end, [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i] is not a bad game, but puzzling choices by developers keep it from claiming a more prominent place in the [i]Resident Evil[/i] canon.

It's classic RE. With that said, RE0 sufferes questionable design decisions taken during its initial development on the N64 which hampers it. The lack of cartridge space on Nintendo's console dictated no item storage boxes, and this was inexplicably retained and taken forward in the move to Gamecube and later versions, where space was a non issue. What this means for you is, like it or not you're going to be backtracking and staring at the inventory screen for longer than is fun. Make no mistake, it is a chore to play more often than not.

RE0 offers the stiffest base difficulty of the series, unfairly so at times. The main antagonist is painfully cringey and weeb (and not in the classic cringey RE sense, either). It looks gorgeous, has puzzles, features switchable characters, and definitely takes its place among the classics of the canon. But it has spikes of fake difficulty which are not challenging, just unfair, and the item juggling and interminable backtracking and inventory study means frustration gets in the way of fun far too often. You'll be reloading save points very frequently due to an unforeseeable monster ganking and if you're going in blind then that can mean at least 10 minutes progress lost, often more. So it's for RE completionists only, and even then, play it last of all.

I played this game after finishing some RE games, but before playing RE1, because I thought playing RE0 first would help me understand that one more when I get to it. With this in mind, I think the plot is a bit shallow, there's barely anything happening in this game. I'm sure it adds something to the original, but it's a bit too simple for me on its own. I also don't really like the main villain, I just didn't find them interesting or entertaining.
I liked that you have 2 main characters (Rebecca and Billy) that you have to control at the same time and they have to work together to solve things. I already knew Reb from Vendetta, and I actually liked Billy so much that I ended up searching for info about him to see if he appears in any other games and no, he doesn't. Dude's nowhere to be seen again, so then why was he here in the first place, when this game is supposed be origin to explain everything? Anyway, I liked playing as 2 characters at the same time or more like, I enjoy this much more than having an AI partner running after me like in RE5&6. Maybe it's creepier to walk in a large mansion alone, but they mostly just talk in cutscenes so I think it was well made. I also think there was more tension when I had to get them to somewhere one by one because I had to be careful about their low health.
I also think the game's beautiful. I liked the atmosphere and soundtrack, I liked exploring. The puzzles are fine. I played on normal and I found the game a bit too easy. I killed pretty much everything and still had way too many ammo left by the end. I mean I killed the Tyrant with like 8 magnum shots I think and it couldn't even move before it died. One boss killed me once, but that was only because Reb had all the stronger weapons at the moment and I had to fight as Billy. Some smaller enemies could be more dangerous than the bosses and I just feel like it was a bit too easy for a survival game. There was nothing challenging in it. One thing I don't like, though, I find it stupid when you can see an enemy chilling on the ground, but you can't shoot it in advance, because it doesn't react to it and you just waste ammo, but it does get up later after you made some progress. I think it's stupid that you can't just shoot it when it attacks you later anyway.  
Then, the problem everyone's complaining about: the inventory-item box problem. Basically, both chara has 6-6 item slots, some items take 2 slots, you don't always know when you'll have to use them next and can't put them in an item box to store them and get them at the next save point. Instead, you have to dump all the stuff you don't use all over the floor and run back for them when they're needed. You also don't know which character needs to carry what, because they might get separated at any time. This was something that I was worried about, because I hate unnecessary backtracking and it can ruin a game for me. Yet, I think I was able to figure out how to make this system work pretty well. I didn't just dump my stuff everywhere, I started with dumping everything at a safe point, then when I made enough progress and everything was mostly clear of enemies, I carried them over to the next one, but mostly just the unused weapons and healing items. If I had a puzzle item, but couldn't use it yet, I just dumped it near the puzzle's location, which I always found in advance. Whenever I checked the current map and saw that I was making my way to the next map, I carried all my stuff nearby in advance, always inching closer to the next save point. This literally made backtracking way less time consuming than going all the way back for everything, if I needed something but left them somewhere without always carrying them closer in advance. The only time when I had to go back more was before I suspected the very last boss happening. Yes, having small inventory and no item box is annoying, dancing around dropped items for 10 seconds before they were willing to pick them up is annoying, but it is manageable and it's not worth a negative review in my opinion. 
I think the game's entertaining, it's not flawless because I found the villain and the plot meh, but I had fun playing it.

I tend to try and write game reviews after I've properly finished it, but I'm making an exception in this case, as I have completed RE ZERO several times since it's release on the game cube as well as it's Wii and HD Xbox port. It's tried and true Resident Evil but with a few mechanics that were experimental at the time. Namely, the character zapping and ability to drop inventory items as and when you wish. In fact, the item box is completely omitted from this entry! 

The original title's side character, Rebecca Chambers takes a share of the lead here, along with new entry Billy Coen. Their characteristics build around the two-character system utilised in Zero. Not only do you have to manage both of their health and ammo/item storage, but use them for certain puzzles or encounters. Rebecca is a medic and can mix herbs and special chemicals, and Billy has more upper body strength for those pesky rusty cranks and can take more punishment in combat; a giant scorpion boss did as much a scratch to him as does a demon horde to Doom Slayer! 

I think Zero is looked upon as a bit of a black sheep in the series, though not as much as the divisive 5 and 6. It's not in anyway bad, it just had a lot to live up to against legacy titles like 2, REmake and Code Veronica. But I have a lot of love for this little gem, it's a few things that stand out on their own merit. The soundtrack that mixes sinister ambience of the original with some of the more epic and mellow/upbeat string and keyboard arrangements from 2 and 3. Rebecca and Billy are honestly a pair of dorks but are totally likeable.

I just love Zero, it stays oldschool but tries some new things without alienating it's routes. Becca isn't the annoying damsel that she was made out in the original title either. Sure she's a little green compared to the main roster but what she lacks in experience she makes up for with spirit, will power, empathy and general desire to do good and see the good in others. 

She also has the best choice in attire for sport activities ever, she could save lives with her posing in gym shorts alone, so thank you for that Rebecca ;) X
What should I say, it's a real nice Resident Evil in the style of the good old days.

RE Zero manages to build up a dense atmosphere with superb visuals and sound design. Compared to the gamecube release the backgrounds look crisp and alive with many details, probably the best static backgrounds in the series. As a proper survival horror game you will find yourself constantly running low on ammunition and healing items. New in Zero is the tag team system: You control both Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen. Via button press you take direct control of one of them or order the other to stay put. The character currently not under your control is taken over by the AI that attempts to dodge and shoot enemies (but is not very reliable). Unfortunately, the devs decided to change the control scheme for Zero. If you played the original or the remake, the tank controls will feel natural, but other buttons like opening the menu, aiming and running are switched around (for the joystick) which leads to confusion and accidental inventory access when you meant to turn around and so on. Only the keyboard can be customised. The enemy design and main story are also rather lacking. The issues are however minor and do not take away from the fun to be had. If you like the original RE games or survival horror in general, totally get this game.

The prequel to the first Resident Evil in full HD.

The story:
It is one day before the mansion incident in the original Resident Evil. You are Rebecca Chambers, a member of the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo team. You were tasked to investigate the many recent murders in where the victims were apparently eaten. You and your team encounter and decide to investigate a stopped train in the middle of the woods. The rest of the story is up to you to discover.

Gameplay:
Very similar to Resident Evil HD, but with a twist, this time you work in duos. Two characters at once. This means you'll have puzzles where you need two characters to solve it. Each character has their own speciality. Rebecca can mix herbs (Used for health), and Billy can push heavy objects. If you haven't played the original Resident Evil (or HD) yet, that game can be described as full with puzzles and zombies where you have to escape the mansion and to solve the mystery of the murders. This can be applied here as well, except that there are even more areas than just one. Starting with the train in the beginning of the game. 

Performance:
I am quite certain that most people will be able to run this. The original game was released in 2002 on the GameCube, this is a HD remaster where the 3D and 2D elements are now in HD or higher. Using V-Sync, my framerate never went below 60 fps.

My experience:
This is the third Resident Evil game I have played fully. (RE1-HD first, RE2 second, RE0-HD third.) And I feel like it's a quality game just like Resident Evil HD. However, there are some things about the game I disliked which prevents it from being just as good as Resident Evil HD. 
The character duo is a nice feature, except that when you're not controlling your partner, an AI takes over.

[i]Resident Evil Ø[/i] will always have a special place in my heart for being the last "classic" RE game. Though the series has already spawned more games then I can keep count of, the core - if not the [i]canon[/i] - for me will always be RE1, RE2, RE3, RE: Code Veronica, and finally REØ. There's just something special and magical about these five games that was never fully recreated in later instalments. I love the detail in the 2D backgrounds, I love how everything is centred around the 'mansion incident', how the events and locations overlap to create an elaborate timeline that is still full of unanswered questions, mystery, and suspense. I love how the background information in files and dialogue add to the world building so that every zombie you encounter is presented as a former human being rather than generic copy-paste cannon fodder. (RE4 may be a phenomenal third person shooter, it certainly is not Resident Evil game if you ask me.)

REØ was the last to use the classic formula of fixed camera angles, lots of key searching, and an emphasis on avoiding the monsters rather than shooting them by the hundreds. I'll take for granted all the flaws: the silly plot, the dodgy controls, the cumbersome item management, the mediocre voice acting, the obstructing camera angles, the puzzles that often stand in no connection to the story... All that is forgiven when you are thrown into the frantic scenario where you are a prey desperately seeking only one thing: survival.

One last word of critique/advice: if this is your first run, play the game on EASY mode. REØ is harder and less forgiving than other RE games. A zombie so much as sneezing in Rebecca's general direction takes away half her health, it seems. Since most of the difficulty comes from backtracking (and there is a lot of that in REØ) and not carrying the right weaponry, the first play-through will probably kick your ass.

I recently beat the REmake remaster and loved it, with my one self-inflicted gripe being the fact that it was way too easy. The reason for this was that I had inadvertently been playing the game on easy because the game doesn't make it obvious which difficulty you're picking at the start. By the time I finished REmake I had probably a dozen healing items, unreasonable amounts of ammo for all of my weapons, like 15 defense items, etc. and that was after clearing out just about every enemy I came across. Once I realized I wasn't in any real danger and could just shoot everything that moved and heal with reckless abandon, the game got boring fast. Backtracking should have been a stressful and calculated endeavor, but in my case it just became a mind-numbing loading door simulator. After that experience, I resolved that I would play the next RE game I tried on the hardest difficulty available to as to challenge myself and raise the stakes a bit. Turns out, that meant playing this game on hard.

After about 8 hours of playtime on hard I was having a blast. The difficulty felt perfect, like I'd be feeling light on ammo and then boom, 15 pistol shots. Then I'd be on danger health and boom, healing spray. It was exactly what I had been looking for in an RE game: where the scarcity of resources adds to the stress without just killing you on loop until you're able to luck into a really clean section. And then, without warning, came a violent difficulty spike. I'm going to keep this spoiler free so I'll avoid specifics, but I will say this occurs roughly halfway through the game. From that point on, this game was nothing but frustration.

Now I know what you're thinking. "Get good, son. This is a RE game on hard - what did you expect?" My frustration wasn't necessarily the difficulty itself, but more being punished for not having played the game before. I can break this down into a few types of situations:

1) Exploration. In this game you play as both Billy, a tough guy (250 HP), and Rebecca, a less-tough girl (150 HP). Because you have control over which player you're using for the majority of the game and the majority of the game can also be completed with just one of them, the winning strategy is often to stash Rebecca somewhere safe and go exploring with Billy. Given that healing items are extremely limited, it usually doesn't make sense to play with Rebecca, because she will need to heal more often after taking the same amount of damage. It also doesn't usually make sense to explore with both characters at once, because doing so just increases the chance of you taking more cumulative damage. However, some puzzles can only be done with both characters, and as the game goes along it starts putting these puzzles farther and farther afield of the safe areas where I stashed Rebecca. So, on a handful of occasions I'd fight my way through some resource-intensive enemy encounters, only to realize that I actually needed Rebecca with me and now she'd need to make the trip herself with very limited weapons. Womp womp.

The other side of the exploration coin simply hinges on knowing which rooms are essential to visit and which enemies are essential to kill. If I knew in advance that a given room didn't have a story-essential item in it, or an elusive healing item, or some shotgun ammo, I would of course not bother wasting my bullets and/or health on the enemies inside. However, given that it's my first playthrough, I'm forced to explore everything just in case. The alternative is backtracking later and wasting even more bullets and/or health. Incidentally, given that there's no item box, the same issue also applies to items.

These issues aren’t unique to RE 0, but they’re more serious flaws in this title because of *how* it is made difficult. Remember the aforementioned difficulty spike? If I had known to expect it, I would have known that I needed to have hoarded a surplus of healing items by that part of the game or risk being stuck with no items and no reasonable way forward. Difficulty should never spike so suddenly so far into a game in which your item consumption throughout the game is a big part of how the game is balanced.

2) Terrible save points. This game uses the classic RE method of doling out ink ribbons that you need to consume in order to save your progress. This adds some glorious tension to just about every encounter, as the stress of having to redo substantial stretches of the game if you die only increases the stress you're under. The trouble, though, is that the game will mercilessly ♥♥♥♥ you on several occasions if you decide to save your ink ribbons. One time I decided not to save I was stun locked and killed from nearly full health the second I stepped out the door of the same room. That one was a blast.

3) Unannounced character splits. In RE 0, each character is limited to six inventory slots. They can exchange items between them when they're right next to each other or next to a dumbwaiter, but other than that their inventories are separate. As you might imagine, problems often arise when Billy and Rebecca are separated without warning. You'll open a door, or pick up an item, etc. and then all of a sudden a cutscene will play, and then boom, one character is incapacitated and the other character is left to fight a boss, run through rooms of agile enemies to rescue the other character, etc.

Again, if you've played the game before, you'll know the split is coming and you'll make sure to give the character that isn't getting incapacitated all of the guns, ammo, and healing items (as if I had any anyway, lmao) so that they're actually able to survive the boss fight. If it's your first time playing, though, you might find yourself playing as an injured Rebecca with 15 pistol rounds and a knife trying to kill a fast, hard-hitting enemy that would best be killed with Molotov cocktails or flame rounds, for example. 

There were certainly ways to address these issues to that they wouldn't be so needlessly punishing for new players. #1 wouldn't be much of an issue if the difficulty stayed reasonably consistent or if difficulty were adaptive. #2 wouldn't be much of an issue if there were item boxes next to pretty much all typewriters like in other RE titles. #3 wouldn't be too much of an issue if your incapacitated character would drop their items or if it were more predictable when your characters were about to be separated. However, taken together, they create an unavoidably punishing experience for first-time players.

--------

With that said, most everything I enjoyed from other RE titles can be found here too (puzzles, horror, resource management, *biohazards*, you name it). I really do like the zombies. They're satisfying to fight, they're dangerous without being fast, and they're unpredictable. Sometimes inanimate corpses will grab at your ankles. Sometimes a zombie's head will explode after two shots and other times you'll have pumped eight pistol rounds into them and knifed them five times before they *finally* die for good. The environments are absolutely gorgeous too and I love how creepy they feel. The fixed camera angles can be a pain if you're using the joystick instead of tank controls, but they're nearly always tastefully chosen and I've grown to really like them. I really did appreciate not being capped to 60 FPS as well.

At the end of the day, though, I just got killed one time too many 45 minutes after my last save because a surprise cut scene & character split screwed me over. I tend to be too much of a completionist in games, so I've been making a point lately to stop playing a game as soon as I realize I’m not having fun anymore. RE 0 hit that threshold tonight. I'm probably 70% of the way through, and at this point I just don't care to finish. I unfortunately can't personally recommend this game for this reason, despite that there's plenty to like here for fans of the series.

Resident Evil Zero takes place right before Resident Evil Remake (there may be some changes between the original beginning, that is the one I played). The main difference from the classic games of the series is that this one you play them simultaneously, with just a few parts separated.  The other VERY divisive mechanic is how you handle items. I have been a Resident Evil fan since the beginning. Having played and loved the original trilogy. But in the early 2000s for some bizarre reason Mikami and Capcom decided to take the series exclusive, first to the Dreamcast with Code Veronica, then finally to the GameCube. Releasing a highly regarded remake of the first game and Resident Evil 4, which quickly lost its exclusive status, returning the series to the fold. Before that though, they released the comparatively unknown Resident Evil Zero. Set just one day before the events of the first game, Zero was supposed to fill in some of the gaps and flesh out the story, while providing a glimpse at Umbrella's history. It would be more than a decade before the game escaped Nintendo's clutches, pushing it further into obscurity. Finally an HD remaster found its way to Steam and my PC.

Starting up this game was a blast from the past. The tank controls, the set camera angles, the pre-rendered backgrounds. It was like playing one of the original games again. Rebecca being the star of the game further magnifies the nostalgia factor. The game quickly introduces us to the other protagonist, ex-marine convict Billy Coen and here is where the game starts showing off its more novel features. Unlike the original trilogy, here you control two characters. You can switch from one to the other at almost any time and you can have them follow you and help fight the various enemies, or wait somewhere safe while you take care of business. Initially, I was skeptical of this system, partly as a result of the whiplash this change caused. But though far from flawless, I did grow to like the mechanic. It helps that the initial area of the game is by far the strongest.

You start the game trapped in a luxurious train, filled with horrors and speeding towards the unknown. This initial area is both excellent and appropriate to the genre, the game's tone and mechanics. It is small, detailed and not too difficult. The pacing is great. You get a few glimpses of the big bad, some backstory via cut-scenes and you get to see the protagonists rapidly come to terms with the fact they are not in Kansas anymore. The game provides you with just enough resources to kill everything and forces you to use both your characters to solve puzzles. The area contains only one leech man and inventory management does not yet become the hassle it will become later on. It really starts the game strong, teaches you what you need to know and keeps you engaged. But it is only the prologue. Soon it comes to an end and as you move to the second main area, clouds begin to gather.

After the train, you find yourself in an old Umbrella training facility, which looks suspiciously similar to the Spencer mansion from the first game. In fact when I first saw the main hall with the staircase I immediately got excited thinking we are back at the legendary house of horrors, before quickly realizing that the layout is just too different. It did leave me somewhat incredulous that Umbrella would have another opulent mansion-like structure with a hidden lab underneath within walking distance of their other much more famous facility. Almost as if the developers could not think of anything better and instead were just aping the original. Nevertheless, a copy of something great does get to reflect some of that greatness. Indeed the training facility as a location is pretty neat. I wouldn't have much to complain if the game successfully aped the original anyway, but as it turns out, it is not similar enough.

Though the game does a good job emulating the classic gameplay of the original games, it falters in the things it does different. The fact you can now control two characters being one of the few key changes that are not negative. Like in the originals inventory management is a big part of the game. This game, however, turns inventory management into medieval torture. Limited item slots are a huge hassle. Even though you now have two characters, it still feels like you have less space. There will be lots of pointless backtracking just to pick up items you couldn't before, or had to drop. But it gets worse, this game does not have an Item box. That's right, no Item box. I don't know what genius at Capcom thought this change would be a good idea, but I do hope they never let them direct a primary school play, much less a game after this. I cannot overemphasize how negatively impactful to the whole experience this change was.

The game is difficult, perhaps the hardest out of the Resident Evil games I've played. But it is difficult in all the wrong ways. The enemies it introduces are some of the most annoying in the series. The leech man is an absurdly difficult opponent to manage, if you don't happen to have fire based weapons. The infected apes are basically mini-Hunters that somehow feel even more agile and durable than the real deal. Then there is that bat boss. Ugh. The enemies are generally hard to deal with due to in-game limitations, like controls and movement. This coupled with the limited resources the game offers you and the aforementioned problematic inventory system, can make it pretty frustrating to slog through the game's later areas. Of course, if you know what enemies await, you can equip yourself correctly. But the only way to know that, is to make sub-optimal choices early on, die and try again. Hardly ideal.

Starting up this game I wasn't entirely sure what to expect. Now that I've finished it I'm not entirely sure what to think of it. At its worst, it caused me a fair amount of frustration. Perhaps it wasn't the case when it was first released, but today it feels like a throwback, a relic of a different era. It is undeniably flawed, but it is also memorable. The story may seem a bit more absurd than usual, I mean controlling BOWs with opera was a feat even the original wasn't campy enough to pull, but it is a true Resident Evil. I am happy to have finally played this game and I will recommend it, but only to mega-fans of the series. For the rest, if interested, you are probably better off watching the game's story on YouTube.

[h1] That other Resident Evil [/h1]
Simply put, the Resident Evil series had grown robust over the years, to the point where even among the major releases some of the games weren’t intended for the limelight by design. Resident Evil 0 is one such “B-side” title. Initially released on Gamecube as a follow-up to 2002 RE Remaster, it was intended to satiate those whom the first game left longing for more. This alone, should flare up the red lights all across the control board, especially for a modern player. Resident Evil HD Remaster is nowadays a title recommendable only for the franchise and oldschool fans. In turn, RE 0 is a rushed expansion to that, offering more of the tedious gameplay and none of the cult status or atmosphere of the original. While RE 0 is not terrible, a title fit exclusively for die-hard RE followers makes for an audience way too narrow for the game’s own good.

[b] That other mansion [/b]
Resident Evil 0 is an immediate prequel to the first game, the game’s events taking place 24 hours before the Spencer’s Mansion incident. The story follows Rebecca Chambers, member of the soon-to-be-missing S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team, dispatched to investigate a strange cannibalism reports on the outskirts of Racoon City. After an emergency landing of their helicopter, Bravo Team comes across the evidence of a death-row escapee Billy Coen and they choose to spread out in pursuit. Soon Rebecca finds Billy in a train full of zombies and the inmate becomes an unlikely ally in a struggle for survival.

Awkwardly enough, the duo finds a second Umbrella facility within an eyeshot from where the events of the first game took place. The derelict mansion that used to be Umbrella’s training facility also hides a secret laboratory and a whole gallery of mutated test subjects running amok. There are even some secret passages operated via overtly convoluted mechanisms too. What a coincidence. 
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2027799372 [/url]
You can now easily tell, that Resident Evil 0 in general is a copy-paste of the first game. To make matters worse, an abridged one. The game is far more linear and blunt in its use of puzzles. Furthermore, the rooms’ cluttered backgrounds no longer have hidden items that would award exploration. Admittedly, the touch of the mad inventor is still present, though most of the meticulously obtained keys serve only to open a single door. In result, RE 0 often feels like you can barely step off the beaten path, complex as it may be. While the original had you circling around, solving a single grand mansion-sized puzzle instead.

[b] Two heads are better than one [/b]
Despite all of the above, the game does deserve a credit where it’s due. Resident Evil 0 introduces a unique twist on the series’ dual protagonist formula – the player gets to control both characters at the same time. This change and the cooperation mechanics coming along with it completely reshape the way you approach tasks at hand. Would you rather clear the way with a single character you can fully control or move in as a team, relying on additional firepower to manage the threat? How to properly divide the supplies among characters? You can only fully control one at a time, alas the number of character swaps will soon exceed that of fired bullets. Especially that the equipment management returns to its quirky roots, having you drop items rather than use global storage chest. Each protagonist has a separate equipment, forcing you to leave, exchange and combine a lot in a bid to make the most of the highly limited room.

Despite still operating on the fixed-camera RE 0 has fewer and better thought-out transitions making them much less confusing. Furthermore, it also makes the character movement feel more fluent and dynamic. It’s a welcome change, especially with the game taking slightly more action-oriented angle. To facilitate said angle, RE 0 features enemies in greater variety and numbers when compared to the first game. New additions include mostly mutated animals, including a giant bat being a boss designed exclusively with malicious intent. Having said all that, most of those are decent twists on what ultimately are tedious mechanics. All the improvements in the world won’t change the fact that the characters control like a tank grinding through mud.

[b] Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster [/b]
Many vices of the title in question won’t change a single aspect in which RE 0 is inherently better than the first RE – being a remaster. Most of the backgrounds are better detailed and much less grainy allowing you to actually see the improvement in graphics. On top of that, once you have beaten the game you unlock two additional game modes, one of which is remaster-exclusive. The extra dubbed “Wesker Mode” has Billy’s model is replaced by that of Albert Wesker from RE 5. Beside a visual change, Wesker now has psychic powers – after a short windup Albert releases a blast from his eyes making the heads of nearby zombies explode. It’s a silly gimmick but a wildly entertaining one. As far as weird extras in Resident Evil games go, this one definitely takes the cake. Too bad only a few players will be persistent enough to beat the game in order to actually reach it.
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2027798931 [/url]
Ultimately, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is not an inherently bad game but one that leaves a lot to be desired. Having it strapped to a cult classic that Resident Evil is with copious amounts of duct tape invites an inevitable comparison RE 0 can hardly stand up to. The title does expand the lore and provides some context to its “parent” game, albeit it does so in a way you start to appreciate that the original chose to keep its questions unanswered. That said, the game can be easily recommended to radical fans of Resident Evil series. To the wider audiences though, RE 0 will remain at best a footnote in the history of the wider franchise. A fate essentially intended for it by the game’s own parent studio from the day one of the development.

Inventory management is a never ending pain, and it only gets worse as you realize that there are no storage chests to hold all of the excess items. The combat isn't completely terrible - when you can actually see what you're fighting. The dialogue and characters are pretty standard for B-Horror movie fare, which is very different from the later entries in the series. I know this isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it's more of a heads up for people coming back to this game after playing the later games in the series. They seem to take a more serious tone later, but this game has bad dialogue that fits right in with the likes of, "You, the master of unlocking".

TLDR: Not having to play using tank controls is nice, but issues from older generations of games still plague this remaster.

I can easily say that this game is my least favourite of the BH/RE games using the Multi Angle camera system and that the HD remaster doesn't bring much to the table over its Gamecube predecessor.

Capcom decided to try some new things at the time with this game and I'll mention them below.

There are no items boxes to manage your inventory. Instead, you must place items on the floor and backtrack to retrieve them.

You control two characters at the same time. If one dies, game over. There are vague options like "Attack" and "Idle" but the AI and and responsiveness is less than desired. What can you expect, considering this is a Gamecube-era game.

The tank controls feel a little less responsive than the BH/RE1 HD remaster but this could be anecdotal at best. Being stunlocked is fun.

There is a choice for non-tank controls, so this option may appeal to players that dislike the original tank controls or want to try something new.

Onto other nitpicks. 

The enemies in this game lack variety, as most are mutated wildlife with the occasional Hunter. It makes sense, lore-wise but may feel like a step backward for some. There's also an enemy called Mimicry Marcus. Consistently killing them completely is fine with flame grenades, but in any other case, it seems they might live and walk around as a ticking time bomb. Speaking of flame grenades, you receive very little in all modes.

I should mention that there are other modes in the game such as Leech Hunter and Wesker Mode. Leech Hunter is uninspired and tedious but offers a short challenge for players interested in infinite ammo unlocks and achievements. Wesker Mode is entertaining for a playthrough and offers some abilities unique to Wesker.

Overall, I like this game but consider it a weaker title among the other legacy games. However, the game does well capturing what it could at the time, which is being a tense survival horror game with emphasis on inventory management and occasional puzzles. The dialogue and cutscenes are just as cheesy as you would expect from that era, too. Oh, and the port of this game is awful. You'll need to find third-party fixes otherwise you may find this game freezing on you or constantly trying to keep task priority (which may lead to crashing).

Pick it up if you can find it on sale or if you're interested in exploring one of the pre-BH/RE4 games.

Hot off the success of [b]Resident Evil (Remake)[/b] and originally a proposed game for the [b]Nintendo 64[/b] console this game came to light in 2002 and the HD remix was as necessary as an HD remix of [b]Resident Evil: Survivor[/b].  Awkward gameplay mixed with poor pacing, sloppy story telling, and atrocious level layout makes RE0 one of the most disappointing classic style REs to date.

[h1][b]Bottom Line Up Front:[/b][/h1]  [b]Resident Evil Zero[/b] is [b]Capcom's[/b] earliest attempt at two survivors simultaneously in a game series that was built on a sole survivor experiences.  Despite [b]RE(Remake)[/b] being released in March of 2002, [b]RE0[/b] was released in November in what appears to only be explained as a rushed development.  [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinji_Mikami]Shinji Mikami[/url][/b], the mastermind behind RE and survival horror, was merely an executive adviser to the games development and it clearly shows as the game has heavy emphasis on faster enemies and gameplay that flows as smooth as a teenagers face.  Enemies are often stacked in pairs and move painfully fast, closing the gap between the player and the adversary.  Historically, classic REs have been criticized for their "tank controls", and it becomes even more problematic due to the enemies capabilities and the terrible camera angles.  The camera angles are often too narrow and often irrelevant and offer players zero advantage; trapping them in a corner while the monsters take turns stunning the player with attacks.  The puzzles are either too easy or so ridiculously complex that players may lose interest or resort to using a guide; one puzzle in particular has players lighting six torches symbolizing the Circle of Life.  There are no hints to signify "Light from the Apex Predator to the bottom of the food chain" or vice versa or "Light the Apex predator to their common prey".  The inventory management is the worst inventory of any RE of its generation (Gamecube/PS2/XBox generations) as each character only gets six slots, players will often over burden themselves and resort to "Leaving"/dropping items behind in one location only to force players later to back track and retrieve the item.   Finally the most criminal offense is the lack of originality in the opponents despite a wide variety of them.  Most bosses are giant [i]Insert scary animal/insect[/i] and lack original thought.  The Hunters (originally featured in RE) were giant frogs that only shared a few characteristics to frogs in appearance but had other features that differentiated them from frogs such as razor sharp teeth and claws.  The monsters in this game that spread the T-virus are leeches (leeches that are the size of a pocket ♥♥♥♥♥), zombie monkeys, and zombie bats and giant zombie bat to list a few,  Despite these flaws; the game still manages to feel like a classic RE often nailing the atmosphere and the desperation of survival.  

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
+ Item dropping (convenient yet also inconvenient) 
+ Game length
+ Enemy variety 

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
- No inventory box
- Pacing
- Gameplay
- Enemies are unoriginal 
- Partner system
- Puzzles
- Map layout (there is literally a room after a 30 second elevator ride that is just a door 3 paces to the left... why?)
- Soundtrack

[b]Closing thoughts:[/b]
Shortly after RE0 and its more action oriented focus, RE would go on to adopt an over the shoulder style that the series still uses today a decade and a half later.  It comes as no surprise that the game was historically praised originally because the game has moments of horrific atmosphere, claustrophobia, and situation based intensity the series is known for.  But it's not easy to overlook the flaws and frustrating experience that comes along with this game.  There are so many tricks the developers pull that create frustrating experiences as opposed to intense challenging ones.  If you're looking for a classic RE experience and you've played all other HD remasters and you truly want to know the origins of RE; don't buy this game.  Watch a [i]Let's Play[/i] on Youtube or a video explanation [b][url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YfLqUshr4n8]such as this one[/url][/b].  It has a long way to go to be as bad as [b]Resident Evil 5[/b] and [b]Resident Evil 6[/b]; but it isn't the quality of players expect from RE like the one's created by [b]Shinji Mikami[/b].

It's funny because you can see how they used some of the item tracking stuff for RE2make and ostensibly RE3make.
There's actually a lot of cool little touches with this game being a N64 prototype originally, then eventually being canned and revived post REmake 1 along with the Outbreak titles. Unfortunately, dwindling sales and enthusiam led the series to RE4-6 which wasn't what the series was at all. 

RE0 despite getting a lot of flack, is easily one of the few games where minor issues being corrected would probably make it much more loved, most of my criticisms being that the game works better switching between the characters, typically leaving one in a safe area(there are a few), playing as the other until both characters are needed which honestly only occurs a few times throughout the long ass campaign. The final fantasy villain actually has a normal appearance, which is that of Marcus whom Birkin and Wesker stole the G virus research from(actually it's amazing but the pettiness of the Umbrella workers is pretty on point commentary for today), he eventually mutates into a horrible Leech Queen that has two stages one reminiscient of the G2 and G1 Birkin form and fights mixed with the final fight of  RE3:Nemesis. The boss mutates and basically you end up Boktai'ing the boss(using sun to kill a giant horrific G monster whose only weakness is acid and sunlight).

The problem is some of the final puzzle work to the boss is poorly communicated, this game is also one of the most merciless titles except for RE2make hardcore and probably RE3make given how it seems Nemesis is even more dynamic than before from the trailers.

The leech enemies aren't even hard to deal with, you have no REmake1 mechanics like the crimson heads so gameplay wise it is probably the most classically styled one between REmake 1 and RE2make, giving a feel of playing somewhere between Remake 1 and the OG 1-3 titles on the playstation.

The last criticism is that the weird monkey enemies need to be completely reworked or trashed, they are a poor replacement in this games bestiary for RE1/3's hunters/spiders. The game has trap rooms where you get trapped into fighting tough monsters(leech monster/mimicry marcus) which only become hilariously easy once you figure out molotovs(which requires gas canisters and wine bottles both of which are hard to spot).

I actually really like the Mimicry Marcus leech monsters, the leeches totally fit into the lore of the series and tone and quite frankly I find them horrific. 

I know that the asymmetrical differences between the two characters also bug people but the series has always had that, Billy is stronger, has less space, has a better weapon but cannot mix chemicals or herbs(which is another way the game ratchets up difficulty and puzzle solutions). Rebecca is similar to Jill/Claire in that she does slightly more damage, is more fragile to the attacks from enemies, and has worse damage roulette numbers in dodging damage, more inventory space, and can mix herbs/chemicals. 

There are tons of little story touches that are totally worth preserving, like when Enrico periodically calls Rebecca for status or orders which is a callback to RE2 Leon and Claire occasionally talking to each other and other moments in the series. There's also stuff via gameplay, and the overall scenario that ends up making it pretty memorable for me even if the story isn't really necessary.

While it isn't BR2049 to BR1 quality, or RDR1 to RDR2, it's a great original RE title that still follows the pre-rendered path that even Code Veronica abandoned. I'm also sorry but nothing, NOTHING in this game is as bad as Nosferatu or Plane tyrant. I refuse to acknowledge these opinions. 

Overall if you've played everything else in the series and want more, the real black sheep of the RE family aside from those terrible gun survivor games, play this because honestly it isn't that bad and is really, actually pretty good in comparison to what came after until RE7,RE2make, RE3make, and probably RE8.

I don't really like the fixed-camera games, but I decided to dive into this one because Rebecca Chambers is my favorite Resident Evil character. Chris, Jill, and Leon all have some form of combat training. Rebecca’s a medic. S.T.A.R.S. recruited her because of her “I graduated from college at the age of 18” intelligence, not because she has any sort of decorated combat record. Despite this, she survived 2 biohazard incidents back-to-back – she began investigating the train at the beginning of Resident Evil 0, survived the Umbrella Research Facility, killed the Queen Leech, went directly to the Spencer Mansion in Resident Evil 1, and survived that. My second favorite character, Claire, also has no (formal) combat training, but didn’t pull as badass of a feat as ~48 straight hours of combat and survival. This is why, in my playthrough, I had Rebecca do the vast majority of all the fighting, despite most people using Billy as he can take way more hits. THIS IS BECKY’S GAME AND SHE’S CARRYING IT, DAMNIT. Err, I’m sorry, I mean this is OFFICER CHAMBERS’S GAME AND SHE’S CARRYING IT, DAMNIT.

I knew what I was getting into from the outset – the price I was going to pay for playing the only game in the series to star Becky. Resident Evil 0, along with Code Veronica, are considered the most difficult in the mainline series. Let’s go through some of the frustrating features.

First, the camera angles. I hate fixed camera angles in these games and this game is no exception. 2 bosses in particular, the bat and Marcus, are incredibly difficult with the camera angles. The bat flies around and the camera means you can’t see it most of the time. The camera changes angles throughout the Marcus fight, which means not only can you not see the boss half the time, but also you’re constantly getting disoriented while he/she/it is slapping you with leech tentacles and grabbing you to exchange your bodily fluids with acid. 

Another reason the camera sucks is the item system. Talk to people about this game and they’ll complain about the lack of item boxes. You instead just drop items on the ground. When you do so, the item just sort of lands somewhere near you, so if it lands in a place the camera can’t quite see, be prepared for a frustrating time trying to find it/pick it back up. If you drop an item near another item, be prepared for a frustrating time trying to pick up the correct item and not the one next to it. An issue unrelated to camera angles is the arbitrary cap on the number of items a room can hold, which means if you try to designate a room for item storage, it’ll inexplicably “fill up” and you’ll need to try to find some other room and organize your items that way. It’s not like the room’s physically too small for these items, either. It smacks of artificial difficulty. Oh, and if you leave some items in a previous area and decide to go back and get them, the game will spawn enemies in your way.

Also related to item management: the hookshot. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hookshot. This thing takes 2 inventory spaces, a full third of the available inventory per character, and you need to carry it through most of the game. Everybody hates this thing and I’m no exception.

Finally, I hate the frogs. You're just walking along and suddenly a frog jumps out of the water, grabs you with its tongue, and eats you. One shot. Dead. Done. WTF CAPCOM.

Anyway, I'll wrap this up. I still think if you want an old-school survival horror game with a kickass heroine and can handle some item-management frustration, you'll highly enjoy this game. It looks amazing graphically, the villain is hilariously hammy, and the gameplay is classic. Go ahead and give it a whirl.

Resident Evil 0 is the last of the "classic" line of Resident Evil games. Originaly developed for Nintendo 64, before being scrapped and remade for Nintento Gamecube, it is a game that operates on a late 90s videogame logic which in the end causes it to be inferior to the Resident Evil Remake that came out few months earlier.

REmake was developed with the intention to improve, polish and perfect the classic Resident Evil formula. Which it did and remains a re-playable classic to this day, almost 20 years later.

Resident Evil 0 - developed simultaneously by an outsourced team - gets the look right, but stumbles in the story and gameplay mechanics department. Why? Because they took the design and mechanics from the old N64 build (being in development in the late 90s) and pretty much porting it to the new build without any polishing or improvements introduced in the REmake.

So, the result is a game that looks and sounds top notch but feels like an older, unpolished Resident Evil title. 

The tank controls are here (along with more modern, alternate controls introduced in the remasters) but there is a weird sliding lag that causes the characters to run a bit further or take a step back when you do not want them to.

The idea of getting rid of the item boxes is sound, but it causes several problems that might bother people -> namely backtracking and impossible level design (magic elevator that takes you from the end game hub all the way back to the main hub, just because the designers needed the player to be able to get to all his dropped items without running all the way back through dozens of screens/enemies).

The story is OK for a 90s game, but after the polished, cinematic, almost-cheese-free presentation of REmake, you are stuck with mindless enemy placement (giant scorpion on a train?), extremely hammy villain and an impossible level geometry. Again it is obivous the designs and mechanics were taken directly from the N64 version without any thought given to the fact that they needed to be given the same treatment as the REmake.

In the end though, RE0 is still a great, sattisfying late cycle RE title and an awesome classic survival horror game. Worth playing, worth re-playing even with the occasional hiccup and frustration caused by the faulty design and mechanics.

If REmake is a pizza, this game is like a calzone. Everyone loves pizza, but not as many people would say they like calzones more than pizza, even if they enjoy both. If you haven't played REmake first, go play REmake first, then come play this if you want more of the same kind of flavor, just arranged a bit differently.

Features:
- Graphics looks incredible, way more cleaner and sharper than REmake's, plus they have a lot more animation with curtains blowing in the wind and light and shadows flickering. The intro section with the rain and the train is amazingly good.

- You can drop items from your inventory anywhere and pick them back up again, which not only makes the game more realistic, it makes it less frustrating if all your slots are full and you just need to grab an item for a second to combine it with something else. If you come across an herb or first-aid spray there's an option to just use it on the spot without ever having to truly pick it up.

- No item boxes. A lot of people dislike this, but if you liked REmake enough to play the Real Survivor mode it is basically just that again. In that mode your item boxes were not connected, so you couldn't put ammo in one box, cross the map, and pick the exact same ammo up in a different room's box; you'd have to walk back to the first box to get it. Because of the previous bullet point every room has the potential to function as an item box, so find a room you feel is close and safe and drop unnecessary items there for safe keeping until you return. All items you have interacted with are marked on your map so it's easy to see where everything is.

- A couple items like the shotgun take up two inventory slots. A lot of people are upset about this too, but consider also you get double the characters as a normal RE game to balance it out, actually giving you 12 slots (six per person). You can exchange items between them as long as they are close so I thought item management was pretty convenient.

- Lots of new enemy types. Most of the ones from REmake are back, but there are mostly new ones you will encounter, which is both a pro and a con since they can be annoying to battle sometimes. But it's still nice to have fresh prey.

- Two characters to play as, which you can control independently or have one tag along. This allows the game to invent new types of puzzles you couldn't have in a truly solo RE game. Like for instance a character might have to stay behind in one room to press a switch to open a door for the other character somewhere else. Nothing truly groundbreaking but it's nice to see some new ways to have to think and plan who does what and with what equipment.

- Bonus modes where you scour the map to find color coded leech sculptures to unlock bonus weapons and ammo, and another where Rebecca gets a different partner.

Overall a very solid game. If REmake is a 10/10 (which it is) this is an 8, if not 9. Item boxes would be convenient, I won't lie, but it's easy to adapt to this new system and shouldn't be a reason for neglecting such a great game.

My only complaint with this game is lack of storage boxes to store your items, so instead you have to drop items that you will be needing later to ground in various rooms. The best way to play the game is to mark every item on your map even if your inventory is full (item will be marked on the map if you try to pick it up even if your inventory is full) so you can easily find what you couldn't pick up by looking at your map. Exploring all unlocked rooms, clearing all the enemies, picking up ammo and health items first with a combat-ready full inventory before picking key items that will unlock new locations is a much better strategy since you will learn easily where you need to go next with the key items available on the map instead of carrying and dropping all key items which some of them will be needed much later. Also, my another humble strategy is to never carry ink ribbons since there will always be three ink ribbons next to each typewriter found in the game. Simply use them and drop them near typewriter. Resident Evil 0 is a direct prequel to the events of Resident Evil 1, and while I personally would not rate it as highly as Resident Evil 1 (HD) it is a fun and interesting entry in the Resident Evil series.  Resident Evil 0 takes the majority of its notes from Resident Evil 1 with a pair of protagonists investigating horrific goings on in a variety of dark and dilapidated locales viewed from fixed camera angles with beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds.  While this might seem like the very definition of Resident Evil 1, Zero changes many key details and elements making it unique, both from a combat and puzzle perspective.  Unfortunately, many of those changes, novel as they are, are cumbersome in comparison to RE1 and its mirror like polish.

You’ll play as either the Courageous STARS Medic Rebecca Chambers, who fan of Resident Evil 1 will recognize, as well as the all new Billy, “Protein Fiend,” Coen, a death row inmate dragged into the survival horror while being transported through the Arklay Mountains.

Zero makes number novel changes to Resident Evil’s regular gameplay.  Particularly in terms of action vs horror and most importantly the dual character control system.  Throughout Zero you’ll play both Rebecca and Billy simultaneously.  You select one character as a “main” character and one as a “partner,” though you can switch those roles at any time with the push of a button.  You’ll move and fight with your main character, while the partner character follows them, and can be manually moved with an alternate stick.  They can also be told to join in the fight, or remain idle.  You’ll get two inventories this time, one for each character.  You don’t get your item box, but can drop and re-pick-up items as you please.

I feel Resident Evil 0’s first stumble is its balance of Action vs Survival Horror.  Zero has more enemies presented more frequently, built up with less horror than in RE1.  You’ll also get more ammo to deal with them all.  As a result, Zero feels less like a horror investigation, and more like an action title with clunky controls and some horror themes.  As well, the dual character system, while commendably unique and offering some interesting puzzles, particularly when the characters must split up, doesn’t always mesh well with greater amount of action.  With more enemies it’s more likely for either or both characters to get hit.  At the same time, the auto attack feature means that rather than dispatching the already wounded enemies with your 60 rounds of pistol ammo, Billy will decide that a precious grenade shot is required if you forget to switch him to idle before swapping to Rebecca.

Getting rid of the item box might be a good way to make players decide which items to bring with them, but I found myself just back tracking in order to pick up items and rearm myself.  Also, key items still take up a whole slot in your small inventory, while larger weapons now take up two each.  This inventory shrinking doesn’t actually increase the tension, as you can just clear rooms one at a time, backtracking and retrieving as needed.

As for story and atmosphere, Resident Evil 0 does do a fair job.  You’ll want to play Resident Evil 1 before you think about playing Zero, as you’ll need RE1 to understand this one, and RE1’s story will be spoilt if you play this one first.  You still get some fun cheezy one-liners, and B-Movie plot we love in Resident Evil games, but the higher focus on action, the lack of horror build up in areas, even with the help of the fixed camera angles, drains out some of the truly scary vibe RE1’s horror provided.  Still, Zero is a beautiful game, and all the talent and art in the background renders is here for you to enjoy.  While not the same horror/investigation plot of RE1, you will get some interesting background for Umbrella, Wesker, Birkin (RE2), and the Virus.
