I recommend the game, but with a few caveats:
The game runs poorly on all but the latest machines because of some technical issue with the frame rate. This can be fixed somehow with unofficial mods, but it's still annoying. Cinematic sequences also might have video and audio de-synched. Again, annoying, and the mods only partially help solve this.
The game itself is a little shorter compared to similar games of the franchise (basically RE1-3).
That said, the game perfectly captures the essence of the survival horror genre in its purest form. Terrifying monsters lurking in an eerie setting; having to manage weapons, ammunition and healing items; the possibility of dying a gruesome death; the hunt for keys and the solving of little puzzles in order to navigate and progress forward in the adventure. In that regard, I don't consider RE0 as good as the other pre-RE4 games (RE4 being the game which changed the original style), but it's a solid add-on to the collection.
RE0 abandons the mechanic of separate playthroughs for two player-controlled characters, typical of RE1 and RE2, and replaces it with one where they both share the same playthrough and are controlled alternately, (which makes it possible to have peculiar puzzles requiring separate control of these characters). It's an interesting and novel mechanic, though at some points it might become tedious and/or unpractical.
The game includes a special mode featuring Wesker as playable character in the main game, and a minigame that grants special weapons for the main game upon completion. Both are available after finishing the main game.
All in all, a solid addition to the series that will certainly please longtime fans of the old school survival horror genre.

To start, I think it's the best-looking Resident Evil game ever made. The backgrounds in the HD Remaster are simply gorgeous. I love how the REmake's HD Remaster looks as well, but this game looks even better.

The core Resident Evil gameplay is intact, with a couple of notable changes. One is that you're controlling two characters at the same time. It's not as complicated as it sounds, and actually ends up being fairly intuitive. Another is that there are no item boxes. Instead of storing items in boxes, you put them on the ground and they'll stay there until you come back and get them. This change is fairly controversial in the RE community, but I don't mind it. In fact, I kind of like it. Any items you put down are marked on the map so you don't have to keep track of where you put stuff - the game does it for you.

I do have three complaints, however:
1. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grappling hook. I suspect that this thing is the main reason people complained so much about the lack of item boxes. It's an item you have to reuse several times throughout the game and it takes up two spaces in your inventory. Meaning, you put it down to make space thinking that you're not going to have to use it again, and then much later on, it's suddenly required, and you have to backtrack across half the game just to pick it up. If it could be used in some other fashion, like as some kind of gimped weapon, then it might not be such a big deal. But as it is, it's a 2-slot key that you have to strategically set down at certain points in the game so that you're not backtracking to get it.
2. The monkeys. These enemies are stupidly unpredictable in an unfair and can be a total pain in the balls.
3. I played RE0 right after playing REmake, and for whatever reason, the default controls for basic actions like aiming and shooting are different, despite the fact that it runs in the same engine as RE1. It's very jarring to go from one game to another that's extremely similar and have to learn a new control scheme. Fortunately, that's not a big problem on Steam because you can just remap the controls, but if I'd gotten this game on a console, I'd be pissed.

Otherwise, this is a good game that's mostly undeserving of the hate it gets. People claiming it's the worst Resident Evil are absolutely full of ♥♥♥♥.

You are introduced to key characters and monsters, but not in a way that prematurely steals lore from the later games in the series. A lot of unique content was put into this prequel too, which really lets it stand up on it's own. RE0HD works as an great introduction to the Biohazard Universe as well as an important juxtaposition in visual quality to the likes of the RE1HD Remaster, and most certainly to the RE2 Remake. [b]A PC port of a remaster of the prequel to the entire Resident Evil series.[/b]

Playing with a keyboard or a controller is entirely up to preference as they're both very much playable with this game. Keyboard and mouse controls are rebindable but you can only change controller buttons through pre-set control schemes like Type A, Type B, etc.
If you've played REmake, this pretty much plays the same minus the change in controls.

The whole plot of the game feels like an afterthought, especially the new protagonist, Billy Coen, whom you never even see again outside of this game's story. The only other and very first mention of his name in a mainline RE game was on the N64 version of RE2, which even then was just random lore at the time.
The story to the whole thing starts off kind of like the first game; a special forces team is sent to investigate bizarre murders that occurred and then everyone gets attacked by zombies & monsters at some point. You first take control of Rebecca Chambers, then shortly after, Billy Cohen joins you and you'll have control of both, each with their own advantages and disadvantages for gameplay.

The gameplay is your usual classic RE deal, tank controls (if you choose to use tank controls), cinematic camera angles, and inventory management. The formula's all there for a classic RE game, but it's made use pretty poorly overall.
The tank controls are still bothersome when you absolutely need to move fast, but that's nothing new. "Alternate" controls allows you to move around like a more traditional character action game like Devil May Cry, but the changing camera angles is extremely annoying with it as you're forced to reorient your analog stick or change the key you're using to keep moving in the direction you were trying to go; it was the same deal in REmake.
In place of a magical storage system, you can now leave items on the ground almost anywhere in the game and you can come back to pick it up later no matter how far you've progressed. It's a very interesting idea, but in this game, it just encourages an insane amount of backtracking, especially after the first half of the game. The game eventually opens a shortcut to the beginning of the game, but that's still a long path.

The first parts of the game start off pretty strong and the backtracking isn't too bad since the first map is more confined. The later maps though just stretch out for way too long.
This game's the weakest of the mainline classic RE games and it's strongly recommended to play any other classic-style RE game first before this one if you really want to check this out.

Kind of going down the list with these ones at the moment, having recently just completed the HD Remaster of the first game, have to say this was generally an interesting prequel with some unique changes to the first but with the same charm all in all.

It had its moments where the partner system felt clumsy and frustrating but after a while it was easier to manage and just great to have two inventories for less hassle. They removed magic item boxes so managing items you wanted to carry or leave behind meant literally dropping stuff on the floor in save rooms, can't say I mind either inventory management type though, a box keeps things tidy and in one place but at the same time been able to drop things wherever you want can potentially make life easier for you in terms of puzzles and progression. I don't feel the need to run through 5 door opening sequences just to stash an item when i can leave it in the most convenient spot possible. Maybe it was a good thing that they changed it, if not for those that asked for it, then at the very least for a new feature to replace another.

Other than the standard zombies that shamble along at varying speeds and the zombie dogs that made only a very brief appearance in the beginning sequence of the game, Zero introduces a handful of new enemies from zombie monkeys, to giant roaches and beyond. Have to admit, I found some of them extremely annoying to deal with and they were usually in unavoidable situations like down very thin hallways and could easily hit both Rebecca and Billy. There are weaknesses they all have but unless you go preemptively looking through guides its a case of trial and error, and then even having the right tools on you at the time to effectively deal with each type of enemy in the first place.

Even on higher difficulties, Zero is fairly generous with ammo and supplies from the get go, only thing I found myself burning through most of the time were healing items until midway through the game but I always have a full clip and at least 50-60 rounds of pistol ammo and 30 rounds of shotgun shells...and those were the weapons I used the most. Grenade Launcher was an as and when situational item so I didn't care about ammo for that, and the Magnum I just dragged and dropped from one save room to the next, leaving it for the last area and final boss before I used it at all.

As before, they implemented the Ink Ribbon and typewriter save style, giving you plenty of ribbons so saving often was never an issue, which is great when its your first time ever running through the game and you don't know what is where and when you might suddenly get jumped by something that takes you completely by surprise and deprives you of either your life or all your healing herbs.

Interesting set of puzzles to solve that require just a little thinking, plenty of areas to explore, goodies to find. Can't say the boss battles were my favourite activities to partake in but I beat them all the same.

Story wise, although it doesn't explain everything very clearly, as a prequel to the original game it gives you a little more insight as to how the mansion incident started. Notes through the game are very vague in telling the origin of the T-Virus and G-Virus so even after beating it you're still like ".....what?". Its the type of game that answered one question and simultaneously creates 5 more in its place. Resident Evil 0, the latest entry of the historical franchise to get the HD remaster treatment offers more of the same survival horror action that fans know and love but also tries to introduce some refreshing new mechanics that spice up the formula, but not without stumbling a bit in the process.

Regarding the port and presentation, RE0 retains all the improvements found in the port of RE1remake, plenty of choice between classic tank controls and modern control scheme, original aspect ratio & widescreen, (both with their pros and cons) plenty of resolutions, smooth 60 fps, and highly detailed and atmospheric backgrounds that seem to have improved a little compared to RE1s somewhat more varying quality. Plus, new effects added to the remaster enhance the mood. Sound is as always excellent. 

Gameplay wise RE0 drops the classic item boxes for a system of gathering and dropping items anywhere on the map adding much more strategy and critical thinking than ever before regarding your inventory management, andthus creating a much more tense feeling of survival horror. However this system also increases the difficulty of the game (perhaps one of the more difficult entries in the franchise) and sometimes turns item management into it's own cumbersome side-quest/chore, forcing alot of backtracking, exchanging recourses as you move along. (Do not worry though there is absolutely no way to lose items permanently anywhere on the map)
- keep in mind that this game too offers various difficulties if you find it daunting -
Another new addition is the partner system - something that future RE games would tamper a bit more with more advanced mechanics in the future. Here you get to switch between (or separate them ) on the spot two characters with different traits and abilities and throughout your game you will need to use this zapping system in order to solve some of the games devious puzzles. It's unfortunate that Rebecca is a little weaker in her defences, making the annoying (but tougher) Billy a more viable option as your main hero - but at least he's not reaching Code Veronica's Steve cringe levels of annoyance.

As for the story, RE0 comes from that peculiar time in Resident Evil history where the games were becoming more stupid, more action packed and adding all kinds of bizzare lore and extremely hokey monsters. In the process, what starts as a game that promises to tell the story of the Bravo Team the night before the mansion incident, evolves into the noncensical and missing the opportunity to actually spend time with the Bravo team itself, besides our main heroine. However, that doesn't mean that it isn't enjoyable (in that classic schlocky RE way) and perhaps it was the better call to make a game that tells something completely new  even if it sometimes becomes convoluted.

As with RE1Remaster, RE0 offers some interesting unlockable modes once you finish the main campaign, the minigame Leech Hunter and the entertaining "Wesker Mode" where you take control of fan favorite dastardly RE villain Wesker and along with an equally evil-looking Rebecca you get to smack soem zombies using your... "RE5-Matrix" powers!

All-in-all, RE0 is a solid entry in the series and the survival horror genre, offering plenty of challenge but also making things a little more frustrating while experimenting with new gameplay concepts. While not the best it is still a fine game on its own. If you're new to the series, I would probably suggest that you start with RE1 instead, experiencing the more celebrated offerings of the RE series (RE1 and 2 especially) and if you like these then get RE0 once you wish to explore the quirckier side of the main series' entries.

This is a pretty good game overall. It looks and plays quite similar to the RE1 remake, with some slight improvements.

They innovated one or two things to the gameplay, letting you solve puzzles with 2 separate playable characters you switch back and forth from and even have a basic way of moving them simultaneously in the same screen and/or swap items. Its neat but you only really do it a few times. Each character has their strengths but you will generally go with the one with statistically better damage when fighting - so the 2nd character feels like a tag-along.

And you're going to need those combat stats because in RE0 they introduce more monsters roaming the halls/mansion. These aren't boss monsters, just annoying super animals that have a ton of health, with attacks that will stun you for a long time, and if you're fighting a few there's a high chance you'll get stuck in an infinite lockstun animation until you die - especially if you have your partner in the same room.

Its almost required to know which guns are effective against these. Pistols ARE NOT. And given where these monsters are in the map, you will have to kill them to solve puzzles. So they're not like new RE games where you can leave them behind and do puzzles in another room.

There's even a funny monster that shows up once near the end (where the save points are far) and since the game trains you to run away if you don't need to kill things, this little slimey dude will one hit kill you for running away. But it also dies quickly if you engage it. It completely defies the logic the game taught you over the many hours of the campaign. That's just a real ♥♥♥♥ move from the designers.

Once you learn the animal weakness it'll mostly be a fun time. You might end up in a very tight spot with very little ammo if you keep going with no knowledge of what guns to save for what monsters, so that'll frustrate you. Expect for that to happen and either reload or survive through it and you'll then know what's what.

So yes, despite the long rant about animal monsters, this game is a classic RE game that's worth playing and replaying. Its one of those games where subsequent playthroughs become relaxing and calming when replaying it instead of scary and unnerving - just like the RE1 remake.

And being able to play these classics in a new remade graphical format and not needing to plug in a old console is the best way to experience it.

I remember playing RE1 when PS2 was out, hated it. Years later, the first time I fully played a RE game was with RE7 launch. Loved it, so, I had to get all the way back again to fully understand what I never dug into as a kid.

Enter RE0. RE0 pretty much explains everything that happened shortly before RE1. RE0 and RE1 remake were both released on the Game Cube and share a very similar artistic and gameplay-wise approach. Fixed camera angles, awkward voice acting (better voice overs tho) stunning visuals, creepy atmosphere galore and a claustrophobic feel that half of the franchise sorely missed after RE4 is what makes RE have that early classic RE feel.

The problem is that it's, quite likely, the most dense of them all with a very odd pacing and some criminally incomprehensible decisions that hurt gameplay. This is the sort of game whose mechanics are scarier than its villains. It's the game that became famous for getting rid of chests, so get ready to spend half of the game backtracking through Christmas presents-filled corridors trying to figure out what was important and what will likely be. Creativity takes a huge hit, forget about AI diversity: you will be fighting zombie animals, over and over and over with very strange hitboxes that may trap you really bad (Hunters, bats and monkeys, mark my words). Some puzzles lack clarity or at least instructions seem to be on holidays. Challenge and imagination are usually well-balanced in RE with non-complex yet engaging puzzles during early RE games, but this time around some objects to solve them are barely used and the game doesn't do much to remind you them and, if so, some puzzles are just dumb trial and error that not even your worst enemy would have thought of.

BUT, all in all, it's the first one (and probably the last so far) that lets you control 2 characters simultaneously: Billy and Rebecca. Sometimes, the game will trigger events for script purposes to rescue your companion through walkie-talkie warnings, well done! Also, It's useful to explore separate rooms to gather different objects together if you are aware of your character's strengths and weaknesses. Also, the game will force you to go solo to make your way to your ally in specific times of the story transferring necessary objects to get back together (this is implemented since very early on and it works). Other than that, plus some team solving-based puzzles, there's not much else to it. A shame that, just when you want to face a boss as a 2 for 1, it's pretty much a 1 VS 1 because Rebecca gets caught by every boss everytime and Billy has to get the Superman cape to rescue the rookie officer that is after him but has no other option but to cooperate with (a big LOL, but you know, human survival instinct). You can tell RE0 had a bigger budget than RE1, a shame it didn't translate to a better story, but it's decent nonetheless. Rendered backgrounds are stunning, a moving picture to say the least, music, effects, etc, all of them show a lot of polish and it's very immersive (because if a RE isn't it, what is?). However, it's mimicing (borderline riping off) those elements that we all loved in RE1, with so much inspiration in it it's hard to give it credit to (the train stage is by far the best, but get ready to stay in Spencer-like mansion and sewer-like sections). Story-wise, well, basically it's S.T.A.R.S' rookie Rebbeca Chambers dealing with the investigation of what was going on behind a strange incident in Arklay Mountains with the convict she's supposed to chase, Billy Cohen after all her team disappeared under very strange conditions. It will remind you of Code Veronica when you see the main villain (Marcus) and some of his powers or how zombies are spawned, adding a supernatural touch to the story (cheesy, but serviceable).

A great game that is hard to recommend for newcomers but worthy nonetheless and a forgotten one. If I seemed to have spent a good chunk of the review ranting make no mistake, it's a beautiful flawed videogame that Capcom developers could have done with their eyes closed and set to cruise control by knowing the RE1 formula that RE0 drinks from. Nonetheless, it incorporates some unique mechanics (some are right, some others are bizarre) here and there that more recent games just don't have anymore.

Try it out and find out the roots of the RE franchise, even if it's hard to get back to or replay twice.

I'm sure others have covered the dumb anime plot that takes itself too seriously, clunky tag team mechanics, and insufferable inventory management. Instead of all that, I'm gonna go over how a simple zombie works, from the perspective of someone who just got done with RE HD Remake.

In classic Resident Evil: A zombie stands in a room, whether alone or in a group, in a calculated position. There's sometimes variance to where he spawns; say, a couple fixed positions he can get instead of just one. After going through the room a number of times, you have a sense of how far he is from each wall, and the exact line you can run through. You can walk up to him to bait him into lunging, then run around. The room is a clockwork challenge, and by replaying it you instinctively design your own solution to it - basically your own (less skilled) version of a speedrun route, based on your resources and such. If you like the RE games on easy instead, and you just shoot through, you know how far you have to stand, how many shots it'll take, how to try for a critical headshot.

In this game: A zombie stands in the only place he could be, which is also the only place to walk through, because the room is a corridor about as wide as a zombie. He spawned there because you were forced to kill the previous zombie that was standing there to pass, and we can't have you getting through a room without shooting, now can we? Even if you cleared it before. Resident Evil 0 is the prequel of Resident Evil 1, revealing the establishment of Umbrella, the hidden truth behind T-virus leaking in the mansion, and a little story background of Resident Evil 2. In my opinion, Resident Evil 0 Remaster surpasses its predecessor Resident Evil 1 in many aspects since it has a more advanced design than Resident Evil 1.

The greatest feature of Resident Evil 0 is you play as two characters: Rebecca Chambers, a rookie STARS with a baby face and starry eyes, whose teammates were mostly killed in the Racoon City incident; Billy Coen, a runaway ex-military tough guy being accused of murder. You have to switch control between them from time to time because you need to use their unique abilities and gears on different occasions. There are some levels that two characters get separated, requiring you to work out problems on each side or make them cooperate. This mechanic is very creative at the time. Even today you can hardly see games with a similar mechanic. However, this doesn't work out very well. As you have to frequently exchange items between the two, this mechanic brings quite some inconvenience. Also in some circumstances, you have no idea which character should be used because in some cases one character can get through the level fairly easily with his/her ability, while for another it is very tough. If you choose the wrong one, you might have to spend extra time fetching items or fighting bosses.

The pro and con list is mainly from comparing with remastered Resident Evil 1. 

+ Movement is less stiff.
+ The game runs smoothly at higher frame rates.
+ Resident Evil 0 was remastered more completely than RE1. The graphics are much better than Resident Evil 1 Remaster which I had to use a texture patch from the community to improve the graphics.
+ Map design is way more friendly and enjoyable. Resident Evil 1 is very confusing especially in the mansion session, not only because the map design is way too complicated, but it also has no hints telling you what is next. It is quite hard for players to navigate and build up a sense of direction from the fixed camera which is placed at different angles in different scenes. On the contrary, the map of Resident Evil 0 is more linear which fits well with the fixed camera and also reduced lots of backtrackings. Items you gather or places you travel often strongly indicate what is next thing should be on your agenda. It brings much more clarity to the game and reduces lots of frustration from cluelessness and getting lost. 

- It has item slots but no item box, which is a pretty lame design choice. If your inventory is full, you have to throw items on the ground and travel back to retrieve the items when it is needed. Or, you have to go back and forth a few times to fetch items to a new place. 
- No autosave. I really hate it because it is a pretty challenging game. If you die without saving, you have to redo tons of progress again,
- Fixed camera still sucks, even it does not suck as much as Resident Evil 1. It is difficult to dodge zombie attacks under camera because it has a bunch of blind spots and makes estimating distance pretty hard. 
- Occasionally, the frame rate significantly drops, which is not acceptable for a game with pre-rendered backgrounds. 
- It can be very unresponsive because the interactive zone is very imprecise. So occasionally you see that the character standing in front of an item, but you just can’t interact with it. You have to move back and forth many times to find the right position. It is annoying.

Some little advice from me. 

Do easy difficulty for the first time. Normal difficulty is hard enough to put you in the loop of replaying the same session again and again. 

Try to dodge as many zombies as you can, and only stop to shoot when necessary, you will otherwise run out of ammo very fast if try to kill all zombies. Resources are very rare even at normal difficulty. Making the characters move solo is a very good strategy because it is much easier to dodge. The way to dodge is to suddenly move backward before a zombie grabs you.

You should play Resident Evil 1 before 0 if you decide to play all, or you may give up playing Resident Evil 1 for it is way more demanding and can bring a much worse experience.  I do think hardcore fans can try whichever they want, and less hardcore fans should just do Resident Evil 0 and skip Resident Evil 1, while ordinary players should just skip these two fixed camera Resident Evil games.

Resident Evil 0 is one of the best games in the series. There, I said it!
RE0 is a prequel to the original Resident Evil, taking place the night before the first RE, and explains some of the events leading up to it. If you've never played Resident Evil 1, and care about the story, this is not where you want to start though, as RE0 spoils some things in RE1. It's better to play these games in release order than in chronological order.

[B]Graphics & Sound [/B]
Resident Evil 0 HD looks great. The game uses high quality pre-rendered backgrounds, and despite having originally been made for a game released in 2002, and only having been lightly touched up for this game, the backgrounds still look amazing. Of course, with pre-rendered backgrounds, the developers are "cheating" a bit, they're basically just a lightly animated image, the game does not have to do any of the hard work in real time. The only 3D models that the game has to work with are the characters, enemies & items.
The sound is also quite good. Most of the weapons have enough weight behind them for them to feel satisfying to use, without sounding as overly powerful as weapons tend to do in games that are more focused on a power fantasy. The groans, and the wet shuffling sound of the zombies sound creepy in a fittingly b-movie way. And the panic-inducing music that plays when you run into a leech zombie (you'll see what you play the game) is fitting and makes you want to get out as soon as possible!

[B]Story & Setting[/B]
The game starts with you, playing as Rebecca Chambers, trying to figure out what's going on with some strange killings in the region. You find a prison transport, with the guards dead, and the prisoner, one Billy Coen, being gone. So now your hunt for the escaped prisoner starts. Of course it's not Billy who's the real danger here, there are far more sinister forces at play, as something is turning the dead into zombies. So now you, and Billy, need to survive.
The story is nothing ground breaking. The early Resident Evil games were very b-horror movie inspired, and RE0 is no exception. You've got zombies, giant insects, and worse things, all trying to kill you. And there's of course an evil villain behind all of this (the game does not hide the fact). But it's a story that's very aware of what it's trying to be, and while it won't win any prizes for great storytelling, it's entertaining, and it does help give you some context for what you're doing. The way the main villain is introduced is a little bit too silly though, and he does not feel very threatening. 

[B]Gameplay[/B]
RE0 is a classic survival-horror game, in the vein of the original Alone in the Dark. This means that you've got fixed camera angles, puzzles to solve, and limited resources. Some hate this, other love it, and personally, I think it works quite well. The camera angles do make turning a corner, or entering a new room a more tense experience than it would have been if you would be able to see everything ahead of you, but it also results in some artificial difficulty, as enemies can ambush you. Most of the time the game is made with this in mind though, and there are only a small handful of spots where the game feels a bit cheap. 
Where RE0 shines, and the reason why I like it more than most other RE games, is in the puzzle department. The old-school survival horror games did borrow some elements from point & click adventure games, and RE0 does this in a good way. There's no moonlogic here, but there are cases where you need to use items to open up new paths, or where you need to solve simple logic puzzles. None of the puzzles are hard, but they do feel surprisingly satisfying. 
Combat is not the games strongest point, although it's not awful. When you enter combat mode (by holding down a button) your character automatically aims in the direction of the closest enemy, and then you just hit the attack button. The trick here is to know when to leave this stance, so you can dodge enemy attacks, and also to know which enemies you should avoid altogether. As resources are limited, you're not meant to kill all the zombies, just the ones that are hard to avoid. Bullets are more plentiful than healing items, so the game encourages you to be better safe than sorry. 
If there's one place where the combat does not work though, it's the bosses. All the bosses apart from one are laughably easy, and the last one just feels cheap. I had a look at some video walkthroughs to see if I was missing something obvious, but most seem to just tank some hits, unless they use a quick-kill method (which seem to be more of an unintended side-effect than something the devs intended). The bosses in this game are simply bad. 

[B]Closing thoughts[/B]
I really like RE0. It's an engaging, slightly creepy, and quite entertaining survival horror game. It lacks some quality of life things, like an item stash, but you've got 12 inventory slots, between the two characters, and a central room that makes for an excellent item dump through most of the game, so I never found the lack of an item chest to actually be a problem. The game also gets a bit too generous with resources in the late game, almost showering you with ammo & healing items, which removes a lot of the tension, but up until that point, I think RE0 is great. It's a lot more forgiving than it might first seem, but this I suspect is by design, the developers wanted the game to feel tense, not frustrating, and thus give the impression of things being more dangerous,  and supplies being more limited, than they really are. So I would highly recommend this game. Just don't expect to be scared, because it's not a scary game, and play RE 1 first if you care about the story.

The gameplay idea of two simultaneous protagonists could have been really interesting but they didn't do enough with it. They could have done a lot more when remastering it. The worst part of the game is probably the inventory management because rather than having item boxes like most of the other games in the series, you just have to leave items on the ground and backtrack whenever you need something you left behind. This is very tedious, especially if you're as obsessive about it as I am. All that said, I still really enjoyed my time here, and I'm terrible at it. A game very intentionally in the style of Resident Evil 1-3 and very similar to REmake HD in general. Tank controls, fixed camera angles, zombies, puzzles, and inventory management. The main difference is the inclusion of two simultaneous protagonists.

The train section is a smart introduction to the classic Resident Evil game-play loop on a smaller scale, allowing players to get used to not only the exploring a slowly expanding setting search for keys and solving puzzles, but also the co-operative synergy between Rebecca and Billy. Everything after that is pretty familiar, including Umbrella's apparent obsession with building secret research facilities under creepy mansions. It's a different one this time.

The main game-play conceit that sets this game apart is the presence of two separate characters. They don't have their own parallel stories. You control both of them. Rebecca has less HP and the ability to mix herbs, She is also smol and thus can fit in small spaces. Billy has more health and masculine upper body strength that allows him push heavy objects around. Unsurprisingly, they become separated at various points. Sometimes you can choose who goes where. Many puzzles require both of them.

On top of this, and seemingly the most unpopular feature, they've changed how the inventory system works, in a few ways. You have twice as much inventory space (kind of), but can only transfer items between characters if they are standing next to each other. Some items (like shotguns, grenade launchers, etc) take up two slots now. There is no storage box, but this is offset by the ability to drop items from your inventory to the ground at will. If you're smart, this can be very efficient, but not having the right items near you when you need them can result in some unfortunate backtracking.

The visuals are a step up from Resident Evil HD, in my estimation. In particular, the backgrounds have a lot more life to them, with many moving elements. Few rooms have the feeling of a static image and it all seems to be higher quality, lacking the occasional obvious compression artifacts encountered at various points in RE1 HD.

The story as delivered by the cut-scenes is awful, but entertainingly so. I don't play these games for the plot anyway. As with REmake, the lore in the form of journals and notes seems to be much better than the cut-scenes.

Overall, I think it's a solid RE game in the classic style, which I now realize I like. Recommended, but probably best played after RE1.

A great, but unfortunatelly underrated RE game. RE0 is amazing for anyone who's looking for a challenging Survival Horror experience, but mainly for it's Partner Zapping feature, it may not be a friendly game for newcomers as it's tricky and takes some time to get used to it. 

RE0 does a great job at changing some things while still staying true to the classic RE formula: There's no magic item boxes here so you have to be careful and plan where you drop things because whenever you want those things back you have to come back to the very room you left them. And the partner zapping is an interesting twist as well, because unlike the other classic RE games, you control one character while the AI handles the other, and you can switch between them on the fly, taking into account each character's strenghts and weaknesses to decide which will be better for the task you need to accomplish. And if you want to succeed, you oftenly have to keep an eye on your AI partner behavior and which weapon she/he has equipped to prevent them from wasting powerful ammo on weak enemies or making other dumb mistakes. 

Those new features can make things more interesting but also more complicated to deal with, hence why not everyone likes them, but I did welcome those additions because they changed things up a bit without screwing up the core gameplay, so I think it's fine.

Map and puzzle design is pretty great too, and the HD remaster did an amazing job on updating the graphics (better than the RE1 Remake HD). The game has some odd pace issues and a few pretty frustrating moments like the giant bat fight, plus it feels like a pretty shoehorned prequel to be honest. But it's overall a pretty solid game. Hardly one of the best RE games but definitely great and worth playing.

I love the RE series, but this game is absolute trash. CAPCOM certainly tried to innovate with this installment, but for all the good ideas and intentions they had almost everything backfired. Some things came close to working but failed to pull it off, other things completely ruined already frustrating mechanics.

Inventory system:
They completely removed item boxes from the game. This is one of the biggest mistakes they made with this installment. You control two characters so sure you can argue that you have 12 inventory spaces, but 2-handed weapons take two slots each plus ammo is 3. If you carry a pistol, shotgun, and ammo that's 5/6 of your slots used up. In REmake you at least have the item boxes, but in RE: 0 you just have to DROP YOUR ITEMS ON THE GROUND. This is horrible and causes excessive back tracking. Back tracking is a core component of RE games, however in RE:0 the back tracking and inventory management went from a gameplay feature to a chore which drained a lot of the fun out of it.

Controlling two characters:
Tbh this isn't too terrible. The AI is very basic, but for the most part it manages to keep your partner out of the way. CAPCOM had a couple sections where the two are split up and you switch back and forth to solve the puzzles that was fun, but there were serious drawbacks as well. Often times you are forced into a situation where you must play as one character by themselves and if you didn't have them fully equipped ahead of time you're just screwed. The only way to successfully navigate portions of this game is to have these sequences sprung upon you, die, and then move items around when you respawn. This isn't challenging, it's requiring the user to know exactly what is coming in order to make it through the section. This just punishes first time players.

Story:
The story is pretty light, but it's not terrible. There's a little bit of background given to REmake that is fun for someone like me who is wanting to do a full run-through of the series. 

Final Verdict:
The game is a series of chores in an RE skin. If you must play through the game you might as well just play on EASY so you can cruise through this excruciating experience with as little pain as possible.

On the positive side, the atmosphere and the permanent tension are present (although if you have played RE 1 you won't be surprised too often). The first half of the game ticks every box of a good classical RE, in particular with an excellent level design.

Now on the negative side:
-the absence of storage chest is baffling. As other reviews pointed it, you lose a good amount of time transferring your extra stuff from one end of the map to another. Except to annoy players, I don't see the point.
-the last map has quite an average, linear and predictable level design.
-last but not least, the scenario is ridiculously basic, predictable, and doesn't bring any interesting element to the story of Resident Evil. This is a shame considering that the game starts with an introduction saying "now we will explain what happened before". The characters are caricatural.

Resident Evil 0 is great to play for the same reasons the first episode was, but from a few aspects it lacked the inspiration that made the first episode a legendary game.

[b]Resident Evil 0[/b] is a survival horror game. The story is simple, virus released, people are zombies, kill everyone and save yourself. Hovewer there is a certain unusual aspect, there are two main characters in this game: Rebecca Chambers an agent from S.T.A.R.S. and Billy Coel escaped convict. They both have to live through the nightmare and defeat mysterious villain and his army of zombies. 

So, in this game you control two characters. Each one has unique ability, which you can use to solve puzzles and progress through the game. It's an interesting concept, which is often used in coop-games, sadly, this game doesn't feature this mode. In this game you control only one of the characters and the second one follows you everywhere. You can also choose one of two tactics(idle - just follow me, attack - follow me and shoot everything). Those work great and sometimes it is wise to let your partner handle the shooting. But when you're low on ammo, it's hard to run through the corridor with your partner and avoid enemies. You have to leave your partner behind and then switch to him and make another run through the corridor. 

To make things even more repetitive your inventory is very limited, you constantly being pressed to leave something behind and then you have to comback for it later. Backtracking quickly becomes a chore. The game also features puzzles like in point'n'click adventure. You have to find something and then use in another room. Sometimes puzzles are a little bit more elaborate and require you to think a little. Also the items that are needed for puzzles take up your inventory space, so you constantly have to think about your inventory. To save in this game, you have to use a typewriter, which requires special ink, which takes space... At times this inventory system feels frustrating, at other times it feels like it's a very unique feature that brings everything together.

Now moving on what I liked about this game, it's an atmosphere, you always feel uneasy in this game. I don't know what's the reason, the strangely placed camera or soundtrack, but there's always a feeling like something evil lurks around in the corner of your eye. And when you finally find a room with typewriter you feel this warm feeling of relief.

I consider myself quite a big fan of Resident Evil, with that I mean, I'm one of the guys who came from Resident Evil 4 and started loving the series after that.

So I decided, after watching a bunch of Resident Evil videos and getting my RE:HYPE up and going again-
That I would start a Resident Evil Chronology playthrough.
Since Resident Evil: Zero is the very first in the timeline, I obviously bought the game and started my playthrough while getting used to fixed perspective and no third person.

Needless to say, this was a lot of fun, like, great fun. The older RE games are seriously masters at making environments.
Sound design, monsters, and locations of loot and enemy spawns after certain actions.
Talking about loot, I see a lot of people complain about how lackluster it is in this game, in my experience, I did not have a problem really, of course I used a lot of healing items, and that seriously messed me up later on in the game (That meant a lot of juking and a lot of skipping fights to get to the next safe room for MAYBE some health items, it's intense fun, trust me)

Graphically? It looks amazing, backgrounds are rendered at 1440p I'm pretty sure, regardless of what setting you choose I have heard, and it shows, it looks amazing!

At starters, I'd like to focus on stuff that's new compared to original:

Because not everybody need to be a hardcore player to enjoy a game. 

And moving on how good this part of Resident Evil franchise is... 
If you ask me, I feel like this game is a great fit to the classic Resident Evil trilogy (1-2-3). Zero have some great locations, like train - it have so great atmosphere of horror, you actually wish there were more if it. It's easily in my "Top 5" of my favorite locations in whole RE franchise. I also like the enemies in this one. There are your usual zombies, hunters, doggies, but also annoying monkeys and Leech Zombies - those guys are really tough cookies. Ever played Resident Evil Remake? Those guys are similar to Crimson Heads. Annoying, and very hard to kill. Also, the choice of bosses is nice: large centipede, scorpion, Tyrant. There are more, but I don't want to spoil everything ;) Of course, we also get a great set of weapons to kill our lovely monsters: hunting gun, molotov cocktails, sub machinegun, and some more similar to those in other Resident Evil games. It's fun to use everything, and kill everything. Well, why wouldn't it be?

There is one thing that is a huge turn-on, and also a turn-off, in this game: difficulty level. The original version (Gamecube) had only two difficulty levels: normal and hard. HD Remaster have one more, and it's easy. Why it could be a good or bad thing? Because, if you ask me, Resident Evil 0 is one of hardest Resident Evil games, and I really mean it. The puzzles in this game are hard to solve, and if you are planning to play without any guides and walkthroughs - you gonna have a (fun) hard time. Unlike in other RE games, this time we have to control 2 characters - Billy and Rebecca. The one is controlled by player, the other by AI, but we can switch to other one whenever we feel like. Also, there are no Item Boxes in this part. Yup, we either lug everything we need, or we do some crazy juggles - taking everything and move from one location, to another, and we do that everytime we move to next place. It's kinda fun, something like another puzzle, but once you forget a big weapon or item needed to make any progress yeah, it can be also annoying. Also, the new enemies spawn sometimes, so moving back means also losing valuable ammo. It's not really so demanding on easy mode, but when you are trying to beat the game on higher difficulty level, without using herbs or saving game (because of achievements), you really need to plan everything out well. For me, that was actually quite fun, but many people won't find it the same, since you need to run around few, or more, times because you can't take or store everything they need.

I'm not sure also why, but I really feel like this part of RE franchise isn't really popular among fans, and players overall. Because it was originally released only on one console, Gamecube? Because it's much less memorable than other RE games? Maybe Bill and Rebecca are more bland than other Resident Evil main characters? I don't know and I won't tell you - I'm just a Resident Evil fanboy ;) If you ever liked any of old Resident Evil games, if you enjoy a survival horror genre which doesn't rely (much) on cheap jumpscares, if you feel like having a good time killing zombies - yup, Resident Evil 0 is a good choice. I had a great time with this game and I'm sure I will replay it many more times in the future.

Resident Evil Zero is a spinoff that tries to be a nice prequel to the first game, promising to explain all important events that led to the Mansion Incident and shed light onto Umbrella backstory some more. It's also a game where you actually get to control two characters at once and you get to drop items instead of keeping them in magic chests. It was originally developed for N64, with developers planning to make use all the cartridge advantages of instant loading. But since N64 was near it's death, they waited and developed it from scratch for Gamecube. It shares same graphical awesomeness as REmake, but it lacks polish of it, despite coming out a bit later. It was being developed by other people after all. Yea, a fixed camera survival horror, possibly the last one before RE4 took over completely.

Technically, they still optimized it horribly for low-end machine. The game still has a forced internal resolution that is bloody high. There is no fan-patch to fix it this time around. Instead I had to learn the glory that is HiAlgo SWITCH software that let me cut every resolution to half. I mean, it was ugly but it worked.

As for settings, well, it's a bit harder to decide. First, widescreen still cuts off the top and bottom lines of backgrounds with camera panning not being present as much. It's quite painful for you can drop items in such way that you will not be able to see them on any camera of a room. Good thing that dropped items are marked on the map so you can still find them instead of forgetting that they existed in the first place. So maybe go with 4:3 aspect this time around. I also couldn't find a control type for gamepad that was similar to old RE controls. As for picking between Alternate and Original type: former allows you move like in 3D action (you push left, you go left on a camera) but is a horrible pick as this is a game that changes camera a lot, not designed for it; latter is just tank control. If you got a gamepad, go with Alternate, as you can still use D-Pad for tank controls and the right analog stick for 3D-action-like movement control of AI partner.


Now, about the game itself. Plot. Oh boy. Who came up with it? Apparently, when it came to make Gamecube version of a game, the writer has already forgot what he wrote for N64 version. And it sure seems like he didn't do a good job. Because the plot in this game is horrible. Well, okay, if you shut off your brain and just enjoy whatever is coming without thinking then maybe it's nice. It starts well, you control the Rebecca from Bravo Team. Sadly, instead of story exploring what happens with Bravo Team, letting you to get familar with their tragedy, she jumps into nearby train and goes choo choo away into weirdass adventure. 
And boy, first, for a prequel it sure has a weird power creep, with a singing opera villian out of Final Fantasy. Second, it fits badly with how Rebecca acts in REmake, even tho REmake changed her personality to be more mature as they knew that Zero was in development. And the third, the game makes no sense even by itself as it screws over geropgraphy. As in, how locations connect with each other. Why is there a RE2 factory look-alike that game doesn't allow us to explore with "there is no need to", how come we meet Bravo Team member so far away randomly after travelling on a bloody train, how we end up being so close to original mansion after all this? And that's ignoring the vertical lift that connects every location that we can abstract away as videogame logic, alike magic chests from previous games, for sake of allowing you to backtrack to pick all items. Clearly, the space had no meaning for the writer. Also, it doesn't explain much of Umbrella backstory, not enough.

Oh, and intro makes a deadly sin of making Resident Evil Survivor canon. Unforgivable.

Also, locations after the amazing train aren't interesting.

Then there is a gameplay. Fixed camera, limited recources. Survival horror that isn't scary. Usual old RE so far. The game is much more stiny with recources on Normal than every other RE, I feel, albeit maybe it's because I awkwardly wasted health items on the train. No, I don't recommend casual player to stick with easy as that mode is too extremely easy, you will be flooded in supplies I heard. Don't try to do Hard on the first walkthrough, that's for sure. Another interest addition that veterans will notice is that the game actually remembers how much you damaged enemies before you left the room. Still resets their positions when you re-enter the room.

So, there are the big two spins on the formula: AI partner and item management. For item management, I can tell you one thing. You can finally drop items. Finally! Because back in older games if you accidently grabbed too much items, you would have to move your butt all the way to magic chest in order to unload. Sounds great? Well, they removed magic chest. Suddenly, everything falls apart. Now you will turn front halls of any location into pirate hideout, a some sort of replacement of magic chest. Pretty similar but this time around anytime you move to a new location, you will be doing a little caravan adventure of moving everything over. Okay, managable, fine. But that's not all. Each of the two characters has only 6 slots. Sure that makes 12 slots in total, but first: a lot of mid-tier weapons require two slots nows. Even one annoying puzzle item that you keep from the beginning only to use suddenly in a location in a middle of a game takes two slots. And then if you plan to actually make use of two characters you kinda want to have them both equipped properly. Especially in a case that game decides to forcefully separate the two characters. What are you going to do now if you are stuck with a mule that has no good weapons? Yea, that's right.

And AI characters. You can either use another character to help you fight or you can use them as a mule. The latter is not preferable on the first walkthrough for the reason explained. Plus, if you don't make use of the partner, then I think it underuses game's main feature, you know. But they aren't that good at fighting alongside. Well, they are OK at shooting, even if they don't shoot as fast as you would have liked. It's kinda weird to have AI that can shoot at enemies in a game with limited recources, that I can say. You can set them to Idle instead of Attack tho. A nice idea, however if you get grabbed by enemy (like, say, instakill frog) then you will not be able to open your status menu in order to set partner to Attack mode and you are screwed. And don't know, I just don't feel that AI partner contributes much to the game. Just that there aren't that many tactical situations to make use of two characters in combat, mostly it's just two shooting right at the entrance until enemy dies.

Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen have different stats. Sounds good, as it's supposed to make you decide at who should go first or such but not in this case. Only, Rebecca can mix herbs, yet she is so weak in health. So that means that you will always control Billy while hangs back as mostly a mule. Lame.

Really, if not forced separations of characters and puzzles that involve the two of them then it wouldn't be interesting much at all. And then I felt that game was mostly wasting a lot of my time with that stupid item management forcing even more backtracking than previous games.

Atmosphere of most locations is great and graphics kickass. Great animated background. I also really like how Rebecca is animated like a rookie when it comes to handling the guns unlike Billy.
Extra modes aren't that fun.

Overall, not sure. I still can't say that it's a bad game. Base gameplay still holds up, I still kinda like having a partner. But objectively, it's a badly designed one. So, I guess I shall just call it the weakest game from the "not bad" RE games. Even beating Code Veronica. Or maybe I just didn't play enough survival horrors so I like whatever I get.
It's a good game, although some of the achievements were a little tedious. It's not my most favorite Resident Evil game, but it's definitely not my least favorite.

Resident Evil 0 easily throws you back into the 90s and delivers an excellent survival horror experience. This HD remaster ist the best version you can get: 

Visuals:

The enviroment looks great and the player models aged well compared to the Nintendo Gamecube version. In general, it look way better than the HD remaster of the original Resident Evil simply due to the fact that there is no difference in background quality. 
While in Resident Evil players could see that some enviroments seem to have been rendered on a lower resolution, at least it looks that way, Zero is consistent. 
Furthermore, Resident Evil 0 uses a lot more motions in the background. Running water, flickering lights, rain and other different light sources do a really good job in bringing the enviroment to life.

However, like in the HD Remaster of Resident Evil, the cgi cutscenes look really bad - like 480p bad.

Sound:

Great and fitting soundtrack as well as audio effects. 
RE 0 supports surround sound (it says "home theater" in the options menu) 
but I didn't really feel it. Maybe I should've pumped up the volume more 
but I got neighbours so that's that.

The dialogues are terrible though and often pretty stupid. I know the the original Resident Evil form 1996 didn't take
itself seriously (the story was basically built around the gameplay - a means to an end) but I expected a lot more from the writers. 
Some actions during cutscenes just simply do not make any sense at all. But OK, we're here for something else. Still, sometimes the interactions between characters was so incredible stupid that it threw me out of the game.

Gameplay/ controls:

Controls have been optimized so that the player is not forced 
to use the original control scheme - which also makes the game a lot easier when it comes to dodging enemies and, in the long run, saves you a lot of time! In general, Resident Evil 0 is anything but clunky. It wasn't on the NGC and it is not on the PC or PS4.

Now to the big difference between Zero and most of the other Resident Evil games: there are no chests and you have 2 characters to play!

On the one hand, the ability to play 2 characters at once or switch in between them opens up room for complex puzzles
and different strategies when it comes to boss battles - or at least one of them. On the other hand, since the players is navigating through tight corridors, it doesn't really make much of a difference. To a certain degree, your 2nd character, if not split up, acts as a mobile chest. And this is the biggest problem Resident Evil 0 has - it basically punishes you for playing well. 
If you save up a lot of ammo for different weapons, it'll get really hard to use all of it or your complete arsenal since every character only has six inventory slots. Some weapons take 2 slots. Really annoying if you want to play around a bit and you are forced to backtrack every 10 minutes. To be clear, you are not forced to waste your ammo, you can put everything on the ground but no matter how big the room is, there is always a limit to the amount of items you can drop on the ground - for some reason. I've found myself basically transforming the first main hall into a pirate's hideout.

Chests would've helped a lot! There are also a couple of puzzles, which shouldn't be a puzzle at all. At some point in the game you have the generic "wooden box - water" puzzle. In every other instance, one character could've easily given the other character a boost up but because reasons it is a puzzle - a very simple one as well.

In addition, after completing the game, you get a small minigame which offers you severals rewards for your next playthrough (depending on how well you did) and a couple of more things, mosty cosmetics.

Overall I can recommend this game without any doubts. It is one of the best horror games out there and one of the few which does not hold your hand during your playthrough with constant autosaves or a waypoint. For 20 bucks, this is a must have.

I didn’t play the original game, nor was I a huge Resident Evil fan, but this game is something else. It’s combined with horror, survival and puzzle elements that I have not experienced in any other games, it’s very unique in its own way and it’s left me with a memorable experience. 

However, please do keep in mind that this is a remaster of a 2002 game( meaning that all they upgraded was the visual perspective of the game, nothing was changed in terms of the gameplay) and it can be very frustrating sometimes. 

Here are several nitpicky things that bothered me the most, if you are okay with the following issues, then you’ll definitely enjoy the game.

-First of all, there is no HUD and there is not guide or hint to help you solve the puzzles. Most of the time you will find yourself clueless and running around the rooms spamming F key on everything. I lost thousands of hair during this process.

-Speaking of moving across different rooms… Gosh I hope they could remove this obnoxious loading screen of opening a freaking door! What on earth is the point of this when you can hit V and switch between characters in different rooms without any delays? Remastered games should rid of these excessive and annoying features that were once necessary due to the technical challenges at the time, but it should not be persevered as a trademark for the game when these technical challenges have been overcome. 

-Inventory management. I’m in between on this one, I understand it’s a survival horror game and there must be limitations on the amount of resources you are allowed to carry, but sometimes you really get screwed for not having something with you that you have just left behind.

-Save points. Probably one of the most punishing games in terms of saving. You get these ink cartridges and you have to use them on typewriters that are scattered only in a few rooms of your current stage. My recommendation is when you see a typewriter, save it, when you played over for 15 mins, go back to that type writer and save it. DO NOT carry ink cartridges with you, just drop them next to the typewriter after saving and pick them up when you want to save, this way you save one extra slot for other things. I can’t count how many times I rage quitted for not saving my progress and dies because I thought I have enough health and resources to advance to the next typewriter location. But then a leech man or an unexpected boss shows up and corner-slaps me to death. Too many uncertainties, you can never be too careful.

But those were just my honest opinions about this game, if those things don’t bother you or maybe you like to be punished by this classic game in such ways, then it’s a perfect game for you. Not to mention it is also an excellent game to get into for the resident evil series.

[h1][b][i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i][/b][/h1]

[h1]Recommended purchase point: [b]25% or more off[/b][/h1]

[i]Resident Evil 0[/i] was developed in tandem with RE1's remake and, like that game, released originally in 2002. It details the events that occured 1 day before [i]Resident Evil[/i]'s story picks up, focusing on the S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team's doomed expedition into the Arklay Mountains. Like [i]Resident Evil[/i], RE0 has two protagonists. Unlike [i]Resident Evil[/i], it expects you to play as both of them at once. This rather unique (until much later) approach yielded a fairly mixed bag of results, but ultimately an enjoyable horror experience.

[h1]STORY[/h1]
What we learned in RE1 was that Bravo Team's helicopter had crashed during their attempt to investigate a string of mysterious murders near Raccoon City. What we learn in RE0 is that things got much stranger after that. 

Near the site of the helicopter crash, a luxury passenger train - the Eclipse Express - lies still and quiet. Rookie S.T.A.R.S. member Rebecca Chambers (the initial protagonist) comes across the train while investigating the area around the crash site. 

Unfortunately for her, the train turns out to be infested with strange leeches, undead passengers, and convicted mass murderer Billy Coen (the second protagonist). Even more unfortunately, the train mysteriously begins to move at high speed once again, stranding the unlikely duo aboard the hurtling death trap.

That's the first hour or two of RE0 and, for better and for worse, the story gets even more absurd as time goes on. If you're already inured to [i]Resident Evil[/i]'s rather "interesting" style of writing, you will likely find it more charming than irritating. That said, 0 should [i]not[/i] be played before [i]Resident Evil[/i] as it very casually and frequently spoils a major plot twist from the original game.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
RE0's gameplay remains very similar to that of [i]Resident Evil[/i]. Players navigate environments with fixed camera angles and tank controls (or brand new relative controls in the HD remaster, which make things easier and more fluid). Weapons and ammunition are scarce (as are healing items), and players must choose carefully when to expend them.

There are however some key differences between RE0 and RE1: Firstly, RE0 does NOT feature an item box mechanic like RE1 does. This makes inventory management exponentially more difficult, and can lead to some herculean feats of backtracking as you attempt to locate a red herb or box of ammo you dropped for space minutes or even hours previously. In this regard I consider RE0 to be directly inferior to RE1's handling of the mechanic.

Secondly, Rebecca and Billy share screen time and top billing as RE0's protagonist. Capcom have gone all in on this partnership, allowing the player to directly control both protagonists at the same time (one with each thumbstick) when they are in the same room. However, the player can also swap direct control at will between the two (barring certain story events) and split them up to solve puzzles that require two characters' presence (or just to keep an injured character safe while you clear a zone of enemies as the other).

These changes create a slightly more polarising experience than RE1, to put it politely - although the core gameplay is as good as ever.

[h1]PRESENTATION[/h1]
In this regard RE0 cannot be faulted. Like RE1, the pre-rendered, incredibly detailed environments married with top-class sound design make RE0 a feast for the senses. Wildly rustling trees in the background, pounding rain on the windows of the train carriage, dead stillness within the lavishly decorated passenger compartments: it is a game that is adept at creating terror through silence and implication, and I admire it for that.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
While overall inferior to its sister game [i]Resident Evil[/i], [i]Resident Evil 0[/i] still has a lot to love about it. I recommend it especially to fans of RE1, but also to everyone with an interest in survival horror - because RE0 is still one of the best out there. Just... wait for a sale before you pick it up.

[i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] (known as [i]Biohazard 0 HD Remaster[/i] in Japan) is a graphically improved version of the classic old-school, third-person survival horror game. 

Whether or not I would recommend this game to you depends on where you stand on the 'old school' aspect. You see, [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] contains some old-school gameplay mechanics that wouldn't cut it today: a lot of running back and forth is unavoidable due to very limited inventory space, there is no way to aim accurately when  shooting, and controls are so clumsy it's sometimes hard to position your character correctly to pick up an item that's right in front of him. 

It's too bad the HD Remaster didn't polish these outdated game mechanics a bit. They greatly upgraded the graphics and they added a second control scheme next to the classic 'tank controls', but that's pretty much it.

If you think you can stomach a few old-school user-unfriendly gameplay mechanics, [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] is certainly worth a playthrough. The game features a good variety of settings and enemies to fight, some good level design for its time, a couple of challenging puzzles, two protagonists with palpable personality, the games' and the movies' iconic antagonist Albert Wesker, and a lot of replayability.


[h1]Story[/h1]

In this prequel to the original Resident Evil game, a team of special forces called S.T.A.R.S. are sent to investigate a string of strange murders on the outskirts of Raccoon City. The team splits up, and rookie soldier Rebecca Chambers goes to investigate a train that's littered with dead people. On the train, she meets escaped convict and ex-Navy lieutenant Billy Coen. When the dead people start to rise and attack her, Rebecca reluctantly decides to team up with Billy in order to try and stay alive.


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] offers three difficulty modes, instead of the original two.  The newly added easy mode is strongly recommended for a first playthrough, especially for new players or for people who want a playthrough with as little frustration as possible.

After finishing the game on any difficulty mode, you unlock a special mode called Leech Hunter. In Leech Hunter mode, you can collect rewards that carry over to the main game, but unfortunately, they only carry over to replays of the same difficulty mode. 

As mentioned in my summary at the start of this review, [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] contains some old-school gameplay mechanics that are plain frustrating and player-unfriendly by today's standards. I'll elaborate…

Both your characters have six inventory slots. The two powerful weapons you'll be able to use during the better part of the game each take up 2 slots. A quest item you need to keep handy until beyond the halfway point also takes up two slots. So that would be one inventory full.

You'll want to carry both your characters' pistols to kill the regular enemies, some ammo for that pistol, ammo for the aforementioned stronger weapons, maybe one healing item, ink ribbons (needed to save the game), and you'll regularly need to make space for quest items (keys and the likes).

To make matters worse, you'll regularly have access to only one of both characters for a while. And lastly, there is no magically linked item box near every save point, as was the case in other games of the series.

All this means you'll be playing the 'inventory management minigame' a LOT: you'll want to drop items you think you won't need for a while in a central place, and run back and forth to that place when needed. 

Picking up items or generally interacting with items can sometimes be a pain. You can't rotate the camera and you can't rotate your characters (unless they're aiming their weapon), so you need to twist and turn them until they're finally able to pick up the item.

You'll be shooting at enemies a fair amount of the time. But the game doesn't offer any real aiming mechanic. While pointing your weapon at something, you can shoot straight ahead, up at the ceiling (only useful if the enemy is standing right on your toes, which you want to avoid, really) or down at the floor right in front of you (same). 

When you click the button to 'aim' your weapon, the character will auto-aim at the nearest enemy. So you'll often just click that button and hope the character registers the enemy and actually aim at him correctly. Speaking of which, that button often failed on me by not responding at all. The only solution was to open the character screen for a second and closing it again. Sometimes it meant having to reload the game, if it happened during a tough fight.

All this sounds a tad frustrating, doesn't it? Well, it is. But if you can deal with a measure of frustration resulting from some clunky game mechanics that were considered normal at the time, you can start to enjoy the good sides of [i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i].

The two player characters, Rebecca and Billy, come to life through their dialogue and their interactions with each other and with the mysterious, dangerous surroundings they find themselves in. The various zones they need to struggle through are varied, and level design is often well-thought-out.

By being able to collect rewards (most notably additional weapons and infinite ammo for certain weapons) that carry over to following playthroughs, a lot of replayability is added. Also, next to the Leech Mode I mentioned earlier, you can unlock Wesker Mode. This allows you to play as Albert Wesker, who has two special abilities that make playing as the iconic nemesis feel really satisfying and a completely different experience. However, the story doesn't change and in cutscenes you still see Billy instead of Albert, so the whole thing doesn't make any sense, but hey…


[h1]Graphics and sound[/h1]

With the 'HD Remaster', the game's graphics have been upgraded. And they look beautiful, especially for a game that's basically 15 years old. 

The game's background music is creepy and adds to the spooky atmosphere, as do ambient sounds. The sound effects are spot on and sound very crisp. I suspect this also has to do with the remaster, but I really don't remember much of my time with the game on my Nintendo GameCube all those years ago.

The voice acting of the protagonists is very good. The aura of mystery and creepiness surrounding Albert Wesker is expressed adequately by his voice actor. The remaining voice acting is below par, though, and sometimes outright terrible.


[h1]DLC[/h1]

There are 5 DLC you can buy. All of them contain just a couple of costumes that alter Rebecca and Billy's look. Priced at €12.95 for all 5, I think this is just ridiculous. I know, nobody forces you to buy them, but still…


[h1]On Steam's extra features[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster[/i] has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.

The 47 Steam Achievements are a challenging bunch. In addition to a few achievements you automatically get for playing through the story, there are a number of achievements for optional actions or more difficult ways to play the game, for example for defeating all the bosses with Rebecca rather than Billy, who's noticeably stronger. And then there are about a dozen or so really, really challenging achievements, like playing the entire game without saving once or without using any healing items whatsoever.
