Whenever someone mentions classic Resident Evil games, usually that term refers to the original trilogy on PlayStation in addition to the Remake of the first game. However, very few seem to include Resident Evil 0 under that umbrella (ha?), which is unfair because not only does this game qualify for it but delivers the kind of quality you would expect from the term “Resident Evil Classics”.

Amongst all the classic Resident Evil titles, Resident Evil 0 feels the most unorthodox of them all due to small changes that affect the way the game is approached without necessarily debunking the classic formula. The most noticeable feature being that you are in charge of two separate characters at the same time: one controlled by you, and the other controlled by the partner AI. Normally this would cause worry knowing how incompetent or inefficient partner AIs are generally like in video games, but considering that you’ll be responsible for most of the heavy-lifting and making all the decisions, all the AI has to do is stay in place or follow, and shoot or stay on idle, and if you ever need to get them out of the way from incoming damage you can always manually take control of your partner with the right analog stick. It might seem all that intimidating or cumbersome, but trust me it works just fine.

The second biggest change comes from a feature that was first introduced in Resident Evil Remake. Remember when after beating the game, you’d unlock a sort of hardcore mode where item boxes had separate inventories? Some of that made it into this game. For starters, there are no item boxes at all. Instead, you have to drop items in rooms and leave them there, and then come pick them up again whenever required. This is a big change in the series where dropping items would have them vanish and you had no way of retrieving them (even Resident Evil 7 does this), which makes inventory management all the less awkward. You’ll also need to manage the individual inventories for both of your characters, who have 6 slots each with some of the bigger guns taking up to two slots by themselves. Deciding on how to divide your items between them is vital as you never know when they’ll be separated again, with a bad inventory potentially leaving one of your characters completely vulnerable. Also, if you have a full inventory but need to say mix a red herb you’re carrying with a green herb you just found, instead of dropping another item to pick up the green herb, you can immediately use it and decide on whether you’d like to use it by itself or combine it with something else.

Now that you have two characters, the game is built in a way to accommodate for that. At times, you’ll have to solve puzzles using both characters simultaneously, and in others both of your characters will be split up either to manage different tasks in order to unlock the next room, or due to unfortunate circumstances unfolding. The puzzles themselves are delicious, often requiring applying common sense rather than just finding the key or combination to a lock. The series had conditioned me to always expect either keys or operation manuals for its various puzzles, so seeing it take this approach is thoroughly refreshing. Moreover, the mechanic of certain solutions requiring the player to examine objects, which was only present in the first game and its remake, makes a spectacular return once more.

If that’s not enough, the level design in this game is stellar; almost Spencer Mansion stellar. Despite the fact that you do start off on a train with linear corridors, the way they stuff that train and make use of space to keep the layout interesting is nothing to scoff at. After the train comes the training facility, or as I like to call it, Spencer Mansion 2.0. It contains a central hub area that branches out into different rooms, some of which spiral around to other sides of the location in intricate and unique ways. While the map doesn’t flow as well everywhere, it still flows well enough to maintain a peculiar dynamic. To top all this with the game’s stunning visual direction that still look just as good if not even better than even Resident Evil Remake.

One complaint I have with the level design comes in the game’s final area, where it feels like two long linear stretches of walking that only intersect twice at the beginning and end. It’s here where the system of dropping items in individual rooms bares its negative qualities the most as anything you leave behind might necessitate long walks back and forth to retrieve them. By far the weakest final area in any of the Resident Evil classics. Another complaint comes in the form of the lackluster boss fights. There are no special mechanics that allow you to tackle some bosses obtusely, such as with Plant 42 or Jack Baker. There’s no bosses that will go as far as to hunt you down like Nemesis, Mr. X or the Bakers. They all involve simply walking into a room and shooting a monster till it dies. The last boss in this game implements the worst possible application for having two playable characters.

At the very least weaknesses to different ammunition types are still in the game, and for one particular brand new enemy in Resident Evil 0, are more necessary than usual, which does make encounters a little annoying if you happen to not have the right type of ammunition at the right time. Other than that, item management can get a little tedious at time especially if you're as meticilous as I am and prefer keeping everything in one place (don't do that), and the grappling hook item eventually becomes a grating dullard that can add a lot of extra playtime due to needing to backtrack and pick it up again whenever it suddenly becomes relevant again between a long portion of the game where it isn't.

Overall, I came out of Resident Evil 0 extremely satisfied. Despite the shortcomings especially in the final stretch of the game, it’s a wonderful addition to the survival horror experience and should be celebrated for some of the risky yet needed diversions it took to its design. Hopefully we’ll see Capcom take notes from this game and apply some of these ideas in future projects.

One final advice: [spoiler]Do not drag around fuel canisters and ink ribbons; each location is plentiful of both, and the item slots they would take up are much better suited for other more vital things.[/spoiler]

Rating: 8/10
Genre: Third Person survival horror

The Good:
+ Pre-rendered backgrounds look gorgeous 

+ Solving puzzles, exploring, opening new shortcuts feels very satisfying. 

+ The new gameplay mechanic is that you now have two playable characters, you control one while the other follows. You can split up and from time to time become separated. Many of the puzzle are designed to make good use switching between characters   
+ Combat feels rewarding, headshot a zombie with a shotgun feels great in addition to every other weapon

+ Leech Hunter/Wesker Mode are nice additions which extend replay value 

+ A choice between camera relative and character relative (tank) controls. Though the game was designed around character relative controls, those that never grew up with this game will find greater comfort with camera relative controls. 

+ Hard mode is much more challenging than Resident Evil 1. Hard mode requires strict resource management and a lot of skill. Those looking for a challenge will find it here.  

+ A Mod that removes door opening animations, though some purists will argue against this

The Average:
+/- Voice acting/cutscene are hilariously bad but its also part of the charm

+/- There are no more item boxes, however you can now freely drop items anywhere you want. The map screen also keeps track of where you left any items. The problem however is that this creates a lot of needless backtracking for no reason whatsoever.    

+/- Though the story fills in a lot of gaps and creates more backstory, it is also obvious Capcom had no intentions of having a prequel to Resident Evil 1 as many story elements feel ‘shoehorned’ in. 

+/- Highly recommended that you use a controller

Conclusion:
Though I really liked this game I felt it was lacking a bit compared to Resident Evil 1. Having new gameplay mechanics were nice however it also lessened the horror aspects of the game, this felt more like an action game.

Resident Evil 0 is a classic that's similar to the other old Resident Evil games such as 1, 2, 3. With this game they introduced a two player system which works well in my opinion, however the game has some flaws which aren't game breaking but rather make the playthrough feel a little annoying at times. Similar to my RE1 review I'll break down some aspects.

[list]
[*]The game is an old classic and regardless of the remaster, still plays like it. I recommend a controller for it.
[*]The horror is subtile, the game rarely consists of straight up jumpscares and relies more on its amosphere and the survival horror aspect of the game, which is the management of your items as your inventory is very limited. It doesn't help that in this game they removed the chests where you could stash your items and introduced the ability to drop items. While the idea to be able to drop items is great, removing the chests was a bad idea as you'll be dropping items a lot throughout the map. Scenarios such as "where did I drop this item?" will happen and it was much better to have the chests where you could stash your items globally rather than backtracking to room's you've been in because you had to drop a useful item.
[*]This game many puzzles. A lot. If you want mere horror induced by jumpscares and atmosphere, this game isn't for you. There's a lot to solve, though don't take me wrong. The puzzles aren't exceptionally difficult and you're not doing someone's master's degree, but every now and then you'll have to think about what you do. As opposed to RE1, the puzzles are confusing at times. [spoiler]For example to get into the lab after a boss fight you need some kind of gun that shoots a hook to get up on the roof (I forgot the name of the gun). This gun is far, far behind unless you took it with you for some unknown reason and it's not too obvious that you need it because you've not needed it for hours prior to the boss fight.[/spoiler]
[/list]

That being said, I recommend this game to anyone looking to play a solid classic in the style of Resident evil 1 and that can get through a few minor flaws.

(This review discusses technical aspects of the remaster. The original game is about an 8/10 and a must play for RE fans.)

A good port/remaster for the most part. Capcom re rendered all backgrounds, something I did not expect after the upscale job they did with REmake's backgrounds. Everything looks nice and crisp. 3D models, lights, and effects also got a boost, and the game runs at 60+ fps. Performance is good and no crashes.

My main complaint would be the widescreen mode; with the exception of the actual gameplay sequences, everything is rendered in true widescreen where you see more to the sides. Cutscenes, menus, loading and puzzle screens all show more in widescreen. Gameplay sections were rendered in the original 4:3 aspect, and in widescreen mode they are blown up to fill the screen, then the camera pans while you move the characters, making you see less. Everything feels close and claustrophobic, like playing a FPS with a reduced FOV. Why make the most important part in 4:3 and do a pan and scan when you have the source material available? I can't find a reasonable explanation. You're still getting a huge visual upgrade if you're playing in 4:3 mode, but the remaster had more potential in this area.

Another point would be the controls. The original game had certain actions bound to one key, for example shoot, action and confirm were one button. The remaster splits these up, adding a new layer of frustration. Sometimes you can confirm using space, others you have to use enter or a left click. Rebinding controls is also tricky and required finding a solution online.

No substantial improvement was done to gameplay. A few examples: 
[list]
 [*]Can't skip door sequences (without a mod). 
 [*]You are still required to confirm climbing (some, but not all) ladders. Why? 
 [*]If your inventory is full you can combine herbs without storing them first, but you can't combine ammo to your weapons.
 [*]Even though the remaster uses a much smaller font, it doesn't show more text on screen, requiring you to press a button every 5 words.[/list]

As a port, performance is good and the game is stable. As a remaster the visual upgrade alone warrants a revisit, and you get a few goodies too. This had potential to be a more refined experience, but we have to make do with what we got.

I just finished playing the Resident Evil HD Remaster, so I figured it would be a great time to give the prequel, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster, a go. One game is not objectively better than the other. However, I found myself enjoying 0 better than 1. I think most people have opposite feelings on the matter, but I just liked far more things better here. 

First off, let's talk about the battle between camera and controls. I have no qualms with the "tank controls" or any of that. This version has a nice new control scheme you can use , along with customizable controls, which allow you to go downward when you push down, left when you press left, etc., unlike the Gamecube releases of these games. However, the RE1 HD Remaster also gives you the new directional controls. The big difference between 1 and 0, is that there are less wacky camera angle changes, in my opinion, and almost none where you will get killed or seriously hurt as a result of this. In RE1, however, this was a massive annoyance to me. I liked this far better in 0.

Second, I found the dialog to be better. Although the lines are often cheesy and dumb, in my opinion, there's more charming stupid dialog than the HD Remaster of RE1. The Playstation version of RE1 had some magnificently cheesy material, while the Gamecube version, unfortunately, was played pretty seriously, and I found the performances to be really dry in it. With 0, the campy, cheesy dialog isn't superb, but it's got enough cornball delivery from people actually trying and putting emotion into their lines that I could get into it.

Third, the character interaction blew that of 1 out of the water for me. Rebecca and Billy are your two playable characters in RE0, and I felt that their interactions with one another as the story progressed, was head and shoulders above anything Chris and Rebecca, or Jill and Barry shared in RE1. I was more interested in them, and if they'd been more popular, I would've liked to see them again in subsequent games. I didn't like Rebecca at all in RE1, but after RE0, I loved her. The writing/directing made her far more likable for me, and Billy was pretty decent. I certainly liked him more than Chris as he is represented in dialog and cutscenes, etc., in RE1.

Fourth, doors are clearly marked by what has them locked. If you're a mega-RE1 veteran, you know which doors the sword key, armor key, etc. open. However, imagine that you don't know and aren't using a walkthrough. The game tells you which key you need when you interact with the door...but your map isn't marked with an icon, and if you just look at a door, it's impossible to tell which key you need unless you are trying to open it. 

In RE0, however, most doors are very memorably marked when you look at them, so you know what type of lock it is. Orange door with flames etched on it? Fire key. Blue door with watery squiggles or some such on it? Water key. Doors with no knob and a clock above them? Solve a clock puzzle. The map isn't marked, but the visual cues on the actual doors themselves in-game make it so much easier for more people to be able to remember which door needs what thing done to open it. I loved this, and found wandering around trying every single door in RE1 each time I got a new key to be tiring and boring.

Fifth, I found this game's "active" story to be far more engaging than the original. A lot of folks probably disagree because nostalgia blinds them, or they might genuinely like something better about the first game's plot. For me, there wasn't really any plot. What I'm referring to by "active" story is the events and things we witness in the game, either real-time or in cutscenes, including flashbacks. In RE1, almost no plot developments ever occurr. RE0 isn't exactly amazing in that department, but outside of background information you read in notes in RE1 (which I do love and think are a lot better than RE0's notes), 

RE1's plot is "split up in mansion, Wesker and <Name> are gone, encounter other survivor and help or get helped, obvious bad guy is obvious, self destruct time, escape hopefully with <Name>, your team member from the beginning and possibly another survivor. RE0 could be simplified, of course, but flashback stuff, things between two villains, dialog and events including Billy and Rebecca...I felt like a lot more happened here, plot-wise. Stuff happened in RE1, but not much of it was story that you witness, and I'm a fan of well-told 

Alright, so with the good out of the way, though, I do want to address things I found to be [i]not[/i] enjoyable for me in RE0. I just said I liked the story better than RE1. That's true, but I do have one issue with it: conflicting information. Rebecca appears in RE1 as a total wuss. However, by the end of RE0, she's pretty badass. With this being a prequel, there's no way Chris should have to save her. I had so many magnum rounds in her pockets at the end of 0 that she should be able to kill Hunters for days and days. She sure wouldn't sit back and let Chris do all the work, realizing he could use a hand.

Something happens in the ending of RE0 which characters would have seen or heard the aftermath of in RE1. Also, a villain reveals the identity of one of his evil proteges near the end of RE1, yet Rebecca never shares this information with Chris in RE0 when she absolutely would tell him this name and what is going on for obvious reasons. I'm sure there are various other continuity errors/issues in the lot.

Next up, the inventory is a mixed bag. There are no item boxes in RE0. Instead of dumping items in an item box and pulling whatever items back out at any other item box in a safe room, you can drop your items anywhere. There are seemingly random maximum numbers of items you can drop per room, but yes, you can ditch stuff almost anyone. On the one hand, it's cool to be able to make your own personal treasure trove of healing items, guns, ammo, etc., but on the other hand, you might find yourself without an item you need, and it's on the opposite end of the game. Although this was annoying having to run back and forth so much, I found it less annoying than doing laps back and forth from kerosine containers to "killed' zombies in RE1. That got so old for me. One big plus, though, is that you control two characters, so you technically have 12 slots for items, which is a lot moe forgiving than the 6-8 in RE1.

Let's see...lastly, the game has an androgynous villain who laughs about doing evil things, speaks a bit pretentiously, has long hair, and wears white robes. I thought he was very cliche in appearance and personality, and he made the game less interesting to me. Oh, and opera randomly plays while he's being evil, because of course it does. At no point did I ever find him scary, cunning, interesting, shocking, cool, formidable (as a wits-matching/evil plan kinda guy, I mean), relatable, or even pitiable. I did not like him and felt bad for the game when he was on-screen, because he was one of the few things I didn't like about it.

Although I've brought up a few things I didn't like about the game, I overall enjoyed it quite a bit; more than RE1, even. For me, the dialog, character interactions/line delivery, less wonky camera angles, the doors having obvious requirements to unlockthem, visible based on the door's appearance itself, and other features made this a good gaming experience for me. If you like older Resident Evil games, it's certainly worth checking out.

It was only a few hours of my life which I'll never get back, vainly testing it out on multiple machines. And what's a few hours, out of a whole lifetime? Useless turds.

   Secondly, I'm giving this game a pretty decent score, but please understand this score comes with reservations. The game has dated somewhat, and was never the very, very best of the RE games in the first place. They've also done such a piss-poor job of updating things like menus and mechanics that I'm not sure how much I can recommend this to anyone who didn't play it the first time 'round. 

   Put it this way: if you're new to not only this but any other old-school, fixed-camera-angle survival horror games, this definitely isn't the place to start. Its mechanics were tricky even back when, what with all the pedantic partner-swapping and ruthless inventory antics, and it's become even less forgiving with time. But for those who have fond if slightly frustrated memories of playing this on the G-Cube...welcome home. You know what to expect.

   The partner-swapping thing, once you get used to it, was actually one of the niftiest things about the game when it first came out. In short, you have to swap frequently between the cute-but-mousy Rebecca Chambers and the surly-but-sexy Billy Coen in order to successfully solve various puzzles, perform specific tasks, etc. They'll get constantly separated, have to closely co-operate, fight side-by-side whenever possible...you name it, this game gets pretty good mileage out of the partner premise. It's more than just a gimmick, in other words; it's absolutely integral to story and gameplay. That said, it also has its irritations, but...I'll leave it up to you to find those out for yourself. Wouldn't wanna spoil ALL your fun.

   Another area where this game excels is atmosphere. Like any great horror game, it has fantastic locations, memorable monsters, and there's no denying that the spiffy new graphics look...well, pretty darned spiffy. I just can't warn the unwary enough about the game's overall difficulty and awkwardness, especially early on.

   You want resource management? Boy, do we have your resource management. The opening couple of hours on the train will test your resource management skills like few games before or since, believe me. You're a better gamer than yours truly if you can manage to procure and/or productively use every item on offer without constantly dropping things and backtracking for them later. For two certifiably butt-kickin' characters, they sure don't seem to be able to carry a lot of stuff between 'em. Useless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

   I still love this game, but a part of me hates it, too. The score below is biased and mostly aimed at veterans, as I've already noted. For everyone else, the risk is yours. Don't say I didn't warn you.

This game was originally released in 2002 and at this point the series had been having a release virtually every year from 1996. So it’s fair to say that the gameplay was beginning to feel about as fresh as one of it’s decomposing enemies.

In an attempt to invigorate the formula you now control 2 characters who you can swap between with a button press. This introduces some clever new puzzles where you must use the characters together or parts where you split up and pass each other items with handily placed dumb waiters. 

It also introduces some problems. Inventory space feels even more limited than other RE games. Larger weapons take 2 out of 6 slots and only Rebecca may mix herbs and chemicals. Meaning that you have to constantly fiddle with the inventory screen which just becomes tedious.

The partner AI is another annoyance. It can be managed with a menu but it will do it’s best to irritate. Such as when it gets in your way and when it doesn’t follow you through doors.

This game also suffers from the syndrome of having enemies off screen in the same room really often. It can be scary to not known where enemies are but you are constantly auto aiming and firing at stuff you cannot see and then listening to hear if they fall down.

The gameplay is never bad and if you can look past the flaws this has some good puzzles and good (but not inspiring) levels. It just lacks something and has some annoyances compared to the best RE games.

Resident Evil 0 was in development hell since around the mid 90's, where it was planned for an N64 release but constantly delayed due to issues in storage inherent with 64MB cartridges. The game's development was moved onto the NGC and  finally saw release in 2002, and in 2016 an HD Remaster was brought out which fortunately made its way to PC. Let's get one thing out of the way: this is a true HD Remaster; you can easily google comparison shots. Short story: this isn't just upscaling-it really does look much better than the previous version. Reason being that they pre-render shots for these classic RE titles, and the assets they had beforehand were actually really high quality and 'downscaled' to Gamecube hardware. So here we're getting a bit more of how it originally looked before being filtered down.

I start with a bit of a history lesson for some context: this is basically old Capcom. This is an RE title from the same Capcom that was at its zenith in the late 90's to mid 2000's. If you enjoyed the RE titles pre-4 (not that 4 was bad or anything) then this is more of the same in similar quality. This game was born in a specific time-period whereby quality was of a particular level.

RE0, as you may have guessed, is a prologue to RE1. It's plot concerns the same cast of characters within Racoon City, and if you like your RE lore you'll enjoy this, albeit there's nothing incredible nor is there a huge revelation here. Rebecca is the star here, along with Billy, an escaped convict. Can't say I'm particularly satisfied with the plot since there was no underground lab as there was in RE1, or family members turned into monsters. There's nothing particularly gripping in the plot, and it all seems to end rather abruptly, but it still holds well as a stand-alone tale. Just don't expect anything amazing.

The game itself is more of what you'd expect: pre-rendered backgrounds and fixed camera angles with, lets face it, god-awful combat. There's nothing worse than moving back a bit and the camera angle switching because of it. RE has never been a series known for its combat, the challenge is in exploring the map and solving puzzles. The tension is in the cinematic camera angles and not knowing whether the next room has an enemy. The fun is in managing your inventory space and running low on ammo. But the fun in RE titles and its are of specialization has never been in its shooting mechanics. Luckily, the game has a button assigned for auto targetting-one push and you automatically target an enemy on the screen. This saves the whole thing: you don't have to worry about losing your target and being impeded in any way by the fixed angles. You get to keep a unique feature and alleviate its short-comings-problem solved.

The partner system is unique and changes things up a bit; ultimately your partner character is really just more storage slots for items when you're together, but you are often seperated and have to work things out until you can meet up once more. It's different, it's not ground-breaking, but it adds some interest to an otherwise similar approach to the formula. You can also drop items on the floor and return to pick them up; gone are those magic boxes that store all of your items. Personally I'm not for it, since you wind up having to backtrack if you leave something important far behind (protip: always keep the grappling hook nearby until you activate the cable car). You wind up leaving items in save rooms anyway so I'm not for it, but it does allow you to just drop an item then and there if you need to pick something else up. It's an interesting idea, but one that needs a bit more refining.

All in all I can't complain; this is from classic Capcom and it shows. It also shows that this is a prologue game that doesn't build too much, but this is also from Capcom's peak so even that is fantastic. Strongly recommended if you loved old RE. Waiting on remakes of RE2 and RE3, Capcom.

[h1]Short version: 71%[/h1]
Resident Evil 0 may feel like just a standalone expansion pack to RE1, but its rich, detailed levels, pseudo co-op mechanics, and more combat-oriented approach will provide plenty of challenge and entertainment for any classic survival horror fan, despite its lack of proper story. 

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Since Resident Evil 0 was created alongside the Resident Evil 1 REmake—even using the same engine—many players consider it the younger sibling of the more famous and mature title. In a sense, they are right, but RE0 is still a good game with some memorable moments that can stand on its own.

RE0 stars one of the most unjustly underused characters from the old games, Rebecca Chambers, and crams an entire day’s worth of excitement into her life that preceded the events of RE1. She ends up as the involuntarily partner of a fugitive, Billy Coen, which in this game translates to a strange single-player co-op mechanic, where we can control either characters at any time, while the computer takes over the other. Although one would think that having two inventories helps in a survival horror, item management is actually even more tedious than in any other old RE, chiefly because of the lack of item boxes (you have to drop items to the ground, leading to quite some backtracking).

Probably the main reason for RE0’s small fame is that it has some gameplay issues. For example, the new enemy types are bland: they are usually just large animals or leeches. On the other hand, players have to face nearly twice as much of them as in RE1.
This enemy density tries to hide the shortcomings of the story: our protagonists essentially never meet anyone and the plot mostly boils down to them going through a set of beautifully rendered stages (the starting luxury train is quite iconic) until they meet an end boss. Sure, there is actually a bit more going on, but in the end, this is probably RE0’s biggest downfall.

[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review [/h1]

Resident Evil 0/Biohazard 0 HD Remaster is a remastered version of the classic survival horror game developed and published by Capcom

This is a prime example of how all remasters should look like. It's a shame that we had to wait for the PC port this long but it still looks and plays really good

It's a really unique game when it comes to it's atmosphere, and somehow, even after so many years, that clunky gameplay is still very catchy. Inventory management with it's low capacity can be a pain, especially on first playthrough, but in the end, I was also OK with it, since it also adds so much to it's tense atmosphere

All in all it's a very good game and I can't wait for the remake of Resident Evil 2!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]

I played this game immediately after REmake, which is a truly stellar game that has stood the test of time. It doesn't provide the incredible artistic experience of Silent Hill (in fact, the writing is laughableb-movie hilarity), but the gameplay and level design embody survival horror better than any other game I've played. It's deeply atmospheric and very punishing.

My main complaint with the REmake was that it gets too easy in the 2nd half on the highest difficulty. Then RE0 came along and had me begging for that. This game is for masochists only. The early RE formula is already unfair - tension is created through fixed camera angles, claustrophobic hallways, a scarcity of ammo and medical supplies, fixed save points where you have to use save items... this game compounds that by having 2 characters you have to keep alive and some nearly indestructible enemies (even after you get the heavy weaponry that made the first game easier).

I very nearly didn't play the rest of the game after experiencing the opening sequence. Many here have stated that the train is the best part of the game, but to me it's the exact opposite. Yes, it's the most novel environment, but that whole sequence is marred by frequent incredibly cheesy cutscenes which ruin any sense of atmosphere, largely thanks to the banter between the two insufferable main characters.

Thankfully, after you escape the train, the cutscenes become far less frequent. Don't expect to gain any insight into the later RE titles from this prequel, as the story is mercifully very scant - it only exists to justify the game's existence, and it barely accomplishes that. Don't think about it too hard, and don't expect it to make sense.

The environments from here on out are basically a re-imagining of the original games, but with higher difficulty and two characters. The bulk of the game is a training facility which looks a whole lot like a mansion, which is followed by an underground lab which mostly looks nothing like a lab (though I hear the lab in this game is actually modelled after the lab from RE2, which I haven't played). Tack on an extra section at the end for novelty and good measure....

The mansion is much smaller than that of the original game (though the basement is larger), and frankly it's a bit of a pale imitation - while the graphics look flashier than REmake overall, the camera angles aren't as artistic and it never feels quite as isolated and distubing as the original while controlling two characters (which require a somewhat wider field of view to fit, eliminating some of that claustrophobia).

But the gameplay more than makes up for that by being much harder. It took me exactly 20hrs to beat this game, which is the same amount of time it took to beat REmake - only my final in-game time on REmake was nearly 10hrs, while this one didn't even reach 6hrs 40min. I spent 2/3 of my time in this game dying and retrying. This game will make you feel very intense anxiety, even beyond the original, and it never gets all that much easier (the final boss is quite difficult this time, as it's even quite resistent to the Magnum - I used up all my ammo and had to carefully run around and take it down with a pistol).

The scarcity of healing items is even more punishing this time around, since you have two characters to keep alive. At any given time, one of them will be dying. Ammo for the shotgun and grenade launcher is even more scarce than in the original, meaning you're basically going to be trying to survive with a pistol (as ammo for that is quite scarce). Except you basically can't kill the game's hardest enemies (abominations, leech zombies) with a pistol without getting killed.

Ink ribbons (for saving the game) are much more common this time around, but I didn't find myself using them more often - mainly because saving would involve backtracking through dangerous areas. The one attempt to make things easier didn't end up helping.

Many have complained about the inventory system, but it didn't strike me as being much worse. Let's be honest - not being able to drop things and having magically interconnected boxes was goofy. I only found myself backtracking marginally more here, and I'm sure it doesn't compare to playing the original on Survival Mode (where boxes are not interconnected). Perhaps this is because I was playing on hard, so there were less items available period. Yes, this frequently turns into 'inventory management: the game' just in terms of figuring out which character needs which item, but the inventory isn't much worse than the standard early RE fare. Heck, you even have twice the space with two characters!

Many have also complained that you can send the wrong character to the wrong place and die. Yes, this game is all about trial and error, and if you keep enough backup saves (which is essential in early RE games anyway), you'll be fine. There's never a point at which you can lose toooo much progress if you save regularly enough and don't always overwrite your saves.

Despite disputing those complaints, I still can't recommend this game to anyone except masochistic completionists who wish the already difficult original game was harder. Objectively, this game is poorly written, the story makes no sense and the main villain is cheesy and random, the environments are recycled, the enemies are unfairly difficult (bat boss fight where it's impossible to aim at the boss thanks to a swarm of tiny bats anyone?), and the mechanics make it that you'll spend half the time in this game moving items back and forth between the two characters, watching door animations, and dying. I enjoyed my time in it quite a lot, to be honest, but I uninstalled it as quickly as I could when I was finished and will certainly never be revisiting it again - it's simply too cruel. If you really want more REmake, just play it again and then wait for REmake2.

The extra modes don't add much - Leech Hunter is basically a survival mode where you try to collect 100 items in the mansion without dying (so, virtually impossible - don't even bother), while Wesker mode is basically a humorous god mode - I can't really see a reason to play the full game with it, though it's moderately entertaining for a few minutes.

After playing Resident Evil 7, I was delighted to learn that there were two remastered classic Resident Evil games available. I have been a Resident Evil fan since playing RE2 back in 1998. This is one of the few REs that I have yet to play so I was delighted to learn that it had been remastered early last year. I have realized that the gameplay mechanics from the older series has not aged well.

Cons:
- Fixed camera angles. Although this has always been an issue with the older RE games, it seems to be a lot worst in this one. There are several miniboss battles that take place in hallways which have camera angles that only focus on the player. This makes the player have to rely solely on audio and the autolock system which brings me to my next point.

- Autolock system. The autolocking system in this game is terrible. The character often choose to lock onto random enemies rather than the closest threat. This was especially annoying during the church bat battle.

- Lack of item boxes. I like the ability to leave items on the ground instead of having to backtrack to an item box. This does become an annoyance when I want to transport a major weapon to another area. Although meant to decrease backtracking, the lack of item boxes actually made me have to backtrack even more.

- Story. The story in this RE is one of the weaker ones in my opinion. The mad scientist who dresses like an anime wizard was just lame.



Pros:
- Buddy system. Each RE has had some sort of gimick. RE0's is the buddy system. I liked how a lot of puzzles required use of both characters and I liked the ability to exchange items. 

- Puzzles: Most of the puzzles were interesting. However, some of the puzzles were not completely logical. Case in point: the prey puzzle in the training facility. All of the clues seem to indicate that you light the fires in the order from the weakest animal to the strongest, yet the actual answer was completely counter intuitive (a wolf is lower than a horse in the food chain?).

It was immersive, dark. The combat was pretty mediocre. The storyline was cheesy. Billy Gives it one thumb up. Get it if you are interested in the RE storyline. But if you want a genuinely fun game this isnt it.

A great prequel to RE series, maybe even better than RE1. Setting is pretty much the same as in RE1. With the exception of (really cool) train sequence at the beginning, you will again find yourself in a villa and underground labs, BUT they are completely different now, with new puzzles, new (and really tough) enemy types and a lot of bossfights.

RE0 is also much, MUCH harder game than RE1, and pretty much harder than even the rest of the RE series. Even on normal difficulty you will find much less ammo, medkits and herbs, and encounter much more enemies, so be prepared for a real survival. You will die a lot of times.

Gameplay stayed the same, except now you control two charaters at the same time. And since crates to store items are not present this time, you will spend a lot of time in inventory managing items between your characters. Inventory management could definitely been more user friendly, but you will get used to it after an hour or two.

Story in RE games was always mediocre, and it's the same in RE0. But it's flow is much better than in RE1, much more things are happening and revealing the story behind T virus and characters behind it was interesting.

All in all it's a great game. If you loved RE1-3, you will also love this one. And now let's hope that waiting on RE Code Veronica and RE2 Remakes won't be too long.

I never owned a Gamecube or a Playstaton 3. I had a Playstation 2. It was there that I discovered the fun survival horror of Resident Evil. I played and beat the original and had beaten Resident Evil 2 many times over 15 years ago. Fond memories.  The series went on without me and I watched the series change. Back in the day when the Resident Evil remake was done, I was excited to see the game get a serious facelift, but I had no way of playing it. Then I learned about Resident Evil 0 and I became mildly curious. An origin story....could be promising. I am so happy that a lot of the RE games have made their way to the PC, enabling me to play the entries that were inaccessible. With the announcement and now release of RE7, I decided it was time to go through the series, see where it all started and watch the mutation of one of the best survival horror franchises. 

For those who love the classic adventure slant of the Resident Evil franchise, this is a must play. When it come to Resident Evil, I will probably always prefer the third person perspective. The tension is high as you never know what is around the corner, until you round the corner. The use of puzzles to advance rather than gunning everything down was wonderful territory to revisit. I enjoyed the herbs, the files, the typewriters, and those famous doors, stairs, and ladders loading screens. But this game is much more than paying homage to the familiar elements of the series. Its a wonderful blend of the old and the new, for me at least.

Chris and Jill....Claire and Leon....and now, Rebecca and Billy. While in previous entries where you had to play two separate campaigns to get a feel for each character, we have two people helping each other in one campaign, and it works out really well. Rebecca may not be a master of unlocking, but she knows how to mix herbs which makes her a strong asset to Billy Coen who is the muscle of the two. The two start a wary alliance but by the end of the game they have come to each others rescue multiple times and have formed a strong bond. There will be times that they have to split up to achieve goals and progress through the game. You can easily switch between the two and choose a Team setting or have one of them go by themselves. On Team setting, the AI Billy or Rebecca has your back, and is very good at covering for you. This served as a strength and weakness for this game. As I controlled Rebecca, it was hard to get scared because I had Billy following and covering with a shotgun. But when circumstances forced Rebecca away from Billy....thats when I would freak. She's a medic. She can shoot a gun, but she does not have the muscle that Joey has. I was always happy when the two met up again. 

Now how does this story fit as an origin story? I think pretty well. In the bounds of the Resident Evil universe it makes sense. Those who have played RE1 and RE2 will probably understand the character relationships better and will enjoy the familiar faces. 

The survival horror aspect is a mixed bag. First off, there are some new monsters that will make you want to run rather than stay and fight. However, I found myself not getting scared so much since I had Rebecca and Billy together so much. My biggest anxiety was my very limited inventory. Rebecca and Billy have very different inventory needs (she is recovery items and small guns and he is the heavy hitter) but the same amount of slots. What I wouldn't have given for those wonderful classic storage bins!! It would have been nice to find a little side pack to add a little more inventory space, but oh well. Instead you have to drop items and pick up others. On the plus side, when you look at the map, you can see all the items you dropped and where they are, so you can go back and retrieve them. Whats annoying is that when you find a puzzle related item, you don't know if you should pick it up or not because the puzzle might not show up for a while. You don't know how long to run around with the grenade launcher or shotgun because it is RE and big baddies can show up at any moment. It really is the scariest part of the game...what do I take with me!?

The game is beautiful. I never saw the original so I can't compare but oh my goodness it is gorgeous in a survival horror kind of way. The controls have two options: the more modern controls or the original. I found myself at home with either, since I prefer the birds eye view. The soundtrack is also very RE. The voice acting was perfect. Rebecca is spunky, strong, resilient, and a great healer. Joey won me over with his entrance and it made me very sad to watch him walk into the sunset. I hope to see him again.

As I finished RE0, I knew another playthrough would be in the future. This game has the feel of a classic RE game with the beautiful modern graphics. Rebecca Chambers is currently high on my favorite RE characters list, and I look forward to seeing her again in Resident Evil as I play as Chris for the first time.

If you're new to Resident Evil, or have not experienced the Old-school resident evil, this is for you.

I had a lot of fun playing this on the Gamecube and am very happy to find that it was handled quite well with this port and remaster.  You have to do a bit of tweaking if you're playing on an NVIDIA powered laptop, but once it's set up properly, the performance is great, as well as the graphics.

This is a solid addition to the franchise that is a must buy for anyone who loves the classic RE style of gameplay or for those that would just like to expand the lore a bit.  It is a prequel to the original game, so it focuses more on the early days of the Umbrella training facility and it's research.  It also provides some back story on Albert Wesker and does a good job of setting the tone for what will eventually occur at the Arklay mansion.

The actual gameplay is very similar to any other classic RE title, focusing on inventory management, atmosphere and puzzles more than grotesqueries and action packed glory.  The game design is solid and it has consistent pacing throughout.

It is a coop game, which turns some people off, but it's done well here.  Rebecca isn't a nuisance that you're constantly rescuing (unlike my least favorite part of RE4), and the game does a good job of creating situations where the two characters need to work together in an un-gimmicky way.  The a.i. is pretty simple, but the game doesn't give it enough room to become problematic, so it works out fine.  You can freely swap between characters and can even move the other character with the right thumbstick which is a nice touch in case they do happen to get in your way.

All in all, this is an excellent part of the franchise that is a steal even if you pay the full retail of $20.

I remember being super excited by RE Zero, and I also remember playing it on Gamecube and loving it. Unfortunately, it seems that I've run into a case of nostalgia blinding me. I adore the Resident Evil series, especially the engine remake with RE1. However, after playing REmake and then following up with Zero, I have to say that Zero is by far one of the worst in the series.

Don't get me wrong, it had a lot going for it. The prequel setup in explaining the genesis of the T-virus and the subsequent events in the series has still held up and is one of my few favorite parts of the game. Along with a partner with their own separate inventory, it features no magic connected item boxes and forces real choices of what to bring with you and what to leave behind, really driving home survival horror. Ammunition scarcity is similarly welcome.

Unfortunately, some of the premises on paper ends up working out as utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when implemented. One glaring flaw, which is the central part of this game, is the partner system. If you don't arm your partner effectively, you may run into story beats where one partner is forced to battle a boss without the other, possibly making the encounter IMPOSSIBLE to win. This happens a few times, and can set back hours of progress if you are forced to reload an earlier save. Further, the idea that partners have their own capabilities is admirable, but not when one is far more durable than the other. 

And remember the ammunition scarcity from earlier? Unlike REmake, which allowed you to decide in some areas whether or not to kill a monster in favor of saving ammo, Zero's cramped and very straightforward environments allow very little choice for making these decisions, much less on where to explore first. You are guided in a bad way, and the game comes off as being on rails at certain points. As a result, ammo scarcity sometimes comes off as unfair, especially in a game that springs encounters on your where you can become separated from your partner and possibly not have the weapons you need to reunite with them.

I am saddened that my nostalgia held this game in a better light when it doesn't really deserve it. It's just bad and eyerolling, and normally nitpicky things, such as the dreaded 2-slot out of 6 hookshot, the large amounts of backtracking for left behind ammo or health items no matter how much planning you have, or some real bullet sponge enemies (looking at you leech zombie), really grind you down to the point of feeling cheated. I got this on a Christmas sale and still feel like I wasted my money. Don't make the same mistake I did. Buy REmake if you haven't, and put on a Let's Play of this game and save yourself the cash.

This is easily the weakest entry of the classic Resident Evil games which consist of RE1, RE2, RE3 and Code Veronica. If you haven't done so already, I strongly suggest you play RE1 Remasted instead, especially since this game will spoil some plot points in RE1.

Why this is a bad RE game can pretty much be summarized with these points:

1. Partner system
2. No storage chests
3. Several items require 2 inventory slots
4. Only 6 inventory slots as opposed to RE1 8 slots

I also thought the environment you explored was a bit meh, but maybe that's just me. The game is also, in my opinion, a lot harder than Resident Evil 1, if that's a good or bad thing depends on you.

Anyway, the partner system. I would very much prefer not to play as 2 characters at once, so I have full control in battle and not a extra character that takes damage and waste shots. It would also add replayability to the game if you had to choose between Rebecca and Billy just like Jill and Chris in RE1.

The inventory system is easily the worst part of the game. Instead of storage chests you now have the ability to drop items on the floor. I've seen some people say this makes it is just like the storage chest just that you can store in every room! Ain't that cute, but it's WRONG! Because storage chests are LINKED, which means once you reach a new area you don't have to backtrack to the previous storage chest to collect any items you need. Which is exactly what you need to do all the bloody time in this game.

Add to the fact that some items, even key items required to progress, can take 2 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ inventory slots. Yeah, you're not going to carry around that hookshot. But then suddenly you see that you require it, well, time to backtrack to the beginning of the game! How fun! And I've seen some people say this system adds strategy, what a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It add tedious backtracking. Backtracking is not necessarily a bad thing, RE1 had a lot in a good way. But this kind of backtracking sucks since you only have to backtrack because the poor inventory system.

I've also seen the argument that 6 inventory slots is not that bad because you have 2 characters, so it is actually 12 slots! The problem with that argument is that they don't acknowledge the fact that many items require 2 slots which was not the case with RE1. If you have a Shotgun and a grenade launcher it took 2 slots in RE1. Now add ammo for each, so 4 slots. You still have 4 empty slots and are free to explore and find new items. In RE0 however, shotgun + grenade launcher takes 4 slots, now add ammo, 6 slots. THAT'S YOUR WHOLE INVENTORY! You literally cannot pick up anything else on that character, you can't even carry a health item.

So you might say, just put the stuff on the other character. Let's assume that character actually has any free slots, the problem then becomes when you have to frequently split up the characters, some times into areas where they can't reach each other. Though normally when that happens you have some kind of item elevator so you can ship items between them. Except for large items! So image Billy has the shotgun and grenade launcher, and Rebecca has the 9mm gun. They can't reach each other and Billy can't give Rebecca his shotgun or g. launcher. So now she has to face whatever enemy is required with the 9mm or load a save game before the split up, IF you have one. This is so bad mechanically and in my opinion completely ruins a would-be decent game.

If you really like Resident Evil, especially the classic gameplay, then ok, it's worth playing. But I had a LOT, a LOT of more fun with RE1 remastered.

Camera angles are sometimes a bit crazy, but thankfully you can hear enemies and aiming always targets them. If you're carefull you shouldn't get sucker punched into face. Though after progressing, enemies might spawn anew in some locations.
*Map - is really usefull in this game - not just to highlight locked doors but to keep track of every item you drop or "tag"(try to pick up and just leave it there) It can even list and highlight items you found so remember to tag them!
*Inventory - a lot of complains about it but it's actually bearable. You can drop things on the ground, they dont disappear. Most of the time you can have one of your characters loaded with extra gun to deal with various threats while another one carry all the stuff you find. Sometimes you will have to do a little bit backtracking and haul stuff a closer to the frontline.
*Partner - most of the time you'll be exploring this dangerous world with buddy, extra firepower comes always handy. So does inventory space. AI is quite decent so you dont have to worry about some bad glitches. And you will need them to solve certain puzzles. But in certain cases it might be helpful to just leave them in safe room, for example if you need to run past some monster(to save ammo and possibly healing), pick up stuff and run away - you can switch to solo.
*Monsters - you'll get them and their varieties, from "easy" monsters to minibosses. Sometimes you'll have to use different tactics + find their weakness to conserve ammo. IE, few molotovs used on certain monsters can save you whole load of pistol bullets against others...
*Atmosphere - I have played only RE3 and this is as close as it gets.
*HD Graphics - can be described as "specatular classic" - it looks like prerendered scenes from original series but it's actually in 3D(you can see it on shadows and lighting). Locations looks unique, no repetitive models...also offers wide screen support.
*Performance - played on Phenom II X3 and HD 7850 2GB - all fluent. Though I have seem some random people with weaker specs complaining. Maybe because they had lower Video RAM? I haven't seen any low res textures/models in this game. And it isn't straight gamecube port either...
---
All in all, I can easily recommend this game for fans of old RE games. People who never played those will have to get used to controls and camera angles first. But it's worth it, because in comparison with modern games it offers unique experience and atmosphere - a game that pretends to be realistic and tough yet you solve this crazy and weird puzzles(yeah, anyone seen doors marked with fire emblem lately??? That's umbrella corp), accompanied by mysterious "what's in the next room" feeling.

Inventory Management and Backtracking: The Game. Resident Evil: Zero is a prequel to the popular survival horror series as the name suggests, and the game mechanics are more archaic and frustrating than the older entries' already infuriating systems. Whether that's an intentional, meta decision or just experimentation gone awry, I couldn't say for sure. The end result is a bad game either way.
 
  RE0 starts out strong. As S.T.A.R.S medic Rebecca Chambers, you're separated from your squad (as tends to happen) and find yourself searching a train for an escaped convict, Billy Coen. The train is a great introductory stage; essentially a long hallway with impressive environmental details and an ever-moving backdrop. You quickly find your liberated prisoner, and he's a real corny douche. Billy's tribal tattoos, spiky hair, and cringy one liners are more than enough to get Rebecca's girl juices flowing, so the two partner up and you're introduced to the concept of playing in tandem with an AI partner. You can set the computer controlled character to follow you, stay put, attack enemies or be passive, and you can exchange items as long as they are on the same screen. The idea is novel and leads to the type of puzzles you would expect, and they each have minor differences and special equipment (Billy can push heavier objects, Rebecca can mix herbs, etc.). Judging by this first stage, things look great in the confined train as you pass objects through dumb waiters and separate to trigger time sensitive switches. As the scope of the game expands, everything quickly falls apart.
 
  Rebecca and Billy both have painfully small inventory slots, so neither of them can be the badly needed pack mule. Struggling with limited space is a staple of the genre, but Resident Evil: Zero pushes it to insufferable levels. The game goes crazy with multiple key items that need to be hauled, combined, and stored and those all eat up precious slots. Anything larger than a handgun (and some key items) take up multiple of your eight squares, plus the ammo needed... add a healing item and you are constantly fiddling and juggling and dropping and swapping and it's obnoxious. Previous games in the series gave you access to a storage box in save rooms that would magically transport items to other save rooms; video game-y? Sure, but it worked to alleviate the finicky nature of what you're doing to a degree. In the aptly named Resident Evil: Zero you just throw crap on the ground.
 
  The dropped objects are physically represented in the room, though you have to take the games' word for it sometimes when your ink ribbon is obscured by foreground objects and you walk in circles jamming 'A' trying to find it while the character remarks over and over about the vintage of the furniture. Even when you can see the items good luck picking up what you want when multiple items are next to each other. Another issue with the floor garbage is it multiplies the need to backtrack exponentially as your weapons, health, and ammo end up scattered all over the entire game as you drop them for key items and are subsequently blocked off, shuffled forward, or split up. It's an inelegant solution to a problem that had already been solved, and the game suffers for it.
 
  After the train the stages devolve from the familiar (another mansion...) to the boring (a sewage treatment plant?), and the story and characters go from cheesy to familiar to bad as well. It all culminates in a boss battle that frequently interjects little cutscenes to throw off your flow; a climax of the bad game design. Then Billy spouts a '90s action movie one-liner and your eyes and the credits roll. Resident Evil: Zero feels like a by-the-numbers Resident Evil game that doubles down on all the worst parts of the genre. It's a real... zero.

I always thought of 'Resident Evil 0' as one of the lesser entries in the series. Not as bad as 'Outbreak', 'Outbreak - File #2', 'Survivor', or 'Dead Aim', but those are the only older entries it beats out. About the only thing this title has going for it is the classic-style gameplay, but even that has it's issues in this one.

#1. Classic Control Scheme Not Included:

R-Trigger - Ready Aim
L-Trigger - Switches Targets While Aiming
A Button - Confirms/Fires
B Button - Run/Cancel (Down+B = 180 Turn)
X Button - Switch Characters
Y Button - Status Menu
Z Bumper - Map

Remember playing this on your Gamecube in 2002 using the above controls? Well, a comparable gamepad control scheme is NOT present here. As a veteran of the originals, I ended up using "Classic Control Scheme D" and still had to make a custom controller wrapper that rotated the functions of B, X, and Y one step clockwise. This is the only way I've found to make the game play like 'Resident Evil - HD Remaster' does. And reload will still end up being R+X instead of R+B. (NOTE: All button references in this section are based on the layout of a Gamecube Controller, not an X-Box Controller)

#2. No Item Boxes:

You must throw everything on the ground when you're not using it, or don't have room for something, then backtrack to pick it all back up again. Constantly. Unless you spend some sessions gathering your items to the central rooms, you'll be ripping your hair out by the finale. If you hated picking up your toys when you were younger, you're probably going to hate this too.

#3. Single-Player Cooperative:

Control two characters throughout the entire game by switching back and forth between them. This is the source of many player's frustrations with this title. The mechanic of switching characters makes certain areas of the game tedious and just plain not fun to play. Usually whenever sending items up and down a lift is involved. This mechanic is also the source of the greater-than-average (for the series) difficulty settings. The developers saddled you with an A.I. partner. At least they know how to fire a gun this time. (That's right, I'm lookin' at YOU, Ashley Graham.)

When all is said and done, 'Resident Evil 0' is not necessarilly a BAD entry in the series, it just doesn't hold a flickering candle to 'Resident Evil - HD Remaster', 'Resident Evil 2', 'Nemesis', or 'Code: Veronica X'. I'd say this one's mostly for veteran players and hardcore fans of the series.

Back in the day, 0 introduced the concept of the leeches that could not only work together very intelligently, but also come together to form a new enemy with extra endurance and reach than the others. The ability to place items in random places when inventory space is needed are more realistic and intuitive features that would have made previous resident evil games a  little easier to handle.

As it is, the tale is well told and gives adventurers items of interest, if only a few. The voices for Rebecca and Billy are well cast and the main villain is pleasingly sinister, albeit underused.

0 is, overall, an atmospheric game that will entertain fans and newcomers alike, but it may seem a little too short. If you want a longer, more in depth experience, seek out Resident Evil 4 or 6. When considering what it is that distinguishes a survival horror game from an action or any other genre, things that come to mind for survival horror fans are usually locked camera angles which can often put the player at a viewing disadvantage, weak or limited combat abilities, low ammo supplies and adventure game exploration in a environment filled with dangerous enemies. What makes a survival horror game different from other genres is that while most games give the player great agency and power over the world, survival horror puts the player at a disadvantage and in a position of weakness. Under those parameters, Resident Evil Zero is undoubtedly a survival horror game.

If inconveniencing the player is part of what makes a game a survival horror game, then Resident Evil Zero may at times have too much of a good thing. While it is a staple of the classic Resident Evil franchise to give the player limited inventory and to juggle items, Zero goes a step further by flooding the player with a multitude of items while also providing no system of storage. The idea was to make item management more organic by forcing the player to pick up and put down items in the game world as necessary rather than being confined to chests. But the management of resources frequently crosses the line from being a source of tension to a source of tedium, and first time players can add whole hours to their play time as they trial and error which items they needed to take and which to leave behind. 

Despite the two character co-op mechanic, this game brings nothing substantially new to the Resident Evil franchise or the survival horror genre. Many of the familiar enemies and settings seen in other games come back here and none of the features makes this game stand out compared to the other entries.  What it does bring is a solid entry into the genre and another hearty full length adventure for fans to sink their teeth into. One quality which stands out in this game versus the other classic Resident Evils is that while they have often been called survival horror, they usually ended up playing more like action games by the end. As early as Resident Evil 2 the games have been empowering the player more than the game advertises and even in the remake there is more bullets than there are enemies to kill by the end of the game. In Resident Evil Zero, especially on hard difficulty, there are truly more threats than there are resources to spare. Perhaps in trying to be how people remembered the classic Resident Evils were like rather than being how they really are, Resident Evil Zero is more survival horror than most of the other Resident Evils.

Playing Zero on hard, I was constantly on the verge of running out of ammo and I was truly worried that I might run out of supplies before I needed them. Zero will still empower the player in time for the end of the game, but first time players will be holding their breath for quite a while before that part arrives. Resident Evil Zero is not an accommodating game. Although released in 2002, this is a game with the design philosophy of 3D playstation 1 games. Many of the features and character control standards of modern AAA games are missing from this title, and it is a very real possibility to get permanently stuck. If you don't mind early 3D game mechanics however, and want to experience a survival horror challenge in what is clearly still a AAA game for its time, then I recommend Resident Evil Zero. 

If you decide to play this game, I recommend that you play it on hard on your first playthrough. A big part of the survival horror experience is entering the unknown, and having to do the cost benefit analysis of risking using supplies versus future need for those supplies. This experience cannot be replicated on repeat playthroughs, and contributes greatly to the horror experience. Here is some spoiler free advice for newer players who might want to take on the challenge of playing this game for the first time on hard which will ensure a more smooth playing experience:

[h1]Create multiple saves[/h1]
Having 20 save slots means that you can create backups to go back to in case you trap yourself in a corner. Going back 3 or even 4 saves is not as dreadful as it might seem since a great deal of play time is trial and error solution finding. A part that might have took you an hour to get through might take 20 minutes or less when you know what items you need and can save time on backtracking. Never put all your saves in one file or you might get irreversibly stuck.

[h1]Use handgun bullets on zombies whenever possible, save the better stuff for the bigger threats[/h1]
Zombies are the low level mooks of this game, and despite what I said earlier, there are usually more handgun bullets than you need. The problem isn't just having ammo, its having the right ammo for the right enemies. Its usually not worth wasting a grenade on a zombie, there are bigger and badder things around the corner that will demand that firepower. A way to make handgun bullets more effective is to bring your partner character with you and have both of them equipped with handguns. Let Billy be the supporting AI since he has more health and shoots more agressively.

[h1] There is more gas than there are bottles to turn into molotovs, don't bother lugging gas cans around. Molotovs are also nearly useless, and don't make that much of a difference [/h1]
This is another flaw of this game. The game leads you to believe that gas is important enough to carry around with you, but it can only create molotovs and there is more of it than you need, which is usually placed around empty bottles in the first place. Any gas you don't immediately use you can almost always ditch. Another thing is that the molotovs are very poor weapons. The attack animation is too slow, the throw range is inconsistent and they don't do very much damage. They are most useful when you encounter leech monsters for the first time, who will often go through a transformation sequence. This gives you a window of time to throw 3-4 molotovs on them guaranteeing their death, but even then they might still get a good hit on you. It might be better to just avoid the leech monsters entirely if you can.

[h1]Keep the hookshot nearby after the train section, it will be needed again later. After the lab is complete, you can safely leave it behind, opening up two whole slots in your characters inventory [/h1]
This always gets people. There is a weird gap after the first section of the game where you use the hookshot once, and then never need it again for the next map. You will need it multiple times in the next map following that one though and people will often leave it all the way back at the beginning of the previous map. Once that section is done though you can ditch it for good, unlike other key items it does not disappear after it no longer serves any use. 

Good luck, have fun, and enjoy true survival horror!

Horror, quite possibly one of the most fun and difficult genres of gaming.  Originating back in the early 1990's on the Playstation One, the Resident Evil One (RE) in the series instantly became the icon for suspense, horror and mystery.  Like all great mysteries, answers to questions get overlooked leaving the player with a thirst un-quenched.  Resident Evil: Zero is that quintessential thirst quencher.  With it's complete fun integrated explanation of game play balanced with all the elements of the series storytelling.  The mystery uncloaked here is a prime example of a prequel meant to be played after having played thru RE:1 first, thus allowing for a  mystery, mystery then answer experience rather than a mystery, answer and mystery solved experience.

         Warning: From here on out there are *SPOILERS* so read at your peril. XP

          The mystery unveiled by the use of yet more mystery.  Lets quickly run through a brief overview of events to give us some feel for the game and story.  Starting out on  a train of the dead, that being a loose and relative thing, our heroine Rebecca Chambers after a lovely intro cut scene investigates.  Just like the first Resident Evil the player is left with a little to go on except micro-sandbox exploration.  Through the use of occasional scripted scenes a team member of STARS ( the police force Rebecca is on) dies from bites and loss of blood from super leeches and a new character/partner Billy Coen (the so called criminal) is introduced as well as the partner system.  Rebecca is attacked by a person made of leeches whom Billy heroically kills, saving Rebecca.  They team up exploring more of the train, while doing so Rebecca gets trapped after fixing a damaged circuit board on the roof of the train and Billy goes to find a tool to get her out.  On the search he gets attacked by a scorpion the size of a Buick, a mass of leech eggs hatch and our heroes have to stop a now run away train.  Managing to do so only to crash into an underground tunnel in a hillside, they somehow manage to survive.  After taking a minute to recover they proceed, only to discover they are in a mansion of the dead, note this one is different than the one in RE:1.  After several puzzles, zombies and a few new enemies we begin to paint a picture on how this whole chain of events came to be as well as reveal the Men behind the scenes and the role they played leading up to RE:1.  Prior to RE:1, and subsequently RE:0, a scientist discovered a means to immortality in the Progenitor virus and proceeded to experiment on how to make it viable.  Leeches where the key.  He the scientist is revealed to be alive, surprisingly because the two men mentioned earlier killed him.  Rebecca and Billy learn how all three villains got started, their dark experiments and after discovering the underground facility by way of a zip-line car and the Doctors revived form and world destructive plans.  They take on the doctor  kill him escape the self-destruction of the facility that then leads to Rebecca's Role in RE:1.  So, overall the game feels adequate to be a stand alone and also very satisfying as a prequel.  Note the partner system allows some choice on who plays what role in some sequences, while in other sequences it is character specific allowing for character development thru personal experiences thus shaping the story.  Flashbacks also play a small role enriching the experience to fill in any of the gaps literature found thru out the game failed to reveal or simply was missed while playing, for the player. 

             New and then kept for future games of the RE series was the partner system.  Though other games in the series had points when two characters would be together for short periods of time, they made both playable but never together.  Important to note also is that a player can switch between characters, single character to allow more complex puzzle solving and save time by switching between characters or have the second character (your choice) follow you, select how aggressive you want them to play burning thru ammo or being defensive and save it along with each respective inventory allows a great deal of freedom and customizablility, all showing the care, detail and standards to which this game was made.  In addition by having a secondary character carry a specific weapon you directly select what kind of weapon and ammo they use.  This intuitive function allows characters to be played with together or separately depending on how easy, challenging  the player wants to make it.   Having properly crafted this partner system the game also manages a decent blend of survival horror with it limited but numerous undead, finite ammo, payoffs of close quarters kills along with puzzles that really require as much as attention to detail as curiosity to truly discover all the secrets often with a worth while payoff.   The detective work to uncover the truth gives a rich lore and is a great driving force if not a the challenge of beating the game in general.   Overall, it's the blending of these elements, their timing and placement that keeps the game fresh and the player coming back for more. 

          Game play is just as good as the original if not slightly more spot on.  Combat is kept honest to the original, basically a 3 level system of up, middle and down attacks with a radial direction and again 3 levels of distance far, medium and close range.  The payoff of range and levels allows for a tactile application of selecting not just targets but relative parts of target Eg. a head shot at close range aimed squarely  and up at the target for max damage/kill shot or medium range with a grenade launcher for a multi kill and no self damage.   General movement controls give that traditional game play of the first RE through a bit wonky/clunky it serves to first add to the terror and suspense in any combat as well as piss off the unexperienced furthering the horror experience.

          The re-release of this game brought with it updated graphics.  This is always a little bittersweet as it changes the visual feel of the game, though in this case it feels like someone cleaned off the screen allowing a more crisp view.   Hilariously though is that there are 3 levels of graphics in this game, game play graphics in HD, low res graphics of most of the cut scenes and one cut scene which they forgot to update at all making it the most entertaining.  Overall though it feels like a healthy mix of old and updated giving its own unique experience.
          The music is identically the same.  Ambient eerie tonal tracks through out the environment help to create the horror without detracting from the immersion with out of place music.  The contrast of the safe rooms' tune emulates a breath of fresh air or a sigh of relief and acts as a synergistic amplifier between rest and tension outside the safe room.

         Bonus or extra content considering the premise of the game seems a little out of place, primarily the costumes, which were earned/unlock in previous version of the game.  Rebecca's cheerleader costume in particular is one such case,  the is fully functional and moves relative to her movements, however.  The major drawbacks to every costume is it's absence in movie cut scene's losing some of its appeal.  The new Wesker mode makes Rebecca totally Smoken' hot and pay homage to RE 5's Jill mind control.  In addition Billy is now Wesker and comes with 2 unique abilities Death Vision a chargeable AOE with head shot ability and Super Speed. Yup no more walking or casual jogging, you can dash across rooms with ease, amazingly helpful for speed runs. There is more but I'm out of space

         Simply, its a solid game made in an era when games had less graphics and were pushed to be engaging and with lasting depth that will always be memorable.

When you bring it to a small room with multiple enemies (which isn't too rare) it's useless. I found myself just using it as a pack-horse and not bringing it to any fights.
