Resident Evil 0's HD remaster is truly noticeable as the game looks great, the mechanics are still the same though (apart from a leaner control scheme) so you can expect a very old fashioned gameplay with all the pros and cons. To expand on that you'll find a pretty atmospheric and challenging survival horror experience with familiar puzzles, quite a few items to carry back and forth to solve them, very limited inventory space and a good amount of bioweapons that'll try to kill you.

The whole item management aspect is part of the old-school charm but can also feel unnecessary fiddly at times, especially when you find out there's a limit to how many items you can leave in each room or have to make a few trips to ensure you have all the items you need in the next area. Story and characters are also pretty shallow and don't really add too many interesting elements to the overarching narrative.

All things considered RE0 is still a worthwhile purchase if you're looking for more old-style survival horror and even more so if you missed it when it came out on Gamecube: it's not the strongest entry of the series but it's decent enough to warrant a playthrough.

When I heard Capcom is going to release Resident Evil 0, I immediately knew this game is going to be a must have for me, because - among many other things - I always wanted to know and experience what happened before the original Resident Evil. Since I've never owned a video game console, I envied those who had the opportunity to play amazing titles that were exclusive to consoles, such as Dead Space 2: Severed, Drakan: The Ancients' Gates and Condemned 2. And of course Resident Evil 0.

After playing it through, I can now understand what an experience it must have been for those who had a Gamecube (the original console it came out to first in 2002) back then. In 2016 it still is incredibly enjoyable. Everything is in place: spooky atmosphere, beautiful underground locations, logical, but sometimes unrealistic puzzles, naive but loveable characters, the herbs, and everything the Resident Evil series is known of.

The game follows the old school Resident Evil scheme from RE 1, 2 and 3. That being said, there are semi-fixed camera positions (there are locations where it follows the character) from a perspective of a monster, which adds to the horror sensation (introduced by the great Alone in the Dark from 1992) and console based controls (good advice: if you want to enjoy the game, get a controller and make sure it's heavy).

The protagonist of the game is Rebecca Chambers, a young medical officer, the girl trapped in one of the rooms from the original Resident Evil. I dare to say she is one of the most loveable characters in gaming history, even though she is a pretty standard Japanese-made female character. Her naiveness and surprised looks can charm even female gamers who would otherwise find her irritating. Not long after the beginning she is joined by an ex-marine, Billy, who had apparently been sentenced to death for murder. After a thrilling zombie infested train ride, the duo begins to investigate an abandoned facility (very similar to the manor from Resident Evil) and of course to escape with their lives.

The story as far as the Resident Evil series go, is very good and we can finally discover how it all started: who was the creator of the T-virus, what species it was tested on originally, how famous characters, such as Wesker came into play and so on. We get a pretty detailed background in Resident Evil lore.

The greatest improvement of the game is the partner system. Almost through the entire game the player gets to control both Rebecca and Billy. Of course only one at a time, but switching between the two is almost immediate. Switching and using them separately is sometimes vital for solving puzzles (pushing two buttons at the same time, etc.). In combat having a partner is also useful, even though in some places it is advised to leave the other one behind, because having two characters also means taking double damage. The attributes of Rebecca and Billy are also different (although only slightly): Rebecca can mix things (in the other RE games everyone was capable of doing this) and can fit into smaller places, while Billy takes less damage from attacks and can push heavier objects (the latter is used only maybe twice throughout the entire game). 
The other thing to point out is that you can leave things anywhere (there are no chests as in RE 1-3), which is a good and a bad thing. Good because with the very limited inventory you can't carry much and you can leave stuff whereever you want to, but it also means that you can't access it later from a storage chest and all you can do is backtrack (even though the items appear on the map). There are also things you have to keep for a long time, the hookshot for example, a tool that takes up 1/3 of your inventory space (you should only throw it away when you find the Magnum in the tram).

The creators came up with quite a lot of new enemies, the leeches above all. As seen in the intro, these little infected creatures are going to stir up a lot of trouble. Besides the good old RE enemies (zombie dobermans, hunters, crows) there are plenty of arch enemies as well, that are all creative enough, but I still liked the ones from the original better. In point of weapons the only new thing here is the molotov cocktail (Billy can also mix this) made of gasoline and empty bottles (so if you find any, mix them immediately) and it's useful against a certain type of enemy (one that is very hard to kill otherwise ;)).

Graphically the game is astonishing. The contrast between the 3d character models and the background is gone, the pin-sharp textures are good to look at and the realistic lighting and shadows also work well. The environment in the train segment is stunning. Rebecca's character is also beautiful, but this can't be said about the others, in Billy's case it looks a bit dated, but overall the characters are well animated, lively and their movement is fluid as it can be.

http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=614339403

I can also praise the sound effects and the tunes, which are both great and add their shares to the atmosphere. Some old sound effects are also known from previous RE games (door creaking, footsteps on metal stairs) which successfully add some nostalgia. The dialogues are a bit childish and may appear they were taken straight out of a B-movie, but hey, it's Japanese after all and still, they are much better than your ordinary RE lines ("That was too close, you were almost a Jill sandwich!" :P)

Resident Evil Zero was originally released on Gamecube in 2002, and was also ported to the Wii in 2008. I never played either of those versions, which means I can't really comment on how faithful this HD remake is, so I will simply judge this version on its own merits. On the whole I enjoyed playing the game, although it does have some problems.

As the name suggests, Zero is a prequel to RE1. There are two playable characters, STARS member Rebecca, and convicted criminal Billy. The player can switch between them at will, with the AI controlling the other character, or you can explore with one character on their own. Billy has more health, is strong enough to move heavy objects, and has a cigarette lighter, whilst Rebecca can mix herbs and other chemicals.

Gameplay contains both the good and the bad of old school survival horror. Combat is a slower pace, there are a small number of monsters, but each one is dangerous. Resource management is key, because ammo and healing items are scarce, so you can't afford to waste any. Puzzles are intelligently designed to require both characters working together.

Unfortunately the fixed camera angles are far more annoying than I remember in RE1. There is a ridiculous number of combat encounters where the monster is off screen, my character is looking at the monster, but I can't see what they see, because I'm forced to look at my character, which makes aiming more difficult than it should be. Thankfully the partner AI is pretty useful, although I'm not sure if "standing still while the AI shoots the monsters" qualifies as playing the game. I'm so glad later games in the franchise dropped the fixed camera angles.

Most of the boss fights are frustrating, because they always disable one character during a cutscene, meaning you can't access their inventory. I always died on the first attempt just because I ran out of ammo, having split my ammo between the two characters. On my second attempt, armed with advanced knowledge of what is about to happen, I gave all my weapons/ammo to the character who wouldn't be disabled and got an easy kill. I don't mind dying in games if I make a mistake, but this felt "cheap".

This game has the same mouse pointer bug that the RE1 HD remake had. If you play with mouse and keyboard, the mouse pointer will constantly be visible on screen. The only solution is to play with a gamepad and push the mouse pointer off screen. Fortunately the controls work well with a gamepad, but I don't understand why Capcom are having so much difficulty figuring out how a mouse works. 

Ultimately I think you need to be an existing fan of the Resident Evil franchise, and be willing to overlook some problems, to enjoy RE Zero. If you've never played Resident Evil before, I would recommend starting with better games such as RE1, or RE Revelations 1 &2, and then grab Zero if you find yourself wanting more.

Resident Evil 0 made its original debut on the Gamecube back in late 2002. The installment set out to clarify the start of the outbreak in Raccoon City in a somewhat "origin story" fashion. The game features two main characters, ex-US Marine Lieutenant Billy Coen, who makes his debut appearance, and S.T.A.R.S. Bravo Team Medic Rebecca Chambers, who appeared in the first Resident Evil game.

Most importantly, let's discuss the HD remaster aspect of this title. Resident Evil 0 runs flawlessly, it's an outstanding port that doesn't suffer from any crashes, bugs, glitches, or framerate drops. I had my framerate set to 85 for the duration of my two playthroughs, and I never saw the rate drop below 83. The optimization is both incredible and commendable. Furthermore, the work that Capcom put into revamping the textures and character models really shines here. Sure, the cutscenes are still old and have not been updated whatsoever; that's nothing new for HD remasters, but everything else has the same sharpness and gleam to it that the Resident Evil HD remaster has. Even the windows have dynamic and clear reflections. The 5.1 audio upgrade really stands out if you have a gaming headset capable of rendering either 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound, and it really helps to tell which direction enemies are going to come from. The subtle ambiance of the game has also been severely upgraded.

So the port and HD upgrades are great, but what about the game itself? Well, RE0 is definitely no RE4, but it's still a decent game and also a highly important one for those who care about the plot of the franchise. Seeing as I never have owned a Gamecube, I never got the chance to play this particular title until now. Throughout the game, you will learn about the origin of the infamous T-Virus and who created it, along with the origins of the Umbrella Corporation, how Albert Wesker got his start, various prototypes and early stages for certain key monsters such as the Lickers, and other tidbits of information that you'll be able to use to piece together information from later games if you have played them.

You start off playing as Rebecca Chambers, on a mission to find criminal Billy Coen who is rumored to have killed 25 people. Your search soon leads you into a train, where all hell breaks loose. Soon you meet up with Billy, who becomes your co-op partner for the remainder of the game. You're able to control both characters both at the same time, and independently. Many times, the characters will have to split up and go separate ways in order to solve puzzles or to get each other out of sticky situations. The main game leads you from the train through the vast Umbrella Training Facility, which is where you will spend about 90% of your time. Although the map of the game isn't incredibly large or varying in comparison to later titles, since RE0 is a prequel the smallness of the world is justifiable.

A huge pain point for Resident Evil 0 is the abysmal lack of storage boxes. Sure, any fan of the franchise has gotten used to dealing with cramped inventory space; it's a staple to the gameplay. Though to my best recollection, every other title in the series has had some form of storage. In RE0, you're left to scattering your items on the floor and then taking on the painstaking task to move every item as you progress into new sections of the game. This might not sound awful, but when coupled with the slow door-opening animations, it really is quite time consuming. It's also extra annoying when the save room (any room with a typewriter) that you're attempting to dump your precious cargo in says that you cannot leave any more items in the room. This leaves you with the option to either forget about the item, or dump it in a different nearby room.

Once you beat the game, you will open up two new modes; Wesker Mode and Leech Hunter. Let me begin by saying that Wesker Mode is just so lazy and tacky that it is painful. This mode simply reskins Billy as Wesker, and gives him two new abilities; Death Stare and Shadow Dash. The cutscenes remain the same, featuring Billy, and Capcom didn't even take the time or put in the effort to change the audio. When playing as Wesker, you will still hear Billy's voice, and people will still refer to him as Billy. However, Wesker is extremely powerful and his Death Stare can kill many enemies in a single hit; zombies, hunters, monkeys, plague crawlers, etc. As well, many bosses are made significantly easier and take only 3-4 hits before they're toast. This is a perfect mode for speed running or grabbing hard to get achievements. However, this mode isn't anything to scream about. Leech Hunter is even more mundane, as you take Billy and Rebecca back into the Training Facility to collect blue and green leech charms; there are 50 of each, you're under no time limit, there are enemies to take care of, and the game is over once you either leave the Facility or die.

The main story of Resident Evil 0 will run you anywhere from 8-15 hours, depending on what difficulty you play on and if you use a guide. After that, there's really not a whole lot to do other than try for some achievements or check out the two modes that are unlocked upon completion; however those may not hold the interest of many. I wouldn't say that this installment is a must play by any means, but it's definitely a worthwhile origin story and those who are major Resident Evil fans should check it out.

After the success of the remaster of the remade Resident Evil, CAPCOM dove back into the archives and remastered Resident Evil 0 (which was developed on the same engine for the Gamecube).

One thing that can be said right off the bat is just how much a work of art the game really is. One of the beauties of this genre and franchise originally was the highly detailed static environments of the original mansion and subsequent environs. When given the level of time, adding on top of that would seem like a rare success but in this case CAPCOM's team emphasized this perfectly. From the train to the training facility and everything thereafter, the player is inundated with shadowplay, detail and an overall enjoyable atmospheric experience. There are some elements that actually look pixelated such as the fireplace in the training facility off the balcony, but they are so rare that they needn't be mentioned.

The sound mastery and soundtrack itself are, yet again, another original that was simply touched up and gained greater eminence because of it. The theme to the training facility might be my favorite track from all of the Resident Evils. It encapsulates that feeling of being trapped in a large, eery place with such perfection. You can hear it 100 times and it still retains, if builds upon, it's original quality. And like many of the franchises' best from pre-RE5, the rest of the soundtrack holds a similar quality that helps create the sensory immersion and atmosphere that made the original so great.

Gameplay wise, it is just as the original which really means not complicated in the least. Very straightforward, and for some, a little sluggish. But not too much so to where it isn't enjoyable even for those who are used to variations on the modern FPS.

The negative aspects of the game really only come from a previous memory of the game. For instance, the faces of Rebecca and Billy have been touched up in certain areas and definitely seem different from the game I remember as a kid. Same can be said with the in-menu faces above the item slots. Also, the FMVs during cutscenes do look slightly dated, but not to the point where it detracts from the story or the game itself.


While I may be a little biased I still give it a solid 8/10 for being shrewdly touched-up version of the original, which supplanted itself in my mind as a child as one of the best horror games ever created.

Its just like the original Resident Evil game, but with extremely upgraded graphics. Very fluid looking and very fun. If a challenge doesn't bother you, pick this one up. Its hard, but its worth it. For a retro style game - 10/10

Resident Evil 0 is a lot of fun. It's more of the campy, gory, spooky good time we enjoy from the RE series and it offers a robust challenge. Lots of dying in this game. This is the last in the series that is essentially an action packed point-and-click adventure game and I appreciate the opportunity to play RE0 once again. Sure the puzzles are not necessarily realistic, but the whole series is always bordering on parody as it is. The level design isn't as strong as in previous titles of the series and some of the environments gave a strong sense of deja vu. The very worst thing about this game, though, is the inventory management. Holy f.ck! Each character can only hold six items and there was always a constant need to switch items between characters, leave items in a room and then have to hike all the way back for them once there was enough room in the inventory. Some items even took up two spots in the inventory. I understand this was a necessary feature for how some of the puzzles were designed, but... how dare they! There is a lot of back tracking in game simply because of the terrible inventory system. The main villain was laughably awful too. Everything he said was re-tarded and he looked like some androgynous NPC from a Final Fantasy game. Don't get me wrong, the puzzle solving, exploration, and blowing away monsters were a grand time and most of the game is spent doing these things. It took around 15 hours to finish the game for the first time. There's definitely incentive to re-play it too; and not just because it's a fun game in general either. After finishing the game for the first time, the ability to play as Wesker is unlocked. This is essentially easy mode. He has an attack that can clear a room faster than grandma's chili. It was a thrill to see groups of enemies all instantly drop dead in unison from a single blast. Boss battles became a breeze. Most only took around 3 blasts from Wesker to kill. There's another mode that wasn't as interesting to me where Rebecca and Billy need to find leech charms scattered throughout the mansion. RE0 still looks pretty good after all these years. Kudos to Capcom for the job they did polishing this game up, getting it ready for this HD release. The water animations stand out as the most impressive part of the presentation. Slime oozes from leeches, water from a filled sink splashes around dripping to the floor, and the rain beats down on top of the train all in convincing fashion, to give a few examples. Even a very simple cut-scene of water flowing from a pipe was impressive to watch. From a technical standpoint, the game ran flawlessly. The frame rate was consistently a rock solid 60fps and the game never crashed. RE0 won't win any converts to the series, but it's still a really good game that I highly recommend, even if it doesn't reach as high levels the series has previously reached.

I've had an amazing time with this game. Being a massive fan of the RE series, especially  the more 'classic' style games, this was the best thing I've played since, well, REmake HD to be honest. The partner mechanic mixed with the limited inventory system makes for some interesting tactical choices. I found myself unequipping the useless AI and using them as a pack mule, using my armed character to scout ahead and my then bringing in the unequipped character as a pack mule. Unfortunately when buddied up, the partner AI is prone to wasting ammo and running straight into the enemies arms and is one of the few cons i have against the game. 

In regards to the inventory management, the ability to drop items is a mixed blessing. While I didnt suffer too much backtracking, I did have to cart myself all the way to an area I visited hours ago as I hadn't been able to bring my grenade launcher with me. With it being just before the final boss, it killed my momentum a little. That said, it does add more depth to the gameplay than the 'magic box' system favoured by the other classic titles and goes a long way to underlining the survival aspect of Survival Horror. 

My playthrough took me 6 in game hours (according to my ranking at the end) or around 8-9 actual hours with deaths and reloads. I found that Normal was actually quite challening, more so than REmake HD. In fact Zero is up there with Code Veronica as personally what I believe to be the most challenging games in the series. With that in mind though the tougher than average difficulty really helped keep me invested in the game. If like me, its your first time playing this since the Gamecube days, then you arent going to have a lot of surplus ammo or healing items even by the end boss. I appreciated this personally, as I find with most RE games, the difficulty drops off sharply after the first half, by which point the 'magic box' has enough ammo and herbs in to last for another full playthough. 

Graphically, I can't fault the presentation at all. While being less atmospheric that REmake, the environments still sing with the HD makeover. Character models, lighting and shadows are all very immersive too. With everything maxed my mid range PC never struggled to keep a 60hz refresh rate.

In terms of story, its probably one of the weaker of the series to be honest. It perhaps takes itself too seriously compared to the more 'B-Movie' values of the earlier installments. The story is serviceable but in all honesty, as a prequel it fails to tell us anything that would be integral to the understanding of the plot of the subsequent games. Dialog and cutscenes are actually quite sparse and it would have probably benefitted the game to have more interaction between the 2 playable characters. As it stands, they barely say a word to each other once their characters have been established. 

There's plenty more I could say but the most important thing is I strongly reccomend the game. I actually enjoyed it a lot more than I did around 10+ years ago when I first played it. If you have the determination and the patience this is a great title thats more than worth the budget price.

Resident Evil 0 deserves more credit.

Of all the more traditional games in the series prior to Resident Evil 4's more action-y gameplay overhaul, 0 receives the most trash talk. It first appeared in 2002, well after all but the most ardent of fans were tired of the survival horror formula and ready for something new. Despite a few minor additions, Resident Evil 0 didn't offer that.

But that's precisely why this Resident Evil 0 HD re-release from Capcom is so useful. With distance from the atmosphere surrounding its release, it's a lot easier to view Resident Evil 0 for exactly what it is: a flawed but generally satisfying and, more importantly, smart take on Capcom's approach to horror.


And yet, aside from the very last area, I found Resident Evil 0's locales interesting enough to alleviate any frustration from backtracking. These are tightly-designed settings, paced perfectly to emphasize tension. I was rarely sent running in a direction I'd already been in without the area suddenly being invaded by a new nightmare creature, or without finding myself unexpectedly stalked by a returning foe. Even as the game advanced and I built up a healthy backpack of ammunition for my guns, I always felt just one or two bad rooms away from losing everything.

For as much as Resident Evil 0 embraces the series' classic gameplay, it also adopts the goofy, heavy-handed and poorly voice-acted storytelling of the franchise's earliest entries. If you're expecting serious drama from Rebecca and Billy, you're in for a disappointment, and don't even get me started on the game's hilariously ineffective villain. But if you love the cornier approach to survival horror, before everything took itself so seriously, it's a blast.

Removed from the moment in time when it debuted, Resident Evil 0 is just a really good classic RE game. It didn't set the standards for this style of game the way Resident Evil 1 did; it's not as ambitious or unblemished as Resident Evil 2. But it's far from the mess that history made it out to be. Whether you're a veteran who's played it before or a new fan who never tried out Resident Evil 0, it's good enough to deserve this second chance.

As you may already know, Resident Evil Zero (RE0) is a prequel to the very first Resident Evil (RE) game. If you remember the opening scene of the first RE, a Special Tactics and Rescue Service (S.T.A.R.S.) team consisting of Jill Valentine, Albert Wesker, Chris Redfield and Barry Burton (Alpha Team) are sent to find out what happened to Bravo Team, with whom they’ve lost contact. The mission of both teams was to investigate mysterious murders that have been happening on the outskirts of Raccoon City. They discover Bravo Team’s downed helicopter in the Racoon Forest, but no sign of survivors. Their search eventually leads them to the legendary mansion from the first game. In RE0, we get to find out what happened to Bravo Team as well as story elements that ties this game to future games. RE0 begins with an Umbrella owned train traveling en-route through the Raccoon Forest. It comes under attack by scary…”leeches”. These leeches seem to be under the control of an androgynous Final Fantasy-esque character who, for some reason, is accompanied by majestic opera music whenever he is on screen. We then cut to the Bravo Team helicopter which is en-route to the outskirts. For reasons unknown, their helicopter is damaged and they are forced to make an emergency landing in the forest. What happens next is for you to find out. I will say this - don’t set your expectations too high story wise. This is honestly B-grade SyFy channel plot material here. However it’s all about the good ol’ survival horror at the end of the day.

RE0 is a very polished remaster. The game runs buttery smooth in 1080p at 60fps (in 16:9 widescreen). Not only that but the game now has added support for 5.1 surround sound, which really amplifies the creepy ambiance. Also added are several new control schemes, so pick one that best suits you. Keep in mind though - this is the same GameCube game from back in the day, just with updated graphics (and sound). If you were hoping that Capcom went the extra mile to remove those tedious loading animations, you are going to be disappointed. [i]Every single time[/i] that you open a door (or climb stairs and ladders) you [i]will[/i] be treated to a "movie" that shows the door opening (or the stairs being climbed etc). Mentally prepare yourself for this.

You control two main characters in the game - S.T.A.R.S. Rookie Rebecca Chambers and alleged criminal Billy Coen. These characters each have their unique traits. For example, Rebecca has the alchemist ability to mix herbs and Billy has the factory-man ability to move heavy boxes. Naturally, the game will present situations in which you need to determine the best character to use at a given time. The character that you choose to take control of is the “Main” character and the other becomes the “Partner” character (and CPU controlled). You can switch who you want as your Main and Partner at any time. You can give orders to your Partner character - such as to follow you, stay put and attack/don’t attack. Learn this mechanic. Also, I should warn you about Rebecca. Be very careful with her as she’s quite a fragile woman. If she even smells the bad breath of a zombie, her health is going to go down. Billy, on the other hand, being a former marine and all, is a tough guy and can take quite a beating before his health drops.

Having two characters to control means that you have two inventories to manage. Sadly, both characters’ inventories are very small and non-upgradeable. Therefore, a huge aspect of the game is item management. You will have to get used to abandoning items in order to make room for higher priority items, then backtracking for the items you left behind at a later time. Here’s a tip. In the mansion area, there’s a save point at the bottom of the stairs when you first get there (the main hall). You will be spending a considerable amount of time running in and out of this area. So you can use this area as a “hub”. A convenient place to leave items you don’t need at the moment. Speaking of save points, here’s an aspect of the game that will surely add to the tension - limited saves! You save by collecting ink ribbons and using them at Typewriters. If you save too much, you might run out of ribbons! So, save wisely.

Now, let’s talk about actually playing the game. All of the game’s locations are pre-rendered, with pre-assigned camera angles. Nothing new if you're an old school veteran but if experiencing this for the first time, get ready for some awkward situations in which you are shooting at things and you can’t even see the things you’re shooting at because they are off-screen. Also, if you’re accustomed to modern RE games, you might have the mindset that headshots are the way to go. This is not the case here. All you need to do is pump bullets into the enemy until they curl up dead on the floor. An exception to this is the shotgun. It is very simple and quite satisfying to obliterate zombie heads with the shotgun. Simply aim up, wait for your victim to walk within range and pull the trigger.

Now it would not be a RE game without special enemies and bosses. The theme of RE0 seems to be - wildlife. You’ve got Frogs, Scorpions, Rabid Dogs, Monkeys, Birds, Bats, Centipedes, Spiders and some weird Leech controlled zombies. Some of these wildlife are boss fights. You can’t avoid them. The rest of them are annoying as hell. Instead of fighting these things, your best bet is to probably avoid them and run the hell away. That’s another decision you will be making a lot - when to fight and when to run. Sometimes the Coward’s route is best.

So how are the boss fights? Well some are more fun than others. Also, almost all of them just happen at random, for no apparent reason. Sometimes you’re going your merry way and all of a sudden, there’s a boss. Oh well. That’s life. The good thing about this is that it adds an element of unpredictability that will keep you on your toes, which I like in a horror game. There is one in particular that annoyed the hell out of me though. The Bat fight. You see, the way the targeting system works in this game is you press the target button and it targets an enemy. Then you press it again and it switches to another. You can’t command the thing to target the enemy you want, as it just cycles through enemies until it gets to the one you want. So, this is the Bat fight. It starts off all well and good because it’s just me and Bat. However when the Bat gets hurt enough, it calls in some minion bats to help it out. So at this point, I’m really irritated because I’m trying to line up a shot on the main Bat but the minions keep getting in the way and my targeting system keeps targeting them instead of the main Bat. Then while that’s going on the main Bat swoops in casually, picks me up and flings me around the room. Thankfully, the other boss fights weren’t as frustrating as that one.

Now let’s talk about game length. I completed the game between 6-7hrs on Normal difficulty and was awarded a B-rank for my troubles. There is a bonus "Wesker Mode" that you unlock once you beat the game that allows you play as the man himself. Plus there’s a ton of replayabiliy if you want to get all of the achievements or a better rank. However looking at some of those achievements (going through the game without healing or saving?) I have a feeling only crazy people will attempt those. They are surely not for me. At the end of it all I did have a good time with this game. Once I got into the groove of things I enjoyed all the strategy involved with managing items & switching between characters to solve puzzles. The story as I mentioned before isn't stellar but RE games aren't known for having stellar plots anyway. I liked it for what it is and if you're a fan, you'll more than likely find it to be a worthy prequel. Whether all of that is worth the $20 asking price is up to you.

One of the weakest of the best is still good, right? Resident Evil 0 is a rather mediocre entry among the absolute best classic Resident Evil titles, which means, it's still way above a lot of classic survival horror wannabes. And in its HD Remake version the game got better. Not just visually, like it mostly was with REmaster (not like it was a bad thing, mind you) - RE0 HD is actually more fun to play than the original GC (and later Wii) release.

Resident Evil 0 itself is a game with a long history of development. Prequel idea started being R&D'ed before RE1 was even released, game was finally shown in some playable state on N64 in 2000, but it seems like a lot of post-train story and gameplay was still not 100% set. After that the development was completely restarted for GC alongside REmake with slight story adjustments for both for continuity. And I think for a lot of people the concept of the "Resident Evil on a train" was something that stuck with them - it sounded interesting and new. And it actually is. Sadly, the Train is only about 1/5 of the entire game.

The game has a lot of intersting concepts - two playable characters at once, change from item boxes to "put item on the ground anywhere", a bit more emphasis on unique abilities of playable characters - something RE1 introduced and since hasn't really been used again in the series. But it's the implementation that makes it all go average instead of great. Playing as two characters is not as fun as it could be, item management is more forced and boring and unique abilities of characters apart from gameplay differences (Billy deals with recoil better and gets hurt less), are very rarely used despite the possibilities. Even the ideas from other games in the series up to that point, are either unused or underused - zombies travel across rooms only once, Crimson Heads are not here, there's no dodging or self-defence items, no creepy pursuing enemies (just an annoying, but often easily skippable, leech-monster), no real scenario variety.

But the main downer is the levels and the overall feel of the game. Story is all over the place, never sticking to any particular tone, with jRPG fabulous-looking evil guy being the main bad, game opening with documentary style narration (but never going back to it), character suddenly referencing the future (because it's prequel, you see?). And yes, it's storytelling in Resident Evil, who cares, right? Well, thing is - no matter how silly a lot of RE stories went, they usually did it with style and in a memorable cool way. RE0 is just "eh, it happened, I guess". And the levels are just... boring. So are the bosses. They all feel like a collection of discarded classic RE ideas put together in one game. It also cannot really choose between the more colorful and stylish look of classic PS1-era REs and the "creepy old" look of REmake, something that was improved a lot in the HD Remaster (original was very gray/yellow-ish), but still feels not as good as other games.

But HD Remaster fixes not just visual issues and makes the game look very good. In addition, it adds several welcome changes in the controls (realtime reload button is a cool thing), most notable of which is the alternative control scheme. Now it was also present in REmaster, however REmake worked perfectly fine with classic tank controls - all the animations felt right, moving and shooting and evading was fun to master and use. In RE0 original tank controls have a slight delay due to additional animation frames for a lot of actions which are simply removed in alt. control scheme, making it a much better option, especially when controlling the partner character, even despite few places, where camera changes to screw up your movement. In addition to that, game also gets a silly and fun to play Wesker mode, where Billy is changed into RE5-style Wesker, who can run at super speed and explode enemies with his aura at will. It's a ridiculous mode, that gets even sillier when you complete it once, as sadly there is no Wesker Leech Hunter, but all the rewards in the game are just unlocked for the second playthrough. It's funny, it's fun, it's a nice way to relax after Leech Hunter or hard mode playthrough, and it's always fun to explode zombie heads with your thoughts.

So, is it a good game to get? Well, if you like classic survival horror and this is the game you've missed before - definitely. If you're a fan of RE series - yep. If you want to get into classic survival horrors - only after you try out better options. REmaster is a better option, but I would've suggested checking RE Director's Cut (just not dual shock ver., if you value your ears), 2 and 3 as well, if possible. And same goes for people who are just checking this out without knowledge of the genre and the series - this is a rather good way, but there are better options to start with.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
Disclaimer: Disregard my hours played as of this review (almost three). I played this extensively on GameCube, finished it on all difficulties, and even went through again using just the rocket launcher. As the gameplay itself hasn’t really changed, this should not be an issue in terms of time spent in-game.

Resident Evil 0 is both good and bad in so many ways, and some of them aren’t even related to this HD remaster. I’m a Resident Evil junkie, and I have been since I got hooked on the PSX original back in 1996, after reading a review of it in Game Informer, one of those things called magazines that you had to buy at stores or wait for it to arrive by mail.

Resident Evil 0 was the last “real” Resident Evil, a slow and methodical game, before Capcom decided the non-stop action and set pieces were the way to go. Not a knock against Resident Evil 4, though. RE4 was a terrific game, it just wasn’t a terrific Resident Evil game.

That said, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster is a fantastic remaster. It shines on PC. The enhanced graphics bring the backgrounds to life, you can read signs and notices that were blurry on the GameCube version, the story (while not the best in the series) does an excellent job of providing more background on Umbrella, and while it introduced a couple of new things to the series (character switching, ability to drop items), it also removed some (such as item boxes).

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*]Graphics are very well done, and Capcom has done an excellent job of bringing the backgrounds to life; both Rebecca and Billy look better than ever
[*]Lots of story to uncover, which gives further insight into the minds of Umbrella’s execs
[*]Puzzles are fun (but haven’t changed), and switching between both characters to solve them feels natural as opposed to a “just because” mechanic
[*]Music is fantastic and sets the mood perfectly
[*]Sound effects are excellent
[*]Enemies are greatly detailed
[*]Decent length
[*]The story, while not the greatest, is still entertaining
[*]Tank controls have been retained (I’m a fan)
[*]Voice acting is as bad as before, but seeing as how it’s a Resident Evil game, that’s fine
[/list]
[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*]Nothing has changed gameplay wise; if you beat this on GameCube way back, you’ll know exactly what to do
[*]Cutscenes appear to be original, and therefore look very low-def compared to the in-game scenes
[*]Not much replaybility, unless you’re looking to catch up on achievements you’ve missed
[*]Micro management is more prevalent, as item boxes are no longer a thing
[/list]
[h1]Summary[/h1]
It’s Resident Evil, you either love it or hate it. It’s great because it’s the slow paced explorative gameplay that Resident Evil was, but it’s sad because it truly is the last of its kind (Resident Evil 4, 5, 6, forthcoming Umbrella Chronicles, etc).

Regardless of your view on the game, it’s well worth the time. It is a great revisit for old fogies like me, and it’s a great survival horror game for newcomers. As long as you don’t compare this to the current crop of horror games, you’ll enjoy yourself.

Somehow, Capcom managed to make this game look even better than Resident Evil 1 HD. I can't place my finger on it but it overall looks crisper. Almost as if they've done more effort than before. Capcom one again brings a classic title to Steam in full HD Glory, an overlooked gem from 2002. They completely remastered every background this time because they had access to the original game files so that's a plus. Everything from the original is carried over along with a few extras made exclusively for the remaster itself.

[b]New stuff included in the Remaster include:[/b]
- Wesker Mode (Beat the game once on any difficulty to unlock)
- Full HD Backgrounds
- Gallery Mode (Includes all the game FMV's, Unlocked from the start and progresses as you do)
- 60 fps (PC Exclusive) consoles are locked to 30, variable frame rate is included.
- New control scheme similar to the action games, various layouts to choose from
- Exclusives costumes, were shown as in game but are actually paid DLC which is typical Capcom
- 5 fan made t-shirts for free if you voted during the campaign 

Already played through the entire campaign and Leech Mode and I had no issues with the gameplay itself. Mechanic/story wise nothing was changed from the original 2002 release which isn't a bad thing. Capcom attempted to bring co-op to the game but it didn't work, pretty obvious why it wouldn't work.

[b]Item Management[/b] is very different from other RE games, this one elimates the need for Item Boxes completely from the start. Newcomers will probably hate the constant backtracking to find items they dropped but old school players will feel right at home. If you are having issues locating items go into your Map and turn on the UI, for some reason reviewers didn't mention this and people are having issues finding it.

[b]Graphic options[/b] are pretty much the game as Remake Remastered from last year, according to most people the backgrounds are locked to 1440 resolution again. Running the game on max settings I was able to play through the entire game without slowdown except the area where you meet your first leech, I think there's a bug here with the flame effects. Other than that I had a constant 60fps experience, also tried variable which for some reason locked the game to 45 fps, tried 30fps for the hell of it and it was too slow for me lol.

Overall, if you're a hardcore RE fan from the early days you should pick it up. If you're newcomer and have patience I'd reccommend trying the game out, just don't expect an action experience this one is a bit slower than the original game but it offers solid gameplay if you give it a chance. Only thing I feel needs work is the control scheme, I dunno who's idea it was to map the run button to X but that needs to be changed. They should have just given the option of using the original gamecube layout.

I'm here to briefly (and straight to the point) tell you about the quality of the Remaster itself. Spoiler-free.
The entire game is one huge eyecandy, every background has been re-rendered, they're at way more higher resolution and do not have obvious compression artifacts. Moving parts of the backgrounds, lighting, shadows, item icons, some 3D objects and bloom were drastically improved along with some character model and font tweaks. Just like in RE1HD you can rebind KB&M controls to your liking (with the exception of mouse, it seems, as it's used for aiming and shooting by default).

The game itself is mostly left unchanged, but it has a couple of extra bonuses added like the Wesker mode where you use RE5 Wesker's special abilities to battle BOWs. This mode is unlocked when you finish the game at least once. There are also extra purchasable DLC costumes if you're into that sorta thing. Worth mentioning that this game supports achievements some of which are rather creative.

As for port itself it's the superior version among the platforms offering you variable framerate refresh rate, 4K resolution, but for whatever reason lacks DoF (blur in distance) which is currently present on PS4. For some with weak/machines with compatibility issues the game might run in slow motion (if you had this issue with RE4UHD, RE1HD then you'll likely have it here). Also currently there's bug with doors stuttering a bit when opened, likely a cache issue (not present on newer graphics cards).

If you care about Survival Horror in this industry and/or oldschool RE then you should pick this up.

After I finished my first playthrough ever of this game (Never played RE0 on GCN), I think it's time for a review.
This is a great game, I'm a long time Resident Evil fan and this game didn't disappoint me at all. While I think it did most things really well, there were some others that I didn't like as much, but I'll get to that later.

Let's start off with the technical stuff. Oh man, this game is a wonderful remaster. The graphics are unbelieveable good, considering that this is originally a game from 2002. The backgrounds, although pre-rendered, have never been so dynamic, it's often hard to distinguish between pre-rendered and actual rendered models because they are both so detailed, pre-rendered backgrounds have never looked so good.
Force Feedback/Controller vibration is also a thing, even during the cutscenes, and it underlines some intense moments very well.
The controls also received an overhaul. In my review of the HD REmaster I complained about the new control scheme, feeling out of place by making character movement look unnatural and that you need to adjust your stick when the camera changes. While the latter problem presists, the movement feels much more natural now. Definitely an improvement.
You can now also set the refresh rate to up to 144 Hz, while the HD REmaster only allowed 60 Hz.

[u]SPOILERS FROM HERE ON IN:[/u]

Next up is the game itself. The gameplay is solid, it might feel strange controlling 2 characters at first, but you'll get used to it. You can switch between the characters almost anytime, and they both have different strenghts and weaknesses.
A weaker point of the game is, in my opinion, the plot. While I love the RE storyline, this one had a few elements that I didn't like. Don't get me wrong, I know Resident Evil isn't know for it's perfect writing, but this one seemed a bit weaker compared to the other games. First off, Marcus in his young/leech/whatever form. The way he looks is just ridiculous, and that chorus like singing...just no. Another point I didn't like so much was Billy's backstory. The guerilla village thing just seemed too forced and didn't fit into the story at all. The message "war is bad" dosen't fit into Resident Evil, we have other game series like Metal Gear for that.
Where this game really shines is level design. It's so good I could talk about it the whole day, but I'll try to keep it short.
First off is are the settings. The train is awesome, the atmosphere of it driving during rain, all the moving objects on the tables...just perfect. The training facility is probably the longest part of the game. One might say it's basically a cheap version of the mansion from RE1, but I would have to disagree. My favoriten part however is the factory. In this part you are seperated from Billy, so you are alone and can only play as Rebecca. Here you will revisit some places from Resident Evil 2, and I would have to lie to say that it didn't make me feel a bit nostalgic.
Then there are also the treatment facility and laboratory, which also have great level design. The way you have to interact with your partner over different rooms is just amazingly thought through, no argument there.

[b]tl;dr[/b]
+amazing level design and atmosphere
+slow paced gameplay, with an overall good character switch system
+excellent soundtrack

-plot has it's weakpoints

Resident Evil 0 was the ninth game in the titanically influential series and arguably the last to showcase a style that modern gaming was fast leaving behind. The pre-drawn environments, the fixed camera angles, the creaky door cinematics that covered the loading times between areas, having to stand in exactly the right bloody spot to pick up an item... they would all disappear quickly after Zero, leaving the radically different masterpiece that was Resident Evil 4 to pick up the pieces. 

Even so, Capcom had already begun to change their gameplan here, introducing a buddy system in which the player freely shared control of the game's two main characters: S.T.A.R.S medic Rebecca Chambers (who you might remember from RE1 as the mostly useless pianist who rescued Chris Redfield's cack-fingered attempts to play Moonlight Sonata) and convicted ex-soldier Billy Coen. Although control of multiple characters was nothing new in the franchise, here it was the centerpiece of the game as most of the puzzles and combat scenarios are engineered to require each character's strengths and to prey on their weaknesses.

I played Resident Evil 0 to death when it originally made its appearance on the Gamecube back in 2002 and, although it did truly rock some ingenuous design, the controls were an absolute horror show especially in any combat scenario. If you've spent any time with the original version, you'll immediately notice how far improved they are in this remaster along with some truly stunning visuals. I'm a sucker for the pre-drawn background art style and it has never looked better than it does here. Also added for a bonus playthrough is Wesker Mode which really does what it says on the tin: blaze through the game as Johnny Bravo's evil twin, sneering and shadow-punching zombies into twitching mulch.

Remaining unchanged, however, is the game's notorious inventory system which truly is the most unforgiving in the entire series. You will often find yourself having to leave useful items behind for sheer lack of carrying space which can mostly be blamed on the Hookshot; a vital piece of equipment that has to be dragged through much of the game while occupying a gluttonous two squares of inventory room. The sheer amount of micromanagement between characters, especially with only Rebecca being able to create healing items, was a pain in arse then and it's a pain in the arse now.

With that said, whatever faults Resident Evil 0 might suffer are relatively minor. It's one of the weaker titles in the franchise but it's certainly far better than the catastrophe that was [b]RE6[/b] and when you consider that it's only really weak in comparison to the mighty original trilogy, the excellent Code Veronica and REMake and the near-flawless Resident Evil 4, well... that's barely a criticism at all really.

The HD Remaster of REmake was put down a bit due to the developers not having original sources for most of the backdrops, so a lot of scenes looked grainy or artifacted, especially if you were playing in HD, and it made 3D geometry like items or puzzle objects stand out awkwardly. In RE0 HD this has been completely fixed, and whether you choose to play in widescreen or in the original aspect ratio everything except the cutscenes looks fantastic. The game still has the same problem with mouse and keyboard play as REmake HD did in that the cursor never goes off screen, so I did play it with a gamepad, but if you can ignore the cursor it controls fine either way. The main new addition aside from the DLC costumes is Wesker Mode, which is an amusing little extra mode where you replay the game replacing Billy with Wesker, complete with a couple of superpowered attacks.

As far as the game in general, I thought it was great. The new mechanic introduced lets you swap between two different characters, which is mainly used to add some spice to the classic Resident Evil puzzles. This means you have a larger combined inventory, but this is offset by what seems to be the most polarizing change - unlike most RE games, there is no magical transporting item box in RE0. Anything you can't carry with you has to be left on the ground somewhere, encouraging you to make caches in certain rooms. Some people will hate this change, and I can understand that, but I thought it added a lot of pressure to manage your inventory and choose carefully what to keep and what to leave behind. Any items that you've interacted with show up on your map, so it isn't a hassle to figure out where you've left something. The game is somewhat faster paced in that you start facing BOWs and acquiring weapons (though not necessarily ammo) to fight them earlier than you probably would in REmake on your first try, but it's still a more resource-scarce and survival-like game than others like Code Veronica. It is shorter than REmake by nature of only having one campaign instead of two like RE1 had, but I found 0's campaign to be a little longer than one of 1's campaigns and on your first playthrough it should serve you a fair amount of time.

In many ways it feels similar to REmake, and some locations will definitely feel familiar, but it keeps things fresh enough to feel more like an encore than a retread. My only real complaint about it is that the train portion of the game is actually fairly short and only makes up a small portion of the game, which disappointed me because I loved the look and atmosphere of it. But overall, if you're a fan of REmake, I can't see any reason not to try this as well, assuming you already haven't in the past decade or so.

This game isn't as good as the REmaster, but it's still great if you're looking for some more classic Resident Evil. Controlling two characters can put a damper on the game for some, but to me it just increases the tension. Another character to look out for means another weapon to keep loaded and another person to keep healthy. 

Item management is a bigger thing here, and there are no item boxes. However you can drop items wherever you like and use some items when picking them up, even if your inventory is full. Both characters have their own item slots (making 12 slots in total), however there are items and weapons that take up more than one slot. Not going to lie, item management can get a little sloppy at times. 

Graphical enhancements are the same as what you would expect after playing the first REmaster, with some character models and pictures being redone. I have run into a couple hiccups with the audio during cutscenes, but it's not even for a second, so it isn't really that bad. 1080p, 60fps goodness is here as well. No 4k resolution support that I am aware of. 

Controls, like the first REmaster, are completely customizable for keyboard and mouse, while controller gets five different preset controls. I recommended keyboard and mouse for the first REmaster, but I may have to recommend a controller this time. Main reason being is that you can control the other character with the other stick without having to switch to the other character. You can still control the other character with the arrow keys (or whatever keys you wish to bind them as). Also, you cannot control one character with the new control scheme (non-tank controls) and then control the other character with classic tank controls. You have to control both characters with the same control scheme. 

The game still keeps the non-hand holding and throwing you into a maze type of game, well if you can really call being on a train a maze. If the game doesn't do it for you right away, get past the train at least. The game opens up a bit after that. The environment will feel a lot more "Resident Evil" then. Plus leech men are probably the freakiest thing you'll encounter.

Resident Evil Zero is a interesting game for the series as it tries new ideas with its dual character gameplay. On one hand its commendable that it stands out from any other Resident Evil game, but on the other, the execution could have been better handled. There are some neat puzzle solving moments using the two separate characters, but overall the game feels a bit underwhelming despite some great promise early on. There’s perhaps too much of an over-familiar feeling due to a reliance on similar locations from the original game. That said, the increased resolution and 60 frames per second make for smooth gameplay experience which is most welcome. So whilst this is perhaps one of the weaker games in the series it’s still worth picking up to play considering its low price point. If you’re a Resident Evil enthusiast who doesn’t want to dust off the old Gamecube then this is a neat game to play for an afternoon and relive some memories in HD. If you’ve never played before then there’s much to like even if there’s vague and fiddly elements to contend with alongside the zombies.

Remember the nights you played Resident Evil Zero on Gamecube? No? I do. 

This game is right for you ...

... when you walk through a dark corridor and you do not know what to expect around the next corner ...

... when you suddenly hear a creepy moan behind the next wall and you're to scared to move forward ... 

First of all here are some simple steps to make sure you get the whole creepy experience out of this game:

- Use a controller (although you can use the keyboard, which is not really recommendable - atleast for me. I don't like it, you could)

- Play at night (or darken your room), you will feel very uncomfortable, trust me

- Don't rush the game like hell. Take your time, explore everything and feel yourself into the world. 

- forget everything about Resident Evil 5, 6, RC:O and similiar games. This is clearly not the same. This is real horror.

So what is Resident Evil 0?

Resident Evil Zero is the prequel to all the beginning of Resident Evil 1 and the following games. 
Its the 07.23.1998, the day before the deadly virus was released in Raccoon City.
This game is full of interesting puzzles, a good story and an oppressive atmosphere.


Pros:

+++ Scary game that will make you feel very lonely and lost
+++ A good background story about what happened before Resident Evil 1
+++ hours of fun playing this game
++ you can play 2 characters
++ a lot of puzzles

What is special about this game?

This Oldschool-Horror Survival Game comes first time with 2 Characters that you can control. (Yes, Resident 5 and so on had also multiple characters). The special thing about these two characters is both of them have their special skills. Rebecca can't take a lot of damage, but she can mix herbs, which can be very useful. Billy got a lighter, which can be helpful for some things. In addition he can take a lot more damage before he will die. In the most time you are playing together, while you can decide with whom you move. You can also decide if your partner will support you in the fight or if he will even follow you or rather stay on his position. This gameplay with both characters CAN make you feel a bit more safe, but don't lean back that much because there will be several situations where you both are lost and on your own, trying to find each other of you. In this case you will feel very lost and desperate. This makes this game so special. You have to keep an eye on both characters, make them survive this game. If one of your characters dies, the game is over. 

How good is the new HD graphic?

While the original Resident Evil Zero on Gamecube was very old fashioned and mushy, this new remastered version comes with some new effects. The game overall looks way better than the old version but you can still see some ugly details which doesn't look that great. Just dont expect too much. It looks just fine, but there is nothing sensational about it. It can be kinda compared with Resident Evil 1 Remastered. 

My final words:

This lets me conclude that this game is really good and it is a REAL Resident Evil. Its not a shooter like the newer games. This game is hard, can be frustrating and brings a lot of fun. You will feel like you felt in Resident Evil 1-3, i will guarantee you. If you never played Resident Evil, but you're a fan of horror-games, then i can also recommend this game for you. For people who want a modern game with a GREAT graphics and a lot of shooting, i really can't recommend this to you, because you might be disapppointed.
